COURSE INTRODUCTION

English for Education Studies I

English for Education Studies I helps teachers and trainee teachers use clear, correct English in everyday school life. You start with simple words for your school and classroom, and build up to describing lessons, writing short notes and talking with learners, parents and colleagues. By the end you will be ready for the A2–B1 final assessment.

5 chapters31 weekly lessonsRead · Listen · Speak · Write

YOUR WEEKLY STUDY PACE

1 course week = 1 calendar week

Study one course week each calendar week. For example, study Week 1 during your first week, then study Week 2 during the following week. Plan to work through the 31 weekly lessons over 31 weeks.

Do not complete several weeks’ lessons in one sitting or fit several course weeks into a single calendar week. Spread each week’s activities across several short study sessions. Give yourself time to listen again, practise speaking and writing, review feedback, and use what you have learned.

If you finish a week’s activities early, use the remaining time to revise and practise. Begin the next course week in the following calendar week.

01 · Useful English for school life

What you will learn

  • Name the people, places and objects in a school and say where things are.
  • Understand and give classroom instructions, rules, praise and feedback.
  • Describe lessons, timetables, children and school days in simple sentences.
  • Read and write short notices, lesson plans, lesson notes and reflections.
  • Talk about teaching, plan a simple activity and hold short conversations with parents and colleagues.

02 · Work through the chapters in order

Your course journey

Chapter IWeeks 1–6

My School in English

People and places, classroom words, subjects and the timetable, classroom instructions, teachers and learners.

Chapter IIWeeks 7–12

Lessons and Learning

School-day routines, describing a lesson, asking questions in class, homework and tests, likes and dislikes.

Chapter IIIWeeks 13–18

Learners and the Classroom

Describing children, classroom rules, praise and feedback, what children can do, supporting a learner.

Chapter IVWeeks 19–24

Reading and Writing for Teaching

Timetables and notices, lesson plans, lesson notes, simple reflections, classroom technology.

Chapter VWeeks 25–31

Talking and Teaching in Simple English

Describing a classroom picture, telling a school-day story, planning an activity, talking with parents and colleagues, case studies from Cambodia, final assessment.

03 · Build your skills step by step

How each week works

  1. Prepare: learning outcomes, an ungraded pretest and a lesson overview.
  2. Learn: key phrases, vocabulary with audio, and a mini story.
  3. Practise: gap-fill and vocabulary activities, five readings, five listening activities and speaking practice.
  4. Use: grammar practice, exercises and sentence practice, then guided writing tasks.
  5. Check: a lesson test, followed by sentence and paragraph writing and a short video activity.

04 · Four categories · one overall mark

How your learning is assessed

Your course mark
AssessmentWeight
Vocabulary challenges and objective exercises20%
Lesson tests, including chapter reviews30%
Paragraph writing20%
Final assessment (Week 31)30%
Total100%

Activities within each assessment category contribute equally to that category’s average. The category averages are then combined using the percentages above. Scored activities without a mark contribute zero until a score is available.

Vocabulary challenges, objective exercises and tests are marked automatically. The 31 paragraph-writing assignments assess how well you answer the task, use relevant vocabulary, form clear sentences, and use grammar and word order. Follow the word range in each task. You will receive feedback to help you improve. Model answers are examples; other suitable answers are accepted.

Practice still matters

Pretests, speaking and video activities, guided writing, sentence practice, gap-fill practice and model-answer activities have a weight of 0% in your overall mark. Use these activities to practise and build confidence. In open-ended sentence practice, compare your response with the model answer; your response is not automatically marked correct or incorrect.

05 · Meet both requirements

How to earn your certificate

100%

Activity completion

Complete all visible course activities and reach 100% progress. This includes practice and speaking activities that carry no grade weight. Meet the completion requirements shown for each activity.

80%+

Overall course score

Achieve an overall weighted course score of at least 80%. This is the combined course mark calculated from the four categories above.

Complete the final assessment and allow your paragraph-writing submissions to finish grading. Check your progress and gradebook to see whether you meet both certificate requirements. Once you are eligible, select Receive Certificate (ទទួលវិញ្ញាបនបត្រ) to access and download your certificate as a PDF.

06 · Steady progress, lasting confidence

How to succeed in this course

Learn one course week per calendar week. Do not rush through several weeks’ lessons in one sitting or one calendar week. Spread your study across the week and allow time to practise, review feedback and improve. Steady weekly learning will help you use English with greater confidence in your own classroom.

TIP 01

Follow a weekly study routine. Complete one course week during each calendar week, in order. Divide the reading, listening, speaking and writing activities across several study sessions. Begin the next course week in the following calendar week.

TIP 02

Read and listen carefully. Follow the instructions, replay the audio when needed, and check the meaning of unfamiliar words. Say the vocabulary and example sentences aloud.

TIP 03

Try each task yourself first. Write your own sentences before opening the model answer. Compare the meaning and sentence structure, then think about how to improve your response.

TIP 04

Use feedback to improve. Read the comments on your writing and review mistakes in exercises and tests. Practise the difficult points again before moving on.

TIP 05

Take every practice activity seriously. Speaking, video and other activities worth 0% still help you develop your English and are part of completing the course. Use opportunities to practise with a colleague or in a classroom situation.

TIP 06

Check your understanding. Before moving to the next lesson, make sure you can understand the key words and use the main language in a simple example of your own.

TIP 07

Keep track of your progress. Check your gradebook and allow time to complete your writing and final assessment. Work towards both certificate requirements: 100% activity completion and an overall course score of at least 80%.

CHAPTER I · WEEK 1

My School: People and Places

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify key people and locations in simple spoken descriptions of a school. L2 Understand
  • Use prepositions of place and school-related vocabulary to describe classroom locations accurately. L3 Apply
  • Describe the main people and places in your school using simple present tense. L3 Apply
  • Locate specific information about school staff and facilities in short descriptive texts. L3 Apply
  • Write a simple paragraph describing the people and places in your own school. L3 Apply
  • Compare school environments with classmates to recognize similarities and differences across educational settings. L4 Analyze · HOTS

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. School people and their roles

Schools have different people who work there. Teachers help students learn. Students come to study.

Example:The teacher is in the classroom.
Connection:You use this English when you talk about your school and the people there.
  • 2. School places and what happens there

A school has many rooms and places. Each place has a different use.

Example:There is a library for reading books.
Connection:You use this English when you describe your school to other people.
  • 3. Where things are in a school

We say where people and things are. We use words like in, on, and at.

Example:The students are in the classroom.
Connection:You use this English when you give directions or explain locations at school.
  • 4. What you do at school

At school, people do different things. Students read, write, and learn. Teachers teach.

Example:I study in the library every day.
Connection:You use this English when you talk about daily activities at school.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
Mr. / Ms. / Mrs.
Mister, Miss, Missus
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Mr. Sok is my teacher at school.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Rm. 5
room five
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
My classroom is room five on the map.
🔉 Spoken Example:
1st floor / 2nd floor
first floor, second floor
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The library is on the first floor.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Office Hrs: 8-5
office hours eight to five
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The office hours are eight to five today.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Cafeteria →
cafeteria this way
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The sign says cafeteria this way.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Staff Only
staff only
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The door says staff only, not for students.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Class 3A
class three A
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I am in class three A this year.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Mon-Fri
Monday to Friday
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
School is open Monday to Friday every week.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. school — A place where students go to learn.
  2. teacher — A person who helps students learn.
  3. student — A person who learns at school.
  4. classroom — A room where students learn together.
  5. library — A place with many books to read.
  6. book — Pages with words and pictures together.
  7. desk — A table where you sit and work.
  8. chair — Something you sit on at school.
  9. board — A big thing on the wall for writing.
  10. pen — A thing you use to write with.
  11. notebook — A book with empty pages for writing.
  12. study — To learn and read about something.
  13. learn — To get new information and skills.
  14. read — To look at words and understand them.
  15. write — To make words with a pen or pencil.
  16. office — A room where people work at school.
  17. cafeteria — A place at school where you eat.
  18. friend — A person you like very much.
  19. class — A group of students learning together.
  20. lesson — A time when you learn something new.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
You learn twenty words about school people and places.
Reading
You read about a school and find information about people and places.
Listening
You listen to descriptions of school locations and identify them.
Speaking
You describe your school and say where things are.
Grammar
You practise there is and there are to describe school places.
Writing
You write a paragraph about the people and places at your school.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary, grammar, and descriptions; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'school' comes from a Greek word that means 'free time' because learning was seen as something enjoyable to do when you were not working!

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). This book has simple pictures and words for school topics. Oxford Picture Dictionary — Oxford University Press (2015). It shows pictures of school places and people with English labels.

▶ Learn English with Simple Stories — Easy English ▶ My School - English for Beginners — BBC Learning English

MINI STORY

My name is Sara. I am a student. I go to school every day. My school is very big.

My classroom is nice. I have a desk and a chair. My teacher is very kind. She writes on the board. I sit with my friend Tom. We study together. We have many books and notebooks. I write with my pen.

In the morning, we learn English. I read and write new words. At lunch, we go to the cafeteria. We eat with our friends. After lunch, I go to the library. I read books there. Today's lesson is very interesting. I like my school very much.

nodes.question: Q1. I go to ___ every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'School' is the place where students go every day to learn.

nodes.question: Q2. My ___ teaches English. She is very nice.
nodes.explanation: → A 'teacher' is a person who teaches students.

nodes.question: Q3. She is not a teacher. She is a good ___.
nodes.explanation: → A 'student' is a person who learns at school. She is not a teacher.

nodes.question: Q4. Our ___ is very big. It has many desks.
nodes.explanation: → A 'classroom' is the room with desks where students learn.

nodes.question: Q5. I read books in the ___. It has many shelves of books.
nodes.explanation: → A 'library' is the place with shelves of books where we read.

nodes.question: Q6. I read this ___. It has a story and it is very interesting.
nodes.explanation: → A 'book' has a story and pages that we read.

nodes.question: Q7. I put my notebook on my ___. It is near the window.
nodes.explanation: → A 'desk' is the table where we put our things. It is near the window.

nodes.question: Q8. This ___ is very comfortable.
nodes.explanation: → We sit on a 'chair', and it can be comfortable.

nodes.question: Q9. The teacher writes on the ___.
nodes.explanation: → The teacher writes on the 'board' so all students can see.

nodes.question: Q10. I write with a blue ___.
nodes.explanation: → We write with a 'pen'.

nodes.question: Q11. I write notes in my ___.
nodes.explanation: → We write notes in a 'notebook'.

nodes.question: Q12. I ___ English every day at school.
nodes.explanation: → We 'study' English at school to learn it well.

nodes.question: Q13. We ___ new words today.
nodes.explanation: → We 'learn' new words when we find out what they mean.

nodes.question: Q14. I ___ books every week.
nodes.explanation: → We 'read' books with our eyes.

nodes.question: Q15. She ___ her name here.
nodes.explanation: → With 'she' we use 'write' to put words on paper. She writes her name.

nodes.question: Q16. The principal works in the ___.
nodes.explanation: → The principal works in the 'office'.

nodes.question: Q17. We eat lunch in the ___. It has many tables and a kitchen.
nodes.explanation: → A 'cafeteria' is the school place with tables and a kitchen where we eat lunch.

nodes.question: Q18. My best ___ sits next to me. We play together.
nodes.explanation: → A 'friend' is a person we like and play with.

nodes.question: Q19. There are twenty students in my ___.
nodes.explanation: → A 'class' is a group of students who learn together.

nodes.question: Q20. Today's ___ is about animals. We learn new words.
nodes.explanation: → A 'lesson' is one time of learning about a topic, like animals.

nodes.text: VOCABULARY CHALLENGE

nodes.question: study — practice
nodes.explanation: → 'Study' and 'practice' have similar meanings, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: teacher — pupil
nodes.explanation: → 'Teacher' and 'pupil' are opposite roles, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: learn — learner
nodes.explanation: → 'Learner' comes from 'learn', so they are in the same word family.

nodes.question: desk — ocean
nodes.explanation: → A 'desk' and an 'ocean' have no connection, so they are unrelated.

nodes.question: friend — buddy
nodes.explanation: → 'Friend' and 'buddy' mean the same, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: come — go
nodes.explanation: → 'Come' and 'go' have opposite meanings, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: write — writer
nodes.explanation: → 'Writer' comes from 'write', so they are in the same word family.

nodes.question: chair — river
nodes.explanation: → A 'chair' and a 'river' have no connection, so they are unrelated.

nodes.question: class — group
nodes.explanation: → 'Class' and 'group' both mean a set of people together, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: student — instructor
nodes.explanation: → 'Student' learns and 'instructor' teaches, so they are opposite roles.

nodes.question: book — booklet
nodes.explanation: → 'Booklet' is made from 'book' (a small book), so they are in the same word family.

nodes.question: library — mountain
nodes.explanation: → A 'library' and a 'mountain' have no connection, so they are unrelated.

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

My First Day at School

Text type: Narrative
My name is Anna. I am a new student. Today is my first day at school.

I meet my teacher. Her name is Ms. Brown. She is very nice. She has a big smile. I see many students in my class. They are friendly. One girl says hello to me.

Ms. Brown shows me the classroom. It is big and clean. I see books and chairs. I am happy at my new school.

questions.prompt: Q1. What is the main idea?

options.text: A. Anna's first day at school
D. Anna goes to the park

questions.explanation: → The whole text is about Anna: 'Today is my first day at school.'

questions.prompt: Q2. Who is Ms. Brown?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'I meet my teacher. Her name is Ms. Brown.'

questions.prompt: Q3. What does Anna see in the classroom?
questions.explanation: → Anna says 'I see books and chairs.'

questions.prompt: Q4. How does Anna feel?

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

This is my school. The library is big and quiet. My teacher is very nice. Students sit in the classroom. We eat lunch in the cafeteria.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Where do you study at school?

I study in the classroom. My classroom is small.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Who is your favorite person at school?

My teacher is my favorite person. She is kind and helpful.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What places are in your school?

My school has a library and a gym. It also has a cafeteria.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Do you like your school?

Yes, I like my school. It is good and clean.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Where do you meet your friends at school?

I meet my friends in the playground. We play there every day.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

There is / There are

We use 'there is' with one thing.

We use 'there are' with two or more things.

Use 'there is' and 'there are' to say what is in a place.

FORMS

FormExample
There is + singular nounThere is a library.
There are + plural nounThere are two classrooms.
Negative: There is not / isn'tThere isn't a gym.
Negative: There are not / aren'tThere aren't any computers.
Question: Is there...?Is there a teacher?
Question: Are there...?Are there desks?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ There are a library.

✓ There is a library.

Use 'there is' with one thing (singular).

✗ There is three students.

✓ There are three students.

Use 'there are' with more than one thing (plural).

✗ Is there books?

✓ Are there books?

Use 'are there' with plural nouns like 'books'.

lessons.titleEn: My School: People and Places — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about people at your school. Name two or three people and their jobs. (20–30 words)

  • Start with 'At my school there is...' or 'My school has...'
  • Name the person and their job (teacher, principal, librarian)
  • Use simple present: is, are, has, have

Key structures: There is / There are, Simple present tense

Model
At my school there is a good teacher. Her name is Mrs. Smith. There is also a librarian. He helps students find books.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words naming two or three people at your school and saying each person's job.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: teacher, principal, librarian, student, school, office, library. Structures: At my school there is...; My school has...; He/She is a...; There is / There are.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names two or three different people at school and gives a clear job for each one, for example 'Mr. Dara is the principal' and 'Mrs. Sokha is a librarian'. Good: Names two people with their jobs, or names three people but one job is missing or unclear. Developing: Mentions only one person with a job, or lists jobs (teacher, librarian) without saying who the people are or where they work. Beginning: Does not name any school people with jobs, or writes about something else such as the school building.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Opens with 'At my school there is...' or 'My school has...' and uses job words such as principal, librarian and teacher correctly, with 'He/She is a...' or 'helps'. Good: Uses the opening phrase or 'There is' and at least two job words correctly; one job word may be replaced by a simple Khmer-influenced choice. Developing: Uses only one job word from the week, or writes 'is' sentences without the 'There is' opening; some job words are wrong, for example 'the principal teaches in library'. Beginning: Uses almost none of the week's job words or structures; sentences are mostly names or single words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Most sentences are correct: 'is' with one person, 'are' with more than one, 'a' before job words (a librarian), and 'she/he' matches the person. Good: Meaning is clear, with one or two small errors such as a missing 'a' ('She is librarian') or 'There are a teacher'. Developing: Several errors make some sentences hard to follow, for example missing 'is' ('Mr. Dara principal') or 'He' used for a woman, but the reader can still guess the idea. Beginning: Errors in nearly every sentence, so it is hard to tell who the people are or what they do.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short, complete sentences, one person at a time, with capital letters for names and full stops. Good: Mostly complete sentences in a sensible order; a capital letter or full stop may be missing. Developing: Sentences run together or the people are mixed up (name and job in different sentences without linking), so the reader must work to follow. Beginning: Words are in a list or jumbled order with no sentence structure.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two or three people with jobs, 'There is' or 'My school has' used well, nearly error-free. | 75-89: Two people with jobs, clear sentences, a few small slips. | 60-74: One or two jobs given; the opening phrase or some job words are weak. | 40-59: Only one person or very unclear jobs; many errors. | 0-39: No school people named, or off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips in job words (libarian, principle); a missing 'a' before a job when the meaning is clear; Khmer-style names such as 'Teacher Sokha'; using 'He' or 'She' for the same person in a clear way; a short extra sentence about what the person does.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-30 words; 17-33 is fine. Under 15 words = cap at 59; 15-19 words = cap at 74. Do not penalise slightly longer answers that stay on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real or imaginary school people and any correct jobs are fine (teacher, principal, librarian, cleaner, guard, nurse). 'My school has a principal and two teachers' is as good as 'At my school there is...'. Names do not need to be Mrs. Smith. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions, unrelated text or a description with no people = 20-35 with a kind note. A copy of the model answer word-for-word = 100 with a note to use own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You named real people and their jobs, like 'Mr. Dara is the principal'. That is exactly what the task asks. 2) Fix: Remember 'a' before a job: 'She is a librarian.' (not 'She is librarian'). 3) Next step: Next time add one more person, for example: 'There is also a cleaner. He cleans the classroom.'

lessons.titleEn: My School: People and Places — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe three places in your school. Say what students do in each place. (30–45 words)

  • Name each place clearly (classroom, library, canteen, gym)
  • Use 'Students...' or 'We...' to say what happens there
  • Connect ideas with 'and', 'also', or start new short sentences

Key structures: Simple present tense, In the / at the + place, Linking: and, also

Model
My school has many places. In the classroom, students learn and write. The library is quiet. Students read books there. In the canteen, we eat lunch. There is also a big gym. Students play sports in the gym.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words describing three places in your school and what students do in each place.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: classroom, library, canteen, gym, office, read, eat, play, study. Structures: In the... students...; at the + place; Students + verb; and / also.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes three different school places (for example classroom, library, canteen) and says one clear thing students do in each. Good: Describes three places but one has no activity, or describes two places clearly with an activity for each. Developing: Names places but gives few activities (for example 'classroom, library, canteen'), or covers only one place well. Beginning: Does not describe places in the school, or describes students without saying where.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses place words and activity verbs correctly (library - read, canteen - eat, gym - play) with 'In the...' or 'at the...', and joins ideas with 'and' or 'also'. Good: Uses at least two place words with matching activities and one linking word or 'In the...' phrase. Developing: Uses place words but the activities do not match the place ('students read in the canteen') or no 'in the' phrases appear. Beginning: Few or no place words from the week; sentences are not about school places.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Simple present is mostly correct: 'Students read', 'We eat', 'The library is quiet', with correct 'in the / at the'. Good: Clear meaning with small errors, such as 'Students reads' or 'in library' without 'the'. Developing: Several errors in verb form and prepositions ('We eating lunch at canteen', 'student play') that slow the reader down. Beginning: Frequent errors in every sentence so the places and activities are unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (20 points). Excellent: Each place gets its own short sentence or two, in a clear order, linked with 'and' or 'also'. Good: Places are clearly separate, with a link or two missing. Developing: Places and activities are mixed in one long sentence or the order jumps back and forth. Beginning: No clear separation between places; reads as a list of words.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Three places each with a matching activity, linking words, very few errors. | 75-89: Three places, most with activities, a few small errors. | 60-74: Two good places or three weak ones; limited linking. | 40-59: One place or mostly word lists; many errors. | 0-39: Not about school places, or off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: 'in classroom' without 'the' when the meaning is clear; spelling slips (canten, libary); using 'we' or 'students' interchangeably; choosing places not in the example (computer room, garden, playground); reasonable activities such as 'students drink water in the canteen'.
LENGTH: Aim for 30-45 words; 27-50 is fine. Under 22 words = cap at 59; 22-26 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any three real school places and sensible activities are fine; it does not need to be classroom, library and canteen. 'There is a library. We read books there.' is fine as well as 'In the library, students read'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to describe your own school next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You wrote about three places and what students do there, like 'Students read books in the library'. 2) Fix: Add 'the' after 'in': 'In the canteen, we eat lunch.' (not 'In canteen'). 3) Next step: Next time add one more sentence with 'also', for example: 'There is also a big gym.'

lessons.titleKm: My School: People and Places — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: My School: People and Places — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about your favorite place at school and your favorite teacher. Explain why you like them. (45–60 words)

  • Start with your favorite place and say why (big, quiet, nice, good)
  • Then write about your favorite teacher and why you like them
  • Use 'because' to give simple reasons, or use 'I like... He/She is...'

Key structures: I like... because..., My favorite... is..., He/She is + adjective

Model
My favorite place at school is the library. It is very quiet. I like to read there. I can find many good books. My favorite teacher is Mr. Brown. He teaches English. He is very kind and helpful. He helps me learn new words. I like his class because it is fun.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about your favorite place at school and your favorite teacher, giving a simple reason for each.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: favorite, library, quiet, big, kind, helpful, teacher, because. Structures: My favorite... is...; I like... because...; He/She is + adjective; It is + adjective.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names a favorite place and gives a reason, then names a favorite teacher and gives a reason, so both halves of the task are complete. Good: Covers both the place and the teacher, but one has no reason or the reason is very short. Developing: Writes about only the place or only the teacher, or gives no reasons ('My favorite place is the library. My favorite teacher is Mr. Brown.'). Beginning: Does not say a favorite place or teacher, or the writing is unrelated to school.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My favorite... is...', 'because' and adjectives such as quiet, big, kind and helpful correctly to explain both choices. Good: Uses 'My favorite... is...' and at least one 'because' or adjective reason. Developing: Uses 'My favorite' but reasons are only 'good' or 'nice', or 'because' is used without a reason after it. Beginning: Few or none of the week's phrases; no adjectives to describe the place or teacher.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Mostly correct 'is' sentences and agreement: 'It is quiet', 'He is kind', 'He helps me', 'I like his class'. Good: Clear meaning with a few errors such as 'He kind', 'She teach English' or 'I like because it quiet'. Developing: Frequent missing 'is', mixed 'he/she' or misplaced 'because', so some sentences are hard to follow. Beginning: Errors throughout; the reader cannot tell who or what is being described.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Place first, then teacher, with reasons following each choice, and short sentences with capital letters and full stops. Good: Two parts are clear; sentence boundaries occasionally slip. Developing: Place and teacher ideas are mixed together, so it is hard to see which reason belongs to which. Beginning: No order; ideas are separate words or phrases.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Place and teacher both with clear reasons, 'because' and adjectives used well, few errors. | 75-89: Both parts present with reasons, small errors. | 60-74: Both parts present but reasons are weak, or one part is thin. | 40-59: Only one part or no reasons; many errors. | 0-39: Off task or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: 'because' used at the start of a sentence; 'He teach' type -s slips if the idea is clear; spelling slips (favorite/favourite are both fine); 'very' used too often; choosing a place other than the library, such as the garden.
LENGTH: Aim for 45-60 words; 40-67 is fine. Under 32 words = cap at 59; 32-39 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any school place and any teacher, real or imagined, named or not are fine. Reasons can use 'because', 'He/She is...' or 'It is...'. The learner may write about a place in a different order from the model. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to write about your own place and teacher.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Your reason is clear: you wrote that the library is quiet. That helps the reader understand your choice. 2) Fix: Add 'is' before the adjective: 'He is kind.' (not 'He kind'). 3) Next step: Next time try one more reason with 'because', like: 'I like his class because it is fun.'

Write about your school. Write about the places and people. Use 20-35 words. (20–35 words)

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.

Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your school: say how it is, name one or two places and say who your teacher is.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: school, big, small, library, cafeteria, classroom, teacher, nice, like. Structures: My school is...; It has...; My teacher is...; She/He is + adjective.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says what the school is like (big, small, nice), names one or two places (library, cafeteria), and says who the teacher is.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My school is...', 'It has...' and 'My teacher is...' correctly with place words and adjectives from the week.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Correct 'is' and 'has' sentences, 'a' before library/cafeteria, and 'she/he' matches the teacher.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short sentences in a sensible order: school, places, teacher, with capitals and full stops.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (cafeteria, libary); 'My teacher name is...' type word order that is clear; using 'canteen' for 'cafeteria'; missing capital letters in names; no mention of liking the school.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-35 words; 17-40 is fine. Under 12 words = cap at 59; 12-16 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any adjectives for the school and any one or two places are fine. The teacher may be named with Mr./Mrs./Ms. or just by title. Extra sentences such as 'I like my school' are good. The model answer is only a reference.

CHAPTER I · WEEK 2

Everyday Classroom Words and Objects

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Classroom objects

Things we use every day in a classroom. They help us learn and teach.

Example:There is a desk and a chair in the classroom.
Connection:You see these things every day in your classroom and read about them in textbooks.
  • 2. Singular and plural nouns

One thing is singular. Two or more things are plural.

Example:There is one book. There are three books.
Connection:You use singular and plural words when you describe your classroom or write about school.
  • 3. Prepositions of place

Words that show where things are. Examples are on, in, and under.

Example:The pen is on the desk.
Connection:Teachers use these words to tell you where to put things in the classroom.
  • 4. Classroom labels and signs

Words on the wall or on things. They tell you what something is.

Example:The sign says 'door' on the door.
Connection:You read labels in your classroom and in school exams.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

🔉 Spoken Example:
Teacher's desk
teacher's desk
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. classroom — A room where students learn.
  2. desk — A table where you sit and work.
  3. chair — A thing you sit on.
  4. board — A thing on the wall for writing.
  5. pen — A thing for writing with ink.
  6. pencil — A thing for writing you can erase.
  7. book — A thing with pages you read.
  8. notebook — A book where you write notes.
  9. teacher — A person who teaches students.
  10. student — A person who learns at school.
  11. bag — A thing you carry books in.
  12. door — A thing you open to enter.
  13. window — A thing you can see through.
  14. eraser — A thing that removes pencil marks.
  15. paper — A thin white thing for writing.
  16. write — To make words with a pen.
  17. read — To look at words and understand.
  18. open — To make something not closed.
  19. close — To make something not open.
  20. clean — Not dirty.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words about classroom objects and actions.
Reading
Read a text about classrooms and find the names of objects.
Listening
Listen to teachers describe classroom objects and where they are.
Speaking
Say the names of classroom objects in your classroom.
Grammar
Learn there is and there are to describe things in classrooms.
Writing
Write sentences about objects in your classroom.
Lesson Test
The test checks all the words and grammar; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In many countries, students say 'desk' for the teacher's big table and for student tables, but some countries have different words for each one.

REFERENCES

Oxford Picture Dictionary for the Content Areas — Oxford University Press (2010). It has pictures and labels for all classroom objects. English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). Unit five teaches classroom words with simple examples.

▶ Classroom Objects for Kids — English Singsing ▶ Learn English: Classroom Vocabulary — BBC Learning English

MINI STORY

My Classroom

I am a student. I go to my classroom every day. The classroom is big and clean. I have a desk and a chair. My desk is brown. My chair is red.

My teacher is very nice. She writes on the board. I write in my notebook. I have a pen and a pencil. My bag has many books. I read my book every day.

The door is white. The window is open. I can see trees. I write on paper. Sometimes I need an eraser. I open my book. I close my notebook. I like my classroom. It is a good place to learn. My classmates are friendly. We study together. The board is clean. Our teacher helps us. I am happy here.

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

This is my pen. The book is on the desk. I have a pencil and paper. The teacher has a board. My bag is under the chair.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What do you have in your bag?

I have a book and a pen. I have my pencil too.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Where is your book?

My book is on the desk. It is a big book.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Do you have a pencil?

Yes, I have a pencil. I have two pencils.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. What is on the teacher's desk?

A book is on the desk. The teacher has paper too.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Is your chair big or small?

My chair is small. It is a good chair.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

There is / There are

We use 'there is' with one thing.

We use 'there are' with two or more things.

Use 'there is' with singular nouns and 'there are' with plural nouns.

FORMS

FormExample
There is + singular nounThere is a book.
There are + plural nounThere are books.
There is not / isn't + singularThere is not a pen.
There are not / aren't + pluralThere are not pens.
Is there + singular?Is there a chair?
Are there + plural?Are there chairs?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ There are a book.

✓ There is a book.

Use 'there is' with one thing (singular).

✗ There is three desks.

✓ There are three desks.

Use 'there are' with more than one thing (plural).

✗ Is there students here?

✓ Are there students here?

Use 'are there' with plural nouns.

lessons.titleEn: Everyday Classroom Words and Objects — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about things in your classroom. Name three objects you see. (20–30 words)

  • Use simple words like book, pen, chair
  • Start with 'I see' or 'There is'
  • Write short sentences

Key structures: I see + noun, There is/are + noun

Model
I see many things in my classroom. There is a big desk. There are chairs. I see books on the desk. There is a board on the wall.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words about your classroom and name three objects you can see.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: desk, chair, book, board, pen, bag, wall, window. Structures: I see + noun; There is a...; There are + plural noun.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names at least three different classroom objects, such as desk, chairs and board, and all of them belong in a classroom. Good: Names two clear classroom objects, or names three but repeats one. Developing: Names only one object, or writes about the classroom in general ('my classroom is big') without naming objects. Beginning: Does not name classroom objects, or writes about something unrelated.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I see...' and 'There is / There are' correctly with week words, choosing 'There are' for chairs or books and 'There is' for a board or a desk. Good: Uses 'I see' or 'There is' correctly with two or more week words; may use 'There is' with a plural once. Developing: Writes object words without a sentence pattern, or mixes up singular and plural ('There is chairs'). Beginning: No week patterns; no classroom object words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Plural -s is correct (chairs, books), 'a' is used before singular nouns, and sentences are complete. Good: Clear meaning, with one or two slips such as 'There are chair' or a missing 'a'. Developing: Several singular/plural or missing-verb errors ('I see desk chair board') that make it hard to read. Beginning: Almost no complete sentences.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short separate sentences, one object idea each, with capitals and full stops. Good: Sentences are clear; punctuation is sometimes missing. Developing: Objects are run together in one long line with 'and' repeated, or in a list without sentences. Beginning: No clear sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Three or more objects with 'I see' or 'There is/are' used correctly. | 75-89: Three objects, small singular/plural slips. | 60-74: Two objects or a weak sentence pattern. | 40-59: One object, or many errors. | 0-39: Not about classroom objects.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (tabel, bord); a missing 'a' when the noun is clear; colour or size words added; objects in a different order from the model; using 'see' for 'have' in a clear way.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-30 words; 17-33 is fine. Under 15 words = cap at 59; 15-19 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any three classroom objects are fine (door, window, clock, fan, bag, ruler). Learners may use 'I see' only or 'There is/are' only, but a mix earns more credit. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to name objects in your own classroom.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You named real things in your classroom, like the desk and the board. 2) Fix: Use 'are' for more than one: 'There are chairs.' (not 'There is chairs'). 3) Next step: Next time add where something is: 'The books are on the desk.'

lessons.titleEn: Everyday Classroom Words and Objects — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe your school bag. Write what things you have in your bag and why you need them. (30–45 words)

  • Name objects: pen, book, notebook
  • Use 'I have' and 'I need'
  • Say why: for writing, for reading

Key structures: I have + noun, I need + noun + for + verb-ing, and (to connect ideas)

Model
I have a school bag. In my bag, I have books and notebooks. I have pens and pencils. I need the pen for writing. I need books for reading. I have a ruler. It is small and blue. My bag is very full.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words describing your school bag: what things you have in it and why you need them.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: bag, pen, pencil, book, notebook, ruler, writing, reading. Structures: I have + noun; I need + noun + for + verb-ing; and (to join nouns); It is + adjective.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Lists several things in the bag (for example pens, a notebook, a ruler) and gives a reason for at least two of them ('I need the pen for writing'). Good: Lists three or more things in the bag but gives a reason for only one, or gives reasons but lists only two things. Developing: Lists objects with no reasons, or says only 'I have a bag' and one object. Beginning: Does not describe the bag or its contents.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I have...' for contents and 'I need... for + writing/reading' correctly, with 'and' joining two nouns ('books and notebooks'). Good: Uses 'I have' and at least one 'I need... for...' phrase correctly. Developing: Uses 'I have' only, or writes 'I need for write' or 'I need pen writing'. Beginning: Few or no week words or patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'for' is followed by -ing (writing, reading), plurals are correct (pens, books), and 'a' appears before singular items. Good: Small errors, such as 'for write' once or a missing plural -s, but the reasons are understood. Developing: Frequent errors in 'for + verb' or plurals ('I need pen for write and read') that change or hide the meaning. Beginning: Errors throughout; the reasons cannot be understood.
- Clarity & organisation (20 points). Excellent: Bag first, then contents, then reasons; sentences are short and easy to follow. Good: Order is clear for most of the text. Developing: Contents and reasons are mixed up so it is unclear which reason belongs to which object. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Contents and reasons both clear; 'I have' and 'I need... for...' used well. | 75-89: Contents and at least one reason, small errors. | 60-74: Contents listed, reasons weak or incorrectly formed. | 40-59: Very short or no reasons. | 0-39: Not about the bag or off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (notebok, pensil); 'for to write' type errors if the reason is clear; extra description such as colour or size; a different list of bag items from the model; using 'because' instead of 'for + -ing'.
LENGTH: Aim for 30-45 words; 27-50 is fine. Under 22 words = cap at 59; 22-26 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any school items are fine (water bottle, lunch box, textbook). Reasons may use 'for writing', 'to write' or 'because I write'. It is fine to write about a teacher's bag. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to describe your own bag.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You listed real things in your bag and said why you need them. 2) Fix: After 'for', add -ing: 'I need the pen for writing.' (not 'for write'). 3) Next step: Next time add one more item and one reason: 'I need a ruler for drawing lines.'

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about your teacher and the classroom. Describe what your teacher uses and what students do in class. (45–60 words)

  • Write about the teacher first, then students
  • Use present simple: writes, reads, sit
  • Connect ideas with 'and' and 'also'

Key structures: The teacher + verb + object, Students + verb, and/also (linking words)

Model
My teacher is good. The teacher uses a board and a pen. She writes on the board. Students sit at desks. We have books. We read and write. The teacher also uses a computer. It is on the desk. We listen to the teacher. We open our books. We write in our notebooks. The classroom is big. It has many chairs and desks.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about your teacher and your classroom: what the teacher uses, and what students do in class.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: board, pen, computer, desk, notebook, write, read, sit, listen. Structures: The teacher + verb + object; Students + verb; We + verb; and / also.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives the teacher part first (what the teacher uses and does, for example a board, pen or computer) and then the student part (sit, read, write, listen), with at least two ideas for each. Good: Covers both teacher and students, but one part has only one idea. Developing: Covers only the teacher or only the students, or lists objects with no actions. Beginning: Does not describe the teacher or the students, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'The teacher uses/writes...', 'Students sit/read...', 'We open/write...' with week objects, and links ideas with 'and' or 'also'. Good: Uses teacher and student patterns with several week words; linking words are limited. Developing: Uses a few week words but patterns are not followed ('teacher board write'). Beginning: Almost no week words or patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: -s is on teacher verbs (writes, uses) and not on students/we verbs (read, sit); objects such as 'on the board' are correct. Good: Meaning clear with some slips, for example 'The teacher write' or 'Students sits'. Developing: Verb forms are mostly wrong or missing ('Teacher board', 'students sit desk'), so the reader must guess. Beginning: Errors in nearly every sentence.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Teacher first, then students, in short separate sentences with capital letters and full stops. Good: The two parts are visible with a few punctuation slips. Developing: Teacher and students ideas are mixed together. Beginning: No order or sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Teacher and students clearly described; verb forms correct; linking words used. | 75-89: Both parts present; a few verb slips. | 60-74: One part thin, or many verb slips. | 40-59: Only one part, or word lists. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (computor); forgetting 'the' before board or desk; using 'she' or 'he' for the teacher; mixing 'we' and 'students'; a different classroom object such as a projector.
LENGTH: Aim for 45-60 words; 40-67 is fine. Under 32 words = cap at 59; 32-39 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any teacher tools (chalk, marker, book) and any sensible student actions are fine. The writer may start with the classroom or the students if both parts appear. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to describe your own teacher and class.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You wrote what your teacher uses and what students do, like 'The teacher uses a board and a pen'. 2) Fix: Add -s for one teacher: 'She writes on the board.' (not 'She write'). 3) Next step: Next time join two ideas with 'also': 'The teacher also uses a computer.'

Write about your classroom. What do you see? What is in your classroom? Use simple words. (20–35 words)

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints

Answer the question and include the requested details.		35

Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your classroom: what things are in it, what colour they are and whether you like it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: classroom, desk, chair, board, bag, white, blue, big, clean. Structures: My classroom is...; It has...; The ... is + colour; I like my classroom.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names at least two objects in the classroom, gives a colour or size for at least one, and says if the learner likes the classroom.

- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: 'is' is used with colours (The board is white), plurals are correct (desks and chairs), and 'it has' is correct.

DO NOT PENALISE: colour spelling (whight, bule); 'the' omitted before classroom objects; a different opinion such as 'I do not like it'; missing capital letters; using 'big' or 'small' instead of a colour.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-35 words; 17-40 is fine. Under 12 words = cap at 59; 12-16 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real classroom items and any correct colours. A negative opinion is fine if written clearly. Mentioning the bag is optional. The model answer is only a reference.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. School subjects

These are the things you study at school. Math, English, and science are school subjects.

Example:Students have English class on Monday.
Connection:You use these words every day in the classroom and when you talk about school.
  • 2. The timetable

A timetable shows when your lessons are. It tells you what subject you have each day.

Example:The timetable shows math at nine o'clock.
Connection:Teachers give you a timetable at the start of term and you read it every week.
  • 3. Days and times

We say the day and the time for each lesson. Monday is the first day of the week.

Example:We have music on Monday at ten o'clock.
Connection:You see days and times on the school timetable and hear them in class announcements.
  • 4. Using 'have' for lessons

We say 'have' to talk about lessons. We have English. She has math.

Example:I have art today.
Connection:You use 'have' when you write or talk about your school day in English.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. subject — A subject is a topic you learn at school.
  2. math — Math is the subject where you learn numbers.
  3. English — English is the subject where you learn English language.
  4. science — Science is the subject about nature and experiments.
  5. history — History is the subject about the past.
  6. art — Art is the subject where you draw and paint.
  7. music — Music is the subject where you learn songs.
  8. timetable — A timetable is a plan showing when classes happen.
  9. lesson — A lesson is one class period at school.
  10. Monday — Monday is the first day of the week.
  11. teacher — A teacher is a person who teaches students.
  12. student — A student is a person who learns at school.
  13. class — A class is a group of students learning together.
  14. study — Study means to learn about something.
  15. learn — Learn means to get new knowledge.
  16. easy — Easy means not hard to do.
  17. difficult — Difficult means hard to do or understand.
  18. favorite — Favorite means the one you like best.
  19. start — Start means to begin something.
  20. finish — Finish means to end or complete something.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
You will learn the names of school subjects and words about the timetable.
Reading
You will read a simple school timetable and find the subjects and times.
Listening
You will listen to a teacher talk about the weekly timetable.
Speaking
You will say your school timetable and talk about your favorite subject.
Grammar
You will practice using have and has to talk about lessons.
Writing
You will write a short paragraph about your school timetable.
Lesson Test
The test checks that you know subject names, times, and have or has; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In many countries, students start school at different times! Some students start at seven in the morning, and some start at nine o'clock. But everyone learns the same subjects: math, English, science, and more!

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). This book has simple lessons about school words and daily routines. Oxford Picture Dictionary — Oxford University Press (2015). It shows pictures of school subjects and classrooms with clear English words.

▶ Learn English - School Subjects — BBC Learning English ▶ Telling the Time in English — English with Lucy

MINI STORY

Anna is a student. She goes to school every day. She looks at her timetable every Monday. The timetable shows all her classes.

Anna has many subjects at school. She has math, English, science, and history. She also has art and music. Her favorite subject is art. She likes to draw and paint. Art is easy for Anna. But science is difficult for her.

Anna's classes start at eight o'clock. Her English teacher is very nice. The teacher helps all students learn. Anna studies every day after school. Her lessons finish at three o'clock. Then she goes home. Anna wants to learn many new things. She is a good student. She likes school very much.

nodes.explanation: → 'Start' and 'begin' mean the same, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: easy — hard
nodes.explanation: → 'Easy' and 'hard' have opposite meanings, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: teacher — teach
nodes.explanation: → 'Teacher' comes from 'teach', so they are in the same word family.

nodes.question: music — mountain
nodes.explanation: → 'Music' and 'mountain' have no connection, so they are unrelated.

nodes.question: lesson — period
nodes.explanation: → 'Lesson' and 'period' both mean a class time, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: finish — continue
nodes.explanation: → 'Finish' means to end, and 'continue' means to keep going, so they are opposites.

nodes.question: study — studied
nodes.explanation: → 'Studied' is a form of 'study', so they are in the same word family.

nodes.question: Monday — apple
nodes.explanation: → 'Monday' is a day and 'apple' is a fruit, so they are unrelated.

nodes.question: subject — course
nodes.explanation: → 'subject' and 'course' both mean a topic that we study, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: difficult — simple
nodes.explanation: → 'difficult' and 'simple' have opposite meanings: difficult is hard, simple is easy, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: student — studies
nodes.explanation: → 'student' and 'studies' share the same root 'study', so they are a word family.

nodes.question: timetable — ocean
nodes.explanation: → 'timetable' and 'ocean' belong to different ideas, so they are unrelated.

Reading Passage

Ana's School Day

Text type: Narrative
Ana is a new student. She is ten years old. Today is Monday. Ana has five classes today.

In the morning, Ana has maths. She likes maths. It is easy. Then she has English. English is hard. But Ana is happy. Her teacher is nice.

In the afternoon, Ana has art. Art is her favourite subject. She can draw and paint. After art, she has PE. PE is fun. Ana can run and play. Her last class is science. Science is interesting. Ana likes her school day.

My Classroom Timetable

Text type: Description
This is my timetable. It is on the wall. The timetable is big and blue. It has five days. It has seven subjects.

On Monday, I have English first. Then I have maths. I have history on Tuesday. I have geography on Wednesday. Thursday is good. I have music and art. Friday is my best day. I have PE in the morning.

The timetable helps me. I can see my classes. I know when I have each subject. I look at it every day. My timetable is very useful.

Important School Notice

Text type: Notice

TO: All Students
FROM: Mr Brown, Head Teacher

There is a new timetable. It starts on Monday. Please look at it.

The new timetable has six classes. Maths is now first. English is second. Lunch is at twelve o'clock. PE is in the afternoon. It is now on Tuesday and Friday.

You can see the timetable in the hall. You can also see it online. Please ask your teacher if you have questions. Thank you.

Mr Brown

contentRef.text:
About School Subjects

Text type: Informational
Students learn many subjects at school. Each subject is different. Each subject is important.

Maths is about numbers. Students count and add. English is about reading and writing. Students learn new words. Science is about nature and the world. PE is physical education. Students move and play sports. Art is about drawing and making things. Music is about songs and sounds.

Students have a timetable. The timetable shows all the subjects. It shows the days and times. Students look at the timetable every day. It helps them know their classes.

Two Different Timetables

Text type: Comparison
Tom and Lisa are students. They have different timetables. Tom's timetable has five subjects. Lisa's timetable has six subjects.

Tom has maths every day. Lisa has maths three times a week. Tom has PE on Monday. Lisa has PE on Friday. Tom likes his history class. It is on Tuesday. Lisa does not have history. She has geography instead.

Both students have English and science. They both like their timetables. But their timetables are not the same. Every student is different.

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

I have English on Monday. Maths is at nine o'clock. We study science on Tuesday. My timetable has seven subjects. History class is very interesting.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What is your favourite subject?

My favourite subject is art. I like art very much.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What subjects do you have on Monday?

I have English and maths on Monday. I have PE too.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Do you like science?

Yes, I like science. Science is good.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. When do you have English class?

I have English on Monday and Wednesday. It is at ten o'clock.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. How many subjects do you study?

I study eight subjects. I have a big timetable.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Present Simple – have

We use 'have' to talk about lessons.

Use 'have' with I, you, we, they.

Use 'has' with he, she, it.

FORMS

FormExample
I / you / we / they + haveI have maths on Monday.
he / she / it + hasShe has English today.
Negative: do not have / does not haveWe do not have art today.
Question: Do / Does + subject + have?Do you have music?
Short answer: Yes, I do. / No, she does not.Does he have PE? Yes, he does.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ She have English today.

✓ She has English today.

Use 'has' with he, she, it.

✗ I has maths now.

✓ I have maths now.

Use 'have' with I, you, we, they.

✗ He do not have art.

✓ He does not have art.

Use 'does not' with he, she, it.

lessons.titleEn: School Subjects and the Timetable — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about your favourite school subject. Say what it is and why you like it. (20–30 words)

  • Name one school subject you like
  • Say it is good or fun
  • Use very simple words only

Key structures: My favourite subject is..., I like... because...

Model
My favourite subject is art. I like art. It is fun. I draw pictures. I use colours. Art is good.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words naming your favourite school subject and saying why you like it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: subject, maths, English, science, art, history, PE, fun, good. Structures: My favourite subject is...; I like... because...; It is fun / good.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names one clear school subject (for example art or science) and gives at least one reason or example, such as 'It is fun' or 'I draw pictures'. Good: Names the subject and gives one simple reason, but the reason is only 'good'. Developing: Names a subject but gives no reason, or names several subjects without choosing a favourite. Beginning: Does not name a school subject.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My favourite subject is...' and 'I like... because...' or 'It is fun' correctly with a subject name from the week. Good: Uses one of the two patterns correctly with a subject word. Developing: Writes the subject word only, or 'I like because' with nothing after it. Beginning: No week patterns or subject words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Sentences are correct: 'is' after the subject, 'It is fun', 'I like art' with no extra -s on 'like'. Good: Clear, with one or two slips such as 'My favourite subject art' (no is). Developing: Several slips like 'I am like maths' or missing 'is', but the idea is still guessable. Beginning: Errors make the meaning unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Subject first, then reason, in 3-5 short sentences with capitals and full stops. Good: Clear order with minor punctuation issues. Developing: Reason comes before the subject, or ideas are joined with no punctuation. Beginning: No sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Favourite subject with a clear reason, both patterns used, nearly error-free. | 75-89: Subject and reason, small slips. | 60-74: Subject with a weak reason. | 40-59: Subject only or many errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: British or American spelling (favourite/favorite, maths/math); 'I like' repeated several times; spelling slips in subject names (scince); short sentences; using 'good' as the only reason.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-30 words; 17-33 is fine. Under 15 words = cap at 59; 15-19 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any school subject is fine (Khmer, maths, science, PE, music, history, English). Reasons may be 'fun', 'easy', 'interesting' or an activity. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer (art) = 100 with a note to use your own subject.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You chose a subject and told me why. 'It is fun' is a clear reason. 2) Fix: Add 'is': 'My favourite subject is art.' (not 'My favourite subject art'). 3) Next step: Next time add one thing you do in the lesson, like 'I draw pictures.'

lessons.titleKm: School Subjects and the Timetable — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: School Subjects and the Timetable — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe your Monday timetable. Write about three or four lessons you have on Monday. (30–45 words)

  • Say what day it is
  • List three or four lessons with times
  • Use 'and' or 'then' to join sentences

Key structures: On Monday I have..., My first lesson is..., Then I have...

Model
On Monday I have four lessons. My first lesson is maths. Then I have English. I have science at eleven. My last lesson is history. I like Monday.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words describing your Monday timetable with three or four lessons, in order, with times if you can.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: Monday, timetable, lesson, first, then, last, maths, English, science, o'clock. Structures: On Monday I have...; My first lesson is...; Then I have...; I have... at + time.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: States that it is Monday and lists three or four lessons in a clear order, with a time for at least one (for example 'science at eleven'). Good: Lists three lessons on Monday with an order but no times, or four lessons with the day missing. Developing: Lists one or two lessons only, or subjects with no day and no order. Beginning: Does not describe a timetable or day.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'On Monday I have...', 'My first lesson is...', 'Then I have...' and a time expression, with subject names spelled recognisably. Good: Uses two of these patterns correctly. Developing: Uses 'I have' once, or lists subjects with commas and no pattern. Beginning: No week patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Correct 'have' (not 'has') with I, 'at nine', 'on Monday', and sentences have verbs. Good: Small slips like 'in Monday', 'at the nine' or 'I has'. Developing: Frequent slips in 'on/at' or missing verbs ('Monday maths English'), but order is guessable. Beginning: Meaning cannot be followed.
- Clarity & organisation (20 points). Excellent: Lessons follow the real order of the day, with first/then/last used to guide the reader. Good: Order is clear but 'then' is repeated or missing. Developing: Order of lessons is unclear. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Monday, 3-4 lessons in order, with times and first/then used. | 75-89: 3 lessons in order, small slips. | 60-74: 2-3 lessons, weak order or no times. | 40-59: 1-2 lessons or heavy errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: time written as 9:00, nine or 9 o'clock; spelling slips (mats, siense); a different day written about, if clearly stated; 'in Monday' when the meaning is clear; not using 'last'.
LENGTH: Aim for 30-45 words; 27-50 is fine. Under 22 words = cap at 59; 22-26 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: The learner's real Monday or an imagined one is fine. Times may be given for all, some or none. A different day is accepted but should be noted. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to write your own timetable.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Your lessons are in a clear order: first maths, then English. That is easy to follow. 2) Fix: Use 'on' with days and 'at' with times: 'On Monday I have science at eleven.' 3) Next step: Next time add the time for each lesson, like 'English at nine.'

lessons.titleKm: School Subjects and the Timetable — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: School Subjects and the Timetable — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about school subjects you like and do not like. Explain your timetable for one day and say which lessons are good or bad. (45–60 words)

  • Name subjects you like and subjects you do not like
  • Say when you have these lessons
  • Use simple words like good, bad, fun, boring

Key structures: I like... but I do not like..., ...is good/bad/fun/boring, I have... on...

Model
