aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about subjects you like and do not like, and describe one day's timetable, saying which lessons are good, fun, boring or hard.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: like, do not like, good, bad, fun, boring, hard, favourite, Tuesday, at nine. Structures: I like... but I do not like...; ... is good / fun / boring; I have... on... at...; My favourite lesson is....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names at least one subject liked and one disliked, says what each is like (fun, boring, hard), and gives the day and time of at least two lessons. Good: Gives liked and disliked subjects with opinions, but the day and times are limited to one lesson. Developing: Gives only likes or only dislikes, or describes the timetable with no opinions. Beginning: No subjects or opinions; off task.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I like... but I do not like...', opinion adjectives (fun, boring, hard) and 'I have... on/at...' correctly. Good: Uses 'like' and 'do not like' plus one opinion word and one timetable phrase. Developing: Uses 'like' only, or writes 'I no like maths'. Beginning: No week patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Negatives use 'do not' correctly, 'is' with adjectives ('Maths is hard'), and day/time prepositions are right. Good: Small errors such as 'I not like maths' or 'in Tuesday', yet meaning is clear. Developing: Many slips in negatives and 'is' ('I no like, maths hard'), so some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Meaning is lost.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Likes first, then dislikes, then the day's timetable, in short sentences with 'but' or 'then'. Good: Sections are visible but 'but' or 'then' is missing. Developing: Likes, dislikes and times are mixed. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Likes, dislikes, opinions and a timetable all included, accurate. | 75-89: All parts with small slips. | 60-74: Likes and dislikes with limited timetable. | 40-59: Only one part, or many errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: 'I don't like' instead of 'I do not like'; spelling slips (boaring); maths/math; using 'bad' instead of 'boring'; a day other than Tuesday.
LENGTH: Aim for 45-60 words; 40-67 is fine. Under 32 words = cap at 59; 32-39 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subjects and any day are fine. Opinions may use fun, good, bad, boring, hard, easy or interesting. The learner may write a real or imagined day. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to write about your own subjects.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You gave opinions about subjects: English is fun, and you said why. 2) Fix: Use 'do not' before the verb: 'I do not like maths.' (not 'I not like maths'). 3) Next step: Next time add the day and time: 'On Tuesday I have English at nine.'

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your school timetable: what subjects you have on different days, when, and which one you like.

TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:

- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'On Monday I have...', day names and 'My favourite subject is...' correctly, with subject names from the week.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Classroom Instructions

Teachers tell students what to do. They use short commands.

Example:Open your book to page ten.
Connection:You hear these words every day in the classroom.
  • 2. Polite Requests

We say 'please' to be kind. We ask, not command.

Example:Please listen to the story.
Connection:Teachers use polite words with students and parents.
  • 3. Imperative Form

A sentence that starts with a verb. It tells someone to do something.

Example:Close the door.
Connection:You see imperatives in textbooks and worksheets.

*[Embedded images on PDF page 126; see source PDF.]* Things we use in class every day. We name them in English.

Example:Take out your pen and book.
Connection:Students need to know these words for all lessons.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

Vocabulary

  1. sit — You are on a chair.
  2. stand — You are on your feet.
  3. open — You move something so you can see inside.
  4. close — You shut something.
  5. listen — You hear with attention.
  6. look — You see with your eyes.
  7. write — You make words with a pen.
  8. read — You see and understand words.
  9. repeat — You say or do again.
  10. stop — You do not continue doing something.
  11. come — You move to this place.
  12. go — You move to another place.
  13. book — It has pages with words inside a cover.
  14. pen — It is a thing you write with.
  15. board — It is a big flat thing on the wall for writing.
  16. chair — It is a thing you sit on.
  17. quiet — Not making noise.
  18. wait — You stay until something happens.
  19. help — You do something good for someone.
  20. turn — You move around or to a different direction.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words about classroom actions and things.
Reading
Read a short text about classroom instructions and find the imperative verbs.
Listening
Listen to a teacher giving instructions and hear the intonation.
Speaking
Say classroom instructions and requests aloud with good intonation.
Grammar
Learn imperative verbs that teachers use to give instructions in class.
Writing
Write five clear instructions for a simple classroom activity.
Lesson Test
The test checks all your skills in classroom instructions; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'please' comes from old French and means 'if it pleases you.' Teachers say 'please' about one hundred times every day!

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching — Jim Scrivener (2011). It shows simple classroom language that all teachers use. Classroom English — Cambridge University Press (2008). It has lists of instructions and requests for everyday teaching.

MINI STORY

Today is Monday. The students come to class. The teacher says, "Good morning! Please sit on your chair." The students sit down.

The teacher says, "Open your book to page five. Look at the board, please." The students open their books. They look at the board. The teacher says, "Please read the text." The students read together. Then the teacher says, "Now repeat after me." The students repeat the words.

One student talks to his friend. The teacher says, "Please be quiet. Stop talking now." The student stops. The teacher says, "Please write your name on the paper. Use your pen." All students write their names. They listen to the teacher. One student needs help. The teacher says, "Wait a moment. I can help you." The class is good today. The students go home happy.

Reading Passage

Maria's First Day at School

Text type: Narrative
Maria is a new student. She is in the classroom. The teacher says, "Sit down, please." Maria sits down. She is happy.

The teacher says, "Open your book." Maria opens her book. The teacher says, "Listen, please." Maria listens. She is a good student.

The teacher says, "Stand up." Maria stands up. The teacher says, "Good work, Maria!" Maria smiles. She likes her new classroom.

contentRef.text:
How to Follow Instructions in Class

Text type: Informational
Good students follow instructions. First, listen to the teacher. Look at the teacher. Be quiet. This is important.

Next, do what the teacher says. If the teacher says "stand up," you stand up. If the teacher says "write," you write. Follow the instructions.

Finally, ask questions. Say "please" when you ask. The teacher will help you. Good students listen, do, and ask. This is how you learn well.

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Please open your book. Close the door, please. Sit down and listen. Can you repeat that? Look at the board.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What do you say when you need help?

I say help me, please. I ask the teacher.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. How do you ask to open the window?

Can you open the window, please? I say please.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What does your teacher say when class starts?

My teacher says sit down. She says open your book.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Do you say please when you ask for something?

Yes, I say please. Please is good and nice.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What do you do when the teacher says listen?

I stop. I listen to the teacher.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Imperative Verbs (Commands and Requests)

We use imperative verbs to give instructions.

Start the sentence with the verb.

Do not use 'you'.

Example: 'Open your book.' To be polite, add 'please'.

FORMS

FormExample
Base verb + object/complementOpen your book.
Please + base verb + object/complementPlease sit down.
Base verb + object/complement + pleaseClose the door, please.
Don't + base verbDon't run in class.
Let's + base verb (suggestion)Let's read together.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ You close the window.

✓ Close the window.

Do not use 'you' in commands. Start with the verb.

✗ Opens your book.

✓ Open your book.

Use base verb form. Do not add -s.

✗ No talk, please.

✓ Don't talk, please.

Use 'Don't' + verb for negative commands.

lessons.titleKm: Simple Classroom Instructions and Requests — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)
lessons.titleEn: Simple Classroom Instructions and Requests — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about what your teacher says in class. Use simple classroom instructions. (20–30 words)

  • Use simple verbs: sit, open, close, listen
  • Start with 'My teacher says...'
  • Write 3 or 4 short sentences

Key structures: Imperative verbs (sit, open, listen), please for polite requests

Model
My teacher says 'Sit down, please.' She says 'Open your book.' She says 'Listen.' I listen to my teacher. She is good.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words about what your teacher says in class, using three or four simple instructions.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: sit down, stand up, open, close, listen, look, please, book. Structures: My teacher says '...'; Imperative: Sit down, Open your book, Listen; please.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives three or four different instructions that a teacher really says (for example 'Sit down', 'Open your book', 'Listen'). Good: Gives two clear instructions, or three with one repeated. Developing: Gives one instruction, or says what the teacher does without any instruction words. Beginning: No classroom instructions.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Starts with 'My teacher says...' and uses imperative verbs (sit, open, close, listen), with 'please' in at least one. Good: Uses 'My teacher says' with two instructions and 'please' or an imperative. Developing: Writes instruction words without 'My teacher says', or uses 'please' wrongly. Beginning: No week verbs or patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Instructions use the base verb ('Open your book', not 'Opens' or 'Opening'), 'says' for one teacher, and 'your' with objects. Good: One or two slips such as 'My teacher say' or 'Open book'. Developing: Several errors like 'Teacher says to sitting', that make instructions hard to understand. Beginning: Meaning is lost.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: One instruction per short sentence, with quote marks or a clear way to show what is said, and full stops. Good: Instructions are clear; quotes or punctuation are missing. Developing: Instructions run together without separation. Beginning: No sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: 3-4 real instructions with 'My teacher says' and base verbs used well. | 75-89: 3 instructions, minor slips. | 60-74: 2 instructions or weak pattern. | 40-59: 1 instruction or heavy errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: missing quote marks; spelling slips (litsen); 'Please sit' or 'Sit, please'; 'the' instead of 'your'; extra sentence like 'I like my teacher'.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-30 words; 17-33 is fine. Under 15 words = cap at 59; 15-19 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real classroom instructions are fine (Stand up, Look at the board, Close the door, Be quiet). Writing the instruction without 'my teacher says' each time is fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to use your own instructions.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You wrote real teacher instructions like 'Open your book' and 'Listen'. 2) Fix: Use 'says' for one teacher: 'My teacher says, "Sit down, please."' (not 'My teacher say'). 3) Next step: Next time add 'please' to one more instruction, such as 'Stand up, please.'

lessons.titleKm: Simple Classroom Instructions and Requests — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: Simple Classroom Instructions and Requests — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about what you say in class when you need something. Describe your classroom requests. (30–45 words)

  • Use 'Can I...?' for requests
  • Use 'please' to be polite
  • Write about pen, paper, help, or going out

Key structures: Can I + verb (Can I go, Can I have), please at the end of requests, Simple present tense

Model
In class, I say 'Can I have a pen, please?' I say 'Can I go out?' I say 'Can you help me?' My teacher is nice. She helps me. I say 'Thank you.'

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words about the requests you make in class when you need something, using 'Can I...?' and 'please'.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: can, please, pen, paper, help, go out, have, thank you. Structures: Can I + verb...?; Can I have a ..., please?; Can you help me?; Thank you.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives three different requests a learner really makes (for example borrowing a pen, asking for paper, asking for help, going out) and may add the teacher's reply. Good: Gives two clear requests, or three requests with one repeated. Developing: Gives one request, or writes only about the teacher. Beginning: No requests.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'Can I have...?', 'Can I go...?' or 'Can you help me?' with 'please' and 'Thank you' used naturally. Good: Uses 'Can I...?' correctly at least twice, with 'please' once. Developing: Uses 'Can I' with the wrong verb form ('Can I going?') or leaves out 'can'. Beginning: No request patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: The verb after 'Can I' is in the base form (Can I go, Can I have), questions have a question mark and 'a' is used before 'pen'. Good: One or two slips such as 'Can I going out' or 'Can I have pen'. Developing: Frequent errors in question form ('I can go out?' or 'Can I to go?'). Beginning: Questions are unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (20 points). Excellent: Each request is in its own sentence, introduced with 'I say' and followed by the polite words. Good: Requests are clear; some punctuation is missing. Developing: Requests are joined together without separation. Beginning: No clear separation.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: 3 polite requests with 'Can I...?' and 'please', accurate. | 75-89: 2-3 requests, small slips. | 60-74: 2 requests, polite words missing or errors in form. | 40-59: 1 request or many errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: missing question marks; 'Can I borrow a pen' instead of 'have'; spelling slips (plese); 'Please' at the start or end; not including 'Thank you'.
LENGTH: Aim for 30-45 words; 27-50 is fine. Under 22 words = cap at 59; 22-26 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic classroom request is fine (Can I have a ruler? Can I open the window? Can you say it again?). Describing the teacher's replies is a good bonus. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to use your own requests.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Your requests are polite and real, like 'Can I have a pen, please?' 2) Fix: After 'Can I', use the base verb: 'Can I go out?' (not 'Can I going out'). 3) Next step: Next time add a reply: 'The teacher says, "Yes, of course."'

lessons.titleKm: Simple Classroom Instructions and Requests — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Simple Classroom Instructions and Requests — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about a typical day in your classroom. Include what the teacher says and what students do. (45–60 words)

  • Describe actions in order: sit, open, read, write, close
  • Use 'we' for students and 'teacher' or 'she/he' for teacher
  • Keep sentences very short and simple

Key structures: Simple present tense (says, listen, write), Imperative forms (Sit down, Open, Close), and to connect actions

Model
We go to class. The teacher says 'Good morning.' We say 'Good morning.' She says 'Sit down, please.' We sit down. She says 'Open your book.' We open our books. She says 'Read page ten.' We read. Then we write. The teacher says 'Close your book.' We close our books. Class is good.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about a typical day in your classroom: what the teacher says and what students do, in order.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: sit down, open, read, write, close, listen, page, please, good morning. Structures: The teacher says '...'; We + verb; She/He says... We...; Then / and.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives at least four steps of the lesson in order, each with a teacher instruction and the matching student action (teacher says 'Open your book', we open our books). Good: Gives three steps with instruction and action, or four steps where some actions are missing. Developing: Gives one or two steps, or only instructions without student actions. Beginning: No lesson steps.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'The teacher says...' with imperatives (Sit down, Open, Read page ten, Close) and 'We + verb' for the students, with 'please' and 'then'. Good: Uses teacher-says and we-verb patterns for most steps, with 'please' or 'then' at least once. Developing: Uses only one pattern or mixes teacher and student verbs. Beginning: No week patterns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: 'says' with she/the teacher and 'say' with we; imperatives in base form; 'We open our books' with correct 'our'. Good: A few slips such as 'The teacher say' or 'We opens'. Developing: Many verb-form errors, though the sequence can still be guessed. Beginning: Not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps follow a believable lesson order (greet, sit, open, read, write, close) with short sentences and 'then'. Good: Order is mostly logical. Developing: Order is mixed (close before open). Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: 4+ teacher-student steps in order, accurate verbs. | 75-89: 3-4 steps, a few verb slips. | 60-74: 2-3 steps, or weak pairing. | 40-59: 1 step or heavy errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: missing quote marks; 'Good morning' repeated; spelling slips; using 'she' for the teacher throughout; not using 'then'.
LENGTH: Aim for 45-60 words; 40-67 is fine. Under 32 words = cap at 59; 32-39 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any believable lesson steps are fine (stand up, look at the board, take out your notebook). Does not have to match the model. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to describe your own class.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You showed what the teacher says and what you do, step by step, like 'She says Open your book. We open our books.' 2) Fix: Use 'says' for the teacher: 'The teacher says...' and 'say' for we: 'We say good morning.' 3) Next step: Next time add 'Then' before a step: 'Then we write in our notebooks.'

Write about your classroom. What does the teacher say? What do students do? (20–35 words)

  • Use simple words.

  • Write about students.
Model
I am in the classroom. The teacher says sit down. We sit down. She says open your books. We open books. We listen to the teacher. We are good students. We learn English every day.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your classroom: what the teacher says and what the students do.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: teacher, students, sit down, open, listen, books, learn, every day. Structures: The teacher says...; We + verb; She says... We....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Gives at least two things the teacher says and shows what students do after each (sit down - we sit; open your books - we open).
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'The teacher says...' with imperatives and 'We + verb' correctly, with week words like sit down, open and listen.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Subject-verb agreement is correct (She says, We sit) and imperatives are in base form.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Teacher and student actions alternate clearly in short sentences.
DO NOT PENALISE: missing quote marks; 'The teacher says sit down' without comma; spelling slips; extra sentences about liking English; using 'students' or 'we'.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-35 words; 17-40 is fine. Under 12 words = cap at 59; 12-16 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any teacher instructions and student actions are fine. The learner may write 'We are good students' as an ending. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to describe your own classroom.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Teacher and learner roles

A teacher helps students learn. Students come to learn new things.

Example:My teacher is very good at helping students.
Connection:You hear this English in every classroom and education book.
  • 2. Classroom activities

Teachers teach lessons. Students read, write, listen and ask questions.

Example:Students write their homework after the lesson.
Connection:Teachers use these words when they give instructions in class.
  • 3. Learning qualities

Good teachers help students. Good students listen and study hard.

Example:Smart students ask questions when they do not understand.
Connection:These words appear in report cards and education textbooks.
  • 4. Teaching and learning materials

Books, homework and exams help students learn. Teachers use these things to teach.

Example:The teacher uses a book in the lesson.
Connection:You see these materials every day in the classroom.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. teacher — A teacher is a person who teaches students.
  2. student — A student is a person who learns at school.
  3. learn — Learn means to get new knowledge or skills.
  4. teach — Teach means to help someone learn something.
  5. classroom — A classroom is a room where students learn.
  6. book — A book is something you read with pages.
  7. homework — Homework is work students do at home.
  8. lesson — A lesson is a time when you learn something.
  9. study — Study means to learn about something.
  10. question — A question is something you ask when you want to know.
  11. answer — An answer is what you say to a question.
  12. write — Write means to make words with a pen.
  13. read — Read means to look at words and understand them.
  14. understand — Understand means to know what something means.
  15. smart — Smart means very good at learning.
  16. easy — Easy means not hard to do.
  17. hard — Hard means not easy to do.
  18. help — Help means to make something easier for someone.
  19. listen — Listen means to hear and pay attention.
  20. exam — An exam is a test to see what you know.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
You will learn twenty words about teachers, students and classrooms.
Reading
You will read a short text about good teachers and learners.
Listening
You will listen for descriptions of teachers and students.
Speaking
You will describe your favourite teacher using simple sentences.
Grammar
You will practise present simple with be, have and do to describe teachers.
Writing
You will write sentences comparing good teachers and motivated learners.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary and grammar, aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word teacher comes from an old word that means to show or point out, so teachers show students the way to learn new things every day.

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). This book teaches simple classroom words with clear pictures. Oxford Picture Dictionary — Oxford University Press (2015). It shows pictures of classrooms, teachers and students with English labels.

MINI STORY

My name is Tom. I am a student. I learn English at school. My teacher is very nice. She helps me every day.

I go to the classroom in the morning. The classroom is very big. I have many books. I read and write every day. I listen to my teacher. The lessons are very interesting.

Today I study new words. Some words are easy. Some words are hard. I do not understand everything. I have a question for my teacher. She gives me the answer. I have homework tonight. Tomorrow I have an exam. I am a smart student. I like to learn!

Reading Passage

My Teacher Ms. Lee

Text type: Narrative
I am a student. My name is Anna. I have a good teacher. Her name is Ms. Lee. She is nice.

Ms. Lee teaches English. She helps me every day. I learn new words. I read books. Ms. Lee is happy when I learn.

I like my teacher. She is my friend too. Thank you, Ms. Lee!

questions.prompt: Q1. Who is the story about?
questions.explanation: → The story is about Anna and her teacher: 'I have a good teacher. Her name is Ms. Lee.'

questions.prompt: Q2. What does Ms. Lee teach?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'Ms. Lee teaches English.'

questions.prompt: Q3. What does Anna do in class?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'I learn new words.'

questions.prompt: Q4. How does Anna feel about Ms. Lee?
questions.explanation: → Anna says 'I like my teacher.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'nice' mean?
questions.explanation: → 'She is nice' and 'She helps me every day' show that nice means kind and good.

Our Classroom

Text type: Description
This is our classroom. It is big. It has many desks. The desks are small. Students sit here. The teacher has a desk too. It is big.

The classroom has a board. The board is white. The teacher writes on the board. We look and we learn. There are books on the shelf. The books are new.

I like my classroom. It is clean. It is a good place to learn.

Note from Teacher

Text type: Notice
Dear Students,

We have class today. Class is at 10 o'clock. Please come on time. Bring your books. Bring your pens too.

Today we learn new things. We read a story. We write sentences. I help you. Ask me questions. I am here for you.

See you in class!

Mr. Park

questions.prompt: Q2. What time is class?

questions.explanation: → 'Please come on time' means come at the right time, not late.

contentRef.text:
What Do Teachers Do?

Text type: Informational
Teachers work at school. They teach students. They help students learn. Teachers teach many things. They teach reading. They teach writing. They teach math too.

Good teachers listen to students. They answer questions. They are patient. Teachers make lessons. They check student work.

Teachers are important. They help us learn. We need good teachers.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

The teacher is nice. My teacher helps me. Students learn at school. She is a good learner. We have a new teacher.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Who is your teacher?

My teacher is Mr. Smith. He is very nice.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Is your teacher good?

Yes, my teacher is very good. I like my teacher.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What do students do at school?

Students learn at school. They read and write.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Are you a good learner?

Yes, I am a good learner. I study every day.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Do you have many teachers?

Yes, I have three teachers. They are all nice.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Present Simple (be, have, do)

We use the present simple to talk about facts and things that happen every day.

The verb 'be' has special forms: am, is, are.

The verb 'have' changes to 'has' for he/she/it.

FORMS

FormExample
I am / you are / he is / she is / it is / we are / they areI am a student. She is a teacher.
I / you / we / they + haveWe have a book.
he / she / it + hasHe has a pen.
Negative: am not / is not / are not (or isn't / aren't)She is not here. They are not late.
Negative: do not / does not + verbI do not like tests. He does not read.
Question: Am / Is / Are + subject?Is she a teacher? Are they students?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ She have a book.

✓ She has a book.

Use 'has' for he, she, it — not 'have'.

✗ He is have a pen.

✓ He has a pen.

Don't use 'is' with 'have'. Just say 'has'.

✗ They is students.

✓ They are students.

Use 'are' with 'they' — not 'is'.

lessons.titleEn: Talking About Teachers and Learners — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about your teacher. Say what your teacher does every day. (20–30 words)

  • Use simple present tense verbs
  • Write about daily teacher activities
  • Keep sentences very short

Key structures: My teacher..., She/He teaches..., and

Model
My teacher is very nice. She teaches English every day. She helps us read and write. We like our teacher. She is kind and patient.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words about your teacher and what your teacher does every day.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: teacher, teaches, helps, explains, kind, patient, every day, lesson. Structures: My teacher is...; She/He teaches...; She/He helps us...; and.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says at least two things the teacher does every day (for example teaches English, helps us read, writes on the board) and adds a quality such as kind or patient. Good: Gives one or two daily actions, with or without a quality. Developing: Only describes the teacher's character ('She is nice') with no actions. Beginning: Does not describe a teacher.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My teacher is...', 'She/He teaches/helps...' and 'every day' correctly, with 'and' to join actions. Good: Uses two of these patterns, with one or two week words. Developing: Uses 'My teacher is' only, or lists verbs without a subject. Beginning: No week language.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: The -s ending is on teacher verbs (teaches, helps), 'is' is present, and he/she matches. Good: One or two slips, such as 'She teach English'. Developing: Many slips like 'My teacher teach and help' or 'He is teach', but the idea is guessable. Beginning: Meaning lost.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short sentences: who the teacher is, what she/he does, what she/he is like. Good: Clear with minor punctuation slips. Developing: Run-on or jumbled sentences. Beginning: No sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: 2+ daily actions with correct -s verbs and a description. | 75-89: Actions and description, small slips. | 60-74: Actions thin or verb slips. | 40-59: Description only, or heavy errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (pesent); 'He is a good teacher' as an extra line; using the teacher's name instead of 'my teacher'; Khmer-style 'teaches us English'; missing 'every day'.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-30 words; 17-33 is fine. Under 15 words = cap at 59; 15-19 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real or imagined teacher is fine. Daily actions can be anything a teacher does (checks homework, plays games, talks to parents). The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to write about your own teacher.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You wrote real things your teacher does, like 'She teaches English every day'. 2) Fix: Add -s for one person: 'She helps us read.' (not 'She help us read'). 3) Next step: Next time add one more action with 'and', for example: 'She writes on the board and checks our books.'

lessons.titleKm: Talking About Teachers and Learners — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe a good learner. Write what a good learner does in class and at home. (30–45 words)

  • Use 'a good learner' to start
  • List simple actions learners do
  • Use connecting words like 'and' and 'also'

Key structures: A good learner..., He/She listens..., also, and

Model
A good learner listens to the teacher. He does his homework every day. He reads books at home. A good learner asks questions in class. He also helps other students. Good learners study hard and learn a lot.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words describing a good learner: what a good learner does in class and at home.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: learner, listens, asks questions, homework, reads, studies, helps, hard. Structures: A good learner...; He/She listens/reads/does...; also; and.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives at least two actions in class (listens, asks questions, helps others) and at least one at home (does homework, reads books). Good: Gives two or three actions but only in class, or one in class and one at home. Developing: Gives one action or only general words like 'good', 'smart', 'kind'. Beginning: Does not describe a learner.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Starts with 'A good learner...' and continues with 'He/She listens...', using also and and to link actions. Good: Uses 'A good learner' and two of the week's verbs. Developing: Uses 'good student' with no verbs from the week. Beginning: No week language.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: The -s is used for 'a good learner' (listens, does, asks) and plurals are right ('Good learners study hard'). Good: A few slips, for example 'A good learner listen to teacher'. Developing: Many verb-form errors ('A good learner is study'), but ideas are guessable. Beginning: Meaning lost.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Class actions first, then home actions, with also/and linking. Good: Class and home ideas are visible. Developing: Class and home are mixed up. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Class and home actions with correct -s and linking. | 75-89: Both settings, small slips. | 60-74: One setting or weak linking. | 40-59: One action or heavy errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: 'he' used for every learner; spelling slips (homwork); plural 'good learners' used throughout; missing 'also'; 'listen to teacher' without 'the'.
LENGTH: Aim for 30-45 words; 27-50 is fine. Under 22 words = cap at 59; 22-26 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible learner behaviours are fine (arrives on time, practises English, helps classmates). 'Good learners...' plural is as good as 'A good learner...'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to use your own ideas.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You gave clear actions for a good learner in class and at home. 2) Fix: Add -s with 'a good learner': 'A good learner asks questions.' (not 'asks question'). 3) Next step: Next time join two ideas with 'also': 'He also helps other students.'

lessons.titleKm: Talking About Teachers and Learners — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Talking About Teachers and Learners — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Compare teachers and learners. Write about what teachers do and what learners do in the classroom. (45–60 words)

  • Start with what teachers do, then what learners do
  • Use simple verbs like teach, learn, help, study
  • Show the difference between teacher and learner roles

Key structures: Teachers teach..., Learners learn..., but, and

Model
Teachers and learners work together in class. Teachers teach new lessons every day. They write on the board. They help students understand. Learners listen to the teacher. They read books and do exercises. They ask questions when they need help. Teachers give homework. Learners do the homework at home. Both teachers and learners are important in education.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words comparing teachers and learners: what teachers do and what learners do, and how their roles are different.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: teach, learn, help, study, explain, homework, lesson, exercise, board. Structures: Teachers teach...; Learners learn...; but; Both teachers and learners....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives at least two things teachers do and two things learners do, and makes a clear contrast (teachers give homework, learners do homework). Good: Gives teacher and learner roles with two actions for one group and one for the other. Developing: Describes only teachers or only learners, or lists actions without showing a difference. Beginning: No teacher or learner roles.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'Teachers teach...', 'Learners learn...' and 'but' or 'and' to contrast, with week verbs such as explain, help, study. Good: Uses both subjects with correct verbs and one linking word. Developing: Uses only 'teacher' and 'student' with is/are sentences. Beginning: None.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Plural subjects take verbs with no -s (Teachers teach, Learners study) and 'They' is used correctly. Good: Some slips such as 'Teachers teaches' or 'They helps'. Developing: Many plural/verb agreement errors; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Teachers first, then learners, with a closing line about both. Good: Both groups described in separate sentences. Developing: Teacher and learner ideas are mixed. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear contrast with 4+ actions, accurate plural verbs. | 75-89: Both roles present, small slips. | 60-74: One role thin or agreement errors. | 40-59: One role only or heavy errors. | 0-39: Off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: 'teacher' singular used instead of plural; spelling slips; missing 'but' if contrast is clear; 'both' omitted; 'They' reference slips.
LENGTH: Aim for 45-60 words; 40-67 is fine. Under 32 words = cap at 59; 32-39 words = cap at 74.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any correct teacher and learner roles are fine; the learner may use 'The teacher...' and 'The student...' in singular. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text = 20-35 with a kind note. A word-for-word copy of the model answer = 100 with a note to write in your own words.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: You showed the difference clearly: teachers give homework and learners do it. 2) Fix: Plural subjects have no -s: 'Teachers teach new lessons.' (not 'Teachers teaches'). 3) Next step: Next time use 'but': 'Teachers explain, but learners ask questions.'

WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write about your teacher or a student. Say their name. Say what they do. Say if they are good. (20–35 words)

  • Use simple words.
  • Write short sentences.

CHAPTER I · WEEK 6

Grammar Practice

There is / There are

We use 'there is' with one thing.

We use 'there are' with two or more things.

Use 'there is' for singular and 'there are' for plural.

FORMS

FormExample
There is + singular nounThere is a desk.
There are + plural nounThere are ten books.
Negative: There is not / There are notThere is not a window. There are not chairs.
Question: Is there...? / Are there...?Is there a teacher? Are there students?
Short answer: Yes, there is. / No, there are not.Are there pens? Yes, there are.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ There are a teacher.

✓ There is a teacher.

Use 'there is' with one person or thing.

✗ There is two rooms.

✓ There are two rooms.

Use 'there are' with two or more things.

✗ Is there books?

✓ Are there books?

Use 'are there' when you ask about more than one thing.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about your school. (20–35 words)

  • Say if your school is big or small.
  • Say what subjects you study.
  • Say if you like your school.
Model
My school is big. It has many classrooms. I study English, maths and science. The teachers are good. I like my school very much. I go there every day.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your own school: say if it is big or small, say what subjects you study, and say if you like your school.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: school, classroom, teacher, student, study, library, lesson, big, new, friend. Structures: My school is big/small.; It has ... classrooms. / There is a ... / There are ...; I study English, maths and ...; I like my school..
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: The paragraph says clearly that the school is big or small, names two or more subjects, and says whether the learner likes the school, plus one extra detail such as the classrooms or the teachers.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses four or more Week 6 words (school, classroom, teacher, library, study, big, new) and writes 'My school is...' plus 'I study...' or 'There is/There are...' correctly.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: 'is' and 'has' are used correctly, 'There is' goes with one thing and 'There are' with many, and any errors are small slips that never block meaning.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short, clear sentences follow a logical order (size, then subjects, then feeling), and 'and' is used to join ideas.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'clasroom' or 'libary'; 'maths' or 'math' (both are fine); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear, e.g. 'My school big'; a missing full stop or capital letter; British or American spelling.
LENGTH: Target is 20-35 words; accept about 18-38. Under 15 words = cap at 50 because the three points cannot all be answered. Over 38 words is fine if the writing stays on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any true school is fine: small village school, big town school, old or new. Any subjects are fine (Khmer, science, PE, not only English and maths). 'It has ten classrooms' or 'There are ten classrooms' are both correct. The learner may say they like or do not like the school if it is clear. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions, writes about something unrelated, or leaves it empty, score 0-20 and ask them to write about their own school. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 and add a note: 'Next time, please use your own sentences about your school.'

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. School day routines

A school day routine is what you do every day at school. It happens at the same time each day.

Example:Students start class at 8 o'clock every morning.
Connection:Teachers use this English when they talk about the timetable in class.
  • 2. Time expressions

Time expressions tell us when something happens. We use them to say the time of day.

Example:We have a break at 10 o'clock.
Connection:You see time expressions in school timetables and textbooks.
  • 3. Daily activities at school

Daily activities are things students do at school. They read, write, and listen every day.

Example:The teacher reads a book to the class.
Connection:Students talk about daily activities in speaking exams and classroom discussions.
  • 4. Sequence words

Sequence words show the order of activities. Words like first, then, and after show what happens next.

Example:First, we listen to the teacher, then we write in our notebooks.
Connection:You use sequence words when you write about your day in exams and homework.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

Vocabulary

  1. school — A place where children go to learn.
  2. class — A group of students who learn together.
  3. teacher — A person who helps students learn.
  4. student — A person who learns at school.
  5. study — To learn about something.
  6. book — Something you read to learn.
  7. write — To make words with a pen.
  8. read — To look at words and understand.
  9. lesson — A time when you learn something.
  10. homework — Work you do at home after school.
  11. break — A short time to rest.
  12. lunch — Food you eat in the middle of the day.
  13. classroom — A room where students learn.
  14. pen — A thing you use to write.
  15. notebook — A book where you write notes.
  16. test — Questions to see what you know.
  17. answer — To say or write a reply.
  18. learn — To get new knowledge.
  19. subject — A topic you study at school.
  20. listen — To hear and pay attention.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words about school days and activities.
Reading
Read a short text about a school day and find the times and activities.
Listening
Listen to a student talk about their school day and write the times.
Speaking
Tell your partner about your typical school day using time words.
Grammar
Practice present simple verbs with he, she, and it in sentences about school routines.
Writing
Write a short paragraph about your daily school routine with time connectors.
Lesson Test
The test checks your understanding of school day vocabulary and present simple tense; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In Cambodia, many students say 'Good morning, teacher' at the start of every lesson. In English, we also say 'Good morning' to show respect and start the day well!

REFERENCES

Oxford Picture Dictionary — Oxford University Press (2015). This book has pictures and words for school activities and classroom vocabulary. Basic English Grammar — Betty Schrampfer Azar (2014). This book explains present simple tense with clear examples for beginners.

MINI STORY

My School Day

I am a student. I go to school every day. My school is big. I have many classes. My classroom is nice. I sit at my desk. I have my book, notebook, and pen.

My teacher is good. The lesson starts at nine. I listen to the teacher. I read and write. I learn new things. My favorite subject is English. I study hard. At ten, we have a break. I eat lunch with my friends.

After lunch, we have more lessons. Today we have a test. I answer the questions. At three, school finishes. I go home. I do my homework. I write in my notebook. I read my books. I like my school day!

Reading Passage

My Friend Tom

Text type: Narrative
My friend is Tom. He is a student. Tom goes to school every day. He gets up at seven o'clock.

Tom eats breakfast at home. He likes bread and milk. Then he goes to school. School starts at eight thirty.

Tom has four lessons in the morning. He has lunch at school. Tom likes his teacher. She is very nice. Tom goes home at three o'clock. He is happy at school.

Our Classroom

Text type: Description
Our classroom is big and clean. It has ten tables and twenty chairs. The tables are brown. The chairs are blue.

There is a big board. The teacher writes on the board. We have books on our tables. We have pens too. The windows are very big. We can see trees outside.

Our classroom has a clock on the wall. It shows the time. We like our classroom. It is a good place to learn.

School Notice Board

SCHOOL NOTICE

Dear Students,

This week we have new times. School starts at eight o'clock. Breakfast is at seven thirty in the dining hall.

Please come on time. Bring your books every day. Bring your pens and pencils too. Lunch is at twelve o'clock.

Do not be late. The gates close at eight fifteen. See you at school!

Mrs. Brown, Head Teacher

School Day Activities

Text type: Informational
Students do many things at school. They learn new things every day. They read books. They write in notebooks. They do math.

Students have break time too. They play with friends. They eat snacks. Some students play football. Some students sit and talk.

After lunch, students have more lessons. They learn English. They learn science. At the end of the day, students go home. They do homework at home.

contentRef.text:
Two Different School Days

Text type: Comparison
Anna and Paul are students. They have different school days. Anna's school starts at eight o'clock. Paul's school starts at nine o'clock.

Anna has five lessons every day. Paul has four lessons. Anna eats lunch at twelve. Paul eats lunch at one o'clock. Anna likes math. Paul likes art.

Both students like school. Anna goes home at two thirty. Paul goes home at three thirty. They are both good students.

questions.prompt: Q1. What does this text compare?

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

I go to school every day. Students sit in the classroom. The teacher reads a book. We eat lunch at school. Children play in the afternoon.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What time do you go to school?

I go to school at eight o'clock. I walk to school.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What do you do in the classroom?

I read and write. I listen to the teacher.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. When do you eat lunch at school?

I eat lunch at twelve o'clock. Lunch is good.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Do you like your school?

Yes, I like my school. My teacher is nice.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What do you do after school?

I play with my friends. Then I go home.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Present Simple

We use the present simple to talk about things we do every day or every week.

Add -s or -es to the verb when the subject is he, she or it.

FORMS

FormExample
I / you / we / they + base verbI go to school.
he / she / it + verb + s/esShe reads books.
Negative: subject + do not / does not + base verbWe do not play.
Question: Do / Does + subject + base verb?Do you study English?
Question: Does + he/she/it + base verb?Does he eat lunch?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ He go to school.

✓ He goes to school.

Add -s or -es for he, she, it.

✗ She does not goes home.

✓ She does not go home.

Use base verb after does not.

✗ Do she like math?

✓ Does she like math?

Use does with he, she, it in questions.

lessons.titleKm: A School Day: Routines and Activities — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)
lessons.titleEn: A School Day: Routines and Activities — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about your morning at school. Say what time you arrive and what you do first. (20–30 words)

  • Start with the time you arrive
  • Use simple verbs like go, see, talk
  • Write short sentences

Key structures: I go to school at..., I see my...

Model
I go to school at eight o'clock. I see my friends. We talk and go to class. The teacher says good morning.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words about your morning at school: say what time you arrive and what you do first.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: school, class, teacher, student, o'clock, morning, friends, talk, lesson. Structures: I go to school at ... o'clock.; I see my ...; We talk and go to class.; The teacher says good morning..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts with the arrival time (e.g. 'at seven thirty') and then says what the learner does first, such as seeing friends, talking or going to class, with one more morning detail. Good: Gives the arrival time and one thing the learner does first, but there is no extra detail. Developing: Gives the time or the first activity but not both, or says only 'I go to school' with no time. Beginning: Does not describe the learner's morning at school, for example writes about home or the weekend.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I go to school at ... o'clock' and 'I see my ...' correctly with a time word and at least two Week 7 words (class, teacher, friends, talk, lesson). Good: Uses 'I go to school at...' correctly and one more Week 7 word or pattern. Developing: Uses only simple words like 'go' and 'school'; the time expression is missing or wrong, e.g. 'I go school eight'. Beginning: Almost no Week 7 language; sentences are unrelated to the given structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple is correct, including 'The teacher says' with -s, and 'at' is used with the time; errors are rare. Good: One or two errors, such as 'The teacher say good morning' or 'I go to school in eight o'clock', but meaning is clear. Developing: Several errors, e.g. missing 'to', no verb, or 'I am go to school', make some sentences unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are hard to understand because of grammar or word order.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short sentences begin with the arrival time and follow the morning in order (arrive, see friends, go to class). Good: Clear, but the order is a little mixed, e.g. the teacher comes before the arrival time. Developing: Ideas are listed without a clear order and the reader must guess what happens first. Beginning: Ideas are scattered or joined in one run-on line with no stops.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Arrival time and first action are clear, with 'I go to school at...' and a Week 7 word; nearly error-free; 20-30 words. | 75-89: Time and first action given; a few small errors. | 60-74: Time or first action is clear but thin; errors, but understandable. | 40-59: Very short or one point only; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'oclock' or 'freinds'; '8:00' written as numbers instead of 'eight o'clock'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing capital letters; using 'go to class' or 'go to school' interchangeably.
LENGTH: Target 20-30 words; accept about 18-34. Under 12 words = cap at 50 because time and first action cannot both be given.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real arrival time and morning routine is fine (flag ceremony, cleaning the classroom, greeting the teacher, saying 'Good morning'). Verbs other than go, see, talk are fine, e.g. 'I meet my friends'. 'I arrive at school at seven' is correct. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or writes unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask them to write about their own morning. Copying the model answer word for word = 100 with the note 'Next time, use your own morning and your own time.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise their time or first action, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "I go to school at seven o'clock".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'The teacher say good morning' -> 'The teacher says good morning.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add what you do after you see your friends.'

lessons.titleKm: A School Day: Routines and Activities — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: A School Day: Routines and Activities — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe what happens in your school day. Include lessons, break time, and lunch. (30–45 words)

  • Write about three different times in the day
  • Use time words like first, then, after
  • Keep sentences very short and simple

Key structures: First, we have..., Then we..., After lunch, we...

Model
First, we have a lesson. We read and write. Then we have a break. I play with my friends. We have lunch at twelve. After lunch, we have two lessons. School finishes at three.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words describing your school day in order, including lessons, break time and lunch, using first, then and after.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson, break, lunch, read, write, play, friends, o'clock, finish, first, then, after. Structures: First, we have ...; Then we ...; We have lunch at ... o'clock.; After lunch, we have ....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes lessons, break time and lunch, covers at least three different parts of the day, and gives at least one time (e.g. 'lunch at twelve'). Good: Covers lessons, break and lunch, but without any time or with very little detail about each part. Developing: Covers only one or two of lessons, break and lunch, or describes only one part of the day. Beginning: Does not describe the school day; the text is about home or a different topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses First, Then and After (lunch) in the right order, and Week 7 words such as lesson, break, lunch, read and write, in patterns like 'First, we have a lesson'. Good: Uses two of the sequence words correctly and some Week 7 vocabulary (lesson, break, lunch). Developing: Uses one sequence word or none, and mostly repeats 'we have' without time or sequence expressions. Beginning: No sequence words and almost no Week 7 vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple is mostly correct (we have, I play, school finishes), with only rare slips such as a missing 's' that do not block meaning. Good: A few errors like 'We has lunch', 'School finish at three' or 'in twelve o'clock', but the meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in verbs or time phrases make some sentences hard to understand. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable because of grammar or word order.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Events are in the correct order of the day (lesson, break, lunch, afternoon), joined by First/Then/After. Good: The order is mostly right, with one event in the wrong place or one missing link word. Developing: Events are listed without order, e.g. lunch before the first lesson with no link words. Beginning: No clear order; the reader cannot follow the day.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Lessons, break and lunch in correct order with First/Then/After and a time; clear and nearly error-free. | 75-89: All three parts covered with sequence words; small errors. | 60-74: Two or three parts covered; simple sentences; understandable. | 40-59: One part or very short; many errors; little order. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'luch' or 'finnish'; 'then' or 'next' used instead of 'after'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; times written as numbers (12:00); a different school pattern, e.g. a morning-only shift.
LENGTH: Target 30-45 words; accept about 27-50. Under 20 words = cap at 50 because three parts of the day cannot be described.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: The learner may describe a different order or schedule (half-day shift, two lessons or six), and may use 'Next' or 'Second' as well as First/Then/After. Any real school day is fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or writes about unrelated things, score 0-20 and ask for their real school day. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write about your own school day.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the sequence, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: you used "First, we have English. Then we have a break".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'After lunch we has two lessons' -> 'After lunch, we have two lessons.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add the time that school finishes.'

lessons.titleKm: A School Day: Routines and Activities — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: A School Day: Routines and Activities — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about your favorite part of the school day and what you do after school. Explain why you like it. (45–60 words)

  • Say which part of the day you like best
  • Use because to give a reason
  • Add what you do when school finishes

Key structures: I like... because..., My favorite time is..., After school, I...

Model
I like lunch time. I like lunch because I see my friends. We eat and talk. My favorite time is break time. We play games. It is fun. After school, I go home. I do my homework. Then I play. I have dinner at six o'clock with my family.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about your favourite part of the school day, give a reason with 'because', and say what you do after school.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lunch, break, lesson, homework, friends, favorite, play, home, finish, fun. Structures: I like ... because ...; My favorite time is ...; After school, I ...; Then I ....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names a favourite part of the day, gives a clear reason with 'because', and says at least two things done after school (e.g. go home, do homework). Good: Names the favourite part and gives a reason, and says one thing done after school. Developing: Names the favourite part but gives no clear reason, or does not mention after school. Beginning: Does not say which part of the day the learner likes, or the text is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I like ... because ...', 'My favorite time is...' and 'After school, I...' correctly with Week 7 words like lunch, break, homework and friends. Good: Uses 'because' and 'After school' correctly, and one or two Week 7 words. Developing: Uses only 'I like...'; 'because' is missing or misused (e.g. 'I like because I play'). Beginning: No target structures and almost no Week 7 words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple is mostly correct ('I like', 'We eat', 'I do my homework') and 'because' joins a full clause; errors are rare. Good: A few errors such as 'I am like lunch' or 'because is fun', but meaning is clear. Developing: Several errors in verbs or sentences, e.g. 'Because I see friends.' as a separate fragment; some parts are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are hard to understand.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Clear order: favourite part, reason, then after school, with short sentences and link words like 'and' or 'then'. Good: Mostly clear; the after-school part comes slightly out of order or without a link. Developing: Ideas are mixed together; the reader has to guess which part is the reason. Beginning: Ideas are scattered or in one run-on line.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Favourite part, reason with 'because', and after-school activities, all clear with Week 7 language; nearly error-free. | 75-89: All three parts present; small errors. | 60-74: Favourite part and one other part; simple language; understandable. | 40-59: Only the favourite part, or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'becaus' or 'homwork'; 'favorite' or 'favourite'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a short reason like 'because it is fun'; starting a sentence with 'Because' (only gently correct it).
LENGTH: Target 45-60 words; accept about 40-65. Under 30 words = cap at 50 because a reason and the after-school part cannot both fit.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any favourite part is fine (English lesson, break, going home, sports). After-school activities can be any real ones: help at home, play, study, eat dinner. 'I like ... because' or 'My favorite time is ... because' both work. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the instructions or writes something unrelated, score 0-20 and ask for their own favourite part of the day. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write your own reason and your own after-school plan.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise their reason, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "I like lunch because I see my friends".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'After school I goes home' -> 'After school, I go home.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add the time you have dinner.'

WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write about your school day. What do you do at school? What time do you start? What time do you finish? (20–35 words)

  • Say what time you start school.
  • Say one or two things you do.
  • Say what time you finish school.
Model
I go to school at eight. I have five lessons. I study English and math. I eat lunch at twelve. I play with my friends. School finishes at three. I go home.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your school day: the time you start, one or two things you do, and the time you finish.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: school, start, finish, lesson, lunch, study, homework, o'clock, friends, go home. Structures: I go to school at ...; I have ... lessons.; I study ... / I eat lunch at ...; School finishes at ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Gives a start time, one or two real activities (e.g. studying English, eating lunch) and a finish time, all about the learner's own school day.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I go to school at...' and 'School finishes at...' correctly and three or more Week 7 words (lesson, lunch, study, homework, o'clock).
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Present simple is mostly correct, including 'School finishes' with -s and 'at' before times; rare errors.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Starts with the start time, ends with the finish time, with the activities in between, in short clear sentences.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'finnish' or 'oclock'; times given as numbers (8:00, 3 pm); 'finish' vs 'end' or 'go home'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; an unusual shift time, e.g. start at seven or one.
LENGTH: Target 20-35 words; accept about 18-38. Under 15 words = cap at 50 because start time, activity and finish time cannot all be given.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real times and activities are fine. 'School starts at eight' or 'I go to school at eight' are both correct. The learner can name any number of lessons or any subjects. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or writes unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask them to write about their own school day. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, use your own times and activities.'
