contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Lesson Steps

A lesson has many parts. Each part comes in order. Teachers plan the steps before class.

Example:First, we read the book. Then, we write the answer.
Connection:Teachers write lesson steps in lesson plans every day at school.
  • 2. Sequence Words

Sequence words show order. We use them to say what comes first, next, and last.

Example:First, open your book. Next, read page ten. Then, answer the question.
Connection:Lesson plans and teaching guides use sequence words to show the order of activities.
  • 3. Instructions

Instructions tell students what to do. Teachers give instructions in every lesson.

Example:Listen to the teacher. Write the answer in your book.
Connection:Teachers give instructions in class and textbooks show instructions for every exercise.
  • 4. Lesson Structure

Every lesson has a start, a middle, and a finish. Good lessons follow a clear plan.

Example:The lesson starts at nine o'clock. We practice for twenty minutes. The lesson finishes at ten o'clock.
Connection:All teachers and textbooks organize lessons with a clear beginning, middle, and end.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Vocabulary

  1. lesson — A time when a teacher teaches students.
  2. teacher — A person who teaches students.
  3. student — A person who learns at school.
  4. start — To begin something.
  5. finish — To end something.
  6. book — Pages with words inside to read.
  7. write — To make words with a pen.
  8. read — To look at words and understand.
  9. listen — To hear words and pay attention.
  10. speak — To say words with your mouth.
  11. question — Something you ask when you want to know.
  12. answer — What you say to a question.
  13. practice — To do something many times to learn.
  14. homework — Work students do at home after class.
  15. class — A group of students learning together.
  16. learn — To get new knowledge.
  17. understand — To know what something means.
  18. repeat — To say or do something again.
  19. explain — To help someone understand something.
  20. example — Something that shows how to do it.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn words about lessons, teachers, and classroom activities.
Reading
Read a simple lesson plan to see the steps in order.
Listening
Listen to a teacher describe the steps in a lesson.
Speaking
Say the steps of a lesson using sequence words.
Grammar
Learn imperative form to give instructions like teachers do in lesson plans.
Writing
Write a short lesson plan with steps in the correct order.
Lesson Test
The test checks your lesson vocabulary and writing; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Teachers around the world use the same lesson steps: start, middle, and finish. A good lesson plan helps students learn better and remember more.

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching: A Guidebook for English Language Teachers — Jim Scrivener (2011). This book shows how teachers plan lessons with clear steps and simple instructions. How to Teach English — Jeremy Harmer (2007). This book explains lesson structure and gives examples of lesson plans in simple English.

▶ Classroom English for Teachers — English with Lucy ▶ ESL Teaching: How to Plan a Lesson — Oxford Online English

MINI STORY

Today I have a lesson. The teacher comes into the class. She says hello. We start at nine o'clock.

First, we open our book. The teacher says, "Read page ten." We read together. Then we listen to the teacher. She speaks slowly. I understand the words. The teacher asks a question. One student gives an answer. It is correct.

Next, we practice new words. We repeat after the teacher. We write the words in our book. The teacher gives us an example. She explains everything clearly. At the end, the teacher gives us homework. We finish the lesson at ten o'clock. I learn many new things today. The lesson is very good.

Reading Passage

Anna's First Lesson

Text type: Narrative
Anna is a new teacher. She is happy. Today is her first lesson. She writes the steps on paper.

First, she says hello to students. Next, she writes on the board. Then, students read a book. After that, they do an activity. Last, she says goodbye.

Anna looks at her steps. The lesson is good. The students are happy. Anna is happy too. She likes teaching.

A Good Lesson Plan

Text type: Description
A lesson plan is very important. It has simple steps. The steps are clear and easy.

The plan shows the lesson time. It shows the lesson activities. It has a start time. It has an end time. Each step is short. Each step is simple.

Teachers read the plan before class. They follow the steps in class. The plan helps teachers. The plan helps students learn well.

How to Plan a Lesson

Text type: Informational
Planning a lesson is easy. Follow these simple steps. First, choose your topic. What do students learn today?

Next, write your activities. Students can read. Students can write. Students can talk. Make the activities fun and easy.

Last, write the time for each activity. Give each activity ten or fifteen minutes. Check your plan. Is it clear? Is it simple? Now you are ready to teach!

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

The teacher says hello to the students. First, we open our books. The teacher writes on the board. Students read and write in class. At the end, we say goodbye.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What does the teacher do first in class?

The teacher says hello. The teacher writes on the board.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What do students do in the lesson?

Students read and write. They listen to the teacher.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Do you open your book in class?

Yes, I open my book. I read my book.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. What happens at the end of the lesson?

We say goodbye. The lesson is finished.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Does the teacher write on the board?

Yes, the teacher writes on the board. We see the words.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Imperative Form (Commands and Instructions)

We use imperative form to give instructions or commands.

Start with the base verb.

No subject is needed.

Use 'Do not' or 'Don't' to make it negative.

FORMS

FormExample
Base verb (+ object)Open the book.
Base verb + noun phraseWrite your name.
Don't + base verbDon't talk now.
Please + base verb (polite)Please sit down.
Base verb + and + base verbListen and repeat.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ You open the book.

✓ Open the book.

Don't use 'you' in instructions. Start with the verb.

✗ Not talk now.

✓ Don't talk now.

Always use 'Don't' before the verb for negative instructions.

✗ Opens the door.

✓ Open the door.

Use base verb only. No -s ending in imperatives.

lessons.titleKm: Describing a Lesson in Simple Steps — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)
lessons.titleEn: Describing a Lesson in Simple Steps — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe what a teacher does at the start of a lesson. Write about the first two steps. (20–30 words)

  • Start with what the teacher does first
  • Use 'first' and 'then' to show order
  • Keep sentences very short and simple

Key structures: The teacher + verb (says, opens, writes), First... then...

Model
First, the teacher says hello. Then the teacher opens the book. The teacher writes the date on the board. Students sit and listen.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words describing the first two steps a teacher does at the start of a lesson, using 'First' and 'then'.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson, teacher, student, start, book, write, board, listen, hello, open. Structures: First, the teacher says ...; Then the teacher opens/writes ...; The teacher + verb-s; Students sit and listen..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes two clear opening steps in order (e.g. the teacher says hello, then opens the book or writes the date) and adds one extra detail about what students do. Good: Describes two opening steps in order, with no extra detail. Developing: Describes only one step, or the steps are from the middle or end of the lesson, not the start. Beginning: Does not describe what a teacher does at the start of a lesson.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'First' and 'then' correctly, writes 'The teacher + verb' (says, opens, writes) and uses at least two Week 8 words such as book, board, listen, start. Good: Uses 'First' and 'then', and 'The teacher + verb' at least once. Developing: Uses only one of 'First/then', or lists actions without 'The teacher'. Beginning: No sequence words and no Week 8 verbs or nouns.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is correct after 'the teacher' (says, opens, writes), and 'Students' takes the base verb; errors are rare. Good: One or two slips, such as 'The teacher say hello' or 'The teacher open the book', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many verb errors, such as 'The teacher is open book' or a sentence with no verb, make some sentences unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps follow real classroom order with First then Then, in short separate sentences. Good: Steps are clear but one link word is missing or the order is slightly odd. Developing: Steps are mixed without order so the reader cannot tell which is first. Beginning: No clear steps; run-on text or single words.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two opening steps in order with First/Then and correct 'The teacher + verb-s'; clear. | 75-89: Two steps with sequence words; a few small errors. | 60-74: Two steps or one clear step with some structures; understandable. | 40-59: One step only or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'wrights' or 'bord'; missing 'the' before board or book; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; imperative forms ('First, say hello.') used as lesson-plan steps; using 'Teacher' without 'the'.
LENGTH: Target 20-30 words; accept about 18-34. Under 12 words = cap at 50 because two steps cannot be shown.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible opening steps are fine: greeting students, checking attendance, writing the date, opening books, reviewing last lesson. 'Teacher' and 'the teacher' are both fine; 'She' can replace 'the teacher' after the first sentence. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or writes unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for the first two steps of a lesson. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, use your own lesson steps.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the order, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "First, the teacher says hello. Then the teacher opens the book".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'The teacher open the book' -> 'The teacher opens the book.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add one thing the students do.'

lessons.titleKm: Describing a Lesson in Simple Steps — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: Describing a Lesson in Simple Steps — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe the middle part of a lesson. Write about what the teacher and students do together. (30–45 words)

  • Write about teacher actions and student actions
  • Use words like 'then', 'next', 'after that'
  • Describe one or two simple activities

Key structures: The teacher + verb / Students + verb, Then, next, after that, Present simple tense

Model
The teacher explains the new words. Students listen and look at the board. Then students read the text. The teacher asks questions. Students answer the questions. Next, students write in their books. They do an exercise.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words about the middle of a lesson, saying what the teacher does and what students do, using then, next or after that.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: explain, question, answer, read, write, listen, practice, repeat, example, exercise. Structures: The teacher explains/asks ...; Students listen/read/answer ...; Then ... Next, ... After that, ...; Present simple tense.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes both teacher actions (e.g. explains, asks questions) and student actions (e.g. listen, read, answer) in one or two clear middle-of-lesson activities. Good: Describes teacher and student actions, but only one activity or with little detail. Developing: Describes only the teacher or only the students, or the activities are from the start or end of the lesson. Beginning: Does not describe the middle of a lesson; the text is off-topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'The teacher + verb' and 'Students + verb' correctly with Then/Next/After that and three or more Week 8 words (explain, question, answer, practice, repeat). Good: Uses 'The teacher + verb' and 'Students + verb' and one sequence word, with two Week 8 words. Developing: Uses simple sentences without sequence words, or only one Week 8 word. Beginning: No Week 8 structures or vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Subject-verb agreement is mostly correct ('The teacher explains' but 'Students read'); errors are rare. Good: A few errors such as 'The teacher ask questions' or 'Students reads', but the meaning is clear. Developing: Many agreement and verb errors make some sentences unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Actions follow a logical order with Then/Next/After that, and teacher and student actions are easy to tell apart. Good: Mostly clear; one link word is missing or two actions are mixed. Developing: The sequence is unclear; teacher and student actions are mixed up. Beginning: No clear sequence; run-on text.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Teacher and student actions in order with Then/Next/After that; correct agreement; clear. | 75-89: Both actors and a sequence word; a few small errors. | 60-74: Teacher and student actions present but thin; understandable. | 40-59: One actor only or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'explan' or 'quesion'; missing articles; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; imperative steps like 'Read the text.'; using 'The students' or 'Students' interchangeably.
LENGTH: Target 30-45 words; accept about 27-50. Under 20 words = cap at 50 because both teacher and student actions cannot be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any middle-of-lesson activities are fine: reading aloud, group work, pair practice, board work, copying words, answering questions. Different verbs from the model are fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for the middle of a lesson. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, use your own lesson ideas.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear action, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "The teacher asks questions. Students answer".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'Students reads the text' -> 'Students read the text.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add "after that" before a new activity.'

lessons.titleKm: Describing a Lesson in Simple Steps — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Describing a Lesson in Simple Steps — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Describe how a lesson ends. Write about the final steps and what happens after the lesson. (45–60 words)

  • Start with what happens near the end
  • Include what the teacher checks or reviews
  • End with how students leave the class

Key structures: The teacher checks..., Finally, at the end, Students + verb (close, put, go)

Model
The teacher checks the answers with the class. Students correct their work. The teacher asks if students have questions. Then the teacher gives homework. Students write the homework in their books. Finally, students close their books. They put their pens away. The teacher says goodbye. Students say goodbye and go home.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about how a lesson ends: what the teacher checks, what homework is given, and how students leave.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: check, answer, homework, question, finish, book, close, goodbye, finally, correct. Structures: The teacher checks ...; Then the teacher gives homework.; Finally, students close/put ...; Students say goodbye and go home..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Covers the end of the lesson fully: what the teacher checks or reviews, homework or a question time, and how students finish and leave (close books, say goodbye). Good: Covers what the teacher checks and how students leave, but homework or another end step is missing. Developing: Covers only one end step, such as 'The teacher says goodbye', with no checking or leaving. Beginning: Does not describe the end of a lesson.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'The teacher checks...', 'Finally...' and 'Students + verb' (close, put, go) correctly with Week 8 words like homework, answer, goodbye. Good: Uses two target structures correctly with at least two Week 8 words. Developing: Uses one structure or relies on the simplest words with no sequence word. Beginning: No Week 8 structures or vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple agreement is mostly correct ('The teacher checks', 'Students put'); errors are rare. Good: A few errors such as 'The teacher check the answers' or 'They puts', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many verb and agreement errors; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps follow a real end-of-lesson order (check, homework, pack up, goodbye) with Then/Finally. Good: Mostly in order; one step is slightly out of place. Developing: Steps are mixed up, e.g. goodbye comes before checking answers. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Checking, homework and leaving described in order with Finally; correct agreement; clear. | 75-89: Most end steps in order; a few small errors. | 60-74: Two end steps; simple language; understandable. | 40-59: One step or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'homwork' or 'goodby'; missing articles; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; imperatives used as lesson steps; 'pack their bags' instead of 'put pens away'.
LENGTH: Target 45-60 words; accept about 40-65. Under 30 words = cap at 50 because the end steps cannot all be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic ending is fine: a quiz, a song, tidying up, giving homework, summarising the lesson. Students may stand up, thank the teacher, or leave in line. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for how a lesson ends. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, use your own ending steps.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear final step, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "Finally, students close their books".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'The teacher check the answers' -> 'The teacher checks the answers.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add one question the teacher asks at the end.'

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about the steps of your English lesson using first, next, then and last.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson, teacher, student, book, read, write, listen, exercise, homework, start. Structures: First, we ...; Next, we ...; Then, we ...; Last, we ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Gives four lesson steps for the learner's own English lesson, one each for first, next, then and last, and says who does each (teacher, students, we).
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses First, Next, Then and Last in correct order, and Week 8 verbs like open, read, write, listen, with 'we' or 'the teacher'.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Verb forms are correct ('we read', 'the teacher writes'); sentences have a subject and verb; errors are rare.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps are in real lesson order and each starts with a different sequence word; short and clear.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'exersice'; missing articles; 'Last' vs 'Finally'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; imperative steps.
LENGTH: Target 20-35 words; accept about 18-38. Under 12 words = cap at 50 because four steps cannot be given.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real lesson steps are fine (not only English; any subject the learner studies). Steps may use 'we', 'the teacher' or 'students'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their lesson steps. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write your own lesson steps.'

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Classroom questions

Questions are things we ask in class. We ask questions to learn new things.

Example:What is the answer to number three?
Connection:You hear these questions every day in your classroom.
  • 2. Polite question forms

We use please and sorry to be polite. Polite words make questions nice.

Example:Can you help me, please?
Connection:Teachers and students use polite words in every lesson.
  • 3. Question words

Question words start questions. They are what, where, who, when, and how.

Example:Where is the book?
Connection:You see question words in textbooks and exams.
  • 4. Asking for help

We ask questions when we do not understand. Questions help us learn better.

Example:Can you repeat that, please?
Connection:You ask for help in class and when you study.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

Vocabulary

  1. question — Something you ask when you want to know.
  2. answer — What you say when someone asks a question.
  3. ask — To say a question to someone.
  4. teacher — A person who helps students learn.
  5. student — A person who learns at school.
  6. class — A group of students who learn together.
  7. understand — To know what something means.
  8. know — To have information in your mind.
  9. help — To make something easier for someone.
  10. repeat — To say something again.
  11. sorry — What you say when you make a mistake.
  12. please — A polite word when you ask for something.
  13. thank you — Words you say to be polite and grateful.
  14. speak — To use your voice to say words.
  15. listen — To use your ears to hear something.
  16. write — To make words with a pen or pencil.
  17. read — To look at words and understand them.
  18. book — Pages with words that you read.
  19. page — One side of paper in a book.
  20. correct — Right and with no mistakes.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words about questions and classroom talk.
Reading
Read a short dialogue about asking questions in class.
Listening
Listen to students and teachers asking and answering questions.
Speaking
Say questions and answers about your class and lessons.
Grammar
Learn question words and how to put them first.
Writing
Write short questions and answers with question marks.
Lesson Test
The test checks your questions and answers; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Teachers ask about four hundred questions every day in class! Good questions help everyone learn better together.

REFERENCES

English for Everyone: Level 1 Beginner — DK Publishing (2016). This book shows how to ask and answer simple questions. Basic English Grammar — Betty Azar (2014). It explains question words in very easy English.

▶ Question Words in English — English with Lucy ▶ Classroom English for Students — Learn English with EnglishClass101.com

MINI STORY

My name is Lisa. I am a student. I go to class every day. My teacher is Mr. Brown. He is very nice.

Today I have a question. I ask Mr. Brown for help. He says, "Please repeat your question." I speak slowly. Mr. Brown listens to me. He understands my question now.

Mr. Brown says, "The answer is on page seven." I open my book. I read page seven. Now I know the answer! I write it in my book. "Is this correct?" I ask. "Yes, very good!" says Mr. Brown. I say, "Thank you, teacher!" I am happy. My class is good. I understand the lesson today.

Maria's First Day

Maria is a new student. She is in class now. The teacher talks about books. Maria does not understand one word.

CLASSROOM RULES

Do you have a question? Raise your hand. Wait for the teacher. Do not shout.

Good questions help everyone learn. Ask questions every day. Be polite. Listen to answers.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

I have a question. Please ask the teacher. Can you help me? I don't understand this. Yes, I know the answer.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Do you ask questions in class?

Yes, I ask questions. I ask the teacher.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What do you say when you don't understand?

I say I don't understand. Please help me.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. How do you answer a question in class?

I put my hand up. Then I answer.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Do you like answering questions?

Yes, I like it. I answer easy questions.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What do you do when you know the answer?

I put my hand up. I say the answer.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Question words (What, Where, Who, When, How)

We use question words to ask for information.

Put the question word at the start.

Then add 'is' or 'do/does' and the subject.

FORMS

FormExample
What + is/do/does + subject...?What is your name?
Where + is/do/does + subject...?Where do you sit?
Who + is/verb...?Who is the teacher?
When + is/do/does + subject...?When does class start?
How + is/do/does + subject...?How do you spell that?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ What your name is?

✓ What is your name?

Put 'is' before the subject in questions.

✗ Where is the pen?

✓ Where is the pen?

This is correct. Do not forget 'is' in the question.

✗ Who you are?

✓ Who are you?

Put 'are' before 'you' in questions.

lessons.titleKm: Asking and Answering Questions in Class — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)
lessons.titleEn: Asking and Answering Questions in Class — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about asking questions in your class. What do you do and say? (20–30 words)

  • Start with 'In my class'
  • Use simple present tense (I ask, I say)
  • Say what you do first, then what you say

Key structures: I + verb (I ask, I say, I put), when + simple present

Model
In my class, I put my hand up. I wait. The teacher says my name. Then I ask my question. I say 'please' and 'thank you'.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words starting with 'In my class' about what you do and say when you ask a question.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: question, ask, teacher, please, thank you, help, class, hand, wait, repeat. Structures: In my class, I ...; I ask my question.; I say 'please' and 'thank you'.; When I have a question, I ....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts with 'In my class' and clearly says what the learner does (e.g. put my hand up, wait) and then what the learner says (the question, 'please', 'thank you'). Good: Says what the learner does and what the learner says, but one part is very short or in a mixed order. Developing: Says only what the learner does or only what the learner says. Beginning: Does not describe asking a question in the learner's class.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'In my class' and 'I + verb' (ask, say, put, wait) correctly, with two or more Week 9 words such as question, please, help. Good: Uses 'I + verb' correctly with at least one Week 9 word (question, ask, please). Developing: Uses only simple words like 'I ask' with no 'In my class' or polite words. Beginning: No Week 9 words or structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple with 'I' is correct (I ask, I say, I wait) and 'The teacher says' has -s; errors are rare. Good: A few errors like 'I am ask' or 'The teacher say my name', but the meaning is clear. Developing: Many errors; sentences with missing verbs or wrong order are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Sentences follow the real order (hand up, wait, ask, thank) with link words like 'Then'. Good: Clear overall; the order is slightly mixed. Developing: Ideas are listed with no order. Beginning: No clear order; run-on text.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Starts with 'In my class', says what they do and say, polite words included; clear. | 75-89: Do and say both covered; small errors. | 60-74: One of do/say with some detail; understandable. | 40-59: Very short or one idea only; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'quesion' or 'pleese'; a question written without a question mark; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'When' or 'Then' freely as linkers; describing a real classroom custom, e.g. standing up to ask.
LENGTH: Target 20-30 words; accept about 18-34. Under 12 words = cap at 50 because do and say cannot both be given.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real classroom habit is fine: raise hand, stand up, say 'Excuse me, teacher', ask a friend first. The question itself can be quoted. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their class habit. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write what you really do in your class.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one action or polite word, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "I say please and thank you".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'I am ask the teacher' -> 'I ask the teacher.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, write the exact question you ask.'

lessons.titleKm: Asking and Answering Questions in Class — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: Asking and Answering Questions in Class — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about answering questions in class. Describe what you do when the teacher asks you a question. (30–45 words)

  • Say what happens when the teacher asks you
  • Describe two different situations (when you know / don't know)
  • Use 'I' to talk about yourself

Key structures: When + subject + verb, I know / I don't know, First... Then...

Model
The teacher asks me a question. I listen. Sometimes I know the answer. I say the answer. Sometimes I don't know. I say 'I don't know' or 'I don't understand'. The teacher is good. She helps me.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words about what you do when the teacher asks you a question, in two situations: when you know the answer and when you do not know.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: answer, question, know, understand, listen, repeat, help, sorry, teacher, correct. Structures: When the teacher asks me, I ...; I know the answer. / I don't know.; I don't understand.; First, I listen. Then I ....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes both situations clearly: what the learner does when they know the answer (e.g. say it) and what they do or say when they do not know (e.g. 'I don't know', 'Please repeat'). Good: Describes both situations, but one is very brief. Developing: Describes only one situation (for example only when they know). Beginning: Does not describe answering the teacher's question.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I know / I don't know', 'I don't understand' or 'Please repeat' correctly with 'When...' or 'First... Then...' and two or more Week 9 words. Good: Uses 'I know' and 'I don't know' correctly and one more Week 9 word or structure. Developing: Uses only 'I know' or only simple verbs; no 'when' or 'first... then'. Beginning: No Week 9 words or structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Negatives with 'don't' are correct ('I don't know', 'I don't understand') and 'The teacher asks' has -s; errors are rare. Good: A few errors like 'I not know', 'I no understand' or 'The teacher ask me', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many errors in negatives and verbs; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: The two situations are clearly separated (e.g. 'Sometimes I know... Sometimes I don't know...') and the order of actions is clear. Good: Both situations are clear but not well separated. Developing: The two situations are mixed together and hard to tell apart. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Both situations described clearly with 'I know / I don't know' and Week 9 language; nearly error-free. | 75-89: Both situations covered; small errors. | 60-74: One situation well, one briefly; understandable. | 40-59: One situation only or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'understan'; 'I no know' (note gently, do not heavily penalise); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'Sometimes' or 'When' to separate the two situations; a missing 'the' before teacher.
LENGTH: Target 30-45 words; accept about 27-50. Under 20 words = cap at 50 because two situations cannot be described.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real reactions are fine: ask a friend, say sorry, ask the teacher to repeat, guess the answer, look in the book. 'I'm not sure' is a good alternative to 'I don't know'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their own reaction. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write what you do in your class.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one situation, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "Sometimes I don't know. I say please repeat".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'I not understand' -> 'I don't understand.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add what the teacher does to help you.'

lessons.titleKm: Asking and Answering Questions in Class — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Asking and Answering Questions in Class — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about good and bad questions in class. Explain what makes a good question and what students should do. (45–60 words)

  • Start by saying what a good question is
  • Give examples of polite words to use
  • Say what students should not do

Key structures: A good question is..., Students can say... / should say..., Don't + verb

Model
A good question is clear and polite. Students can say 'Can you help me, please?' or 'I have a question'. They say 'Excuse me' first. They wait for the teacher. Bad questions are rude. Don't say 'What?' or 'I don't understand this'. Say 'Can you repeat, please?' Good questions help students learn.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words saying what a good question is, giving polite words students can use, and saying what students should not do.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: question, please, excuse me, thank you, repeat, help, polite, clear, wait, rude. Structures: A good question is ...; Students can say ... / should say ...; Don't + verb; Can you repeat, please?.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says what a good question is, gives at least two polite words or phrases (e.g. 'Excuse me', 'Can you help me, please?'), and says one or two things students should not do. Good: Covers all three parts, but with only one polite phrase or one 'Don't' sentence. Developing: Covers only one or two parts, e.g. polite words but nothing about what not to do. Beginning: Does not say what makes a good question; off-topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'A good question is...', 'Students can say...' or 'should say...' and 'Don't + verb' correctly, with Week 9 phrases like please, excuse me, repeat. Good: Uses two of the target structures correctly, with some polite phrases. Developing: Uses one structure; 'Don't' is missing or wrong (e.g. 'Not say what'). Beginning: No target structures and few Week 9 words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'Don't + base verb' and 'can/should + base verb' are correct, and 'A good question is' is complete; errors are rare. Good: A few errors like 'Don't says' or 'Students can says', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many errors in modals and 'Don't'; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order is clear: what a good question is, polite words, then what not to do, in short sentences. Good: Mostly clear; the parts are not in a clear order. Developing: Ideas are mixed so it is hard to tell the good advice from the bad. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Good question, polite phrases and 'Don't' advice all clear with Week 9 language; nearly error-free. | 75-89: All three parts present; small errors. | 60-74: Two parts clear; understandable. | 40-59: One part or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'polit' or 'repete'; question marks left out of quoted questions; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'should' or 'can' interchangeably; a different definition of a good question (clear, short, polite).
LENGTH: Target 45-60 words; accept about 40-65. Under 30 words = cap at 50 because three parts cannot be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Other polite phrases are fine ('May I ask a question?', 'I'm sorry, I don't understand'). Other 'Don't' advice is fine (don't shout, don't laugh at questions, don't talk during the lesson). The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for good-question advice. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write your own advice for students.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a polite phrase or tip, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "Students can say excuse me".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'Don't says what' -> 'Don't say what.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, add one more polite phrase.'

WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write about asking questions in your English class. Write 20-35 words. What do you do? How does your teacher help you? (20–35 words)

  • Say what you do in class.
  • Say what the teacher does.
  • Use simple words like ask, answer, help.
Model
I am a student. I go to class every day. Sometimes I have a question. I raise my hand. My teacher sees me. She answers my question. She helps me. I say thank you. She is very nice.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about asking questions in your English class: what you do and how your teacher helps you.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: question, ask, answer, help, teacher, class, student, thank you, please, understand. Structures: I have a question.; I ask my teacher.; She/He answers my question.; The teacher helps me..
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says what the learner does in class (e.g. have a question, raise a hand, ask) and how the teacher helps (answers, repeats, explains), with one extra detail like 'I say thank you'.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses ask, answer and help correctly with 'I + verb' and 'The teacher/She + verb-s', plus other Week 9 words (question, thank you, understand).
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is correct for the teacher ('She answers', 'The teacher helps me'), and 'I' sentences are correct; errors are rare.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Learner actions come first, then the teacher's help, in short sentences, with an optional closing sentence.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'quesion'; missing question marks or quote marks; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'He' or 'She' for the teacher; 'I am a student' style opening sentences.
LENGTH: Target 20-35 words; accept about 18-38. Under 12 words = cap at 50 because both parts cannot be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real classroom habit is fine, and the teacher may help in any way (repeats, explains, shows an example, checks the book). The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their own class. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, use your own sentences about your class.'

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Homework and assignments

Homework is work you do at home. Teachers give homework to students every day or every week.

Example:Please finish your homework by Friday.
Connection:You hear this in class when teachers give you work to do at home.
  • 2. Tests and exams

A test has questions. You answer questions to show what you know.

Example:We have a spelling test on Monday.
Connection:Teachers write about tests in class announcements and on the board.
  • 3. Marks and grades

A mark is a number for your work. Good marks show you did well.

Example:She got 85 marks on her test.
Connection:You see marks on your tests and in your report card.
  • 4. Study habits

Study habits are the ways you study. Good study habits help you learn better.

Example:I study for one hour every evening.
Connection:You talk about study habits with your classmates and teachers.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. homework — Homework is work you do at home after class.
  2. test — A test is questions that check what you know.
  3. mark — A mark is a number that shows how good your work is.
  4. pass — Pass means to do well enough on a test.
  5. fail — Fail means to not do well on a test.
  6. study — Study means to learn about something from books.
  7. answer — An answer is what you write or say for a question.
  8. question — A question is something you ask when you want to know.
  9. correct — Correct means right, not wrong.
  10. wrong — Wrong means not right, not correct.
  11. easy — Easy means not hard to do.
  12. hard — Hard means not easy, difficult.
  13. exam — An exam is a big test at the end of a term.
  14. write — Write means to make words with a pen or pencil.
  15. read — Read means to look at words and understand them.
  16. book — A book is something you read with many pages.
  17. page — A page is one sheet of paper in a book.
  18. teacher — A teacher is a person who helps students learn.
  19. good — Good means nice, great, or doing well.
  20. bad — Bad means not good, not nice.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
You learn twenty words about homework, tests, and marks.
Reading
You read a teacher's announcement about homework and test dates.
Listening
You listen to students talking about their test marks and study habits.
Speaking
You talk about your homework and how you study with a classmate.
Grammar
You practice present simple to say what students do every day or every week.
Writing
You write sentences about your homework and your test marks.
Lesson Test
The test checks all vocabulary, grammar, and reading skills; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'homework' is used all over the world, but in some places, teachers call it 'home task' or 'home study'!

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). This book teaches simple words about school and tests. Basic English Grammar — Betty Azar, Pearson (2014). This book explains present simple verbs very clearly.

▶ School Vocabulary for Beginners — Easy English ▶ Present Simple Tense Explained — BBC Learning English

MINI STORY

My name is Anna. I am a student. I study every day.

Today I have a test. I read my book. I look at every page. The test has ten questions. I write all my answers. Some questions are easy. Some questions are hard. I think my answers are correct.

My teacher checks the test. She gives me my mark. I pass! I get a good mark. I am happy. Yesterday I did my homework. I study hard. My teacher is happy too.

Next week we have a big exam. I need to study more. I read my books every night. I want to pass the exam. I do not want to fail. Good marks are important. I work hard at school.

Reading Passage

Anna's Good Mark

Text type: Narrative
Anna is a student. She has homework today. She writes the homework at home. She works for one hour.

Today is the test day. Anna is happy. The test is easy. She knows the answers.

The teacher gives the marks. Anna has a good mark. It is an A. She is very happy. She calls her mother. Her mother is happy too.

questions.prompt: Q1. What is the story about?

options.text: C. A student and her test

questions.explanation: → The story is mostly about Anna, a student, and her homework and test.

questions.prompt: Q2. How long does Anna work?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'She works for one hour.'

questions.prompt: Q3. What happens after the test?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'The teacher gives the marks' after the test day.

questions.prompt: Q4. How does Anna feel about the test?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'Today is the test day. Anna is happy.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'mark' mean here?
questions.explanation: → Anna has 'a good mark. It is an A.' So a mark is a grade.

contentRef.text:
My Classroom

Text type: Description
This is my classroom. It is big. There are many desks here. The students sit at the desks. They do tests here.

The teacher has a big desk. The desk is red. On the desk there are many tests. There are marks on the tests. Some marks are good. Some marks are bad.

The students have homework books. The books are on the desks. The homework is in the books.

questions.prompt: Q3. Where are the homework books?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'The books are on the desks.'

questions.prompt: Q4. The classroom is:

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'many' mean?
questions.explanation: → 'There are many desks here' means there are a lot of desks.

contentRef.text:
Message from Teacher

Text type: Notice

To: Class 3A
From: Mr. Brown

Hello students!

The test is on Friday. Please do your homework. Read pages 10 to 15. Write the answers in your book.

Bring a pen to the test. Bring a pencil too. The test is at 9 o'clock. Please come early.

Good luck!

Mr. Brown

questions.prompt: Q2. When is the test?

questions.prompt: Q3. What pages do students read?

contentRef.text:
How to Do Homework

Text type: Informational
Homework is important. Here is how to do homework well.

First, sit at a desk. The desk is quiet. Read the homework questions. Read them two times. Then write the answers. Write slowly. Check your work.

Do homework every day. Do it after school. Do not do homework late. Do homework early. This is good for you. You get good marks!

questions.prompt: Q1. What is the text about?
questions.explanation: → The text is mostly about doing homework well: 'Here is how to do homework well.'

questions.prompt: Q2. Where should you sit?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'First, sit at a desk.'

questions.prompt: Q3. What should you do after reading?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'Read the homework questions... Then write the answers.'

questions.prompt: Q4. When is good to do homework?

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'check' mean?
questions.explanation: → 'Check your work' comes after writing, so it means look at it again.

contentRef.text:
Two Students

Text type: Comparison
Tom and Lisa are students. Tom does not like homework. He does homework fast. He does not check his work. His marks are bad. He is sad.

Lisa likes homework. She does homework slowly. She checks her work. She asks questions. Her marks are good. She is happy.

Tom sees Lisa's marks. Now Tom works slowly too. He checks his work now.

questions.explanation: → The text is about Tom and Lisa, two students who do homework in different ways.

questions.prompt: Q2. How does Tom do homework at first?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'He does homework fast.'

questions.prompt: Q3. Who has good marks?
questions.explanation: → The text says about Lisa, 'Her marks are good.'

questions.prompt: Q4. What does Lisa do?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'She checks her work.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'now' mean?
questions.explanation: → 'Now Tom works slowly too' means at this time, not before.

What is Your Homework?
A1 — Listen and Answer

Aisha: Hi Rafael. Do you have homework?
Rafael: Yes, I have homework.
Aisha: What is your homework?
Rafael: I have math homework.
Aisha: Is it easy?
Rafael: No, it is hard.
Aisha: I have English homework.
Rafael: Is it easy?

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

I do my homework every day. The test is on Monday. I have a good mark. She writes the answers in her book. We study for the test at home.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Do you do homework every day?

Yes, I do homework every day. I write in my book.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. When do you have tests?

I have tests on Friday. We have one test every week.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Do you like tests?

No, I don't like tests. Tests are hard.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. What marks do you get?

I get good marks. My marks are good in English.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Where do you do your homework?

I do my homework at home. I study in my room.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Present Simple (Affirmative, Negative, Questions)

We use present simple for things we do every day or every week.

For I, you, we, they we use the base verb.

For he, she, it we add -s or -es.

FORMS

FormExample
I / you / we / they + verbI do homework every day.
he / she / it + verb + s/esShe does homework every day.
Negative: do not / does not + verbHe does not do tests.
Question: Do / Does + subject + verb?Do you have homework?
Short answer: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.Does she study? Yes, she does.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ He do homework every day.

✓ He does homework every day.

Use 'does' with he, she, it.

✗ She don't like tests.

✓ She doesn't like tests.

Use 'doesn't' with he, she, it.

✗ Do he get good marks?

✓ Does he get good marks?

Use 'Does' in questions with he, she, it.

lessons.titleEn: Homework, Tests, and Marks — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about your homework. Say what homework you do. (20–30 words)

  • Say what subject the homework is
  • Say when you do homework
  • Use simple present tense

Key structures: I do..., I have...

Model
I do homework every day. I have English homework. I write words. I read books. My homework is not very hard.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words about your homework: what subject it is and when you do it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: homework, study, write, read, book, page, easy, hard, every day, question. Structures: I do homework ...; I have English homework.; I write / I read ...; My homework is easy/hard..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says what subject the homework is (e.g. English, maths) and when the learner does it (e.g. every day, at night), with one more detail such as what they write or read or how hard it is. Good: Gives the subject and the time, with no extra detail. Developing: Gives only the subject or only the time. Beginning: Does not describe the learner's homework.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I do homework', 'I have ... homework' and 'I write/read...' correctly with Week 10 words such as homework, study, easy or hard. Good: Uses 'I do' or 'I have' correctly and two Week 10 words. Developing: Uses only 'homework' and basic words; no target pattern. Beginning: No Week 10 words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple is correct ('I do', 'I have', 'It is hard'); past tense, if used, is also acceptable; errors are rare. Good: A few errors like 'I does my homework' or 'I have a homework', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many verb errors; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Short clear sentences in a sensible order: subject, time, what they do, how it feels. Good: Mostly clear; the order is slightly mixed. Developing: Ideas are listed with no order. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Subject, time and an extra detail about homework, with Week 10 language; clear and nearly error-free. | 75-89: Subject and time given; small errors. | 60-74: One of subject/time plus a simple detail; understandable. | 40-59: Very short or one idea; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'homwork'; 'a homework' (note gently; homework is uncountable); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; past tense where it fits the meaning; missing capital letters.
LENGTH: Target 20-30 words; accept about 18-34. Under 12 words = cap at 50 because subject and time cannot both be given.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subject and any real habit is fine: homework for children the learner teaches, homework from a course, reading at night. Present simple or past tense are both fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their own homework. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write about your own homework.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one detail, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "I have English homework every day".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'I does homework' -> 'I do homework.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, say if your homework is easy or hard.'

lessons.titleKm: Homework, Tests, and Marks — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: Homework, Tests, and Marks — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about tests at school. Say how you feel about tests and what you do. (30–45 words)

  • Say when you have tests
  • Say what tests you have
  • Say how tests make you feel

Key structures: I have... / We have..., I feel..., Tests are...

Model
I have tests at school. We have a test every week. I study for tests. Tests are hard. I feel scared. My teacher helps me. I try to do well. I get marks after the test.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words about tests at school: when you have tests, what tests you have, and how tests make you feel.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: test, exam, study, hard, easy, mark, pass, fail, question, feel. Structures: I have a test every week.; We have ... tests.; I feel scared/happy.; Tests are hard/easy..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says when the learner has tests (e.g. every week, at the end of the month), what kind of tests (e.g. English test, exam), and how tests make them feel, with a reason or action (e.g. study). Good: Covers when, what and the feeling, but one part is a single short phrase. Developing: Covers only one or two of when, what and feeling. Beginning: Does not describe tests; the text is off-topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I have / We have a test', 'I feel ...' and 'Tests are ...' correctly with Week 10 words like test, exam, study, hard, easy. Good: Uses two of the structures correctly and some Week 10 words. Developing: Uses 'test' but no feeling words or target patterns. Beginning: No Week 10 words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'have', 'feel' and 'is/are' are correct ('Tests are hard'); present simple or past tense are used correctly; errors are rare. Good: A few errors such as 'I am feel scared' or 'Test is hard', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many errors; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order is clear: when, what, feeling, what they do, in short sentences. Good: Mostly clear; feeling and facts are slightly mixed. Developing: Ideas are mixed; hard to tell what is fact and what is feeling. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: When, what kind and feeling about tests, with Week 10 language; clear and nearly error-free. | 75-89: All three parts present; small errors. | 60-74: Two parts clear; understandable. | 40-59: One part or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'scarred' or 'exsam'; 'Test is hard' (note gently, 'Tests are hard' is the target); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; past tense where it fits; feelings other than the model (nervous, happy, worried).
LENGTH: Target 30-45 words; accept about 27-50. Under 20 words = cap at 50 because when, what and feeling cannot all be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real test habits are fine (weekly quiz, monthly test, final exam, driving test). Feelings can be positive or negative: happy, nervous, worried, calm. Present or past tense. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their own test experience. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write how you feel about your tests.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a detail or feeling, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "Tests are hard. I feel scared".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'I am feel scared' -> 'I feel scared.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, say what you do to get ready for a test.'

lessons.titleKm: Homework, Tests, and Marks — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Homework, Tests, and Marks — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about marks you get. Say what marks are good or bad and how you feel about your marks. (45–60 words)

  • Say what marks you get
  • Say if marks are good or bad
  • Say what you do to get good marks

Key structures: I get..., My marks are..., I am happy / sad

Model
I get marks for my homework. I get marks for tests. Good marks are A and B. Bad marks are D and F. I have good marks in English. My marks are not very good in math. I am happy with my English marks. I study hard every day. I want to get good marks. My parents see my marks. They are happy too.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about the marks you get: which marks are good or bad, how you feel about your marks, and what you do to get good marks.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: mark, good, bad, pass, fail, study, homework, test, happy, sad. Structures: I get marks for ...; My marks are good/not good.; I am happy/sad with ...; I study hard to get good marks..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says what marks the learner gets, which marks are good or bad (e.g. A/B good, D/F bad), how the learner feels, and what they do to get good marks. Good: Covers marks, good or bad, and a feeling, but not what they do to improve. Developing: Covers only one or two of these: marks, good or bad, feeling, action. Beginning: Does not describe the learner's marks.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I get...', 'My marks are...' and 'I am happy/sad' correctly with Week 10 words like mark, good, bad, study, test, pass. Good: Uses two of the structures correctly with several Week 10 words. Developing: Uses 'mark' and basic adjectives with no target patterns. Beginning: No Week 10 words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple (get, are, study) is mostly correct, or consistent past tense is used correctly; errors are rare. Good: A few errors like 'My mark is not good in math' or 'I am get a good mark', but meaning is clear. Developing: Many errors; tense switches or missing verbs make some parts unclear. Beginning: Most sentences are not understandable.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Clear order: marks, good or bad, feeling, what they do, in short sentences, with link words like 'and' or 'but'. Good: Mostly clear; the order is slightly mixed. Developing: Ideas are listed with no link and the order is unclear. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Marks, good or bad, feeling and action all clear with Week 10 language; nearly error-free. | 75-89: Most parts present; small errors. | 60-74: Two or three parts; understandable. | 40-59: One part or very short; many errors. | 0-39: Off-topic, copied or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'mak' or 'happey'; different marking scales (percent, A-F, numbers out of 10); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; past tense where it fits; mixing 'maths' and 'math'.
LENGTH: Target 45-60 words; accept about 40-65. Under 30 words = cap at 50 because four parts cannot be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any marking system is fine (A-F, percent, scores out of 10 or 100). The learner may write about their own marks or the marks of students they teach or support. Present or past tense. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions or unrelated text, score 0-20 and ask for their own marks. If the model answer is copied exactly, give 100 with the note 'Next time, write about your own marks.'
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one clear idea, quoting it, e.g. 'Good: "I study hard every day".' 2) Fix: One correction with an example, e.g. 'My mark is not good in math' -> 'My marks are not good in maths.' 3) Next step: One small action, e.g. 'Next time, say what mark you want to get.'

WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write about a test you have at school. Write 20 to 35 words. Say what test it is. Say if it is easy or difficult. Say what mark you usually get. (20–35 words)

  • Say what test it is.
  • Say if it is easy or difficult.
  • Say what mark you usually get.
Model
I have an English test every month. It is easy. I study at home. I get a good mark. My mark is A. I am very happy.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Expressing preferences about school subjects

We say which subjects we like and which we do not like. We give simple reasons why.

Example:I like math because it is easy.
Connection:Teachers ask you about your favourite subjects in class and on forms.
  • 2. Talking about school subjects

We name the subjects we study at school. We talk about them with other students and teachers.

Example:My favourite subject is art.
Connection:You use these words every day in the classroom and in your homework.
  • 3. Using like and don't like

We use like to say we enjoy something. We use don't like to say we do not enjoy something.

Example:She likes English but she doesn't like history.
Connection:This grammar helps you talk about your feelings in class discussions and tests.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Vocabulary

  1. like — You enjoy something or you think it is good.
  2. dislike — You do not enjoy something or you do not think it is good.
  3. favourite — This is the one you like the most.
  4. subject — A subject is a topic you study at school.
  5. math — Math is the subject where you learn about numbers.
  6. English — English is the language from England and America.
  7. science — Science is the subject where you learn about nature.
  8. history — History is the subject where you learn about the past.
  9. art — Art is the subject where you draw and paint.
  10. music — Music is the subject where you learn about songs.
  11. study — Study means to learn about something at school.
  12. learn — Learn means to get new knowledge about something.
  13. easy — Easy means not hard or difficult to do.
  14. hard — Hard means difficult to do or understand.
  15. interesting — Interesting is something that makes you want to know more.
  16. boring — Boring is something that is not interesting at all.
  17. fun — Fun means enjoyable and making you happy.
  18. teacher — A teacher is a person who helps you learn.
  19. class — A class is a group of students learning together.
  20. homework — Homework is work you do at home for school.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
You will learn the names of school subjects and words for likes and dislikes.
Reading
You will read short texts about students' favourite and least favourite subjects.
Listening
You will listen for subject names and reasons people like or dislike them.
Speaking
You will say which subjects you like and give simple reasons why.
Grammar
You will practise using like and don't like with he, she, and it.
Writing
You will write sentences about your favourite subjects and your reasons.
Lesson Test
The test checks you can use like and don't like correctly; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In English, we say math in America and maths in Britain, but both words mean the same subject!

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). This book teaches school subject words and how to talk about likes and dislikes. Basic English Grammar — Betty Azar, Pearson (2014). This book explains how to use like with different subjects clearly.

▶ School Subjects Vocabulary — English with Lucy ▶ Talking About Likes and Dislikes — British Council LearnEnglish

contentRef.text:
Talking About School Subjects

Text type: Informational
Students talk about subjects at school. They say 'I like' or 'I do not like'. They can say their favourite subject too.

To say you like something, use 'I like'. Example: 'I like Music.' To say you do not like something, use 'I do not like' or 'I don't like'. Example: 'I don't like History.'

You can also say why. Use 'because' and then say the reason. Example: 'I like Art because it is fun.' This helps people understand you better.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

I like English. It is fun. My friend does not like maths. What is your favourite subject? She likes art. She likes music too. We have science today. I like science.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What is your favourite subject?

My favourite subject is English. I like it very much.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Do you like maths?

Yes, I like maths. It is good.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What subject do you not like?

I do not like history. It is boring.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Why do you like English?

I like English. It is fun and easy.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Does your friend like science?

No, my friend does not like science. She likes art.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Present Simple with 'like' and 'don't like'

We use 'like' to say what we enjoy.

We use 'don't like' to say what we do not enjoy.

Add '-s' after 'like' for he, she, it.

FORMS

FormExample
I / you / we / they + likeI like maths.
he / she / it + likesShe likes art.
I / you / we / they + don't likeWe don't like tests.
he / she / it + doesn't likeHe doesn't like homework.
Do + I / you / we / they + like?Do you like science?
Does + he / she / it + like?Does Tom like English?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ He like music.

✓ He likes music.

Add -s for he/she/it.

✗ I doesn't like history.

✓ I don't like history.

Use 'don't' with I/you/we/they.

✗ She don't like PE.

✓ She doesn't like PE.

Use 'doesn't' with he/she/it.
