lessons.titleKm: Likes, Dislikes, and Favourite Subjects — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)
lessons.titleEn: Likes, Dislikes, and Favourite Subjects — Guided Writing Task 1 (20–30 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about your favourite subject. Say what it is and why you like it. (20–30 words)

  • Start with 'My favourite subject is...'
  • Use 'I like it because...'
  • Keep sentences very short and simple

Key structures: My favourite... is..., I like... because...

Model
My favourite subject is English. I like it because it is fun. We read books and write stories. The teacher is very nice.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-30 words that start with 'My favourite subject is...' and give a reason with 'I like it because...'.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: subject, favourite, like, fun, easy, interesting, English, math, art, teacher. Structures: My favourite subject is...; I like it because...; It is fun / easy / interesting..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Names one school subject as the favourite and gives a clear reason (for example 'because it is fun'), and adds a small detail such as what they do in class or who the teacher is. Good: Names the favourite subject and gives a reason, but the reason is very thin (only 'good') or there is no extra detail. Developing: Names a subject but gives no reason, or the reason does not connect (for example 'I like math. I go school.'). Beginning: No favourite subject is named, or the text is about something else.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses both 'My favourite subject is...' and 'I like it because...' correctly, and at least one week adjective such as fun, easy or interesting. Good: Uses one of the two key sentences correctly and one week word, but the other is missing or changed (for example 'My favourite is art'). Developing: Uses the structures only partly, such as 'I like because fun', or uses only general words like 'good'. Beginning: Neither key sentence appears and no subject or opinion words from the week are used.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Short sentences are correct, including 'it is' and 'I like', with no more than one or two small slips such as a missing 's' or article. Good: The meaning is clear, but there are some errors like 'It fun' (missing is), 'I am like English' or 'I like it because is easy'. Developing: Many errors in each sentence (missing verbs, wrong word order), so the reader must guess some meaning. Beginning: Almost every sentence has errors and the main idea cannot be understood.
- Clarity & organisation (10 points). Excellent: Subject first, then reason, in very short sentences that are easy to read, with capital letters and full stops mostly used. Good: Subject and reason are in the right order and the text is easy to follow. Developing: The reason comes before the subject or sentences run together, so the order is confusing. Beginning: Ideas are scattered and the text is hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Favourite subject and a clear 'because' reason in own words, both key structures used, 20-30 words, very few slips. | 75-89: Subject and reason are clear; one key structure is missing or a few small errors. | 60-74: Subject is named but the reason is weak or unclear; several grammar errors. | 40-59: Very short, no reason, or hard to understand; little week language. | 0-39: Off task, copied instructions, or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (for example 'favorite' or 'maths'); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing or extra articles when meaning is clear; capital letters and punctuation; any school subject or any sensible reason; missing 's' on 'likes' if the learner writes 'my friend' (this task is about 'I').
LENGTH: Aim for 20-30 words. Accept about 17-35 words with no penalty. Under 17 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subject (English, math, science, history, art, music) and any simple reason are fine, e.g. 'My favourite subject is history. I like it because it is interesting.' The model's extra lines about books and the teacher are not required. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions, unrelated text or text in Khmer only: score 0-20 and ask the learner to write again. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking the learner to use their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the subject and reason the learner chose, quoting their words (for example 'I like it because it is fun' is a clear reason). 2) Fix: Give one correction with an example, such as: 'Write "It is fun", not "It fun". Example: I like art because it is fun.' 3) Next step: Add one more short sentence next time about what you do in your favourite class.

lessons.titleKm: Likes, Dislikes, and Favourite Subjects — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)
lessons.titleEn: Likes, Dislikes, and Favourite Subjects — Guided Writing Task 2 (30–45 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about subjects you like and subjects you do not like. Give two examples of each. (30–45 words)

  • Use 'I like...' and 'I do not like...'
  • Say why for each subject
  • Write one sentence for each subject

Key structures: I like... because..., I do not like... because..., and, but

Model
I like English and art. English is fun and easy. Art is good because I can draw. I do not like math and science. Math is hard for me. Science has many long words. I am not good at it.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 30-45 words about two subjects you like and two you do not like, with a reason for each.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: like, don't like, hate, love, easy, hard, boring, interesting, science, history. Structures: I like... because...; I do not like... because...; joining ideas with 'and' / 'but'.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Gives two subjects they like and two they do not like, with a reason for each of the four, one short sentence per subject. Good: Gives two liked and two disliked subjects, but one or two reasons are missing or only 'good' / 'bad'. Developing: Gives only one liked and one disliked subject, or most subjects have no reason. Beginning: Writes about only likes or only dislikes, or does not answer the task.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I like...' and 'I do not / don't like...' with subject names, and reason words such as easy, hard, boring, interesting or fun; may join ideas with 'and' or 'but'. Good: Uses both like and don't like correctly, but reasons use only simple words like 'good' or 'bad', or 'because' is missing. Developing: Uses 'like' correctly but writes the negative form wrongly or avoids it (for example 'I no like math'). Beginning: Does not use like / don't like, or uses unrelated vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Negatives are correct ('I do not like math') and 'it is' is used correctly; no more than two small slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but there are errors like 'I not like math', 'I don't likes science' or 'Math is hards'. Developing: Frequent errors with negatives and missing is/are make several sentences unclear. Beginning: Errors in almost every sentence; the reader cannot tell what the learner likes.
- Clarity & organisation (10 points). Excellent: Likes are grouped together, then dislikes, with one clear sentence per subject and 'but' or 'and' used well. Good: Likes and dislikes are mostly separated and easy to follow. Developing: Likes and dislikes are mixed, so the reader cannot see which are which. Beginning: No clear order; hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two likes and two dislikes, each with a clear reason, correct negatives, 30-45 words. | 75-89: Four subjects given; one or two reasons missing or a few small errors. | 60-74: Fewer than four subjects or several reasons missing; negatives sometimes wrong. | 40-59: Only one side (likes or dislikes) or very short; hard to understand. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'don't' or 'do not' (both are fine); missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; choosing any subjects, including less common ones.
LENGTH: Aim for 30-45 words. Accept about 26-52 words without penalty. Under 26 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Learners may use 'love' or 'hate' instead of 'like' and 'do not like', and may choose any reasons (hard, boring, too long, teacher is strict). One sentence with 'and' for two subjects is fine if both have reasons. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear liked or disliked subject with its reason, quoting the learner (for example 'Math is hard for me'). 2) Fix: Correct one negative or missing-verb error with an example, such as: 'Write "I do not like science", not "I no like science". Example: I do not like history because it is boring.' 3) Next step: Check that each of your four subjects has its own reason before you send.

lessons.titleKm: Likes, Dislikes, and Favourite Subjects — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Likes, Dislikes, and Favourite Subjects — Guided Writing Task 3 (45–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about your best friend's favourite subject. Say what subject they like, why they like it, and what they do in class. (45–60 words)

  • Start with your friend's name
  • Use 'He likes...' or 'She likes...'
  • Write about what happens in the class

Key structures: My friend... likes..., He/She likes it because..., In class, he/she...

Model
My best friend is Anna. Her favourite subject is music. She likes it very much. Music is fun for her. In class, she plays the piano. She sings songs too. The teacher says Anna is very good. I like music too but Anna is better than me.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 45-60 words about a best friend: name, favourite subject, why he or she likes it, and what he or she does in class.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: favourite, subject, likes, loves, fun, interesting, class, teacher, study, learn. Structures: My friend... likes...; He / She likes it because...; In class, he / she....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Starts with the friend's name, names the friend's favourite subject, gives a reason, and says two or more things the friend does in class (for example 'she plays the piano and sings'). Good: Gives the friend's name, subject and a reason, but only one thing or none about what the friend does in class. Developing: Names the friend and a subject but no reason, or writes mostly about the learner's own likes instead of the friend's. Beginning: Does not write about a friend, or the text does not answer the task.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'He/She likes...', 'He/She likes it because...' and 'In class, he/she...' correctly, with subject names and an adjective such as fun or interesting. Good: Uses 'likes' and one other key phrase correctly, but 'In class, he/she...' or the reason is missing. Developing: Uses key phrases only partly, or keeps 'I like' instead of changing to he/she. Beginning: None of the key structures appear.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is used well ('she likes', 'he plays'), with at most two small slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but the -s is sometimes missing ('She like music', 'He play football') or he/she is mixed up. Developing: Missing -s, he/she confusion and missing verbs in most sentences, but some meaning is clear. Beginning: Errors throughout; the reader cannot follow the description.
- Clarity & organisation (10 points). Excellent: Moves clearly from friend's name to subject, to reason, to class activities, with 'she/he' linking sentences. Good: Mostly in a sensible order and easy to follow. Developing: Ideas jump between the learner and the friend, which is confusing. Beginning: No clear order; hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Friend's name, subject, reason and class actions all clear; he/she -s mostly correct; 45-60 words. | 75-89: All parts present but thin, or a few third-person errors. | 60-74: Friend and subject given but reason or class activity missing; several -s errors. | 40-59: Short, mostly about the learner, or hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; a real or imagined friend; using the friend's name instead of he/she in every sentence.
LENGTH: Aim for 45-60 words. Accept about 40-70 words without penalty. Under 40 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any friend, subject and class activities are fine (for example 'In class, he draws pictures and shows the teacher'). A final sentence comparing with the learner's own liking, as in the model, is optional. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the friend's details the learner chose, quoting their words (for example 'She sings songs in music class'). 2) Fix: Correct one third-person error with an example, such as: 'Write "She likes music", not "She like music". Example: In class, he plays football and helps his friends.' 3) Next step: Read your text once and check every he/she sentence for -s.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write about your likes and dislikes at school. What subjects do you like? What subjects don't you like? Why? (20–35 words)

  • Say your favourite subject.
  • Say why you like it.
  • Say one subject you don't like.
Model
I like English. It is fun. I also like art. I draw pictures. I don't like math. It is difficult. My favourite subject is English. I am happy in English class.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words that give your favourite subject and why you like it, and name one subject you do not like.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: favourite, like, don't like, fun, difficult, boring, art, math, English, happy. Structures: My favourite subject is...; I like it. It is fun.; I don't like... It is difficult..
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: States a favourite subject, says why they like it, and names one subject they do not like (with a reason), all in a short connected paragraph.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My favourite subject is...', 'I like...' and 'I don't like...' correctly, with adjectives such as fun, easy, difficult or boring.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Simple present sentences are accurate ('It is fun', 'I don't like math'), with one or two small slips at most.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Likes come first, then the dislike, with the ideas in a sensible order, and an optional closing sentence.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; 'math' or 'maths'; 'do not' versus 'don't'.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-35 words. Accept about 17-42 words without penalty. Under 17 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subjects and reasons are fine. Learners may skip 'My favourite subject is' if they clearly say 'I like English best' or similar, as long as one subject is clearly the favourite. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.

contentRef.text:
CHAPTER II · WEEK 12

Chapter 2 Review: Lessons and Learning

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify key points about different teaching methods in a simple classroom discussion. L2 Understand
  • Use present simple tense to describe lessons and learning activities accurately. L3 Apply
  • Describe a favorite lesson from school using present simple tense and basic adjectives. L3 Apply
  • Recognize main ideas in short texts about effective teaching and student learning experiences. L3 Apply
  • Write a simple paragraph summarizing what makes a good lesson for learners. L3 Apply
  • Compare own learning preferences with classmates to recognize different ways people learn best. L4 Analyze · HOTS

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

lesson noun

Phonetic: LES-sun

Meaning: a time when a teacher teaches students

Khmer: មេរៀន

Example: The English lesson is at 9 o'clock.

learn verb

Phonetic: LURN

Meaning: to get new knowledge or skills

Khmer: រៀន

Example: I learn English every day.

teacher noun

Phonetic: TEE-chur

Meaning: a person who teaches students

Khmer: គ្រូ

Example: My teacher is very kind.

student noun

Phonetic: STOO-dent

Meaning: a person who learns at school

Khmer: សិស្ស

Example: She is a good student.

class noun

Phonetic: KLASS

Meaning: a group of students learning together

Khmer: ថ្នាក់

Example: There are twenty students in my class.

book noun

Phonetic: BOOK

Meaning: pages with words that you read

Khmer: សៀវភៅ

Example: I read my English book every night.

study verb

Phonetic: STUH-dee

Meaning: to spend time learning something

Khmer: សិក្សា

Example: We study math on Monday.

write verb

Phonetic: RITE

Meaning: to make words with a pen

Khmer: សរសេរ

Example: Please write your name here.

read verb

Phonetic: REED

Meaning: to look at words and understand them

Khmer: អាន

Example: I can read this sentence.

homework noun

Phonetic: HOME-wurk

Meaning: work students do at home after school

Khmer: កិច្ចការផ្ទះ

Example: I do my homework every evening.

test noun

Phonetic: TEST

Meaning: questions to see what students know

Khmer: ការប្រឡង

Example: We have a test on Friday.

classroom noun

Phonetic: KLASS-room

Meaning: a room where students have lessons

Khmer: ថ្នាក់រៀន

Example: Our classroom is very clean.

easy adjective

Phonetic: EE-zee

Meaning: not hard or difficult

Khmer: ងាយស្រួល

Example: This lesson is very easy.

hard adjective

Phonetic: HARD

Meaning: difficult and not easy

Khmer: ពិបាក

Example: Math is hard for me.

question noun

Phonetic: KWES-chun

Meaning: something you ask when you want to know

Khmer: សំណួរ

Example: I have a question for the teacher.

answer noun

Phonetic: AN-sur

Meaning: words you give to a question

Khmer: ចម្លើយ

Example: The answer is on page five.

understand verb

Phonetic: un-der-STAND

Meaning: to know what something means

Khmer: យល់

Example: Do you understand this word?

practice verb

Phonetic: PRAK-tiss

Meaning: to do something many times to learn

Khmer: ហ្វឹកហាត់

Example: I practice English every day.

repeat verb

Phonetic: ree-PEET

Meaning: to say or do something again

Khmer: និយាយឡើងវិញ

Example: Please repeat the sentence.

help verb

Phonetic: HELP

Meaning: to make something easier

Khmer: ជួយ

Example: The teacher can help

MINI STORY

Anna is a new student. She is in class 1A. Her teacher is Mr. Lee. He is a good teacher.

Every day Anna has English lessons. The classroom is big and clean. She sits with her friend Tom. They learn many new words. They read books. They write in their notebooks. Sometimes the lesson is easy. Sometimes it is hard.

Anna does her homework every evening. She studies English for one hour. She practices speaking English. When she has a question, she asks the teacher. Mr. Lee always helps her. Anna understands English better now. Next week they have a test. Anna is ready. She can answer all the questions.

nodes.text: GAP-FILL

nodes.question: Q1. The English ___ is at 9 o'clock.
nodes.explanation: → A 'lesson' is a class that starts at a set time, like nine o'clock.

nodes.question: Q2. I ___ English every day.
nodes.explanation: → We 'learn' English when we get better at it every day.

nodes.question: Q3. My ___ is very kind.
nodes.explanation: → A 'teacher' teaches students, and a teacher can be kind.

nodes.question: Q4. She is not a teacher. She is a good ___.
nodes.explanation: → A 'student' goes to school to learn. She is not a teacher.

nodes.question: Q5. There are twenty students in my ___.
nodes.explanation: → A 'class' is a group of students. There are twenty in it.

nodes.question: Q6. I read my English ___ every night. It has many pages.
nodes.explanation: → A 'book' has many pages that we read.

nodes.question: Q7. We ___ math on Monday.
nodes.explanation: → We 'study' a subject like math at school.

nodes.question: Q8. Please ___ your name here.
nodes.explanation: → We 'write' our name with a pen.

nodes.question: Q9. I can ___ this sentence.
nodes.explanation: → We 'read' a sentence with our eyes.

nodes.question: Q10. I do my ___ every evening.
nodes.explanation: → We do our 'homework' at home in the evening.

nodes.question: Q11. We have a ___ on Friday. We write the answers on paper.
nodes.explanation: → A 'test' is when we write answers on paper to show what we know.

nodes.question: Q12. Our ___ is very clean.
nodes.explanation: → A 'classroom' is a room, so it can be clean.

nodes.question: Q13. This lesson is very ___. I know all the answers.
nodes.explanation: → 'Easy' means not hard. We know all the answers.

nodes.question: Q14. Math is ___ for me. I do not understand it.
nodes.explanation: → 'Hard' means not easy. We do not understand it.

nodes.question: Q15. I have a ___ for the teacher.
nodes.explanation: → A 'question' asks something. We ask the teacher.

nodes.question: Q16. The ___ to question three is on page five.
nodes.explanation: → An 'answer' replies to a question, like question three.

nodes.question: Q17. Do you ___ this word?
nodes.explanation: → We 'understand' a word when we know its meaning.

nodes.question: Q18. I ___ English with my friends.
nodes.explanation: → We 'speak' English when we talk with friends.

nodes.question: Q19. Please ___ the sentence after me.
nodes.explanation: → 'Repeat' means to say it again after the teacher.

nodes.question: Q20. The teacher can ___ you with your homework.
nodes.explanation: → A teacher can 'help' you with your homework.

nodes.text: VOCABULARY CHALLENGE

nodes.question: learn — study
nodes.explanation: → 'learn' and 'study' both mean to get knowledge, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: easy — difficult
nodes.explanation: → 'easy' and 'difficult' have opposite meanings: easy is not hard, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: teacher — teach
nodes.explanation: → 'Teacher' comes from 'teach', so they are in the same word family.

nodes.question: book — mountain
nodes.explanation: → 'book' and 'mountain' are about very different things, so they are unrelated.

nodes.question: hard — challenging
nodes.explanation: → 'hard' and 'challenging' both mean not easy, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: easy — hard
nodes.explanation: → 'Easy' and 'hard' have opposite meanings, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: practice — practical
nodes.explanation: → 'practice' and 'practical' share the root 'practice', so they are a word family.

nodes.question: classroom — ocean
nodes.explanation: → 'classroom' and 'ocean' belong to different ideas, so they are unrelated.

nodes.question: help — assist
nodes.explanation: → 'help' and 'assist' both mean to give support to someone, so they are synonyms.

nodes.question: write — erase
nodes.explanation: → 'write' and 'erase' have opposite meanings: write puts words on paper, erase takes them off, so they are antonyms.

nodes.question: student — study
nodes.explanation: → 'student' and 'study' share the root 'study', so they are a word family.

nodes.question: homework — banana
nodes.explanation: → 'Homework' is school work and 'banana' is a fruit, so they are unrelated.

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

My First Lesson

Text type: Narrative
My name is Anna. I am a teacher. Today is my first day. I am happy. I am nervous too.

I go to the classroom. I see ten students. They are young. They smile at me. I smile back. I say hello. They say hello too.

I teach numbers today. We count to ten. The students are good. They learn fast. I like teaching. Today is a good day.

questions.prompt: Q1. What is the story about?

options.text: B. Anna's first day as a teacher
C. Anna's last day at school

questions.explanation: → The story is mostly about Anna's first day as a teacher: 'Today is my first day.'

questions.prompt: Q2. How many students does Anna see?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'I see ten students.'

questions.prompt: Q3. What does Anna teach first?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'I teach numbers today.'

questions.prompt: Q4. How does Anna feel today?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'I am happy. I am nervous too.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'nervous' mean?
questions.explanation: → Anna is happy and nervous on her first day, so nervous means a little worried.

contentRef.text:
Our Classroom

Text type: Description
Our classroom is big. It is clean. It has white walls. There are six windows. The windows are open. We have fresh air.

There are twenty desks in the room. The desks are blue. There is one big desk. That is the teacher's desk. We have a board too. The board is green.

We like our classroom. It is a good place. We learn here every day. We have lessons here. We are happy students.

questions.prompt: Q1. What is this text about?
questions.explanation: → The text is mostly a description of a classroom: its walls, windows, desks and board.

questions.prompt: Q2. What color are the desks?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'The desks are blue.'

questions.prompt: Q3. How many windows are there?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'There are six windows.'

questions.prompt: Q4. Is the classroom small or big?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'Our classroom is big.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'fresh' mean?
questions.explanation: → The windows are open and 'we have fresh air', so fresh means clean and nice.

contentRef.text:
Message from Teacher

Text type: Notice

To: All Students
From: Mr. Brown

Hello students! We have a test next week. The test is on Monday. It is about Chapter 2.

Please study at home. Read your book. Do the exercises. Learn the new words. Come to class early. Bring a pen.

Do you have questions? See me after class today. I can help you. Good luck with your studies!

Mr. Brown

questions.prompt: Q1. What is this message about?
questions.explanation: → The message says 'We have a test next week.'

questions.prompt: Q2. When is the test?

options.text: A. The test is on Sunday
B. The test is on Monday
C. The test is on Friday
D. The test is on Tuesday

questions.explanation: → The text says 'The test is on Monday.'

questions.prompt: Q3. What should students bring?

options.text: B. Students should bring a pen
D. Students should bring a bag

questions.explanation: → The text says 'Bring a pen.'

questions.prompt: Q4. Who wrote this message?

options.text: D. The head teacher wrote it

questions.explanation: → The message says 'From: Mr. Brown'.

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'study' mean?
questions.explanation: → 'Please study at home. Read your book.' So study means to learn and read.

contentRef.text:
How to Be a Good Student

Text type: Informational
Do you want to learn well? Here are some tips. They are easy.

First, listen to your teacher. Look at the board. Write notes. Ask questions when you don't understand. Second, do your homework every day. Practice makes you better. Read your books at home.

Third, be on time for class. Come early. Don't be late. Bring your book and pen. Be ready to learn. These tips help you. You can be a good student!

questions.prompt: Q1. What is this text about?
questions.explanation: → The text is mostly about tips to learn well: 'Here are some tips.'

questions.prompt: Q2. What should you do first?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'First, listen to your teacher.'

questions.prompt: Q3. When should you do homework?

options.text: A. Do homework once a week
C. Do homework on Sundays only

questions.explanation: → The text says 'do your homework every day.'

questions.prompt: Q4. Should you be late for class?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'Come early. Don't be late.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'on time' mean?
questions.explanation: → 'Be on time... Come early. Don't be late' means not late and not early.

contentRef.text:
Two Ways to Learn

Text type: Comparison
Sara likes to study alone. She sits at home. She reads her book. It is quiet. She can think well. She learns slowly. She understands everything.

Tom likes to study with friends. They sit together. They talk about lessons. They help each other. It is noisy. But Tom learns fast. He has fun too.

Both ways are good. Sara and Tom are both good students. They learn in different ways. What about you? How do you like to learn?

questions.prompt: Q1. What is this text comparing?
questions.explanation: → The text compares how Sara and Tom learn: 'They learn in different ways.'

questions.prompt: Q2. How does Sara like to study?
questions.explanation: → The text says 'Sara likes to study alone. She sits at home.'

questions.prompt: Q3. Who studies with friends?

options.text: B. The teacher studies with friends

questions.explanation: → The text says 'Tom likes to study with friends.'

questions.prompt: Q4. Are both ways good?

options.text: A. No, only one way is good
C. Yes, both ways are good

questions.explanation: → The text says 'Both ways are good.'

questions.prompt: Q5. What does 'alone' mean?
questions.explanation: → Sara 'likes to study alone' and it is quiet, so alone means by yourself.

contentRef.text:
Grammar Practice

Present Simple

We use present simple for things we do every day or every week.

We also use it for facts and things that are always true.

FORMS

FormExample
I / you / we / they + verbI study English.
he / she / it + verb + s/esShe learns new words.
Negative: subject + do not / does not + verbWe do not learn on Sunday.
Question: Do / Does + subject + verb?Do you study at home?
Negative short form: don't / doesn'tHe doesn't teach today.
Question answer: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.Does she teach? Yes, she does.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ He study every day.

✓ He studies every day.

Add -s or -es for he, she, it.

✗ She don't read books.

✓ She doesn't read books.

Use doesn't (not don't) with he, she, it.

✗ Do she learn English?

✓ Does she learn English?

Use does (not do) in questions with he, she, it.

nodes.text: EXERCISES

nodes.question: Q1. I ___ English every Monday.
nodes.explanation: → I goes with the base verb in present simple.

nodes.question: Q2. She ___ her lessons at home every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit, so we use present simple. 'She' takes 'does'.

nodes.question: Q3. We ___ to school every day.
nodes.explanation: → We takes the base verb in present simple.

nodes.question: Q4. The teacher ___ in the classroom every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit. The teacher is one person, so we add -s.

nodes.question: Q5. Do you ___ your homework at home?
nodes.explanation: → After Do in a question, we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q6. He ___ not like tests.
nodes.explanation: → He needs does before not in present simple negative.

nodes.question: Q7. They ___ books in the library.
nodes.explanation: → They takes the base verb in present simple.

nodes.question: Q8. My teacher ___ me new words.
nodes.explanation: → My teacher is one person, so we add -es.

nodes.question: Q9. Does she ___ in this class?
nodes.explanation: → After Does in a question, we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q10. I ___ not understand this lesson.
nodes.explanation: → I needs do before not in present simple negative.

nodes.question: Q11. The students ___ questions in class every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit. 'The students' is plural, so we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q12. She ___ her book every evening.
nodes.explanation: → She is one person, so we add -s to the verb.

nodes.question: Q13. We ___ not study on Saturday.
nodes.explanation: → We needs do before not in present simple negative.

nodes.question: Q14. Do they ___ English on Tuesday?
nodes.explanation: → After Do in a question, we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q15. The lesson ___ at nine o'clock every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit. The lesson is one thing, so we add -s.

nodes.question: Q16. My friend ___ French at school every week.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every week' shows a habit. My friend is one person, so we add -s.

nodes.question: Q17. I ___ my teacher every day.
nodes.explanation: → I takes the base verb in present simple.

nodes.question: Q18. Does your class ___ at ten?
nodes.explanation: → After Does in a question, we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q19. He ___ not write in his notebook.
nodes.explanation: → He needs does before not in present simple negative.

nodes.question: Q20. You ___ good work in class every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit, and 'you' takes the base verb in present simple.

nodes.question: Q21. The children ___ in the classroom every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit. 'The children' is plural, so we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q22. She ___ her hand when she knows.
nodes.explanation: → She is one person, so we add -s to the verb.

nodes.question: Q23. Do you ___ with a pen?
nodes.explanation: → After Do in a question, we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q24. We ___ our homework after school every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit, and 'we' takes the base verb in present simple.

nodes.question: Q25. The school ___ at half past three every day.
nodes.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit. The school is one thing, so we add -es.

nodes.question: Q26. They ___ not listen in class.
nodes.explanation: → They needs do before not in present simple negative.

nodes.question: Q27. Does he ___ his notebook to class?
nodes.explanation: → After Does in a question, we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q28. My classmates ___ hard every week.
nodes.explanation: → My classmates is plural, so we use the base verb.

nodes.question: Q29. It ___ not help me learn.
nodes.explanation: → It needs does before not in present simple negative.

nodes.question: Q30. I ___ to my teacher every day.
nodes.explanation: → I takes the base verb in present simple.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write about your favorite lesson at school. Say what you learn and why you like it. (20–35 words)

  • What is your favorite lesson?
  • What do you do in the lesson?
  • Why do you like it?
Model
My favorite lesson is English. I learn new words. I read books. I write sentences. The teacher is very good. I like English a lot. It is fun.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 20-35 words about your favorite lesson at school: what the lesson is, what you do in it, and why you like it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson, learn, teacher, class, book, read, write, study, easy, hard. Structures: My favorite lesson is...; I read / write / learn...; I like it because...; The teacher is... / It is fun..
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names a favorite lesson, says at least two things they do in it (for example 'I read books. I write sentences.'), and gives a reason for liking it.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My favorite lesson is...' plus classroom verbs such as read, write, learn, study and words like book, teacher, easy or fun, correctly in context.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Present simple sentences are mostly correct ('I read books', 'The teacher is good'), with one or two small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Lesson first, then activities, then the reason, in a short paragraph that flows well.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (including 'favorite' or 'favourite'); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; a past-tense answer (for example 'I learned new words') if it is clear; choosing any subject or lesson, not just English.
LENGTH: Aim for 20-35 words. Accept about 17-42 words without penalty. Under 17 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any lesson (math, science, art, English) and any activities are fine, in present or simple past. The model's line about the teacher is optional. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Age groups in childhood

Children are grouped by age into stages. Each stage has a special name in English.

Example:A teenager needs different activities than a toddler does.
Connection:Teachers use these words when they plan lessons for different age groups.
  • 2. Physical appearance

Physical appearance means how someone looks. We describe hair, eyes, height, and skin.

Example:The child has blonde hair and freckles on her face.
Connection:Teachers write reports describing each child's physical features for school records.
  • 3. Emotions and feelings

Emotions are feelings like happy, sad, or angry. Children show emotions in their faces and actions.

Example:The shy child does not want to speak in class.
Connection:Teachers describe children's feelings when they talk to parents about classroom behaviour.
  • 4. Adjective order

When we use many adjectives, opinion words come before fact words. Adjectives go before the noun.

Example:She is a happy young girl with curly hair.
Connection:Education books and reports use correct adjective order to describe children clearly.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
We say adjective plus noun, like 'tall boy' in English.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. toddler — A toddler is a young child who is learning to walk.
  2. teenager — A teenager is a young person between 13 and 19 years old.
  3. curly — Curly hair has many curves and is not straight.
  4. blonde — Blonde hair is light yellow in color.
  5. freckles — Freckles are small brown spots on the skin.
  6. chubby — Chubby means slightly fat in a cute way.
  7. shy — Shy means nervous and uncomfortable with other people.
  8. brave — Brave means not afraid to do difficult or dangerous things.
  9. excited — Excited means very happy and full of energy.
  10. upset — Upset means unhappy or worried about something.
  11. smile — To smile means to make a happy expression with your mouth.
  12. cry — To cry means to have tears coming from your eyes.
  13. giggle — To giggle means to laugh in a quiet silly way.
  14. playful — Playful means liking to play and have fun.
  15. curious — Curious means wanting to know about everything.
  16. tired — Tired means needing rest or sleep.
  17. tall — Tall means having a greater height than others.
  18. short — Short means not tall in height.
  19. friendly — Friendly means kind and nice to other people.
  20. energetic — Energetic means having a lot of energy and activity.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words that describe children's age, looks, and feelings.
Reading
Read short texts about children and find words that describe them.
Listening
Listen to descriptions of children and notice the adjectives used.
Speaking
Say sentences describing a child's age, appearance, and feelings aloud.
Grammar
Practice putting adjectives in the correct order before nouns in descriptions.
Writing
Write simple sentences that describe children using adjectives and present tense.
Lesson Test
The test checks your understanding of describing children; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In English, we can use up to seven adjectives before one noun! But most teachers use only two or three adjectives when they describe children in reports.

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). Unit 8 teaches adjectives for describing people's appearance and feelings clearly. Basic English for Teachers — Oxford University Press (2015). Chapter 3 shows how teachers describe students in simple English sentences.

▶ Describing People - Appearance and Personality — BBC Learning English ▶ Adjective Order in English — English with Lucy

MINI STORY

My New Friend

Today I met a new friend at the park. Her name is Lucy. She is seven years old. Lucy has beautiful blonde hair. It is long and curly. She also has freckles on her nose. Lucy is quite tall for her age. She wears a big smile on her face.

Lucy is very friendly and playful. We run and jump together. She is so energetic! Lucy is also very curious. She asks me many questions about my family. We giggle when we play hide and seek. I am so excited to have a new friend.

Later, Lucy's little brother comes to the park. He is a toddler with chubby cheeks. He is a bit shy at first. But soon he is brave and plays with us too. When it is time to go home, we are all very tired. Lucy says goodbye with a big smile.

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

My Little Sister Emma

Text type: Narrative
My sister Emma is seven years old. She is very small for her age. She has long brown hair and big green eyes. Her hair is always messy in the morning. She loves wearing her red dress every day.

Emma is usually a happy child. She smiles and laughs a lot. But sometimes she gets angry when I play with her toys. Last Tuesday, she was very sad. Our cat was sick. Emma cried for two hours. She loves animals very

much.

Today Emma is excited because it is her birthday tomorrow. She is talking all the time about her party. She wants a big cake with pink flowers. Emma is jumping around the house. She cannot sit still for one minute. I think she is a sweet little girl.

The Children in My Class

Text type: Description
There are fifteen children in my English class. They are all different ages. The youngest student is only nine years old. His name is Tom. The oldest student is thirteen. Her name is Sarah. Most children are ten or eleven years old.

How Children Show Their Feelings

Text type: Informational
Children show their feelings in many different ways. Young children cannot always use words. They show feelings with their face and body. A happy child usually smiles. Their eyes look bright. They often laugh and play.

When children feel sad, they may cry. Their face looks down. Sad children are often very quiet. They do not want to play or talk. Angry children sometimes shout or stamp their feet. Their face becomes red. Scared children hide behind their parents. They hold hands very tight.

Teachers and parents can help children with feelings. They can ask simple questions like 'How do you feel today?' They can teach children words for feelings. Children need to learn feeling words like happy, sad, angry, and scared. This helps them talk about feelings better.

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

The little girl is five years old and has long brown hair. My brother is ten and he feels happy today.

The baby has blue eyes and very short black hair. She looks sad because her friend is not at school. The boy is tall for his age and has green eyes.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Can you describe what a child in your family looks like?

My little sister is six years old. She has short black hair and brown eyes. She is very short and has a small nose.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. How can you tell when a child is feeling happy?

A happy child usually smiles a lot. They laugh and play with their friends. Their eyes look bright and they talk more.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What does a tired child look like?

A tired child looks very sleepy. Their eyes are small and red. They move slowly and want to sit down.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Can you describe a baby you know?

My baby cousin is one year old. She has no hair yet and big brown eyes. She is very small and cute.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. How do children show they are angry or upset?

Angry children often cry or shout loudly. Their face becomes red and they close their hands. Some children do not want to talk.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Adjective Order and Placement

Adjectives describe nouns.

In English, adjectives go BEFORE the noun.

When we use two or more adjectives, opinion words (nice, happy) usually come before fact words (young, tall, blue).

FORMS

FormExample
one adjective + nounShe is a happy child.
opinion adjective + fact adjective + nounHe is a cute little boy.
subject + be + adjectiveThe girl is sad.
subject + look/feel + adjectiveThe baby looks tired.
subject + have + adjective + nounThey have brown eyes.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ She is a child happy.

✓ She is a happy child.

Adjectives go BEFORE the noun in English.

✗ He is a boy tall young.

✓ He is a tall young boy.

Opinion (tall) comes before age (young) before the noun.

✗ The children is excited.

✓ The children are excited.

Use 'are' with plural nouns like 'children'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe a child in your family or a friend's child. Include their age and how they look. (40–60 words)

  • Start with the child's name and age
  • Describe their hair colour and eye colour
  • Add one more thing about how they look

Key structures: He/She is... years old, He/She has... hair and... eyes

Model
My cousin Tom is six years old. He has short black hair and brown eyes. Tom is quite tall for his age. He always wears a red jacket. Tom has a big smile on his face. He looks very happy most of the time.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words describing a child you know: name and age, hair colour, eye colour, and one more thing about how he or she looks.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: curly, blonde, freckles, tall, short, chubby, toddler, teenager, smile, friendly. Structures: He / She is... years old.; He / She has... hair and... eyes.; He / She is tall / short.; He / She has freckles..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Starts with the child's name and age, gives hair colour and eye colour, and adds one more detail about looks (height, freckles, clothes or smile). Good: Gives name, age, and hair and eye colour, but the extra look detail is missing or very general ('he is nice'). Developing: Gives the name and age but describes only hair or only eyes, or mixes in many things that are not looks. Beginning: Does not describe a child's appearance, or leaves out the age and the hair and eyes.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'is... years old' and 'has... hair and... eyes' correctly, with at least two appearance words such as curly, blonde, tall, short, freckles or chubby. Good: Uses both key sentences, but only basic words (black, long, big) and no new appearance words. Developing: Uses one key sentence partly, such as 'He have black hair' or 'He is six year', and few week words. Beginning: Neither key sentence appears; no appearance vocabulary from the week.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'has' for hair and eyes, 'is' for age and height, and 'years' correctly, with at most two small slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but errors such as 'He have hair', 'She is six year old' or 'He has tall' appear. Developing: Frequent confusion of is/has and missing verbs ('She black hair'), so some lines are unclear. Beginning: Errors throughout; the child cannot be pictured.
- Clarity & organisation (10 points). Excellent: Name and age first, then hair and eyes, then the extra detail, with he/she used to link sentences. Good: Mostly in a sensible order and easy to read. Developing: Details are mixed up or the name is repeated in every sentence. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Name, age, hair, eyes and an extra look detail, with is/has used correctly; 40-60 words. | 75-89: All required details are present; thin vocabulary or a few is/has errors. | 60-74: One required detail missing (age, hair or eyes); several errors. | 40-59: Very short or mostly unrelated to looks; hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; a real or imagined child; 'colour' or 'color'.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words. Accept about 35-70 words without penalty. Under 35 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any child (a niece, student or neighbour) and any appearance details are fine. The model's lines about the red jacket and the smile are examples only. Black hair and brown eyes are fine; new words like curly or freckles are a bonus. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear picture of the child, quoting the learner (for example 'She has curly black hair and brown eyes'). 2) Fix: Correct one is/has error with an example, such as: 'Write "He has black hair", not "He is black hair". Example: Sophea is seven years old. She has long hair.' 3) Next step: Add one new word from this week, such as freckles or curly, in your next description.

WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about a child's feelings during their first day at school. Explain how the child feels and why. (60–80 words)

  • Say how the child feels at the beginning
  • Explain why the child feels this way
  • Describe how their feelings change during the day

Key structures: The child feels... because..., At first... but then..., When... he/she...

Model
Lily is five years old. On her first day at school, she feels nervous. She feels this way because everything is new. At first, Lily cries and holds her mother's hand. But then she meets other children in her class. They play games together. After lunch, Lily feels much better. She smiles and talks to her new friends. By the end of the day, Lily feels happy and excited.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words about how a child feels on the first day at school: the feeling at the start, why, and how the feeling changes during the day.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: shy, nervous, upset, excited, happy, cry, smile, giggle, curious, brave. Structures: The child feels... because...; At first... but then...; When..., he / she....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Names the child's feeling at the start, gives a reason with 'because', and describes a clear change later in the day (for example from nervous to happy) with something that causes the change. Good: Gives the starting feeling and a reason, and says the child feels different later, but the cause of the change is missing. Developing: Gives one feeling only, with no reason or no change during the day. Beginning: Does not describe a child's feelings on the first day, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'feels... because...', 'At first... but then...' and 'When...' correctly, with at least two feeling words from the week (nervous, shy, upset, excited, happy) and actions such as cry, smile or giggle. Good: Uses two of the three structures and some feeling words, but mostly basic ones like happy and sad. Developing: Uses one structure partly (for example 'At first he cry but then happy') and few week words. Beginning: No key structures; no feeling vocabulary from the week.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third-person present is mostly correct ('she feels', 'he cries', 'they play'), with at most two small slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but errors like 'She feel nervous', 'He cry' or 'because is new' appear. Developing: Repeated errors in verb forms and missing be-verbs make some lines hard to understand. Beginning: Errors in almost every line; the story cannot be followed.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Tells the day in order (start, reason, change, end) with linking words like at first, then, after lunch. Good: Mostly in time order and easy to follow. Developing: Events are out of order or not linked. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Start feeling, reason and a clear change with a cause, key structures used well; 60-80 words. | 75-89: Feeling, reason and change all present; a missing cause or a few errors. | 60-74: No clear change in feeling or weak reason; several errors. | 40-59: Very short or only one feeling; hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; a real or invented child; mixing present and simple past if the story is still clear.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words. Accept about 52-92 words without penalty. Under 52 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any child, age, feeling and reason are fine (for example missing mother, new teacher). The change can be small, such as shy to happy after playing a game. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the feeling change the learner shows, quoting their words (for example 'At first he is shy, but then he plays with friends'). 2) Fix: Correct one verb-form error with an example, such as: 'Write "She feels nervous", not "She feel nervous". Example: At first Dara cries, but then he smiles.' 3) Next step: Use one more feeling word from this week, such as excited or upset, in your next story.

lessons.titleKm: Describing Children: Age, Looks, and Feelings — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Describing Children: Age, Looks, and Feelings — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Describe two children who look different and have different feelings. Compare them using simple sentences. (80–110 words)

  • Describe the first child's age, looks, and feelings
  • Describe the second child's age, looks, and feelings
  • Use words like 'but' or 'however' to show differences

Key structures: The first child is... but the second child is..., One child has... while the other has..., They both... but...

Model
There are two children in the playground. The first child is a girl called Emma. She is eight years old. Emma has long blonde hair and green eyes. She is very tall. Emma feels happy today because she got a good mark. She is laughing with her friends. The second child is a boy called Jake. He is nine years old. Jake has short red hair and blue eyes. He is quite short. Jake feels sad today. He lost his favourite pen. Jake sits alone and looks down at the ground. Emma and Jake are very different today.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words comparing two children who look different and feel different, giving each child's age, looks and feelings, and using 'but' or 'however' to show the difference.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: tall, short, curly, blonde, freckles, excited, upset, shy, energetic, tired. Structures: The first child is... but the second child is...; One child has... while the other has...; They both... but....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Describes both children fully (age, looks and feelings for each, with a reason for a feeling) and clearly shows at least two differences between them. Good: Both children have age, looks and feelings, but one child has less detail or a difference is not made clear. Developing: Describes one child well but the second only briefly, or gives looks without feelings. Beginning: Describes only one child or does not compare.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'but' or 'however' to contrast, with 'One child has... while the other has...' or similar, and several week words for looks (curly, blonde, freckles, tall, short) and feelings (shy, excited, upset, tired). Good: Uses 'but' correctly at least once and some week words, but does not use 'while' or 'however'. Developing: Writes two separate descriptions with little or no contrast words. Beginning: No contrast structures and little week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Uses is/has/feels with he/she correctly, and keeps the two children's pronouns straight; only a few slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but is/has slips ('He is brown hair') or he/she mix-ups appear. Developing: Many is/has errors, he/she confusion and missing verbs, making the comparison unclear in places. Beginning: Errors throughout; cannot tell which child is which.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: First child, then second child, then a closing comparison, so the reader can easily see who is who. Good: Mostly clear which child is being described. Developing: Details switch between children without warning. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two children each with age, looks, feelings, and clear contrast with 'but' or 'however'; 80-110 words. | 75-89: Both children described; contrast is weak or a few errors. | 60-74: One child much weaker, or no real comparison; several errors. | 40-59: Only one child or very short; hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; any invented children and settings (playground, classroom, home); using 'and' or full stops instead of 'while'.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words. Accept about 70-125 words without penalty. Under 70 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any two children, ages and feelings are fine. Contrast can be shown with but, however, while or 'the other child'. The model's playground scene is only an example. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear contrast the learner wrote, quoting them (for example 'Emma is tall, but Jake is short'). 2) Fix: Fix one is/has or he/she slip with an example, such as: 'Write "He has short red hair", not "He is short red hair". Example: One child has curly hair while the other has straight hair.' 3) Next step: Check that both children have an age, a look and a feeling before you send.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about a child you know. Describe their age, what they look like, and how they feel. (40–60 words)

  • Say how old the child is.
  • Describe their hair and eyes.
  • Say how they feel or what they are like.
Model
My cousin Lisa is seven years old. She is small and slim. She has curly blonde hair and big blue eyes. Lisa is very cheerful and friendly. She smiles a lot and likes to play with other children. Sometimes she feels shy when she meets new people. Lisa loves animals and she is kind to everyone.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about one child you know: how old he or she is, what he or she looks like (hair and eyes), and how he or she feels or what he or she is like.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: curly, blonde, freckles, tall, shy, friendly, playful, curious, cheerful, smile. Structures: He / She is... years old.; He / She has... hair and... eyes.; He / She is shy / friendly / playful.; He / She feels... when....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says the child's age, describes hair and eyes, and says how the child feels or what the child is like, with at least one example (for example 'She smiles a lot').
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'is... years old', 'has... hair and... eyes' and a feeling or personality sentence correctly, with several week words such as curly, shy, friendly, playful or curious.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Present simple with he/she is mostly correct (has, is, smiles, likes); one or two small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Age, looks, then feelings in a short paragraph, with he/she linking the sentences.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; 'colour' or 'color'; describing a child the learner invents.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words. Accept about 35-70 words without penalty. Under 35 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any child, age and details are fine. Learners may describe feelings with 'feels...' or personality with 'is...'. The model's lines about animals and being kind are optional. The model answer is only a reference.
