contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Classroom rules

Classroom rules tell students what they must do or cannot do. They help everyone learn well together.

Example:Students must arrive on time and listen to the teacher.
Connection:Teachers write these rules on posters or say them at the start of class.
  • 2. Giving instructions

Teachers give instructions to tell students what to do. They use clear and simple words.

Example:Please raise your hand if you have a question.
Connection:You hear instructions every day in the classroom and read them in textbooks.
  • 3. Modal verbs for rules

We use special verbs like must, should, can and can't to talk about rules. They show if something is necessary or allowed.

Example:You must do your homework and you should participate in class.
Connection:These verbs appear in school rules, exam instructions and teacher feedback.
  • 4. Polite behaviour

Polite behaviour means being respectful and kind to others. It makes the classroom a good place to learn.

Example:Students should not interrupt when the teacher is speaking.
Connection:Teachers talk about behaviour in class and write about it in reports.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
correct or allowed
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
A tick means the behaviour is correct or allowed.
🔉 Spoken Example:
wrong or not allowed
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
A cross shows that the action is wrong or not allowed.
🔉 Spoken Example:
turn off your phone
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
This sign means you must turn off your phone.
🔉 Spoken Example:
be quiet
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The quiet symbol means you should not make noise.
🔉 Spoken Example:
raise your hand
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The hand symbol tells students to raise their hand.
🔉 Spoken Example:
not allowed or forbidden
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
This sign shows that something is not allowed or forbidden.
🔉 Spoken Example:
!
important or warning
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
An exclamation mark shows the rule is important or a warning.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Must / Should / Can / Can't
modal verbs for rules
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
We use must, should, can and can't as modal verbs for rules.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. rule — A rule tells you what you can or cannot do.
  2. behave — To behave means to act in a good or bad way.
  3. listen — To listen means to pay attention to sounds or someone speaking.
  4. respect — To respect means to be polite and show you care about someone.
  5. quiet — Quiet means making little or no noise.
  6. raise — To raise means to lift something up higher.
  7. permission — Permission is when someone says you can do something.
  8. interrupt — To interrupt means to stop someone when they are speaking or working.
  9. polite — Polite means having good manners and being nice to others.
  10. arrive — To arrive means to get to a place.
  11. late — Late means not on time or after the right time.
  12. homework — Homework is work that teachers give students to do at home.
  13. turn off — To turn off means to stop a machine or device from working.
  14. pay attention — To pay attention means to watch or listen carefully to something.
  15. disturb — To disturb means to make noise or do things that bother others.
  16. follow — To follow means to do what someone says or what a rule says.
  17. tidy — Tidy means clean and with everything in the right place.
  18. borrow — To borrow means to use something that belongs to someone else temporarily.
  19. share — To share means to let someone use something that belongs to you.
  20. participate — To participate means to join in and take part in an activity.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words about classroom rules and good behaviour.
Reading
Read classroom rules on posters and notices and find the modal verbs.
Listening
Listen to teachers giving instructions and identify the rules they say.
Speaking
Talk about classroom rules and explain why they are important.
Grammar
Use must, should, can and can't to write and say classroom rules.
Writing
Write a short list of five to eight classroom rules.
Lesson Test
The test checks your understanding of rules vocabulary and modal verbs, and your pass mark is seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In Japan, students clean their own classrooms every day because it teaches respect and responsibility. This is a classroom rule that helps students learn good behaviour while keeping the school tidy!

REFERENCES

English Grammar in Use — Raymond Murphy (2019). Unit 26 explains modal verbs for rules and obligation very clearly. Oxford Picture Dictionary — Oxford University Press (2015). The classroom section shows vocabulary about school rules with helpful pictures.

▶ Modal Verbs for Rules and Obligations — English with Lucy ▶ Classroom English for Teachers — British Council LearnEnglish

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play the full vocabulary list with definitions and example sentences:

rule noun

Phonetic: rool

Meaning: something that tells you what you can or cannot do

Khmer: ច្បាប់

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The first rule is to raise your hand.

behave verb

Phonetic: bi-HAYV

Meaning: to act in a good or bad way

Khmer: ប្រព្រឹត្តខ្លួន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Students must behave well in class.

listen verb

Phonetic: LIS-en

Meaning: to pay attention to sounds or someone speaking

Khmer: ស្ដាប់

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Please listen to the teacher carefully.

respect verb/noun

Phonetic: ri-SPEKT

Meaning: to be polite and show you care about someone

Khmer: គោរព

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: We must respect all our classmates.

quiet adjective

Phonetic: KWY-et

Meaning: making little or no noise

Khmer: ស្ងាត់

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The classroom is very quiet during the test.

raise verb

Phonetic: rayz

Meaning: to lift something up higher

Khmer: លើក (ដៃ)

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Raise your hand before you speak.

permission noun

Phonetic: per-MISH-un

Meaning: when someone says you can do something

Khmer: ការអនុញ្ញាត

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Ask for permission before you leave the room.

interrupt verb

Phonetic: in-ter-UPT

Meaning: to stop someone when they are speaking or working

Khmer: និយាយកាត់

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Do not interrupt when the teacher is talking.

polite adjective

Phonetic: po-LYTE

Meaning: having good manners and being nice to others

Khmer: សុភាពរាបសា

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: It is polite to say please and thank you.

arrive verb

Phonetic: a-RYVE

Meaning: to get to a place

Khmer: មកដល់

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Students must arrive on time every day.

late adjective

Phonetic: layt

Meaning: not on time or after the right time

Khmer: មកយឺត

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: He is always late for morning class.

homework noun

Phonetic: HOME-werk

Meaning: work that teachers give students to do at home

Khmer: កិច្ចការផ្ទះ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: We have homework to finish for tomorrow.

turn off phrasal verb

Phonetic: tern awf

Meaning: to stop a machine or device from working

Khmer: បិទ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Please turn off your phone in class.

disturb verb

Phonetic: pay a-TEN-shun dis-TERB

Meaning: to watch or listen carefully to something to make noise or do things that bother others

Khmer: រំខាន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: You must pay attention during the lesson. Do not disturb other students when they work.

follow verb

Phonetic: FAH-low

Meaning: to do what someone says or what a rule says

Khmer: ធ្វើតាម

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: We must follow the classroom rules every day.

tidy adjective

Phonetic: TY-dee

Meaning: clean and with everything in the right place

Khmer: មានរបៀបរៀបរយ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Keep your desk tidy and organized.

borrow verb

Phonetic: BAH-row

Meaning: to use something that belongs to someone else temporarily

Khmer: ខ្ចី

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?

share verb

Phonetic: shair

Meaning: to let someone use something that belongs to you

Khmer: ចែករំលែក

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: We should share our books with friends.

participate verb

Phonetic: par-TIS-i-payt

Meaning: to join in and take part in an activity

Khmer: ចូលរួម

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: All students must participate in group

MINI STORY

Maria is a new student in Class 5B. She wants to behave well and follow all the classroom rules. Every day, she arrives on time and never comes late. She always keeps her desk tidy and organized.

In class, Maria tries to pay attention to all the lessons. She is very polite to everyone. When she wants to speak, she raises her hand first. She never interrupts when the teacher is talking. Maria does not disturb other students during their work. She stays quiet during tests.

Maria always asks for permission before she borrows anything. She likes to share her books with classmates. She participates in all group activities. Maria respects her teacher and all her friends. She remembers to turn off her phone in class. Every evening, she completes her homework carefully. Maria is a good student because she follows the rules!

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

Maria's First Day

Text type: Narrative
Maria was very nervous on her first day at school. She walked into the classroom and saw many students. The teacher smiled and said, "Welcome, Maria. Please sit down."

Maria sat down and took out her notebook. The teacher explained the classroom rules. "Always raise your hand before speaking," she said. "Be quiet when others are talking. Come to class on time every day."

Maria listened carefully. She wrote the rules in her notebook. At lunch time, Maria forgot to raise her hand. She just started talking. The teacher stopped and looked at her. "Remember the rule, Maria," she said kindly. Maria felt embarrassed. She said sorry and raised her hand. After that day, Maria always remembered the rules. She became a good student.

Our Classroom Rules Poster

Text type: Description
Our classroom has a big poster on the wall. The poster is blue and yellow. It shows all our classroom rules. There are pictures next to each rule.

The first rule says, "Listen when the teacher talks." The picture shows a student with ears. The second rule says, "Put up your hand to speak." There is a picture of a hand in the air. The third rule says, "Be kind to

everyone." Two students are smiling in this picture. The fourth rule says, "Keep the classroom clean." The picture shows a tidy desk.

Our teacher made this poster with the class. We all helped choose the rules. Now everyone can see the poster every day. It helps us remember good behaviour. The poster makes our classroom a better place.

contentRef.text:
Message from Mr. Brown

Text type: Notice

To: All Students in Class 5B
From: Mr. Brown, Class Teacher
Date: Monday, 15th January

Dear Students,

I have some important information about our classroom rules. Starting next week, we will have new rules. Please read them carefully.

Rule 1: Arrive at class before 8:30 every morning. Rule 2: Bring all your books and pens to class. Rule 3: Do not eat or drink in the classroom. Rule 4: Switch off your mobile phones during lessons. Rule 5: Respect all teachers and classmates.

If you break these rules, you will get a warning. After three warnings, I will call your parents. I want everyone to learn well. Good behaviour helps everyone in the class. Please follow these rules every day.

Thank you for your help.

Mr. Brown

contentRef.text:
Why Classroom Rules Are Important

Text type: Informational
Classroom rules help students learn better. Rules make the classroom a safe place. Everyone knows what to do. This is good for all students.

Rules help in many ways. First, they stop students from talking loudly. When the room is quiet, everyone can hear the teacher. Second, rules teach respect. Students learn to wait for their turn. They learn to be polite. Third, rules keep students safe. For example, students should not run in the classroom. Running can cause accidents.

Teachers make rules with their students. This is important. When students help make rules, they follow them better. Good rules are simple and clear. Everyone can understand them easily. When students follow rules, the whole class works well together.

contentRef.text:
Two Different Classrooms

Text type: Comparison
Class 3A and Class 3B are very different. Both classes have the same teacher, Mrs. Lee. But the students behave differently.

In Class 3A, students follow all the rules. They arrive on time every day. They raise their hands before speaking. They listen when others talk. The classroom is always clean and tidy. Students help each other with their work. Mrs. Lee is happy with this class.

In Class 3B, students often break the rules. Some students arrive late. They talk when the teacher is speaking. They do not raise their hands. The classroom is often messy. Students sometimes fight with each other. Mrs. Lee feels tired after teaching this class.

Mrs. Lee wants Class 3B to be like Class 3A. She talks to them about good behaviour every week.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Students must be quiet when the teacher is talking. We should raise our hand before we speak in class. Everyone needs to bring their books and pens to class. We must not use our mobile phones during lessons. Good students always arrive on time for their lessons.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What do you do when you want to ask a question in class?

I raise my hand and wait. The teacher calls my name. Then I can speak and ask my question.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Why is it important to be quiet when the teacher talks?

Because we need to listen and learn. If students are noisy, we cannot hear the teacher. Everyone must be quiet.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What happens if a student is late for class?

The student misses important information. The teacher might be unhappy. It is better to arrive on time every day.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Can you name two things students should bring to class?

Students should bring their books and pens. They also need their notebooks. These things help us to study and write.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Why should we not use mobile phones during lessons?

Mobile phones stop us from learning. We must pay attention to the teacher. We can use our phones after class.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs: must / should / can / can't

We use modal verbs to talk about rules and behaviour.

'Must' means you have to do something.

'Should' means it is a good idea.

'Can' means it is allowed.

'Can't' means it is not allowed.

FORMS

FormExample
must + base verb (obligation)Students must listen to the teacher.
should + base verb (advice)You should raise your hand before speaking.
can + base verb (permission)You can borrow a pencil from me.
can't + base verb (prohibition)You can't eat food in the library.
don't have to + base verb (no obligation)We don't have to wear uniforms on Friday.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ Students must to arrive on time.

✓ Students must arrive on time.

Never use 'to' after modal verbs like must, should, can.

✗ He cans ask questions in class.

✓ He can ask questions in class.

Modal verbs never add -s for he/she/it.

✗ You no can talk during the test.

✓ You can't talk during the test.

Use can't (cannot) for prohibition, not 'no can'.

nodes.question: Q13. You ___ return library books after two weeks. That is the rule.

nodes.question: Q16. Students ___ be quiet during silent reading time. It is a strict rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q17. You ___ copy from other students. It is cheating.
nodes.explanation: → Cheating is wrong, so copying is not allowed.

nodes.question: Q18. We ___ try to arrive five minutes early. It is good to be ready.
nodes.explanation: → Being ready is a benefit, so arriving early is good advice.

nodes.question: Q19. Students ___ wear hats inside the building. Please take them off.
nodes.explanation: → The instruction to take hats off shows wearing them is not allowed.

nodes.question: Q20. You ___ write with a pen or a pencil. Both are fine.
nodes.explanation: → Both being fine means students are free to choose either one.

nodes.question: Q21. We ___ throw paper on the floor. Use the bin instead.
nodes.explanation: → The instruction to use the bin shows throwing paper on the floor is not allowed.

nodes.question: Q22. You ___ share your books with classmates if they forget theirs. It is kind, but not a rule.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q23. Students ___ hand in their essays by Friday. That is the last day.
nodes.explanation: → The last day means students have to hand in essays by Friday.

nodes.question: Q24. It is allowed. You ___ drink water during class. Keep a bottle on your desk.
nodes.explanation: → The action is allowed, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q25. We ___ forget to sign out when we leave early. It is important.
nodes.explanation: → Something important that we must not forget is a prohibition on forgetting.

nodes.question: Q26. Students ___ listen carefully when the teacher explains something new. This is good advice, not a rule.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q27. You ___ sit on the desks. Chairs are for sitting.
nodes.explanation: → Chairs being for sitting shows sitting on desks is not allowed.

nodes.question: Q28. We ___ close the windows before we leave. The teacher gave a rule, so we have no choice.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q29. You ___ use the computer lab on weekends. It stays open.
nodes.explanation: → The lab staying open means students are allowed to use it on weekends.

nodes.question: Q30. Students ___ push other students in the corridor. It is dangerous.
nodes.explanation: → Something dangerous is not allowed for safety reasons.

lessons.titleEn: Simple Rules and Classroom Behaviour — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about three important classroom rules. Explain why these rules help students learn. (40–60 words)

  • Choose three simple rules like raising hands, listening, or being on time
  • Say what each rule is in a short sentence
  • Explain how the rules help the class work well

Key structures: We must / should + verb, because / so

Model
Every classroom needs good rules. First, students must listen when the teacher talks. Second, we should raise our hand before speaking. Third, everyone must arrive on time. These rules help because the class stays quiet and organized. When we follow rules, we can all learn better.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about three classroom rules and explain how these rules help students learn.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: rule, listen, respect, quiet, raise, permission, polite, arrive, late, pay attention. Structures: Students / We must + verb; Students / We should + verb; because / so; These rules help....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: States three different classroom rules, each in its own short sentence, and explains how the rules help the class (for example 'so the class stays quiet and we can learn'). Good: States three rules but the explanation of how they help is very short, or states two rules with a good explanation. Developing: Gives only one or two rules and no real explanation, or lists rules that repeat each other. Beginning: Does not give classroom rules, or the text is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'must' and 'should' correctly with a base verb (listen, arrive, raise your hand, be polite) and uses 'because' or 'so' to give the result. Good: Uses must or should correctly for most rules, but 'because' or 'so' is missing. Developing: Uses modals but adds the wrong verb form, for example 'must to listen' or 'should listens', or gives rules as plain statements. Beginning: No modal verbs and no rule vocabulary from the week.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Modal + base verb is correct in nearly every rule ('must listen', 'should raise'), with at most two small slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but errors appear such as 'must listens', 'should to raise' or 'arrive on the time'. Developing: Repeated modal errors and missing subjects make several rules hard to understand. Beginning: Errors throughout; rules cannot be understood.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Rules come in a clear order (First, Second, Third) followed by one sentence about the result. Good: Mostly clear order; the result sentence is short. Developing: Rules and explanation are mixed together. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Three clear rules with must / should, a reason for how they help, 40-60 words. | 75-89: Three rules and a reason; a few modal errors or a thin explanation. | 60-74: Only two rules or no clear explanation; several errors. | 40-59: Very short or rules unclear; hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; 'raise your hand' written as 'raise hand'; using 'have to' instead of 'must' if the meaning is clear.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words. Accept about 35-70 words without penalty. Under 35 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any three sensible rules (no phone, tidy desk, share books, do homework, be polite) are fine, and 'can't' or 'don't' may be used for a negative rule. The model's wording 'Every classroom needs good rules' is not required. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear rule the learner wrote, quoting them (for example 'Students must listen to the teacher'). 2) Fix: Fix one modal error with an example, such as: 'Write "Students must listen", not "Students must listens". Example: We should raise our hand before we speak.' 3) Next step: Finish with one 'because' sentence that says why the rules help.

lessons.titleKm: Simple Rules and Classroom Behaviour — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Simple Rules and Classroom Behaviour — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe good and bad behaviour in the classroom. Give two examples of each and explain the results. (60–80 words)

  • Start with good behaviour and give two clear examples
  • Then write about bad behaviour with two examples
  • Say what happens when students behave well or badly

Key structures: When students..., they..., but / however, First... Second...

Model
Good behaviour helps everyone in class. When students listen carefully, they understand the lesson better. When they help classmates, everyone feels happy and safe. However, bad behaviour causes problems. Some students talk loudly during lessons. This makes it hard for others to hear. Other students arrive late and disturb the class. Bad behaviour means less learning time. Teachers feel stressed and students cannot focus on their work.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words about good and bad classroom behaviour: two examples of each, and what happens when students behave well or badly.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: behave, respect, polite, interrupt, disturb, late, share, participate, follow, pay attention. Structures: When students..., they...; First... Second...; However / But, ...; Students should not interrupt..
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Gives two clear examples of good behaviour and two of bad behaviour, and says what happens as a result in both cases (for example 'they understand the lesson' or 'it is hard for others to hear'). Good: Gives two good and two bad examples, but the results are missing for one side or are very short. Developing: Gives only one good and one bad example, or gives examples without any results. Beginning: Writes only about good or only about bad behaviour, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'When students..., they...' and contrast words (But / However) with week behaviour words such as listen, respect, interrupt, disturb, share or arrive late. Good: Uses 'When students...' or a contrast word correctly, and some week words. Developing: Lists behaviours with only simple words (good, bad) and no week structures. Beginning: No week vocabulary or structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple after 'when' is correct ('When students listen, they learn'), and plural verbs are right; at most two slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but slips like 'When students listens', 'They is late' or 'it make noise' appear. Developing: Many verb-form errors and run-on sentences make several lines unclear. Beginning: Errors throughout; unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Good behaviour first, then a clear turn to bad behaviour with 'However' or 'But', each with its results. Good: Good and bad parts are mostly separated. Developing: Good and bad examples are mixed together. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two good and two bad behaviours with results, 'when... they...' used well, 60-80 words. | 75-89: Four examples; some results missing or a few verb errors. | 60-74: Fewer than four examples or no results; several errors. | 40-59: Only one side, or very short; hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; using 'if' instead of 'when'; simple results such as 'the teacher is angry'.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words. Accept about 52-92 words without penalty. Under 52 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any good and bad behaviours are fine (helping classmates, shouting, using a phone, being late). Results can be simple. Learners need not use the exact model examples. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear good or bad example with its result, quoting the learner (for example 'When students talk loudly, others cannot hear'). 2) Fix: Fix one verb error with an example, such as: 'Write "When students listen, they learn", not "When students listens, they learn".' 3) Next step: Check that each example has a result before you send.

lessons.titleKm: Simple Rules and Classroom Behaviour — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Simple Rules and Classroom Behaviour — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write a guide for new students about classroom behaviour at your school. Include what they should do, what they should not do, and why it matters. (80–110 words)

  • Welcome new students and introduce the topic in your first sentence
  • List three things students should do and three things they should not do
  • End by explaining why good behaviour is important for everyone

Key structures: You should / must + verb, Don't / Never + verb, It is important to..., because / so that

Model
Welcome to our school! Here are some important rules about classroom behaviour. You should always bring your books and pens to class. You must listen when the teacher speaks. It is important to be polite and respect other students. However, there are some things you must not do. Don't use your phone during lessons. Never eat or drink in class. Don't shout or run in the classroom. These rules are important because they help everyone feel safe. When we follow the rules, we create a good learning environment. Teachers can teach well and students can study without problems. Good behaviour makes our school a better place for everyone.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write an 80-110 word guide for new students: welcome them, give three things they should do and three things they should not do, and finish by explaining why good behaviour matters.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: rule, respect, polite, quiet, turn off, disturb, tidy, borrow, share, participate. Structures: You should / must + verb; Don't / Never / You must not + verb; It is important to...; because / so that.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Opens with a welcome and topic sentence, gives three things to do and three things not to do, and ends by explaining why good behaviour is important for everyone. Good: Has a welcome and about two or three do's and don'ts each, but the ending reason is short, or one part has only two items. Developing: Gives a few rules but misses the welcome or the ending, or lists only 'do' or only 'do not'. Beginning: Does not give a guide for new students, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'You should / must...', 'Don't / Never...' and 'It is important to...' with week words such as turn off, disturb, polite, tidy or share, and ends with because / so that. Good: Uses should / must and Don't correctly, but lacks 'It is important to...' or 'because'. Developing: Uses only one structure, such as 'You must' for everything, or writes negative rules without don't / never. Beginning: No modal or imperative structures from the week.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Modals and commands are followed by the base verb ('Don't use', 'You must listen'), with at most two slips. Good: Understandable, with errors such as 'You should to bring', 'Don't using phone' or 'Never eating'. Developing: Many errors with modals and negatives; some rules are unclear or sound as if they mean the opposite. Beginning: Errors throughout; rules cannot be understood.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Welcome, then do's, then don'ts, then why it matters, with linking words such as However, because. Good: Mostly in order, with some mixing of do's and don'ts. Developing: Rules are in a jumbled list with no start or ending. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Welcome, three do's, three don'ts and a clear reason why behaviour matters, with good modals; 80-110 words. | 75-89: All parts present; slightly short lists or some modal errors. | 60-74: Missing welcome, ending or several rules; frequent errors. | 40-59: Very short, only one type of rule, or hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; using 'must not' / 'don't' / 'never' interchangeably; rules from the learner's own school, not the model's rules.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words. Accept about 70-125 words without penalty. Under 70 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible rules are fine (bring books, listen, be polite, no phones, no eating, no running). The welcome can be one short sentence, and the ending can use 'because' or 'so that'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a helpful rule for new students, quoting the learner (for example 'You must listen when the teacher speaks'). 2) Fix: Fix one modal or negative error with an example, such as: 'Write "Don't use your phone", not "Don't using your phone". Example: You should bring your book to class.' 3) Next step: End with one sentence that begins 'It is important to...' to explain why.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about good classroom behaviour. Describe what students should do and why it is important. (40–60 words)

  • Say what students should do in class.
  • Give two or three examples of good behaviour.
  • Explain why good behaviour helps learning.
Model
Good classroom behaviour is very important for learning. Students should arrive on time and listen carefully to the teacher. They must raise their hands before speaking and be polite to everyone. When students follow these rules, the classroom is quiet and everyone can work well. Good behaviour helps us learn better and makes the class a nice place for everyone.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about good classroom behaviour: what students should do (two or three examples) and why good behaviour helps learning.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: behaviour, arrive, listen, polite, respect, raise, quiet, follow, pay attention, participate. Structures: Students should + verb; Students must + verb; When students follow the rules, ...; Good behaviour helps....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says what students should do with two or three clear examples of good behaviour and explains why good behaviour helps learning.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'should' / 'must' with week words (listen, arrive on time, raise their hands, respect, polite) and a result sentence such as 'When students follow the rules, the class is quiet'.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Modals take the base verb and plural subjects agree ('Students should listen'), with one or two small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Opening topic sentence, then examples, then why it helps, in short connected sentences.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; 'behavior' or 'behaviour'; using 'have to' instead of 'must'.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words. Accept about 35-70 words without penalty. Under 35 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible good behaviours and reasons are fine. The first sentence does not have to match the model. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.

contentRef.text:
CHAPTER III · WEEK 15

Giving Praise and Simple Feedback

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify specific praise words and simple feedback expressions in spoken classroom exchanges L2 Understand
  • Use common adjectives and simple present forms to express positive feedback clearly L3 Apply
  • Give simple praise and constructive feedback to classmates using appropriate intonation L3 Apply
  • Recognise feedback language and praise expressions in short teacher comments and notes L3 Apply
  • Write short positive feedback comments for classmates using basic praise vocabulary L3 Apply
  • Reflect on how giving respectful feedback supports positive learning relationships L4 Analyze · HOTS

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Positive feedback language

Words teachers use to tell students they did something good. They help students feel happy about their work.

Example:Well done, your essay is excellent and very clear!
Connection:You hear this language when teachers talk to students in class.
  • 2. Constructive feedback language

Kind words that help someone improve their work. They show what is good and what needs more work.

Example:You should check your spelling, but your ideas are creative.
Connection:Teachers write this in comments on homework and tests.
  • 3. Modal verbs for advice and suggestions

Special verbs like should, must, can, and could. They help us give feedback in a polite way.

Example:You could try harder next time to make fewer mistakes.
Connection:Teachers use these verbs when giving advice to students in school.
  • 4. Strengths and weaknesses in learning

A strength is something you do well. A weakness is something you need to improve.

Example:Your strength is careful writing, but grammar is a weakness.
Connection:You see these words on report cards and in parent meetings.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
A+
A plus
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
You got an A plus because your work is excellent.
🔉 Spoken Example:
B-
B minus
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Your grade is B minus, so you should improve a little.
🔉 Spoken Example:
check mark or tick
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The teacher put a check mark next to your correct answer.
🔉 Spoken Example:
cross or X
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
A cross means your answer has a mistake in it.
🔉 Spoken Example:
9/10
nine out of ten
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
You got nine out of ten, so well done!
🔉 Spoken Example:
*
star
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The teacher drew a star because your work is creative.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Good!
Good exclamation mark
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The comment says good exclamation mark at the top.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Keep up the good work.
Keep up the good work period
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The note says keep up the good work period at the end.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. praise — Words that show you think someone did something good.
  2. feedback — Helpful comments about someone's work or actions.
  3. excellent — Very very good.
  4. improve — To make something better than before.
  5. mistake — Something wrong that you do or say.
  6. well done — Words you say when someone does something good.
  7. try harder — To put more effort into doing something.
  8. effort — The energy and work you put into doing something.
  9. correct — Right, with no mistakes.
  10. neat — Clean and tidy, organized well.
  11. progress — Getting better at something over time.
  12. creative — Showing new and interesting ideas.
  13. careful — Giving attention to avoid mistakes.
  14. comment — Words that give your opinion about something.
  15. grade — A letter or number showing how good your work is.
  16. clear — Easy to understand or see.
  17. confident — Feeling sure about what you can do.
  18. strength — Something you are good at doing.
  19. weakness — Something you are not good at doing.
  20. keep up — To continue doing something at the same good level.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words teachers use to give praise and feedback.
Reading
Read short teacher comments and find the praise and feedback words.
Listening
Listen to teachers giving feedback and notice their intonation and modal verbs.
Speaking
Practice saying praise and feedback sentences with the right friendly intonation.
Grammar
Learn should, must, can, and could to give advice in feedback.
Writing
Write short positive feedback comments for your classmates using praise vocabulary.
Lesson Test
The test checks all feedback language skills, and seventy percent is pass.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Research shows students learn better when they hear specific praise like 'Your paragraph is very clear' instead of just 'Good job!' Telling students exactly what is good helps them understand their strengths.

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching: The Essential Guide to English Language Teaching — Jim Scrivener (2011). This book has clear examples of classroom feedback language teachers actually use. How to Teach English — Jeremy Harmer (2007). Chapter seven shows how to give praise and correction in simple English.

▶ Classroom English for Teachers — English with Lucy ▶ Giving Feedback to Students — British Council LearnEnglish

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play the full vocabulary list with definitions and example sentences:

praise noun/verb

Phonetic: PRAYZ

Meaning: words that show you think someone did something good

Khmer: ការសរសើរ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The teacher gave praise to the student for good work.

feedback noun

Phonetic: FEED-bak

Meaning: helpful comments about someone's work or actions

Khmer: មតិកែលម្អ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: My teacher gives me feedback on my homework every week.

excellent adjective

MINI STORY

Maria is a new student in English class. Her teacher, Miss Chen, always gives helpful feedback to all students. Today, Miss Chen reads Maria's writing and smiles.

"Well done, Maria! Your story is very creative and interesting. Your writing is clear and neat. You made good progress this month," says Miss Chen. Maria feels confident and happy. Miss Chen writes some comments on the paper. "You have only two small mistakes here. Please be more careful with spelling next time. That is your weakness, but reading is your strength!"

Maria reads the teacher's feedback. She sees her grade is excellent! "Thank you for your praise," says Maria. "I will try harder to improve my spelling." Miss Chen smiles and says, "Your effort is wonderful. Keep up the good work!" Maria knows that mistakes help her learn. She feels ready to work on her next essay. Good feedback helps students become better learners.

Reading Passage

My Teacher's Kind Words

Text type: Narrative
Last week, I felt worried about my English test. I studied hard every night. I read my books and did all the homework. But I thought my writing was not good.

On Friday, Ms. Chen gave back our tests. She smiled at me. She said, "Your essay was very clear and interesting." She wrote nice words on my paper too. She wrote, "Good job! Your ideas are great. Next time, check your spelling." I felt so happy.

Now I know what I do well. I also know what to practice more. Ms. Chen's words helped me feel confident. Her feedback was kind but also useful. I will work on my spelling for the next test. Good feedback makes learning easier and more fun.

A Great Classroom Helper

Text type: Description
Mr. Lee is a sports teacher at our school. He is tall and friendly. He always wears a blue jacket and white shoes. He teaches football and basketball every Tuesday and Thursday.

Mr. Lee is very good at giving praise. When students try hard, he smiles and says, "Well done!" He claps his hands when someone scores a goal. He also gives helpful feedback. If your kick is wrong, he shows you the right way. He says, "Try it like this. Bend your knee more." He never shouts or gets angry.

All the students like Mr. Lee. His positive words make us want to practice more. We learn quickly because he explains things clearly. He makes sports fun and easy to learn. Everyone feels good in his class.

To: All Music Club Members

Hello everyone! Thank you for coming to our concert practice yesterday. You all worked really hard. I want to give some praise and feedback.

Great things: The singing was beautiful and loud. Everyone remembered the words. The drummers kept good time. Well done to everyone!

Things to improve: We need to start together at the same time. Also, please stand up straight when you sing. This helps your voice sound better. Let's practice these two things next week.

Best wishes, Sarah

How to Give Good Feedback

Text type: Informational

Giving good feedback is an important skill. It helps people learn and improve. Here are some simple tips.

First, always say something positive. Start with praise. Say what the person did well. For example, "Your drawing has beautiful colors." This makes people feel good. Then, give one or two suggestions. Be specific and clear. Say, "Maybe draw the eyes a bit bigger." Don't say too many things at once. This can confuse people.

Also, be kind and friendly. Use a nice voice. Smile when you talk. Never laugh at mistakes. Everyone makes mistakes when they learn. Good feedback should help, not hurt. Remember to say "please" and "thank you."

When you give good feedback, people listen better. They feel happy to improve. Practice giving feedback to your friends and family.

Two Different Teachers

Text type: Comparison

I have two teachers at school. They give feedback in very different ways.

Mrs. Park teaches math. She is strict but fair. When I do good work, she writes "Excellent" on my paper. She uses a red pen to show my mistakes. Then she explains the right answer. She says, "Look at step three. You need to add, not subtract." Her feedback is clear and direct. I always know what to fix.

Mr. Santos teaches art. He is relaxed and cheerful. He looks at my paintings and says, "I love these colors!" He asks questions like, "What feeling do you want to show?" He doesn't tell me exactly what to change. He wants me to think and decide.

Both teachers help me learn. Mrs. Park's way is clear and quick. Mr. Santos's way makes me think more. I like both styles.

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Good job! Your homework was very good this week. You worked hard on this project. Well done! Your writing is better now. Please check your spelling next time. That was excellent! You helped your friend with the problem. Try to speak louder. But your answer was correct!

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. How do you feel when your teacher says 'well done' to you?

I feel very happy when my teacher says well done. It makes me want to work harder. I feel good about my work.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Can you tell me about a time when someone gave you good feedback?

My teacher said my story was interesting last week. She told me to add more details. I was happy and wrote more.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What nice words can you say to a classmate about their work?

I can say good job or well done. I can say you tried hard. I can also say that looks great!

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Why is it important to give praise to other students?

Praise makes students feel happy and confident. They want to do better next time. It helps everyone feel good in class.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What can you say if a friend's homework has a small mistake?

I can say your work is good. But maybe check this part again. I think there is a small mistake here.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs: should, must, can, could (for advice, obligation, ability,

suggestions) Modal verbs help us give praise and feedback.

'Should' gives advice.

'Must' shows something is necessary.

'Can' and 'could' talk about ability or make suggestions.

They come before the main verb without 'to'.

FORMS

FormExample
should + base verb (advice)You should practise more often.
must + base verb (strong necessity)You must finish your homework today.
can + base verb (ability or permission)You can answer questions very well.
could + base verb (polite suggestion or past ability)You could try writing longer sentences.
Negative: modal + not + base verbYou should not worry about mistakes.
Question: Modal + subject + base verb?Should I read this again?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ You should to study more.

✓ You should study more.

Never use 'to' after modal verbs.

✗ He cans speak English well.

✓ He can speak English well.

Modal verbs never add -s in third person.

✗ You must not be late is important.

✓ You must not be late.

Modal + verb is enough; do not add extra words.

lessons.titleKm: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about why teachers should give praise to students. Explain what happens when students receive praise. (40–60 words)

  • Start with a sentence about why praise is important
  • Give one or two examples of what praise does
  • Keep sentences short and simple

Key structures: Simple present tense (helps, makes, feels), Because (to give reasons)

Model
Teachers should give praise to students because it makes them happy. When students hear 'Good work!' they feel confident. Praise helps them try harder next time. Students learn better when they get kind words from their teacher. It makes the classroom a nice place.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about why teachers should give praise, and what happens when students receive praise.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: praise, feedback, well done, excellent, confident, effort, try harder, improve, progress, happy. Structures: Teachers should give praise because...; Praise helps / makes students...; When students hear '...', they feel....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Opens with why praise is important and gives one or two clear effects on students (for example they feel confident or try harder), with a short example of praise words. Good: Gives why praise is important and one effect, but no example of what a teacher says. Developing: Says praise is good but gives no reason or effect, or repeats the same idea. Beginning: Does not write about praise, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'because' and present-simple result verbs such as 'helps' and 'makes' correctly, with week words like praise, confident, effort, try harder or well done. Good: Uses 'because' or 'helps / makes' correctly, with a few week words. Developing: Uses simple words only (good, happy) and no key structure. Beginning: No week vocabulary or structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is right in 'praise helps' and 'it makes them happy', with at most two slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but slips like 'Praise help students' or 'it make them feel' appear. Developing: Frequent verb errors and missing subjects make some lines unclear. Beginning: Errors throughout; unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Opening reason, then effects, then a short closing idea, in short easy sentences. Good: Mostly in order and easy to follow. Developing: Ideas are mixed or repeated. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear reason why praise matters and one or two effects with an example, key verbs correct; 40-60 words. | 75-89: Reason and effect present; no example or a few errors. | 60-74: Reason or effect missing; several errors. | 40-59: Very short or unclear; little week language. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; 'students' or 'children' used for learners; praise phrases that are different from the week's list.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words. Accept about 35-70 words without penalty. Under 35 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any reasons are fine (confidence, happiness, motivation, learning better). The learner may use the model's 'Good work!' or other praise such as 'Well done!' or 'Excellent!'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear reason or effect the learner wrote, quoting them (for example 'Praise makes students confident'). 2) Fix: Fix one verb error with an example, such as: 'Write "Praise helps students", not "Praise help students". Example: When teachers say "Well done!", students feel happy.' 3) Next step: Add one real praise phrase in quotation marks next time.

lessons.titleKm: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about different ways to give praise and positive feedback in the classroom. Give examples of what teachers can say or do. (60–80 words)

  • Start by saying there are many ways to give praise
  • Give at least three different examples with actual words or actions
  • Use phrases like 'for example' or 'also' to connect ideas

Key structures: Can/could (for suggestions), For example, also (linking words), Imperatives (Say, Give, Write)

Model
There are many ways to give praise in class. For example, teachers can say 'Excellent work!' or 'You did really well!' They can also write nice comments on homework like 'Great effort!' or 'Keep it up!' Teachers can give students a smile or a thumbs up too. Some teachers use stickers or stars on good work. All these things show students that their work is good.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words about different ways to give praise in the classroom, with at least three examples of what teachers can say or do.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: praise, well done, excellent, great, comment, grade, neat, creative, keep up, effort. Structures: There are many ways to give praise.; For example, teachers can say '...'; They can also write / give...; Keep it up! / Say '...'.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Starts by saying there are many ways to praise, then gives at least three different examples with actual words ('Excellent work!') or actions (a smile, a sticker, a written comment). Good: Gives two or three examples, but one is vague (for example 'say nice words') or the opening sentence is missing. Developing: Gives only one example, or gives three examples that are almost the same. Beginning: Does not give examples of praise, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'For example', 'also' and 'can / could' correctly, and includes real praise phrases from the week such as Well done, Excellent, Keep it up, Great effort. Good: Uses 'can' and either 'for example' or 'also', and one or two praise phrases. Developing: Gives examples without linking words, or uses 'can' wrongly ('teachers can says'). Beginning: No linking words and no praise phrases from the week.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'Can' + base verb is correct throughout ('can say', 'can write'), with at most two small slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but slips such as 'teachers can says', 'give a smiles' or 'write comment' appear. Developing: Frequent modal and plural errors make several sentences unclear. Beginning: Errors throughout; unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Opening sentence, then examples joined with 'For example' and 'also', then a short closing line. Good: Examples are in a clear list but connectors are few. Developing: Examples are a jumble with no connectors. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Opening sentence, three or more different examples with real words or actions, linking words and 'can' used well; 60-80 words. | 75-89: Three examples present; thin linking or a few errors. | 60-74: Only two examples or vague ones; several errors. | 40-59: One example or very short; hard to follow. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; missing quotation marks around praise phrases; using 'may' or 'could' instead of 'can'.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words. Accept about 52-92 words without penalty. Under 52 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible ways to praise are fine (words, smiles, thumbs up, stickers, stars, notes on homework, telling parents). The learner does not need the model's exact phrases. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a specific example the learner gave, quoting it (for example 'Teachers can say "Well done!"'). 2) Fix: Fix one error with an example, such as: 'Write "Teachers can say", not "Teachers can says". Example: They can also write "Great effort!" on homework.' 3) Next step: Add one more way to praise that uses an action, such as a smile or a sticker.

lessons.titleKm: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about how to give helpful feedback that includes both praise and suggestions for improvement. Explain why this balance is important for student learning. (80–110 words)

  • Begin by explaining that good feedback has two parts
  • Give a clear example showing both praise and suggestion
  • Explain why students need both positive and improvement comments
  • End with how this helps students learn better

Key structures: First...then/but (sequencing and contrast), Should (for advice), This helps/This makes (showing results)

Model
Good feedback should have two parts. First, teachers should say what the student did well. Then they should give one or two ideas for improvement. For example, a teacher can say 'Your essay has good ideas, but check your spelling next time.' This helps students feel good about their work. At the same time, they learn what to do better. Students should not feel bad when they get feedback. They should feel ready to improve. When teachers give praise and helpful suggestions together, students learn faster. This balance is very important for good learning.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words explaining that good feedback has praise and suggestions for improvement: give an example with both parts, explain why students need both, and say how this helps learning.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: feedback, praise, improve, mistake, suggestion, strength, weakness, progress, correct, careful. Structures: Good feedback should have two parts.; First..., then...; ..., but you should...; This helps / This makes students....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Says good feedback has two parts, gives one example comment with both praise and a suggestion, explains why students need both, and ends by saying how this helps learning. Good: Has the two parts and an example, but the explanation of why both are needed or the ending is thin. Developing: Writes about praise or about suggestions but not both, or gives no example comment. Beginning: Does not explain feedback, or is off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'First... then...', 'but' and 'should' for advice, and 'This helps / This makes' for results, with week words like improve, mistake, strength, weakness, progress. Good: Uses should and either 'but' or 'First... then', with some week words. Developing: Uses 'should' only once, or no sequencing and contrast words; vocabulary stays at good / bad. Beginning: No week structures or vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'Should' + base verb and the example comment are correct ('You should check your spelling'), with at most two slips. Good: Meaning is clear, but errors like 'should to check', 'this help students' or 'students feels' appear. Developing: Repeated modal and verb-ending errors; some sentences are unclear. Beginning: Errors throughout; unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Moves in order: two-part idea, example comment, why both are needed, how it helps learning. Good: Mostly in order with some jumping. Developing: Ideas are mixed with no clear order. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two-part feedback explained, example with praise and suggestion, reason and result, key structures; 80-110 words. | 75-89: All parts present; short explanation or a few errors. | 60-74: Only praise or only suggestions, or missing example; several errors. | 40-59: Very short or unclear; little week language. | 0-39: Off task or not understandable.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; missing quotation marks around the example comment; 'ideas for improvement' written as 'ideas to improve'.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words. Accept about 70-125 words without penalty. Under 70 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any example comment with praise and a suggestion is fine (for example 'Your picture is neat, but you should add a title'). The learner may use 'could' instead of 'should'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for a new attempt. If the model answer is copied word for word, give 100 with a note asking for their own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a good example comment the learner wrote, quoting it (for example 'Your story is clear, but you should check your spelling'). 2) Fix: Fix one modal error with an example, such as: 'Write "You should check your spelling", not "You should to check spelling". Example: This helps students feel confident.' 3) Next step: End with one sentence that begins 'This helps...' to show the result.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about giving feedback to a classmate. Describe what you said and why feedback is helpful. (40–60 words)

  • Say what work your classmate did
  • Give one piece of praise
  • Give one helpful comment to improve
  • Explain why feedback is useful
Model
Last week, my classmate Maria showed me her poster. I told her the colors were very beautiful. Then I said she could add more text. I think feedback is helpful because it helps us learn. Maria was happy with my comments. She improved her poster and it looked fantastic. Good feedback helps everyone do better work.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about giving feedback to a classmate: the work they did, one piece of praise, one helpful suggestion, and why feedback is useful.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: feedback, praise, well done, beautiful, neat, improve, comment, creative, careful, helpful. Structures: I said / told... that...; You could / should add...; Feedback helps us...; because.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says what work the classmate did, gives one clear praise comment and one clear suggestion for improvement, and explains why feedback is useful.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses praise words (beautiful, neat, creative, well done), a polite suggestion with 'could' or 'should', and 'because' or 'helps' for the reason.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Verb forms are accurate whether in past (I said, she showed) or present, and 'could / should' take the base verb; one or two slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Tells what happened in order (work, praise, suggestion), then why feedback helps.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; capital letters and punctuation; mixing past and present tense if the meaning is clear; an imagined classmate or situation.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words. Accept about 35-70 words without penalty. Under 35 words: cap the total at 60. Longer is fine if still on task.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Past tense (as in the model) or present tense are both fine. Any classmate's work (poster, essay, drawing, presentation) is fine, and the learner may use 'could', 'should' or 'try to'. The model answer is only a reference.

contentRef.text:
Video Evidence

This is your performance evidence for this lesson. Record a 3-minute video of yourself presenting this week's topic in English. Speak naturally — notes are fine, reading a script word-for-word is not.

Present in your own words: Giving Praise and Simple Feedback

CHECKLIST

  • ☐ Introduce the topic in one or two sentences
  • ☐ Use at least five of this week's key terms correctly

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Developmental milestones

Important skills that children learn at certain ages. Each child grows and learns at their own speed.

Example:Most children can walk by eighteen months old.
Connection:Teachers use this language when they write reports about children.
  • 2. Physical abilities

Things children can do with their bodies. These include moving, jumping, and using their hands.

Example:Five-year-old children can usually run and jump well.
Connection:You will read this language in education textbooks and child development guides.
  • 3. Cognitive abilities

Things children can do with their minds. This includes reading, counting, and remembering things.

Example:Most six-year-olds can count to twenty.
Connection:Teachers talk about these skills in classroom discussions and parent meetings.
  • 4. Social and emotional skills

Ways children learn to play with others and control their feelings. This takes time to develop.

Example:Young children cannot always share their toys with friends.
Connection:Early childhood educators observe and record these skills in daily notes.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. able — When you can do something because you have the skill.
  2. unable — When you cannot do something because you don't have the skill.
  3. skill — Something you can do well after learning and practising.
  4. ride — To sit on a bike or animal and control it.
  5. swim — To move through water using your arms and legs.
  6. climb — To go up something using your hands and feet.
  7. tie — To make a knot with string or rope.
  8. count — To say numbers in the right order like one, two, three.
  9. draw — To make pictures with a pencil or pen.
  10. read — To look at words and understand what they mean.
  11. write — To make letters and words with a pen or pencil.
  12. spell — To say or write all the letters of a word correctly.
  13. catch — To take hold of something moving through the air with your hands.
  14. throw — To make something fly through the air from your hand.
  15. jump — To push yourself up into the air with your legs.
  16. run — To move very fast on your feet.
  17. sing — To make music with your voice.
  18. dance — To move your body to music in a fun way.
  19. share — To let other people use your things too.
  20. help — To make something easier for another person to do.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words about children's abilities and physical actions.
Reading
Read a short text about what children can do at different ages.
Listening
Listen to teachers describing what young children are able to do.
Speaking
Say sentences about what children at different ages can and cannot do.
Grammar
Practise using can and cannot to talk about children's abilities.
Writing
Write simple sentences about what young learners are able to do.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary and grammar about child development; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In English, we say 'can' and 'cannot' for every person — I can, you can, he can, they can. The word never changes, which makes it very easy to use!

REFERENCES

From Birth to Five Years: Practical Developmental Examination — Mary Sheridan (2014). This book helps you learn simple English to describe child development stages. Child Development: An Active Learning Approach — Laura Levine and Joyce Munsch (2018). It uses clear language to explain what children can do at each age.

▶ Child Development Milestones — Zero to Three ▶ Physical Development in Early Childhood — Khan Academy

MINI STORY

My name is Sarah and I teach young children. Every day I watch what they can and cannot do.

In my class, most children are able to read simple books. They can write their names and count to fifty. Some children can spell easy words too. They love to draw pictures of animals and people. During break time, the children run and jump in the playground. They can throw and catch balls together. A few children can ride bicycles now. Some can swim but others are still unable to swim alone.

The children also learn important skills. They can share toys with friends. They help me clean the classroom. On Friday, we sing songs and dance together. I am very happy when I see children climb and try new things. Every child learns at their own speed. Some things are easy and some are difficult. But every child can do something special!

Reading Passage

My Little Brother Tom

Text type: Narrative
My brother Tom is three years old. He can do many things now. He can run very fast in the garden. He can climb the stairs by himself. Tom can also say many words like 'mummy', 'daddy', and 'dog'. He loves talking all day!

But Tom cannot do some things yet. He cannot ride a bike. He cannot write his name. He tries to write, but he only makes funny lines. Tom cannot swim without his special arm bands. He is afraid of the deep water.

Last week, Tom tried to tie his shoes. He cannot do it. Mum helps him every morning. Tom gets angry sometimes. But I tell him, 'Don't worry, Tom. You will learn soon!' Every child learns new things slowly. Tom is learning every day. Next year, he will be able to do more things. I am proud of my little brother.

contentRef.text:
Children at Sunny Day Nursery

Text type: Description
Sunny Day Nursery has children from two to five years old. The children have different abilities. The two- year-olds can walk and run around the room. They can pick up toys and put them in boxes. They can say simple words like 'yes' and 'no'. But they cannot dress themselves completely. They need help with buttons and zips.

The four-year-olds can do much more. They can draw pictures with crayons. They can count to ten in English. Most of them can use scissors carefully. They can put on their coats without help. Some children can even write their first names! They are very proud when they show their work.

The five-year-olds are the oldest group. They can read simple books with small words. They can ride bikes in the playground. They can help younger children with their activities. These children cannot do everything, but they learn something new every single day.

Message from Green Park Primary School

Text type: Notice
Dear Parents,

Next week is Sports Day! We want all children to join in. Please read this information about what your child can and cannot bring.

Your child CAN bring: a water bottle, a sun hat, and comfortable sports shoes. They can bring a small snack for break time. Children can also bring a camera to take photos of their friends.

Your child CANNOT bring: fizzy drinks, sweets, or chocolate bars. They cannot bring pets or toys from home. Children cannot bring mobile phones. We have a school phone for emergencies. They cannot wear jewellery during sports activities. It is not safe.

Please remember: young children cannot stay in the sun too long. We will have shade areas. Children who cannot run can do other activities. Every child can take part! There are games for everyone.

Sports Day starts at 9 o'clock on Friday 15th June. We finish at 2 o'clock. We hope to see you there!

Mrs Sarah Johnson Head Teacher
