contentRef.text:
What Can Children Do at Different Ages?

Text type: Informational
Children grow and learn new skills every year. Here is some information about typical abilities at different ages.

Babies (0-1 year): Babies can cry when they are hungry. At six months, most babies can sit up. At one year, many babies can stand up and say one or two words. They cannot walk far or use a spoon properly yet.

Toddlers (1-3 years): Toddlers can walk and run. They can throw and kick balls. Two-year-olds can say short sentences. Three-year-olds can draw circles and use the toilet by themselves. They cannot read or write yet.

Young children (4-6 years): Four-year-olds can hop on one foot. They can tell simple stories. Five-year-olds can usually write some letters. Six-year-olds can ride a bike without help. They can also play games with rules. But they cannot do difficult maths or read long books.

Remember: every child is different! Some learn faster. Some learn slower. This is completely normal.

Emma and Jack: Two Different Learners

Text type: Comparison
Emma and Jack are both seven years old. They are in the same class at school. But they can do different things.

Emma can read very well. She reads books every night before bed. She can spell long words like 'elephant' and 'computer'. Emma can also play the piano. She practices every day after school. But Emma cannot swim yet. She is scared of water. She also cannot ride a bike. She fell off last year and now she is afraid.

Jack loves sports. He can swim very fast. He can also ride his bike to school. Jack can climb trees in the park. He is very strong and active. But Jack cannot read as well as Emma. He finds reading difficult. He can read short words, but long words are hard. Jack cannot play any musical instruments either.

Their teacher, Miss Brown, says both children are doing well. Emma and Jack are learning at their own speed. Next year, they will both learn new skills and get better.

Children at Different Ages

Hello everyone. Today I want to talk about children. Children can do different things at different ages. When

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

Young children can run and jump, but they cannot drive cars. A five-year-old child can draw pictures but cannot write long stories. Most children can ride a bike when they are seven years old. Babies cannot walk or talk when they are very small. Ten-year-old children can read books but cannot vote in elections.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What can young children do at the playground?

Young children can play on the swings and slide. They can run around and play with their friends. They have lots of fun there.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Can a three-year-old child read books alone?

No, a three-year-old child cannot read books alone. They are too young to read. But they can look at the pictures.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What is something that teenagers can do but young children cannot?

Teenagers can stay home alone, but young children cannot. Teenagers can also cook simple meals. Young children need help with these things.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. At what age can children usually start school?

Children can usually start school at five or six years old. They learn to read and write at school. They also make new friends.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What cannot children do until they are eighteen years old?

Children cannot drive a car until they are eighteen. They cannot vote in elections either. These things are only for adults.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Can / Can't (Ability and Permission)

We use 'can' to say someone is able to do something or has permission.

We use 'can't' (cannot) to say they are not able or do not have permission.

The form stays the same for all subjects.

FORMS

FormExample
Subject + can + base verbChildren can learn new words quickly.
Subject + can't / cannot + base verbYoung babies can't walk yet.
Can + subject + base verb + ?Can your sister swim?
Question: Yes, subject + can / No, subject + can'tYes, she can. / No, she can't.
Negative question: Can't + subject + base verb + ?Can't he ride a bike yet?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ He cans ride a bike.

✓ He can ride a bike.

Can never takes -s with he/she/it.

✗ She can rides a bike.

✓ She can ride a bike.

After can, always use the base verb without -s or -ing.

✗ Do you can swim?

✓ Can you swim?

Questions with can do not need do/does.

nodes.text: EXERCISES

nodes.question: Q1. My baby sister is only six months old, so she ___ walk.
nodes.explanation: → A six-month-old baby is too young to walk, so she is not able to do it.

nodes.question: Q2. Tom is five years old and he ___ count to one hundred.
nodes.explanation: → Tom has the ability to count to one hundred, so we use can.

nodes.question: Q3. In our school, children ___ use the computer room at lunch time.
nodes.explanation: → The school allows children to use the room, so they have permission.

nodes.question: Q4. My three-year-old son ___ read books yet, but he likes pictures.
nodes.explanation: → The word 'yet' shows he does not have the ability now.

nodes.question: Q5. Anna is seven and she ___ ride her bike without help now.
nodes.explanation: → Anna has learned the skill, so she has the ability to ride alone.

nodes.question: Q6. Students ___ bring phones to class because the teacher says no.
nodes.explanation: → The teacher has a rule against phones, so students do not have permission.

nodes.question: Q7. Most four-year-olds ___ write their names, but not full sentences.
nodes.explanation: → The sentence says they are able to write their names.

nodes.question: Q8. Children under twelve ___ watch this film; it is only for teenagers.
nodes.explanation: → The film has an age rule, so younger children do not have permission.

nodes.question: Q9. My daughter is eight and she ___ speak two languages very well.
nodes.explanation: → She has learned both languages, so she has the ability to speak them.

nodes.question: Q10. Babies ___ understand everything, but they listen to your voice.
nodes.explanation: → Babies do not have the ability to understand all words yet.

nodes.question: Q11. In this playground, children ___ play football after school finishes.
nodes.explanation: → The playground allows football, so children have permission to play.

nodes.question: Q12. Jake is only two, so he ___ tie his shoes by himself.
nodes.explanation: → At age two, Jake is too young to have this skill.

nodes.question: Q13. Children ___ eat sweets in the library because it is a quiet place.
nodes.explanation: → The library has a rule against eating, so children do not have permission.

nodes.question: Q14. My nephew is six and he ___ swim across the pool now.
nodes.explanation: → He has learned to swim, so he has the ability to do it.

nodes.question: Q15. Pupils ___ leave the classroom during the lesson without asking first.
nodes.explanation: → The rule is that pupils must ask, so they do not have permission to leave freely.

nodes.question: Q16. Most children ___ draw pictures before they learn to write.
nodes.explanation: → Children develop the ability to draw before writing, so they are able to do it.

nodes.question: Q17. Students ___ use dictionaries in the exam; the teacher allows it.
nodes.explanation: → The teacher allows dictionaries, so students have permission to use them.

nodes.question: Q18. My little brother is four and he ___ spell his own name. He learned it last month.
nodes.explanation: → This shows ability or possibility, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q19. Children ___ run in the school hall because the floor is slippery.
nodes.explanation: → The floor is dangerous, so the school does not allow running there.

nodes.question: Q20. At age ten, most kids ___ tell the time on a clock.
nodes.explanation: → Most ten-year-olds have learned this skill, so they have the ability.

nodes.question: Q21. Young children ___ sit still for two hours during a long film.
nodes.explanation: → Young children do not have the ability to stay still for such a long time.

nodes.question: Q22. Teenagers ___ borrow books from the adult section in our library. The library allows it.
nodes.explanation: → The action is allowed, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q23. My cousin is nine and she ___ play the piano beautifully.
nodes.explanation: → She has learned to play, so she has the ability to play beautifully.

nodes.question: Q24. Children ___ bring toys to school on Fridays for show and tell. The school allows it.
nodes.explanation: → The action is allowed, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q25. A five-year-old ___ understand difficult maths problems in secondary school books.
nodes.explanation: → Secondary school maths is too hard for a five-year-old, so they do not have the ability.

nodes.question: Q26. In this class, students ___ choose their own reading book every week. The teacher allows it.
nodes.explanation: → The action is allowed, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q27. Most seven-year-olds ___ dress themselves without help from parents.
nodes.explanation: → By age seven, most children have learned to dress alone, so they have the ability.

nodes.question: Q28. Pupils ___ shout in the classroom because it disturbs other students.
nodes.explanation: → Shouting disturbs others, so it is not allowed in the classroom.

nodes.question: Q29. My eight-year-old neighbour ___ cook simple meals like toast and eggs.
nodes.explanation: → At age eight, the child has learned to cook simple things, so they have the ability.

nodes.question: Q30. Children under five ___ go on the big slide because it is too high.
nodes.explanation: → The slide is too high for safety, so young children do not have permission.

lessons.titleKm: Talking About What Children Can and Cannot Do — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Talking About What Children Can and Cannot Do — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about what young children aged 2-3 can and cannot do. Use simple examples from everyday life. (40–60 words)

  • Start with what children at this age can do
  • Add what they cannot do yet
  • Use 'can' and 'cannot' in your sentences

Key structures: can + verb, cannot + verb

Model
Young children aged two or three can do many things. They can walk and run. They can say simple words like 'mum' and 'dad'. They can eat with a spoon. However, they cannot read or write. They cannot ride a bike yet. They cannot swim without help from adults.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about what children aged 2-3 can do and cannot do yet, using can and cannot with everyday examples.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: can, cannot, walk, run, ride, swim, eat, read, write, yet. Structures: can + verb; cannot + verb; cannot ... yet.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: The text is about children aged 2-3 and gives at least two believable things they can do (for example walk, run, eat with a spoon) and at least two things they cannot do yet (for example read, ride a bike). Good: The text gives both a can part and a cannot part for age 2-3, but with only one example on one side, or two examples that are almost the same. Developing: Only things children can do, or only things they cannot do, are given; or the examples do not fit age 2-3 (for example 'two-year-olds can write a letter'). Beginning: One or two unclear sentences, or the text is about a different age or topic, so the task is not really answered.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses can and cannot several times with week verbs such as walk, run, eat, ride, swim, read, write, and adds 'yet' at least once (for example 'They cannot swim yet'). Good: Uses both can and cannot at least twice and mostly week verbs, but does not use 'yet' or repeats the same verb. Developing: Uses can or cannot only once or twice, or writes 'is can' / 'don't can' instead of cannot, with very few week verbs. Beginning: No can or cannot sentence, or the writer uses only words from outside the week.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Every can/cannot sentence has the base verb after it ('They can run') and the sentences are complete with capital letters and full stops. Good: Mostly correct, with one or two slips such as 'can runs', 'can to eat' or 'cannot ride bike' that do not stop the reader understanding. Developing: Repeated errors after can (for example 'can walking', 'cannot to read') or missing subjects, but the message can still be guessed. Beginning: Almost every sentence has errors, so it is hard to know what children can or cannot do.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Says first what children can do, then uses 'but' or 'however' to turn to what they cannot do yet, so the reader sees two clear parts. Good: The can sentences and cannot sentences are mostly grouped, with one sentence out of place. Developing: Can and cannot ideas are mixed in a list with no clear order, so the reader must work to follow. Beginning: Ideas are too few or too jumbled to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two or more can and two or more cannot sentences for age 2-3, with 'yet', and very few errors. | 75-89: Both parts present with believable examples; a few verb-form errors. | 60-74: Message clear but only one example on one side, or several errors after can. | 40-59: Mostly one-sided or very short; can/cannot often wrong. | 0-39: Little or nothing about age 2-3; no can/cannot sentences.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'cannt' or 'swin'; 'can not' written as two words; missing 'a' or 'the' (for example 'eat with spoon'); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a missing 's' on 'two year olds'.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59 because there is not room for both can and cannot parts; over 65 is fine if still on topic.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic abilities are fine (say simple words, climb stairs, kick a ball, draw lines; cannot tie shoelaces, count to 100, read books). Using 'is able to / is unable to' is also acceptable. The model's exact examples are not required. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: If the learner pastes the task instructions, writes about another age group or unrelated text, give 0-20 and ask them to write about age 2-3. If the model answer is copied word-for-word, give 100 and note that next time they should use their own sentences.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a specific can or cannot sentence the learner wrote, for example their example about a child eating or running. 2) Fix: Correct the most common verb error, for example: 'Write: They can run (not: They can runs).' 3) Next step: Add one more thing children cannot do yet, using 'yet', for example 'They cannot read yet.'

lessons.titleKm: Talking About What Children Can and Cannot Do — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Talking About What Children Can and Cannot Do — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Describe the abilities of primary school children aged 6-8. Write about their physical and learning skills for a teacher training class. (60–80 words)

  • Include both physical activities and school learning
  • Use linking words like 'also' and 'but'
  • Give specific examples teachers can observe

Key structures: can + verb, also/but, at this age

Model
Children aged six to eight can do many things at school. They can read simple books and write short sentences. They can count to one hundred. These children can also ride bikes and play football. They can follow classroom rules. But they cannot sit still for very long. They cannot understand difficult words yet. At this age, children learn best through games and fun activities. Teachers need to give them short tasks.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words for a teacher training class about the physical and learning skills of children aged 6-8, using also, but and 'at this age'.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: skill, able, unable, count, draw, climb, ride, tie, read, write. Structures: can + verb; also / but; at this age.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes children aged 6-8 with at least one physical skill (for example ride a bike, play football, climb) and at least one school skill (for example read short books, count to 100), and gives at least one limit with an example a teacher could actually see. Good: Includes both a physical skill and a school skill but the examples are general (for example 'they can do many things') or there is no limit given. Developing: Covers only physical skills or only school skills, or the examples are for the wrong age (for example 'they can drive' or 'they cannot walk'). Beginning: Almost no information about ages 6-8; one or two unclear sentences.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses can and cannot with week verbs (ride, count, tie, read, write) and links ideas with 'also' and 'but' correctly, and includes 'at this age' or a similar phrase. Good: Uses can/cannot and at least one of also or but correctly; 'at this age' is missing or placed awkwardly. Developing: Uses can/cannot but no linking words, or puts also/but in the wrong place (for example 'They also can' is fine, 'They but can' is not). Beginning: No clear use of can/cannot or linking words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Base verb after can/cannot, 'they' used with the right verb, and sentences are complete; one small slip at most. Good: A few errors (for example 'They can reads', 'children can plays football') but meaning is clear. Developing: Many sentence-level errors such as missing verbs ('Children also football') or wrong verb forms after can. Beginning: Errors make most sentences hard to understand.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Groups physical skills together and learning skills together, then ends with what teachers should notice or do, so the paragraph reads in a clear order. Good: Physical and learning skills are both there, but the order is sometimes mixed. Developing: A list of separate sentences with no grouping or linking. Beginning: Hard to follow or too short to have an order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Physical and school skills with observable examples, also/but used well, few errors. | 75-89: Both skill types covered; linking words present; minor errors. | 60-74: Only partly covers physical or learning skills, or no linking words. | 40-59: Short, general and with frequent errors after can. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'children' / 'childrens' mix-ups; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; using 'but' at the start of a sentence like the model.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Below about 45 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Other skills are fine (jump rope, skip, write their name, read a clock, share, follow rules). Learners may use 'also' or 'and' for adding, and 'but' or 'however' for limits. The model answer is only a reference. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted task text, text about another age group or unrelated writing: score 0-20 and ask for ages 6-8. A word-for-word copy of the model answer gets 100 with a note to use own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a physical or school example the learner gave, such as riding a bike or counting. 2) Fix: Fix the most important error with a model, for example: 'Write: They can also play football (not: They also can plays football).' 3) Next step: Add one limit with 'but', for example 'But they cannot sit still for long.'

lessons.titleKm: Talking About What Children Can and Cannot Do — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Talking About What Children Can and Cannot Do — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Compare what babies and five-year-old children can do. Write this information for parents in a childcare centre newsletter. (80–110 words)

  • Start with what babies can do
  • Then explain what five-year-olds can do
  • Show clearly how children develop and grow

Key structures: when/while, can/cannot, but/however

Model
Babies and five-year-old children are very different. When babies are born, they cannot do much. They cannot walk or talk. They can only cry, sleep and drink milk. Babies need help with everything. However, five-year-old children can do a lot. They can walk, run and climb. They can talk in full sentences. They can dress themselves and use the toilet alone. These children can play games with rules. They can also learn letters and numbers. They can share toys with friends. While babies need adults all the time, five-year- olds can do many things by themselves. This shows how much children learn and grow.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words for a childcare centre newsletter comparing what babies can and cannot do with what five-year-olds can do, so parents see how children grow.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: baby, able, unable, walk, talk, climb, dress, tie, skill, yet. Structures: can / cannot; when / while; but / however.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts with babies (what they cannot do and the few things they can, for example cry, sleep, drink milk), then explains five-year-olds with several abilities (for example talk in sentences, dress themselves), and ends with a sentence about growing and learning. Good: Covers both babies and five-year-olds with at least two points each, but the comparison or the closing idea about growth is missing. Developing: Writes mostly about only one age group, or the abilities given for the two ages are not clearly different. Beginning: Very little about babies or five-year-olds; no comparison.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses can and cannot for both ages, and connects the two groups with when or while and with but or however in correct sentences (for example 'While babies need adults, five-year-olds can do many things alone'). Good: Uses can/cannot well and one connector (when, while, but or however) correctly. Developing: Uses can/cannot but connectors are missing or wrongly used (for example 'While but babies cannot walk'). Beginning: Little use of can/cannot and no connectors.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Accurate verb forms after can/cannot, correct 'babies' plural and 'they' agreement, with no more than two small errors. Good: Some errors such as 'babies cannot walks' or 'five-year-old children can talks' but the meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in verbs, plurals ('babys') and sentence structure; the reader sometimes has to guess. Beginning: Many errors in every sentence; meaning is unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Has a clear order: babies first, then five-year-olds, then a closing line, with connectors that make the contrast obvious to parents. Good: The order babies then five-year-olds is clear, but the ending is missing or the connectors are few. Developing: Babies and five-year-olds are mixed together, so the contrast is hard to see. Beginning: Ideas are too short or mixed to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear baby-to-five comparison with a closing idea, connectors used well, few errors. | 75-89: Both ages covered with some connectors; minor errors. | 60-74: Both ages mentioned but the comparison is weak or connectors are missing. | 40-59: Mostly one age or many errors. | 0-39: Off task or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'beby'; missing hyphen in 'five-year-olds'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a missing 'the' or 'a'; a slightly informal newsletter tone.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words, cap at 59 because the comparison cannot be complete.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any believable abilities are acceptable (babies: smile, crawl, hold a toy; five-year-olds: hop, draw, count, share). 'But' or 'however' and 'when' or 'while' may be swapped if the grammar is right. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for the baby versus five-year-old comparison. Word-for-word copy of the model answer gets 100 with a note to write in own words next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear contrast the learner made between babies and five-year-olds. 2) Fix: Show the key correction, for example: 'Write: While babies cannot walk, five-year-olds can run (not: While babies cannot walks...).' 3) Next step: Finish with one sentence about growing, such as 'Children learn new skills every year.'

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about what a young child (age 3-5) can and cannot do. Give examples of their abilities. (40–60 words)

  • Say how old the child is.
  • Write two or three things the child can do.
  • Write one or two things the child cannot do yet.
Model
My cousin Lucy is four years old. She can run very fast and jump high. She can sing songs and draw pictures. Lucy can count to twenty. But she cannot tie her shoelaces yet. She cannot read words. She is learning new things every day. I think she is very clever.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about one child aged 3-5: say the age, two or three things the child can do, and one or two things the child cannot do yet.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: can, cannot, yet, run, jump, sing, draw, count, tie, years old. Structures: He/She is ... years old; can + verb; cannot ... yet.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: States the child's age (3, 4 or 5), gives two or three abilities and one or two things the child cannot do yet, all believable for that age.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Writes 'He/She is four years old', uses can for abilities and cannot with 'yet' for limits, with week verbs like run, jump, sing, draw, count, tie.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'is' correctly with the age, he/she matches the child, base verb after can/cannot; only tiny slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order is age, then abilities, then what the child cannot do yet, optionally ending with a short comment about the child.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; '4 years old' written with a number; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a missing full stop here and there; using a real child (own child, cousin) or an imaginary child.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any child aged 3-5, real or invented, and any believable abilities. 'My son', 'my niece' or a student's name are all fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or off-topic writing: 0-20 with a request to describe one child. Copied model answer word-for-word: 100 and ask for own sentences next time.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Identifying learner difficulties

Finding out what problems a student has with learning. Teachers need to know what is hard for each student.

Example:Can you explain what is difficult for you in this lesson?
Connection:Teachers ask these questions every day in the classroom when students need help.
  • 2. Giving learning advice

Telling students what they should do to improve. Good advice helps students learn better and feel confident.

Example:You should practice reading every day to improve your English.
Connection:You will read this advice in textbooks and hear it from teachers in class.
  • 3. Supporting different learners

Helping each student in the way they need. Not all students learn the same way or have the same problems.

Example:Some learners need more time, so teachers must be patient with them.
Connection:Teachers use these ideas when they plan lessons and work with students in the classroom.
  • 4. Encouraging progress

Making students feel good about their learning and helping them continue. Encouragement helps learners try hard and not give up.

Example:Don't worry about mistakes—they help you learn and make progress!
Connection:You will see this language in feedback from teachers and in education books.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
I don't understand.
I don't understand.
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The student said, 'I don't understand this word.'
🔉 Spoken Example:

Can you help me?
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
When you need support, you can say, 'Can you help me?'
🔉 Spoken Example:
You should...
You should...
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The teacher said, 'You should practice every day.'
🔉 Spoken Example:

I need to...
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The learner wrote, 'I need to repeat this lesson.'
🔉 Spoken Example:

It's difficult.
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Many students say, 'Grammar is difficult for me.'
🔉 Spoken Example:
Can I try again?
Can I try again?
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
After a mistake, you can ask, 'Can I try again?'
🔉 Spoken Example:
I'm confused.
I'm confused.
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
If you don't understand, say, 'I'm confused about this question.'
🔉 Spoken Example:
You must...
You must...
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The teacher explained, 'You must listen carefully in class.'
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. help — Help means to make something easier for someone.
  2. support — Support is help that you give to someone.
  3. learner — A learner is a person who is learning something new.
  4. explain — Explain means to tell someone about something so they understand.
  5. patient — Patient means able to stay calm and not get angry.
  6. understand — Understand means to know what something means.
  7. practice — Practice means to do something many times to get better.
  8. encourage — Encourage means to give someone confidence to do something.
  9. mistake — A mistake is something wrong that you do or say.
  10. repeat — Repeat means to say or do something again.
  11. listen — Listen means to pay attention to sounds or words.
  12. confused — Confused means not able to think clearly or understand.
  13. progress — Progress is improvement that happens over time.
  14. confident — Confident means feeling sure about what you can do.
  15. difficult — Difficult means not easy to do or understand.
  16. slowly — Slowly means at a low speed, not fast.
  17. improve — Improve means to become better at something.
  18. try — Try means to make an effort to do something.
  19. feedback — Feedback is comments that help someone do better.
  20. question — A question is something you ask when you want information.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words about helping learners and giving support in class.
Reading
Read short messages from students about their learning problems and what help they need.
Listening
Listen to teachers and students talking about difficulties and asking for help.
Speaking
Practice asking and answering questions about problems a learner is having in class.
Grammar
Use modal verbs like should, must, can, and need to when giving advice to learners.
Writing
Write simple sentences that give helpful advice to a learner who needs support.
Lesson Test
The test checks all the skills from this lesson, and 70 percent is a good score.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'encourage' comes from old French and means 'to make someone brave.' When teachers encourage students, they help them feel brave enough to try new things and learn from their mistakes!

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching: The Essential Guide to English Language Teaching — Jim Scrivener (2011). This book explains how teachers can support learners with different needs in simple English. How to Teach English — Jeremy Harmer (2007). Chapter 4 talks about helping students and giving feedback in clear, easy language.

▶ Classroom English for Teachers — British Council LearnEnglish ▶ English for Teachers — Cambridge English

MINI STORY

Maria is a new learner in our class. Sometimes she feels confused about the lessons. They are difficult for her. She makes mistakes when she writes.

I try to help Maria every day. I sit with her and explain the homework slowly. She listens carefully to me. I am patient when she does not understand. I encourage her to ask questions. When she makes a mistake, I help her learn from it. We practice together after class.

Now Maria is making good progress. She can repeat new words correctly. She feels more confident in class. The teacher gives positive feedback about her work. Maria is happy because she can improve her English every week. She understands that learning takes time and support from friends.

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

Maria Helps Her Friend

Text type: Narrative
Maria sat next to Tom in class. Tom looked sad. He did not understand the math homework. Maria saw his empty notebook. She asked, "Do you need help?" Tom said yes quietly.

Maria took out her notebook. She showed Tom her work. She explained each step slowly. Tom listened carefully. He asked questions. Maria answered with patience. She drew pictures to make it easier.

After twenty minutes, Tom smiled. He said, "Now I understand! Thank you so much." Maria felt happy too. She helped her friend learn something new. The next day, Tom finished his homework. The teacher was pleased. Tom thanked Maria again.

How to Help Someone Study

Text type: Informational
Do you want to help a friend with their studies? Here are some easy steps. First, find a quiet place to work. Turn off the TV and music. You both need to focus.

Second, ask your friend what they do not understand. Listen carefully to their answer. Do not tell them all the answers quickly. Instead, explain things step by step. Use simple words. Give examples. Be patient and kind. If they make mistakes, do not laugh. Help them find the correct answer.

Third, check their work together. Ask questions like "Do you understand now?" Take breaks if you work for a long time. Give them time to think. After studying, say something positive. Tell them they did well. Good support makes learning easier and more fun.

Anna and Ben both help other students at school. But they help in different ways. Anna likes to work one-on- one with students. She meets one person at a time. They sit together at a table. contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Some students need extra help with their school work. A good teacher listens carefully to the student's problems. You can explain the lesson again in a simple way. It is important to be patient and kind with learners.

Helping a student makes them feel happy and confident.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. How can you help a student who doesn't understand the lesson?

I can explain the lesson again slowly. I can use simple words and examples. I can also ask them questions to check.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Why is it important to be patient with students who need support?

Students learn at different speeds. If you are patient, they feel safe. They are not afraid to ask questions.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What can you do if a student feels sad or worried about studying?

I can talk to them and listen carefully. I can help them with their problems. I can tell them they can do it.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Can you give an example of helping a classmate with their homework?

Yes, my friend didn't understand maths. I showed her the steps slowly. We did the exercises together and she understood.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What are good ways to encourage a learner who finds studying difficult?

You can say positive things like 'Good job!' You can give them small, easy tasks first. You should smile and be friendly.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs: should, must, can, need to

Modal verbs help us give advice, talk about rules, and say what is possible.

We use 'should' for advice, 'must' for strong rules, 'can' for ability or permission, and 'need to' for necessary things.

FORMS

FormExample
should + base verb (advice)You should help your friend with homework.
must + base verb (strong rule / obligation)Teachers must listen to all students.
can + base verb (ability / permission)I can explain this question again.
need to + base verb (necessary action)He needs to ask for help today.
Negative: should not / must not / cannot / do not need toYou must not ignore a student's question.
Question: Should / Must / Can + subject + base verb?Should I repeat the instructions?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ You should to help him.

✓ You should help him.

Never use 'to' after modal verbs like should, must, or can.

✗ She musts ask the teacher.

✓ She must ask the teacher.

Modal verbs never add -s, even with he/she/it.

✗ I can to answer your question.

✓ I can answer your question.

Use the base verb after 'can', not 'to + verb'.

nodes.question: Q1. The teacher says all students ___ bring a pencil to class every day. It is a rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q2. You ___ sit next to Anna if she feels nervous in class.
nodes.explanation: → This is good advice to help Anna, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q3. I ___ explain this grammar point again if you don't understand. I am happy to, and it is not a duty.
nodes.explanation: → This shows ability or possibility, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q4. Students ___ talk during the test; it is not allowed.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'must not'.

nodes.question: Q5. He ___ practise reading every day to improve his English.
nodes.explanation: → Daily practice is necessary for improvement, so 'needs to' is correct.

nodes.question: Q6. We ___ help classmates who have difficulty with their homework.
nodes.explanation: → Helping classmates is good advice, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q7. The school rules say students ___ wear a uniform every day.
nodes.explanation: → School rules create a strong obligation, so 'must' is correct.

nodes.question: Q8. Maria ___ use a dictionary during the reading activity if she wants.
nodes.explanation: → 'Can' shows that Maria has permission to use a dictionary.

nodes.question: Q9. You ___ shout at a student who makes a mistake. It is against the rules.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'must not'.

nodes.question: Q10. Tom ___ finish his homework by tomorrow because the teacher will check it.
nodes.explanation: → Finishing by tomorrow is necessary because of the deadline, so 'needs to' is correct.

nodes.question: Q11. Teachers ___ give extra time to students who work slowly.
nodes.explanation: → Giving extra time is good advice for helping slow learners, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q12. You ___ copy answers from your friend during the exam; it is cheating.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'must not'.

nodes.question: Q13. Sara ___ ask the teacher questions after class if she is confused.
nodes.explanation: → 'Can' shows that Sara is able and allowed to ask questions.

nodes.question: Q14. All students ___ attend the safety training next Monday; it is required.
nodes.explanation: → Attendance is required, so 'must' shows this strong obligation.

nodes.question: Q15. You ___ spend some time each day reviewing your notes to remember better. This is advice, not a rule.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q16. We ___ wait for everyone to finish before we leave the classroom.
nodes.explanation: → Waiting is necessary because everyone must finish first, so 'need to' is correct.

nodes.question: Q17. Students ___ bring their own lunch or buy food at the canteen. They can choose.
nodes.explanation: → The action is allowed, so we use 'can'.

nodes.question: Q18. You ___ speak loudly in the library; other people are reading.
nodes.explanation: → Speaking loudly in a library is against the rules, so 'must not' is correct.

nodes.question: Q19. If a student feels unwell, the teacher ___ send them to the nurse.
nodes.explanation: → Sending an unwell student to the nurse is good advice, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q20. Every learner ___ bring a notebook to write new vocabulary words.
nodes.explanation: → A notebook is necessary for vocabulary work, so 'needs to' is correct.

nodes.question: Q21. You ___ encourage a shy student to speak in small group activities.
nodes.explanation: → Encouraging shy students is good advice, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q22. I ___ help you with your project after school today if you want.
nodes.explanation: → 'Can' shows that I am able and willing to offer help.

nodes.question: Q23. Teachers ___ arrive late to class; it sets a bad example.
nodes.explanation: → Being late is against professional rules, so 'must not' is correct.

nodes.question: Q24. You ___ check your work carefully before you give it to the teacher.
nodes.explanation: → Checking work is good advice to find mistakes, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q25. Students ___ submit their essays by Friday or they will lose marks.
nodes.explanation: → The deadline creates a strong obligation because of the consequence, so 'must' is correct.

nodes.question: Q26. A good tutor ___ explain difficult topics in simple words for learners.
nodes.explanation: → Using simple words is good advice for tutors, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q27. If you don't understand, you ___ raise your hand and ask immediately.
nodes.explanation: → 'Can' shows that you have the ability and permission to ask.

nodes.question: Q28. We ___ prepare all materials before the lesson starts tomorrow morning.
nodes.explanation: → Preparing before the lesson is necessary, so 'need to' is correct.

nodes.question: Q29. You ___ give positive feedback when a struggling student tries hard.
nodes.explanation: → Giving positive feedback is good advice for motivation, so 'should' is correct.

nodes.question: Q30. Learners ___ use their phones during the exam; it is strictly forbidden.
nodes.explanation: → Using phones in exams breaks a strict rule, so 'must not' is correct.

lessons.titleKm: Helping a Learner Who Needs Support — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Helping a Learner Who Needs Support — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about how you know a learner needs support. Describe what you can see or hear. (40–60 words)

  • Describe what the learner looks like or does
  • Mention what the learner might say
  • Use simple present tense for general facts

Key structures: Present simple (looks, seems, asks), Modal verb 'can' for possibility

Model
Sometimes a learner needs extra support in class. You can see this when they look confused or worried. They often ask many questions or they stay very quiet. They might not finish their work on time. Their body language shows they feel nervous or upset about the lesson.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about how a teacher knows a learner needs support, describing what the learner looks like or does and what the learner might say.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: support, learner, confused, worried, nervous, quiet, question, mistake, difficult, finish. Structures: Present simple (looks, seems, asks); can for possibility; They might say ....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes at least two things the teacher can see (for example looks confused, stays quiet, does not finish work) and gives at least one thing the learner might say, such as 'I don't understand'. Good: Describes one or two signs of needing support but does not include what the learner might say, or the signs are very general. Developing: Gives only a general sentence ('The learner has a problem') with no visible sign, or describes the teacher instead of the learner. Beginning: Does not explain how to know a learner needs support; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses week words such as confused, worried, quiet, mistake, difficult and present simple verbs like 'looks', 'seems' and 'asks' correctly, with 'can' or 'might' for possibility. Good: Uses several week words and some present simple, but not looks/seems or can for possibility. Developing: Uses one or two week words only, or writes 'he is look confused'. Beginning: No week vocabulary; writes in general words only.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is used correctly (the learner looks, asks, stays) and sentences are complete; one slip at most. Good: Some errors, such as 'The learner look confused' or 'She not understand', but the meaning is clear. Developing: Many missing verbs or wrong forms ('is ask', 'not finish'), so some sentences need guessing. Beginning: Grammar makes most sentences unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Moves in order from what you see, to what the learner does, to what the learner says, with simple linking such as 'and' or 'or'. Good: Signs are grouped sensibly with a small order problem. Developing: Signs are listed one by one with no link. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: At least two visible signs plus what the learner may say, accurate third-person verbs. | 75-89: Signs are clear; one part is thin; small errors. | 60-74: Understandable but general or with many -s errors. | 40-59: Very short or mostly unclear. | 0-39: Off topic or not enough text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'confuse' for confused; missing -s that is still understandable; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'student' instead of 'learner'; missing articles.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Other signs are fine (does not look at the teacher, plays with a pen, copies from friends, has a low voice, says 'It is too hard'). Writing in 'you' or 'the learner' or 'they' are all acceptable. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for signs a learner needs support. Word-for-word copy of the model answer gets 100 with a note to write own sentences next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a specific sign the learner noticed, for example 'stays quiet' or 'looks worried'. 2) Fix: Correct one verb form, for example: 'Write: The learner looks confused (not: The learner look confused).' 3) Next step: Add what the learner might say, for example 'He may say, "I do not understand."'

lessons.titleKm: Helping a Learner Who Needs Support — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Helping a Learner Who Needs Support — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about what you can do to help a learner who needs support. Give practical examples of helpful actions. (60–80 words)

  • Give two or three different ways to help
  • Use 'can' or 'should' to give advice
  • Include what to say and what to do

Key structures: Modal verbs 'can' and 'should' for advice, Sequencing with 'first', 'then', 'also', Imperative forms for instructions

Model
There are many ways to help a learner who needs support. First, sit with them and speak in a calm, friendly way. You can ask simple questions like 'What part is difficult for you?' Then explain the problem slowly and clearly. Use easy words and give examples. You should also check their work and give positive feedback. Be patient if they make mistakes. You can also give them extra time to finish their work.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words giving two or three practical ways to help a learner who needs support, including what to say and what to do.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: help, explain, patient, understand, example, slowly, feedback, practise, encourage, extra time. Structures: can / should for advice; First, then, also; imperatives (Sit with them, Use easy words).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives two or three different, practical ways to help, includes at least one thing to say (for example 'What part is difficult for you?') and at least one thing to do (sit with the learner, give extra time). Good: Gives two ways to help but does not include both something to say and something to do. Developing: Gives one way to help or only general advice ('help them a lot') with no practical action. Beginning: No clear advice; off topic or too short.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'can' or 'should' for advice correctly, orders ideas with First/Then/Also, and uses imperatives like 'Explain slowly' and week words such as patient, example, feedback. Good: Uses can or should and at least one sequence word, with some week vocabulary. Developing: Uses advice language once, or writes 'You should to explain'. Beginning: No advice structure; only statements.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Base verb after can/should and correct imperatives; sentences complete; one small slip at most. Good: Errors such as 'should explains', 'You can to ask' or missing 'the' that do not stop understanding. Developing: Frequent verb form errors or fragments; some advice is hard to follow. Beginning: Errors make the advice unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Advice follows a clear order with First, Then and Also (or similar), so a new teacher could follow the steps. Good: Order is mostly clear; sequence words are few. Developing: Advice is a list without order or links. Beginning: Ideas are mixed and hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Two or three practical actions with something to say, clear sequence, accurate can/should. | 75-89: Good advice, order clear, minor errors. | 60-74: Advice understandable but thin, or few sequence words. | 40-59: Very short or general; many structure errors. | 0-39: No usable advice or off task.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'should' used where 'can' would also work; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; commands without 'please'.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Under about 45 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible help is acceptable (use pictures, pair with a friend, repeat the instruction, praise small progress, give easier tasks). 'Then', 'next', 'after that' may replace First/Then. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted task instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for ways to help a learner. Word-for-word copy of the model answer gets 100 with a note to use own sentences.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one practical idea the learner suggested, for example sitting with the learner or giving extra time. 2) Fix: Correct one structure, for example: 'Write: You should check their work (not: You should to checks their work).' 3) Next step: Add one sentence of what you can say, in quotation marks.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about why helping learners is important and how it makes them feel. Include what happens when learners get good support. (80–110 words)

  • Explain the benefits of giving support
  • Describe how the learner feels before and after help
  • Mention what the learner can do after receiving help

Key structures: Present simple for facts and routines, Conjunctions 'because', 'when', 'so', Comparative adjectives (more confident, better)

Model
Helping a learner who needs support is very important because it changes how they feel about learning. When a learner gets help, they feel less worried and more confident. They understand the lesson better and they can do the work. This makes them happier at school. Good support also helps learners believe in themselves. They try harder and they don't give up easily. When teachers and classmates give support, learners make progress and feel proud of their work. Everyone can learn well when they have the right help and encouragement. A positive learning environment helps all students succeed.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words explaining why support is important, how the learner feels before and after help, and what the learner can do after getting help.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: support, confident, worried, progress, understand, encourage, patient, proud, better, give up. Structures: because / when / so; comparatives (more confident, better); present simple for facts.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Explains at least one benefit of support, describes feelings before help (for example worried, confused) and after help (for example more confident, happier), and says what the learner can do after help. Good: Covers benefit and feelings, but one part is missing, usually what the learner can do afterwards. Developing: Mentions that support is good but gives no clear before/after feelings or results. Beginning: Very little relevant content; off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses because, when and so correctly to give reasons and results, uses at least one comparative like 'more confident' or 'better', and week words such as progress, worried, proud. Good: Uses two of the target structures correctly, with some week words. Developing: Uses one connector or no comparative, or 'more better'. Beginning: No target structures or week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple correct (learners feel, a teacher gives), comparatives formed correctly, sentences complete; one or two small slips. Good: Some errors ('more better', 'he feel') but the meaning is clear. Developing: Many errors with verbs and comparatives; some sentences unclear. Beginning: Grammar errors hide the meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Moves in a clear order: why support matters, then before-help feelings, then after-help feelings and abilities, with connectors linking them. Good: The order is mostly clear but connectors are few. Developing: Ideas are listed without a clear order. Beginning: Too short or mixed to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Benefit, before/after feelings and result all clear; connectors and comparatives correct. | 75-89: Most parts present; small errors. | 60-74: One part missing or connectors weak. | 40-59: Very general or short, many errors. | 0-39: Off task or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'confidence' used instead of 'confident' if the idea is clear; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; a missing comma before because/so.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any believable benefit and feeling is fine (less afraid, happier, tries harder, asks questions, does homework alone). Learners may write about their own experience of being helped. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or off-topic writing: 0-20 and ask for the topic. Word-for-word copy of the model answer: 100 with a note to use own words.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear before/after idea the learner wrote, for example feeling worried then confident. 2) Fix: Fix the key error, for example: 'Write: They feel more confident (not: They feel more better).' 3) Next step: Add one sentence with 'so' showing a result, such as 'She is happy, so she asks questions.'

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about helping a learner who needs support. Explain what you can do to help. (40–60 words)

  • Say who needs help and why.
  • Explain how you can help them.
  • Say why helping others is good.
Model
Some students struggle with English. They need extra help. I can sit with them and explain new words. I can be patient and kind. We can practice speaking together. When I help someone, they feel more confident. Helping others makes me happy too. Everyone learns better when we work together.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words saying who needs help and why, how you can help them, and why helping others is good.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: help, support, learner, explain, patient, practise, confident, understand, kind, together. Structures: I can + verb; They need ...; When I help ..., they feel ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says who needs help and why (for example a classmate who finds English difficult), explains at least two things I can do (sit with them, explain words, practise together), and gives one reason helping is good.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I can ...' with week verbs like explain, sit, practise, and week words such as patient, confident, support, and links with 'when' or 'because'.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Subject-verb agreement and base verb after can are right ('He needs help', 'I can explain'); only small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Three parts in order: who needs help, how I help, why it is good.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'student' or 'friend' instead of 'learner'; missing -s on 'need'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; imaginary or real examples.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any person who needs help and any reasonable help (a child in my class, a colleague learning English, a neighbour). The model's English-learning example is not required. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Instructions pasted or unrelated writing: 0-20, ask to write about helping. Model answer copied word-for-word: 100, with a note to use own sentences.

contentRef.text:
CHAPTER III · WEEK 18

Chapter 3 Review: Learners and the Classroom

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify key information about different types of learners in short classroom descriptions. L2 Understand
  • Use present simple and classroom vocabulary to describe learner needs and behaviours. L3 Apply
  • Describe different learning styles and basic classroom management situations using simple sentences. L3 Apply
  • Understand short texts about classroom environments and how different learners participate. L3 Apply
  • Write simple sentences comparing two types of learners or classroom arrangements. L3 Apply
  • Reflect on own learning preferences and share ideas with classmates about effective classrooms. L4 Analyze · HOTS

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

classroom noun

Phonetic: KLAS-room

Meaning: a room where students have lessons at school

Khmer: ថ្នាក់រៀន

Example: Our classroom has twenty desks and many books.

learner noun

Phonetic: LER-ner

Meaning: a person who is learning something new

Khmer: អ្នករៀន

Example: Every learner in the class works hard.

teacher noun

Phonetic: TEE-cher

Meaning: a person who helps students learn new things

Khmer: គ្រូ

Example: My teacher explains the lesson very well.

lesson noun

Phonetic: LES-sun

Meaning: a time when a teacher teaches students something

Khmer: មេរៀន

Example: We have an English lesson every Monday morning.

homework noun

Phonetic: HOME-werk

Meaning: work that students do at home after school

Khmer: កិច្ចការផ្ទះ

Example: I finish my homework before dinner every day.

study verb

Phonetic: STUH-dee

Meaning: to learn about something by reading or practicing

Khmer: សិក្សា

Example: I study English for two hours every day.

practice verb

Phonetic: PRAK-tis

Meaning: to do something many times to get better

Khmer: ហ្វឹកហាត់

Example: We practice speaking English in class every week.

notebook noun

Phonetic: NOTE-book

Meaning: a book with empty pages for writing notes

Khmer: សៀវភៅកត់ត្រា

Example: She writes new words in her notebook.

whiteboard noun

Phonetic: WITE-bord

Meaning: a white board on the wall for writing

Khmer: ក្តារខៀន

Example: The teacher writes the answers on the whiteboard.

question noun

Phonetic: KWES-chun

Meaning: something you ask when you want to know

Khmer: សំណួរ

Example: Can I ask a question about the homework?

answer noun

Phonetic: AN-ser

Meaning: what you say or write to a question

Khmer: ចម្លើយ

Example: The answer to question three is very easy.

understand verb

Phonetic: un-der-STAND

Meaning: to know what something means or why it happens

Khmer: យល់

Example: I understand the lesson because the teacher explains well.

explain verb

Phonetic: eks-PLANE

Meaning: to make something clear so others can understand

Khmer: ពន្យល់

Example: Can you explain this word to me please?

group noun

Phonetic: GROOP

Meaning: some people who work or play together

Khmer: ក្រុម

Example: We work in a group of four students.

activity noun

Phonetic: ak-TIV-i-tee

Meaning: something that people do for fun or learning

Khmer: សកម្មភាព

Example: Our classroom activity today is a reading game.

helpful adjective

Phonetic: HELP-ful

Meaning: useful and making things easier for someone

Khmer: ចេះជួយអ្នកដទៃ

Example: My teacher is very helpful when I ask questions.

difficult adjective

Phonetic: DIF-i-kult

Meaning: not easy to do or understand

Khmer: ពិបាក

Example: This English exercise is difficult for me.

mistake noun

Phonetic: mis-TAKE

Meaning: something wrong that you do or say

Khmer: កំហុស

Example: I made a mistake on the test yesterday.

improve verb

Phonetic: im-PROOV

Meaning: to get better at something or make something better

Khmer: កែលម្អ

Example: I want to improve my English speaking skills.

listen verb

Phonetic: LIS-sun

Meaning: to use your ears to hear

Khmer: ស្ដាប់

Example: Please listen to the

MINI STORY

My name is Sara. I am a learner at Green Hill School. I study English every day in my classroom. My classroom is big and bright. We have a whiteboard and many desks.

My teacher, Mr. Brown, is very helpful. He explains every lesson carefully. When I don't understand something, I ask a question. He always gives a good answer. Sometimes the homework is difficult, but I practice every day. I write new words in my notebook.

Today we did a fun activity in class. We worked in a group of five students. We listened to a story and answered questions together. I made one mistake, but that's okay. Everyone makes mistakes when they learn. I want to improve my English. I practice speaking, reading, and writing every week. Learning English is not easy, but it's very interesting!

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

Anna's First Day Teaching

Text type: Narrative
Anna was nervous on her first day as a teacher. She walked into the classroom early in the morning. The room was quiet and empty. She put her books on the desk. She wrote her name on the board.

The students came in at eight o'clock. They looked at Anna with big eyes. Anna smiled at them. She asked their names. The students were shy at first. Then one boy started talking. His name was Tom. Soon all the

students were talking and laughing.

Anna felt happy. The classroom was now full of noise and energy. She learned that good teachers listen to their students. They make the classroom a friendly place. Anna knew this was just the beginning of her teaching journey.

questions.prompt: Q1. What is this story mainly about?

options.text: A. Anna's first day as a teacher
C. How to write on a board

questions.explanation: → The story is mostly about Anna's first day as a teacher: she meets her students and feels happy.

questions.prompt: Q2. What did Anna do before the students came?

options.text: C. She wrote her name on the board

Important Message from the School

To: All Students and Parents
From: Mrs. Johnson, Head Teacher
Date: Monday, 15th March

Dear Students and Parents,

We are making some changes to help our learners. Starting next week, classes will begin at 8:30 instead of 8:00. This gives students more time in the morning. We want everyone to arrive fresh and ready.

We are also starting a homework club. It will be on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Students can stay after school until 4:30. Teachers will help with homework. This club is free for all students.

Please remember to bring your books every day. Keep your classroom clean. Respect your teachers and classmates. Working together makes learning better for everyone.

If you have questions, please email me or call the school office.

Thank you, Mrs. Johnson

contentRef.text:
How Students Learn Best

Text type: Informational
Students learn in different ways. Some students learn best by listening. They like when the teacher talks and explains things. These students remember what they hear. They often like music and stories.

Other students learn by looking at things. They need to see pictures, words, and colors. These students like books with many photos. They enjoy videos and drawings. They remember things they see on the board.

Some students learn by doing activities. They need to move and touch things. These students like games, sports, and hands-on projects. They remember things better when they practice. Good teachers use all these ways in the classroom. They talk, show pictures, and plan activities. This helps every student learn well.

Two Different Learners

Text type: Comparison
Meet Sarah and David. They are both in Class 5B. But they are very different learners. Sarah loves reading books. She is quiet in class. She likes to work alone. Sarah writes notes in her notebook. She studies at home every evening. Tests are easy for her.

David is different. He loves group work and talking with friends. He learns when he works with other students. David likes projects and activities. Sitting quietly is hard for him. He sometimes forgets to do homework. But he is very good at presentations.

contentRef.text:
Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs (must, should, can, may)

Modal verbs show necessity, advice, ability or permission.

We use 'must' for rules and strong necessity.

We use 'should' for advice and suggestions.

We use 'can' for ability and permission.

We use 'may' for polite permission.

FORMS

FormExample
must + base verbStudents must bring their books every day.
should + base verbTeachers should speak clearly in class.
can + base verbChildren can ask questions in lessons.
may + base verbYou may leave the classroom now.
Negative: modal + not + base verbStudents must not run in class.
Question: Modal + subject + base verb?Can I open the window?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ Students must to sit down.

✓ Students must sit down.

Never use 'to' after modal verbs.

✗ Teacher cans help you.

✓ The teacher can help you.

Modal verbs never add -s for he/she/it.

✗ We should not to talk loudly.

✓ We should not talk loudly.

No 'to' after modals, even in negative.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about your classroom. Describe what is in it and why you like it. (40–60 words)

  • Say what furniture is in your classroom.
  • Describe the walls and windows.
  • Explain why you like your classroom.
Model
My classroom is big and bright. We have twenty desks and chairs. The teacher has a desk at the front. There is a white board on the wall. We also have three windows. Fresh air comes in. I like my classroom because it is clean and comfortable. We can learn well here.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about your classroom: what furniture is in it, what the walls and windows are like, and why you like it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: classroom, desk, chair, whiteboard, window, wall, notebook, learner, comfortable, clean. Structures: There is / There are; We have ...; I like my classroom because ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names at least three things in the classroom (for example desks, chairs, whiteboard), says something about the walls and windows (colour, number, what is on them), and gives a reason for liking the classroom.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'There is' for one thing and 'There are' for many correctly, uses 'We have' and 'I like ... because ...', with five or more classroom words such as desk, chair, whiteboard, window, wall.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: There is/are agrees with singular and plural, plurals such as 'desks' and 'windows' are right, and sentences are complete; one or two small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Goes in the order of the task: furniture, then walls and windows, then why I like it, so the reader can picture the room.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'whiteboad'; a missing 'the' or 'a'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; describing a real or imagined classroom; 'blackboard' instead of 'whiteboard'.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any classroom (own school, a dream classroom) and any believable objects (fan, shelf, door, pictures, books) are fine. 'I like it because it is clean' works as the reason. The model answer is only a reference. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or text about something else: 0-20 and ask for a classroom description. Word-for-word copy of the model answer: 100 with a note to describe your own classroom next time.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Timetable information

A timetable shows when classes start and finish. It tells you the room number and the subject.

Example:The Math class is on Monday at 9:00 in Room 12.
Connection:You read timetables on classroom walls and in school apps every day.
  • 2. Notice board messages

A notice gives important information about changes or events. Teachers put notices on the wall or send them online.

Example:Notice: The exam is postponed to Friday at 2:00 p.m.
Connection:You read notices at school to know about cancelled classes and new schedules.
  • 3. Prepositions for time and place

We use small words like at, on, and in to say when and where. They come before times and days.

Example:My lesson is at 10:00 on Tuesday in Room 5.
Connection:Teachers and students use these words to describe schedules and locations clearly.
  • 4. Spoken timetable announcements

Teachers say times, rooms, and subjects out loud. You listen and write the important details.

Example:Please attend the Science lesson at 3:00 in Room 8.
Connection:You hear announcements at school and in teacher meetings every week.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:
