🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. timetable — A list showing the times when things happen.
  2. notice — A written message that gives information to people.
  3. class — A group of students who learn together.
  4. schedule — A plan showing when things will happen.
  5. room — A space inside a building with walls.
  6. subject — A topic you study at school.
  7. break — A short time when you stop working.
  8. start — To begin doing something.
  9. finish — To complete or end something.
  10. period — A length of time for one lesson.
  11. lesson — A time when a teacher teaches students.
  12. teacher — A person who helps students learn.
  13. change — To become different or make something different.
  14. important — Something that matters a lot.
  15. cancel — To stop something that was planned.
  16. Monday — The first day of the week.
  17. exam — A test to check what you know.
  18. postpone — To move something to a later time.
  19. location — The place where something is.
  20. attend — To go to and be present at something.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words about timetables, notices, and school schedules.
Reading
Read a school timetable and notice to find times and room numbers.
Listening
Listen to a teacher announce class times and room changes.
Speaking
Describe your weekly class schedule to another student.
Grammar
Use at, on, and in correctly with times and days in timetables.
Writing
Create your own simple weekly timetable with subjects and rooms.
Lesson Test
The test checks vocabulary, grammar, and reading timetables; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'timetable' is used in British English, but American teachers usually say 'schedule' for the same thing!

Maria's First Day Mix-Up

Text type: Narrative
Maria started at Green Valley School last Monday. She looked at her new timetable on Sunday night. The timetable said Maths was at 9 o'clock. English was at 10 o'clock. She felt happy because she likes English.

On Monday morning, Maria went to Room 12 for Maths. But the room was empty. She asked another student for help. The student said, "Maths is in Room 21, not Room 12." Maria looked at her timetable again. She read the room number wrong!

Maria learned something important that day. She must read her timetable carefully. Now she checks the time, the subject, and the room number. She also writes notes on her timetable. Maria never goes to the wrong room now. She is happy at her new school.

Tom's School Timetable

Text type: Description
Tom's school timetable is on a white piece of paper. It shows five days: Monday to Friday. Each day has six lessons. The timetable has three columns. The first column shows the time. The second column shows the subject name. The third column shows the room number.

Tom's first lesson starts at 8:30 every day. His last lesson finishes at 3:15. There is a lunch break from 12:00 to 1:00. Tom has different subjects each day. On Monday, he has Science, English, and History. On Tuesday, he has Maths, Art, and Music.

Tom keeps his timetable in his school bag. He looks at it every morning. The timetable helps Tom know where to go. It also helps him bring the right books. Tom's timetable is very useful. He never forgets his lessons now.

NOTICE TO ALL STUDENTS

There are changes to the timetable next week. Please read this notice carefully.

How to Read a School Timetable

Text type: Informational
A school timetable is a very useful thing. It shows your lessons for each week. Reading a timetable is easy when you know how.

First, find the day you want. The days are usually at the top. They go from Monday to Friday. Then, look down that column. You will see your lessons for that day. Each lesson has a time, a subject, and a room number. Some timetables also show the teacher's name.

Look at the times carefully. Most schools have breaks between lessons. There is usually a long lunch break too. Check what time each lesson starts and finishes. This helps you be on time.

Always keep your timetable with you. Put it in your bag or folder. Some students take a photo on their phone. This way, you can check it anytime. A timetable helps you stay organized at school.

Two Different School Timetables

Text type: Comparison
Anna and Ben go to different schools. Their timetables are not the same.

Anna's school day starts at 8:30. She has six lessons every day. Each lesson is 45 minutes long. Anna has a 15-minute break at 10:30. Her lunch break is one hour long. It starts at 12:15. Anna's school finishes at 3:30. She likes her timetable because the lessons are short.

Ben's school day starts earlier, at 8:00. He has five lessons each day. Each lesson is one hour long. Ben has a 20-minute break at 10:00. His lunch break is 45 minutes. It starts at 12:00. Ben's school finishes at 3:15. He likes his timetable because he has longer breaks.

Both Anna and Ben use their timetables every day. Their timetables are different, but both are good. Each school has its own way.

Yes, I have a timetable at school. It shows all my lessons for the week. I look at it every morning.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What information can you find on a timetable?

A timetable shows times and activities. It tells me when my lessons start and finish. I can see what subject I have next.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Where do you usually see notices in your school?

I see notices on the walls and doors. There are notices in the classroom too. The main notice board is near the office.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Why is it important to read notices at school?

Notices give important information about school events. They tell us about changes or special activities. I need to read them carefully.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. Can you tell me about a notice you read recently?

Yes, I read a notice about sports day yesterday. It said sports day is next Friday. We need to bring our sports clothes.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Prepositions of Time (at, on, in)

We use 'at' for clock times and specific moments.

We use 'on' for days and dates.

We use 'in' for months, years, seasons and parts of the day.

FORMS

FormExample
at + clock timeThe class starts at 9:00.
at + specific momentThe library closes at lunchtime.
on + day / dateWe have English on Monday.
in + month / year / seasonThe exam is in June.
in + part of dayThe meeting is in the morning.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ The lesson is in 10:00.

✓ The lesson is at 10:00.

Use 'at' with clock times, not 'in'.

✗ The test is in Monday.

✓ The test is on Monday.

Use 'on' with days of the week.

✗ School starts on September.

✓ School starts in September.

Use 'in' with months, not 'on'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write a short paragraph about your school timetable. Describe what subjects you study on Monday. (40–60 words)

  • List the subjects you have on Monday
  • Include the time for each lesson
  • Say which subject you like best

Key structures: Present simple tense (I have, We study), Time expressions (at 9 o'clock, in the morning)

Model
My Monday timetable is very busy. I have maths at 9 o'clock. Then I study English at 10 o'clock. After break, we have science and history. In the afternoon, I have art class. Art is my favourite subject on Monday because I like drawing and painting.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about your school timetable on Monday: list the subjects, give the time of each lesson, and say which subject you like best.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: timetable, subject, lesson, class, break, start, finish, morning, afternoon, favourite. Structures: I have ... at ... o'clock; in the morning / in the afternoon; I study ...; My favourite subject is ... because ....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Lists at least three Monday subjects, gives a time for each (or for most), and names the favourite subject with a short reason. Good: Lists two or three subjects with times for some of them and names a favourite, but a time or the reason is missing. Developing: Lists subjects without times, or gives times but no favourite subject. Beginning: Does not describe a Monday timetable; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I have maths at nine o'clock' patterns correctly, adds 'in the morning/afternoon' or 'after break', and uses week words such as subject, lesson, break, start, finish. Good: Uses 'I have ... at ...' correctly several times, but little time vocabulary beyond the clock. Developing: Uses 'at' with times incorrectly ('in 9 o'clock', 'on the morning') or has very few week words. Beginning: No time expressions or timetable words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Present simple correct with I/we, prepositions 'at' for clock times and 'in' for parts of the day are right, and sentences are complete. Good: A few errors ('I has maths', 'in 9 o'clock') but the timetable is easy to understand. Developing: Frequent errors in verbs or prepositions; some lines are only subject names with no sentence. Beginning: Errors hide the meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Subjects are in time order through the day with Then/After break, and the favourite subject comes last. Good: Most subjects are in order with a small mix-up. Developing: Subjects and times are mixed with no clear order. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: At least three subjects with times in order, favourite with reason, accurate at/in. | 75-89: Subjects and most times present; small errors. | 60-74: Times or favourite missing, or several preposition errors. | 40-59: Very short list with little structure. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'sciense'; times written as '9:00' or 'nine o'clock'; 'maths' or 'math'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a missing capital letter on Monday.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subjects and times are fine, including a real timetable or an invented one (Khmer, maths, PE, science). 'At 8:00' and 'at eight' both work. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask for the Monday timetable. Copied model answer word-for-word: 100 with a note to use your own timetable.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear subject-and-time sentence the learner wrote. 2) Fix: Correct one error, for example: 'Write: I have English at ten o'clock (not: I has English in ten o'clock).' 3) Next step: Add 'after break' or 'in the afternoon' to show the order of your day.

lessons.titleKm: Reading a Simple Timetable and Notice — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Reading a Simple Timetable and Notice — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write a paragraph explaining how to read a school notice. Help a new student understand what information to look for. (60–80 words)

  • Explain where to find notices in school
  • List the important information in a notice
  • Give advice about checking notices regularly

Key structures: Imperatives (Look at, Check, Read), Modal verbs (should, can, need to), Sequencing words (first, then, also)

Model
Reading a school notice is easy. First, look at the title to know the topic. Then read the date and time carefully. The notice shows where the event happens. You should also check who needs to attend. Some notices are for all students, but others are only for one class. You can find notices on the board near the office. Check the notice board every day so you don't miss important information about tests, trips, or school events.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words telling a new student how to read a school notice: where to find notices, what information to look for, and why to check them regularly.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: notice, title, date, time, room, place, attend, check, notice board, important. Structures: Imperatives (Look at, Read, Check); should / can / need to; First, then, also.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says where notices are found (for example the notice board), lists at least three kinds of information to look for (title, date, time, room, who must attend) and advises checking regularly with a reason. Good: Gives where to find notices and two items of information, but advice about checking regularly or the reason is missing. Developing: Only says notices are important or lists one item, with no where or how. Beginning: Does not explain how to read a notice; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses imperatives (Look at the title, Check the date) and should/can/need to correctly, orders with First/Then/Also, and uses notice words like date, time, room, attend. Good: Uses at least imperatives or should, plus a sequence word, with some notice words. Developing: Uses advice language once, or writes 'You should looking' / 'Must to read'. Beginning: No advice structure; only statements.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Base verb after should/can/need to, imperatives without a subject, complete sentences; one small slip at most. Good: Errors such as 'You should reads', 'Need check the date' or missing 'the' but the advice is clear. Developing: Frequent verb-form errors and fragments; some advice is hard to follow. Beginning: Errors make the advice unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps go in an order a new student can follow: where to find it, then title, then date/time, then room, then check again. Good: Steps are clear with a small order problem. Developing: Steps are listed without order or linking words. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Where to find notices, three or more items to check, and advice on checking, in clear order with accurate imperatives. | 75-89: Good advice with two or three items; minor errors. | 60-74: Understandable but missing the where or the checking advice. | 40-59: Very short or general; many errors. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'must' used in place of 'should'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; using 'board' alone for 'notice board'.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Under about 45 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Notices may be found on the board, the office door, the school gate or a class group chat. Any sensible items to check are fine (who it is for, what to bring, the deadline). The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask how to read a school notice. Copied model answer: 100 with a note to write your own advice next time.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one useful tip, for example checking the date or the room. 2) Fix: Correct one structure, for example: 'Write: You should check the date (not: You should checking the date).' 3) Next step: Add one sentence with 'also' to give a second tip.

lessons.titleKm: Reading a Simple Timetable and Notice — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Reading a Simple Timetable and Notice — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write a paragraph comparing your Monday and Friday timetables. Explain which day you prefer and why. (80–110 words)

  • Describe the subjects on both days
  • Compare the two days using comparative language
  • Explain your preference with clear reasons

Key structures: Comparative forms (more fun, easier, better than), Conjunctions (but, because, and, so), Present simple for routines

Model
My Monday and Friday timetables are quite different. On Monday, I have maths, English, science, and history. These subjects are difficult and I have lots of homework. Friday is better because I have art, music, and PE. These lessons are more fun and more interesting than Monday lessons. On Friday afternoon, we finish early at 2 o'clock. Monday finishes at 4 o'clock, so it is a longer day. I prefer Friday because the subjects are easier and more enjoyable. I also like Friday because the weekend starts after school. My friends and I are always happy on Friday!

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words comparing your Monday and Friday timetables, saying which day you prefer and why, with comparative language.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: timetable, subject, lesson, break, finish, homework, easier, more fun, favourite, prefer. Structures: comparatives (easier, more interesting, better than); but / because / and / so; present simple for routines.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes the subjects on both Monday and Friday, compares them (for example length of day, difficulty, fun), says which day is preferred, and gives at least two clear reasons. Good: Describes both days and says which is preferred, but gives only one reason or only a weak comparison. Developing: Describes only one day well, or says 'I like Friday' without reasons. Beginning: Very little about either timetable; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses at least two comparatives correctly (easier, more interesting, better than), links with but/because/so, and uses timetable words like subject, break, finish, homework. Good: Uses one or two comparatives and one or two connectors correctly. Developing: Uses a comparative incorrectly ('more easy', 'more better') or no connectors. Beginning: No comparatives or connectors.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Comparatives are formed correctly, present simple agrees with the subject, and sentences are complete; one or two small slips. Good: Errors like 'Friday is more easy than Monday' or 'We finish at 2 o'clock' mix-ups, but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent comparative, 'than' and verb errors; some sentences hard to follow. Beginning: Errors hide the meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Gives Monday, then Friday, then the comparison and preference with reasons, in a paragraph that flows. Good: Order is clear but the comparison is only in the last sentence. Developing: Monday and Friday details are mixed together. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Both days compared, clear preference with two reasons, comparatives and connectors accurate. | 75-89: Both days described; preference and reason present; minor errors. | 60-74: One day weak or only one reason. | 40-59: Mostly one day or many comparative errors. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'more easy' if the rest of the sentence is clear (note it, but score the meaning); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; times written as '2pm' or 'two o'clock'; missing articles.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any two days may be used if the learner explains, but Monday and Friday are expected. Any reasons are fine (fewer lessons, favourite subject, weekend, less homework). The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask for a Monday versus Friday comparison. Copied model answer: 100 with a note to use own timetable.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear comparison or reason the learner gave. 2) Fix: Correct one comparative, for example: 'Write: Friday is easier than Monday (not: Friday is more easy than Monday).' 3) Next step: Add one more reason with 'because' or 'so' for your favourite day.

questions.question: Q23. The art show is ___ the afternoon next Friday.
questions.explanation: → We use 'in' with parts of the day.

questions.question: notice — announcement
questions.explanation: → 'notice' and 'announcement' both mean a message that tells people something, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q20. All students must ___ the meeting.
questions.explanation: → 'Attend' means to go to a meeting.

questions.question: Q6. My favorite ___ is English. I also like math and science.
questions.explanation: → A 'subject' is something we study, like English, math or science.

questions.question: Monday — elephant
questions.explanation: → 'Monday' and 'elephant' belong to different ideas, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q13. The exam timetable shows maths is ___ Monday morning.
questions.explanation: → We use 'on' with days of the week.

questions.question: cancel — stop
questions.explanation: → 'cancel' and 'stop' both mean to not go on, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q19. The ___ of the class is room 101.
questions.explanation: → The 'location' is the place. The class is in room 101.

questions.question: timetable — plan
questions.explanation: → 'timetable' and 'plan' both mean a list of what will happen and when, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q17. The music room is free ___ Wednesday afternoons.
questions.explanation: → We use 'on' with days of the week, even with a part of the day.

questions.question: exam — umbrella
questions.explanation: → 'exam' and 'umbrella' do not connect in meaning or form, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q14. Sports day is always ___ June every year.
questions.explanation: → We use 'in' with months.

questions.question: attend — attendance
questions.explanation: → 'attend' and 'attendance' share the root 'attend', so they are a word family.

questions.question: finish — continue
questions.explanation: → 'Finish' means to end, and 'continue' means to keep going, so they are opposites.

questions.question: Q26. The history class finishes ___ 3:00 this afternoon.
questions.explanation: → We use 'at' with exact clock times.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about your school timetable. Say what lessons you have on one day. Include times. (40–60 words)

  • Say which day you are writing about
  • Write what lessons you have
  • Include the times of your lessons
Model
On Tuesday, I have four lessons. My first lesson is English at 9:00 am. Then I have Math at 10:00 am. After break, I have Science at 11:00 am. My last lesson before lunch is History at 12:00 pm. I like Tuesday because I have my favorite subjects.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about the lessons you have on one day, naming the day and giving a time for each lesson.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: timetable, lesson, subject, first, then, after break, start, finish, o'clock, favourite. Structures: On Tuesday, I have ...; My first lesson is ... at ...; Then I have ... at ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names the day, lists at least three lessons, and gives a time for every lesson.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'On Tuesday', 'My first lesson is ... at ...', 'Then I have ... at ...' and 'after break' correctly.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Have/is used correctly, prepositions on/at are right, and sentences are complete; only tiny slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Lessons follow the real order of the day with first, then, after break, last.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; times written as 9am, 9:00 or nine; 'math' or 'maths'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing capital letters on days.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any day of the week and any subjects; real or invented timetable. The model's Tuesday is not required. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask for one day's lessons. Copied model answer: 100 with a note to write your own day.

contentRef.text:
CHAPTER IV · WEEK 20

Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify the main stages and activities when hearing a lesson plan explained. L2 Understand
  • Use present simple tense and sequencing words to describe lesson plan components. L3 Apply

  • Complete a partially written lesson plan template with appropriate teaching activities. L3 Apply
  • Evaluate how clearly a lesson plan communicates learning goals to other teachers. L4 Analyze · HOTS

questions.question: Q26. ___ in complete sentences, not just words.
questions.explanation: → This instruction tells students how to write their answers.

questions.question: teacher — teach
questions.explanation: → 'Teacher' comes from 'teach', so they are in the same word family.

questions.question: Q2. ___ to the teacher when she explains the task.
questions.explanation: → This is a command telling students what to do, so we use the imperative.

questions.question: Q20. Let's ___ yesterday's lesson before the test.
questions.explanation: → We 'review' a lesson when we look at it again.

questions.question: Q18. ___ the pictures and describe what you see.
questions.explanation: → This tells students to look at pictures and then describe them.

questions.question: Q27. ___ eat or drink in the computer room.
questions.explanation: → This is a negative instruction about computer room rules.

Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Lesson Plan Structure

A lesson plan has parts in order. Each part tells teachers what to do and when.

Example:The lesson plan shows three activities: warm-up, practice, and review.
Connection:You see lesson plan structures in teacher training books and when you prepare classes.
  • 2. Sequencing Activities

Teachers put activities in a good order. First activities are easier, then harder activities come next.

Example:First, students listen to the story. Then they answer questions about it.
Connection:You read sequencing words like 'first' and 'then' in lesson plans and teaching guides.
  • 3. Lesson Plan Components

A lesson plan has important parts: objectives, materials, time, and activities. Each part gives different information.

Example:The materials section lists: board, markers, and picture cards.
Connection:You write these components when you plan lessons or read other teachers' plans.
  • 4. Giving Instructions

Teachers use command sentences to tell students what to do. These sentences start with a verb.

Example:Open your books to page ten and read the text.
Connection:You use imperatives every day when you give instructions in the classroom.

Vocabulary

  1. lesson — A lesson is a time when a teacher teaches students something.
  2. plan — A plan is ideas you write before you do something.
  3. teacher — A teacher is a person who helps students learn at school.
  4. student — A student is a person who goes to school to learn.
  5. activity — An activity is something that students do to learn or practice.
  6. goal — A goal is something you want students to learn or do.
  7. practice — Practice means to do something many times to get better.
  8. explain — Explain means to help someone understand by telling them clearly.
  9. time — Time is minutes or hours when something happens.
  10. material — A material is a thing that teachers and students use in class.
  11. topic — A topic is the main subject or idea you learn about.
  12. step — A step is one part of something you do in order.
  13. instruction — An instruction is words that tell you how to do something.
  14. group — A group is some students who work together on something.
  15. task — A task is a small piece of work someone must do.
  16. check — Check means to look at something to see if it is correct.
  17. simple — Simple means easy to understand or do, not difficult.
  18. ready — Ready means prepared and able to do something now.
  19. finish — Finish means to complete something and stop doing it.
  20. review — Review means to look at or study something again.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words about lesson plans, teaching, and classroom activities.
Reading
Read a simple lesson plan and find the objectives, materials, time, and activities.
Listening
Listen to a teacher explain their lesson plan and identify the main steps.
Speaking
Describe the activities in a lesson plan using sequencing words like 'first' and 'then'.
Grammar
Learn imperatives to give instructions, just like teachers do in lesson plans.
Writing
Complete a lesson plan template by writing activities for each stage.
Lesson Test
The test checks if you can read and complete a simple lesson plan; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Teachers around the world use similar lesson plan formats with objectives, activities, and timing, so you can read lesson plans from many different countries!

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching: The Essential Guide to English Language Teaching — Jim Scrivener (2011). This book shows clear examples of lesson plan stages and how to write them. Practical English Language Teaching — David Nunan (2003). It explains lesson planning vocabulary and gives sample lesson plan templates for teachers.

▶ How to Write a Lesson Plan — Cambridge English ▶ Lesson Planning for Teachers — British Council TeachingEnglish

MINI STORY

Maria is a new teacher at a small school. Today she writes her first lesson plan. The topic is about animals. She writes the goal at the top: students will learn eight animal names.

Maria plans three simple activities for her students. First, she will explain the new words. Then students will practice saying them in groups. The final task is to write sentences. She writes the time for each step. The whole lesson is 40 minutes.

Maria prepares all the material she needs. She has pictures of animals and worksheets. She also writes clear instructions for each activity. At the end, students will check their work together. Maria feels ready to teach. She will review her plan one more time before class starts tomorrow.

Reading Passage

Maria's First Lesson Plan

Text type: Narrative
Maria is a new teacher at Green Valley School. Last week, she wrote her first lesson plan. She was very nervous. Her plan was for a science lesson about plants.

Maria wrote the lesson plan on her computer. First, she wrote the topic at the top. Then she wrote what students will learn. She planned three activities. The first activity was looking at pictures of plants. The

second activity was a short video. The last activity was drawing a plant.

Maria showed her lesson plan to Mr. Brown. He is the head teacher. Mr. Brown read the plan carefully. He smiled and said it was very good. Maria felt happy. She used the lesson plan in her class on Monday. The students enjoyed all the activities. Maria now writes a lesson plan every week.

contentRef.text:
What a Lesson Plan Looks Like

Text type: Description
A lesson plan is a simple paper or document. It helps teachers teach better. Most lesson plans are one or two pages long. They are usually on white paper or on a computer.

At the top of a lesson plan, you can see important information. There is the date and the subject name. There is also the topic of the lesson. For example, the topic might be 'Animals' or 'Numbers'. Below this, there is a list of what students will learn. This part uses simple, clear words.

The middle part shows the activities for the lesson. Each activity has a time, like '10 minutes' or '15 minutes'. Teachers write what students will do. At the bottom, there is a section for materials. This lists things the teacher needs, like books, pens, or pictures. Some lesson plans also have a part for homework.

Email About Lesson Plans

To: All New Teachers
From: Principal Johnson
Date: September 5th
Subject: Writing Your Lesson Plans

Dear Teachers,

Welcome to Riverside School! I want to help you with your lesson plans. Please write a lesson plan for every lesson. Keep your plans simple and short.

Your lesson plan must have these parts: the date, the subject, the topic, and the activities. Write how long each activity takes. Also write what materials you need. You can use the lesson plan template on our school

website. The template is easy to use.

Please send me your lesson plans every Friday. Send them by email before 4 p.m. I will read them and give you feedback. If you have questions, come to my office. I am here Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Good luck with your teaching!

Best wishes, Principal Johnson

contentRef.text:
How to Read a Lesson Plan

Text type: Informational
Reading a lesson plan is easy. You just need to understand the different parts. Here is how to do it.

First, look at the top of the page. Read the date, subject, and topic. This tells you what the lesson is about. Next, find the learning goals. These explain what students will learn. Learning goals often start with words

like 'Students will understand' or 'Students will know'.

Then, read the activities section. This shows what happens in the lesson. Activities are usually in order from first to last. Look at the time for each activity. Add all the times together. This shows how long the whole lesson takes. Finally, check the materials list. This tells you what things you need. Common materials are books, papers, pencils, and computers. Now you can understand any simple lesson plan!

contentRef.text:
Two Different Lesson Plans

Text type: Comparison
Mr. Lee and Ms. Ahmed both teach English. They both write lesson plans, but their plans look different.

Mr. Lee writes very short lesson plans. His plans are only half a page long. He writes the topic and three or four activities. He does not write the time for each activity. He keeps all his lesson plans in a blue notebook. Mr. Lee says short plans are quick to write. He can remember the details in his head.

Ms. Ahmed writes long, detailed lesson plans. Her plans are one or two pages long. She writes everything: the topic, the goals, the activities, the times, and the materials. She also writes questions she will ask students. Ms. Ahmed keeps her plans on her computer. She says detailed plans help her remember everything. Both teachers are good teachers. Their students learn well. There is no perfect way to write a lesson plan.

Parts of a Simple Lesson Plan

A2 — Listen and Answer

🎧 Listen to the recording and answer the questions that follow:
contentRef.transcript:
Parts of a Simple Lesson Plan
A2 — Listen and Answer

Hello everyone. Today I will talk about lesson plans. A lesson plan has different parts. First, it has a title. The
title tells us the topic. For example, 'Learning Numbers' or 'My Family'. Next, we see the date and time. This
shows when the lesson happens. The plan also shows how long the lesson is. Most lessons are thirty or forty-
five minutes long.


The lesson plan has an aim. The aim tells us what students will learn. Then we see the activities. Activities
are things students do in class. They can read, write, talk, or play games. At the end, we find materials.
Materials are things we need for the lesson. They can be books, pictures, or cards. A good lesson plan is clear
and easy to read.

A2 — Listen and Answer

contentRef.transcript:
My First Time Reading a Lesson Plan
A2 — Listen and Answer

My name is Sokha. I remember my first lesson plan. My teacher gave it to me last month. I was nervous
because I didn't understand it. The plan had many new words. But my teacher helped me. She explained
everything slowly.


The lesson plan was about fruit. The aim was simple. Students needed to learn eight fruit names. The lesson
started with a warm-up game. Then students looked at pictures of fruit. They said the names together. After
that, students wrote the words in their notebooks. At the end, they worked in groups. They made fruit
posters with colored paper. The lesson was fifty minutes long. I enjoyed reading the plan. Now I understand
lesson plans better. They help teachers organize their work. They make lessons more interesting for students.

contentRef.text:
Why Lesson Plans Are Important

A2 — Listen and Answer

🎧 Listen to the recording and answer the questions that follow:
contentRef.transcript:
Why Lesson Plans Are Important
A2 — Listen and Answer

Good morning, class. Today I want to explain lesson plans. Why are they important? A lesson plan helps
teachers prepare. Teachers know what to do in every lesson. They don't forget important activities. This
makes teaching easier and better.


Lesson plans also help students. When teachers follow a plan, lessons are clear. Students understand what
they will learn. They know what activities come next. The lesson has a good beginning, middle, and end.
Everything is organized well. Students can also see the plan sometimes. They can read the aim and the
activities. This helps them prepare too. Good lesson plans save time. Teachers don't waste time in class. They
use every minute well. Students learn more when lessons are well planned. That's why every teacher needs to
write lesson plans.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

A lesson plan shows what the teacher will do in class. It tells the topic, time, and activities for students. Good lesson plans have a clear beginning, middle, and end. Teachers write the materials they need, like books or paper. Reading a lesson plan helps you understand the class better.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What is a lesson plan?

A lesson plan is a paper with teaching ideas. It shows what the teacher will teach in class. It helps teachers remember their activities.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What information do you usually find in a lesson plan?

A lesson plan has the topic and the time. It also shows the activities and materials. Some plans have homework too.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Why do teachers write lesson plans?

Teachers write plans to organize their class time well. Plans help them remember what to teach. It makes teaching easier and clearer.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Can you name one part of a simple lesson plan?

One part is the warm-up or beginning activity. This helps students start thinking about the topic. It usually takes five or ten minutes.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. How can reading a lesson plan help a student teacher?

It helps them learn how to organize a class. They can see good examples of activities. Then they can write their own plans better.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Imperatives (Commands and Instructions)

We use imperatives to give instructions or tell someone to do something.

Start with the base verb (no 'to').

For negative instructions, use 'Do not' or 'Don't' + base verb.

FORMS

FormExample
Positive: base verbRead the text on page five.
Negative: Do not / Don't + base verbDo not talk during the test.
Please + base verb (polite)Please write your name here.
Let's + base verb (suggestion for group)Let's practice the new words together.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ To open your books to page ten.

✓ Open your books to page ten.

Don't use 'to' before the verb in imperatives.

✗ You write your answers in the notebook.

✓ Write your answers in the notebook.

Don't use 'you' at the start of an imperative.

✗ Not use your phone in class.

✓ Do not use your phone in class.

Use 'Do not' or 'Don't' for negative imperatives, not just 'Not'.

lessons.titleKm: Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe what a lesson plan looks like. Write for someone who has never seen one before. (40–60 words)

  • Start with what a lesson plan is
  • Say what sections or parts it has
  • Mention how it helps teachers

Key structures: Present simple (is, has, shows), Linking words (and, also)

Model
A lesson plan is a short document for teachers. It has several parts. It shows the lesson topic and the date. It also has a list of activities. Each activity has a time, for example ten minutes or twenty minutes. The lesson plan helps teachers remember what to do in class.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words for someone who has never seen a lesson plan: say what it is, what parts it has, and how it helps teachers.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson plan, topic, goal, activity, material, time, teacher, student, step, check. Structures: A lesson plan is ...; It has / It shows ...; also / and.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts by saying what a lesson plan is, names at least two parts it contains (for example topic, goal, activities, time, materials), and says how it helps teachers (remember what to do, save time). Good: Says what a lesson plan is and names one or two parts, but how it helps teachers is missing or very general. Developing: Only says 'A lesson plan is good' without parts, or lists parts without saying what a lesson plan is. Beginning: Does not explain a lesson plan; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'A lesson plan is ...', 'It has/shows ...' correctly, joins ideas with also or and, and uses at least four week words (topic, goal, activity, material, time). Good: Uses is/has/shows correctly and one linking word, with about three week words. Developing: Uses one structure, writes 'It have' or 'It show', or uses one or two week words. Beginning: No target structures or week words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is right (it has, it shows, it helps), plurals such as 'activities' are right; sentences complete. Good: Errors like 'It have a topic' or 'a activities' that do not block meaning. Developing: Frequent verb and article errors; some sentences are hard to follow. Beginning: Errors hide the meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order is what it is, then what is in it, then how it helps, with 'also' linking the parts. Good: The three ideas are present with a small order problem. Developing: Sentences are separate and the order is hard to see. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Defines a lesson plan, names two or more parts, says how it helps, accurate it has/shows. | 75-89: Definition and parts present; small errors. | 60-74: Understandable but parts or helping idea missing. | 40-59: Very short or confused. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips such as 'materal'; missing articles (a/the); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'lesson plan' written as one word; missing -s that does not block meaning.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible parts are fine (date, class, aims, steps, homework, assessment). Another way to say how it helps is also fine (stay organised, know the time, feel confident). The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask for a description of a lesson plan. Copied model answer: 100 with a note to write own sentences.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear part of the lesson plan the learner named. 2) Fix: Correct one verb, for example: 'Write: It has a topic and a goal (not: It have a topic and a goal).' 3) Next step: Add one sentence about how a plan helps, for example 'It helps teachers save time.'

lessons.titleKm: Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Explain the main parts of a simple lesson plan. Write for a new teacher who wants to understand the basic structure. (60–80 words)

  • Name three or four main parts of a lesson plan
  • Explain what each part contains
  • Use simple examples to make it clear

Key structures: Present simple for describing (contains, includes, lists), Sequencing (first, then, finally), Articles (a, an, the)

Model
A simple lesson plan has four main parts. First, it has the lesson information at the top. This includes the date, the class name, and the topic. Then, it lists the lesson aims. These are the things students will learn. Next, there is a section for materials. This shows what the teacher needs, like books or pictures. Finally, the plan shows the activities. Each activity has a short description and a time limit.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words for a new teacher naming three or four main parts of a simple lesson plan and explaining what each part contains, with examples.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: topic, aim, goal, material, activity, time, date, class, practice, explain. Structures: The plan includes / contains / lists ...; First, then, next, finally; articles a / an / the.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names three or four distinct parts (for example lesson information, aims, materials, activities) and explains what each one contains with a small example (such as date and class, books and pictures, ten-minute speaking activity). Good: Names three parts but explains only one or two of them, or examples are missing for some. Developing: Names one or two parts, or gives names without any explanation. Beginning: Does not describe parts of a lesson plan; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses descriptive verbs (includes, contains, lists, shows) correctly, orders with First/Then/Next/Finally, and uses articles a/an/the in phrases like 'the lesson aims' and 'a list of activities'. Good: Uses includes/has and two sequence words correctly; articles mostly right. Developing: Uses 'has' only, few or no sequence words, or drops articles often. Beginning: No target structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third-person -s is right (it includes, the plan lists), articles and plurals are correct; one small slip at most. Good: Errors like 'It include the date', 'a materials' or missing articles but the explanation is clear. Developing: Frequent verb or article errors; some parts are hard to follow. Beginning: Errors hide the meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Parts are given in the order they appear in a plan, each linked by First/Then/Next/Finally with its explanation next to it. Good: Order is mostly clear. Developing: Parts are listed with no order or links. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Three or four parts each explained with an example, sequence words and verbs used accurately. | 75-89: Three parts with most explained; small errors. | 60-74: Two or three parts named but little explanation. | 40-59: Very short or only one part. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; dropped articles that do not block meaning; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'objectives' for 'aims'; 'chapter' or 'section' for 'part'.
LENGTH: Aim for 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Under about 45 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any logical set of parts is fine (topic and date, aims, materials, warm-up, main activity, review, homework). Sequence words may be second, after that, last. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask for parts of a lesson plan. Copied model answer: 100 with a note to use own parts and examples.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a part the learner explained clearly with an example. 2) Fix: Correct one error, for example: 'Write: The plan lists the materials (not: The plan list materials).' 3) Next step: Add an example for each part, such as 'For example, books or pictures.'

lessons.titleKm: Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Reading a Short, Simple Lesson Plan — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Describe how reading a lesson plan can help a teacher prepare for class. Write for teachers who want to improve their teaching. (80–110 words)

  • Explain why reading the plan before class is important
  • Give examples of what teachers can prepare
  • Mention how it saves time and makes teaching easier
  • Use connecting words to link your ideas

Key structures: Modal verbs (can, will, should), Linking words (because, so, before, when), Present simple and future with will

Model
Reading a lesson plan before class is very important for teachers. When teachers read the plan, they can see what materials they need. They can prepare books, worksheets, or pictures before the lesson starts. They also know how much time each activity needs. This helps them use classroom time well. If teachers read the plan carefully, they will feel more confident. They know what to do first, second, and last. The lesson plan also shows the aims. Teachers can check these aims after the lesson. This helps them see if students learned the new things. A good lesson plan makes teaching easier and more successful.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words explaining why teachers should read the lesson plan before class, what they can prepare, and how it saves time and makes teaching easier.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson plan, prepare, material, aim, activity, time, confident, worksheet, before, check. Structures: can / will / should; because / so / before / when; present simple and will.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Explains why reading the plan before class matters, gives at least two things a teacher can prepare (for example books, worksheets, pictures, timing) and says how it saves time or makes teaching easier. Good: Gives a reason and one thing to prepare, but saving time or ease of teaching is missing. Developing: Says reading the plan is good without examples of what to prepare. Beginning: Does not explain the benefit; unclear or off topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses can, should or will correctly, links ideas with because, so, before or when, and includes week words such as prepare, material, aim, confident. Good: Uses one modal and one connector correctly, with some week words. Developing: Uses 'will' as 'will to prepare' or no connectors; few week words. Beginning: No target structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Base verb after can/will/should, and present simple correct after when and if; only one or two small slips. Good: Errors like 'teachers can prepares', 'will saves time' but the meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors with modals and verbs; some sentences unclear. Beginning: Errors hide the meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Flows from why reading the plan matters, to what teachers can prepare, to the time-saving result, with connectors showing cause and result. Good: Order is clear, but connectors are few. Developing: Ideas are listed with no links. Beginning: Hard to follow.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Reason, two or more preparation examples and time-saving result, with modals and connectors accurate. | 75-89: Main ideas present; small errors. | 60-74: One idea missing or connectors weak. | 40-59: Short and general; many errors. | 0-39: Off topic or too little text.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'must' instead of 'should'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; a missing comma after when/if.
LENGTH: Aim for 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Other preparation is fine (practise the activity, find a picture, copy handouts, plan the board, check the aims after class). Both 'will' and present-simple forms are acceptable for results. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 and ask for why teachers read the lesson plan. Copied model answer: 100 with a note to use own examples.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a good example of preparation or a clear reason that the learner gave. 2) Fix: Correct one modal or connector error, for example: 'Write: Teachers can prepare pictures (not: Teachers can prepares pictures).' 3) Next step: Add one sentence with 'so', such as 'The plan shows the time, so teachers can finish on time.'

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about what is in a lesson plan. Say what information a lesson plan has. Write 40-60 words. (40–60 words)

  • Say what the lesson topic is
  • Say what students will learn
  • Say what activities are in the lesson
Model
A lesson plan has important information for teachers. It shows the lesson topic and objectives. It says what students will learn. The plan lists all activities and materials. It also shows how long each part takes. Teachers use lesson plans to teach well. A good plan helps students learn better.

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about the information in a lesson plan: the lesson topic, what students will learn, and the activities.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson plan, topic, goal, student, learn, activity, material, time, teacher, practice. Structures: It shows / says / lists ...; Students will learn ...; The plan has ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: States a lesson topic, says what students will learn (the aim), and names at least two activities, optionally adding time or materials.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'It shows/lists ...' and 'Students will learn ...' correctly with at least four week words (topic, goal, activity, material, time).
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Third-person -s and 'will + base verb' are correct, plurals 'students' and 'activities' correct; only tiny slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order follows the task: topic, what students will learn, then the activities.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; missing articles; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'objective' for 'goal'; a missing -s.
LENGTH: Aim for 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words, cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any believable topic and activities, real or invented (animals, family, my town; a game, a reading task, a short quiz). The model answer is only a reference.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Lesson notes

Short written records that teachers make after a lesson. They help teachers remember what happened and what students learned.

Example:The teacher wrote notes about the lesson in her notebook.
Connection:Teachers write lesson notes every day at school to plan better lessons.
  • 2. Teaching stages

The different parts of a lesson, from start to finish. Each stage has a different activity or purpose.

Example:The first stage was a warm-up, and the last stage was review.
Connection:You see teaching stages in lesson plans and teacher training books.
  • 3. Lesson summary

A short version of what happened in a lesson. It includes only the most important points.

Example:The lesson summary said students learned five new words and played a game.
Connection:Teachers write summaries in their notebooks and on school reports.
  • 4. Student responses

The answers and reactions that students give during a lesson. Teachers write notes about them.

Example:The teacher noted that students answered the questions well and enjoyed the activity.
Connection:You record student responses in lesson notes and teaching journals.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Vocabulary

  1. lesson — A period of time when a teacher teaches students.
  2. note — Something you write down to remember information.
  3. write — To make words or numbers with a pen or pencil.
  4. teacher — A person who teaches students in a school.
  5. important — Something that you need to know or remember.
  6. remember — To keep something in your mind and not forget.
  7. topic — The main subject that you talk or write about.
  8. explain — To help someone understand something by telling them about it.
  9. example — Something that shows what you mean or how something works.
  10. main — The most important or largest one.
  11. point — One piece of information or one idea.
  12. notebook — A book with empty pages for writing notes.
  13. short — Not long or not taking much time.
  14. subject — One area of study like math or English.
  15. information — Facts or details about something.
  16. review — To look at or study something again.
  17. understand — To know what something means or how it works.
  18. summary — A short version that has only the main ideas.
  19. list — A group of names or things written one under another.
  20. useful — Something that helps you or is good for you.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty words about lessons, notes, and teaching like lesson, important, and summary.
Reading
Read sample lesson notes and find the main points about what happened.
Listening
Listen to teachers describe their lessons and identify the key teaching stages.
Speaking
Talk about a lesson you taught or saw using past simple verbs.
Grammar
Use past simple verbs to write what happened in a lesson.
Writing
Write short notes about a lesson including the aim, activities, and student responses.
Lesson Test
The test checks if you can write clear lesson notes; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Many teachers around the world write lesson notes in English, even when they teach in other languages, because English is the language of international teacher training.

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching: The Essential Guide to English Language Teaching — Jim Scrivener (2011). This book shows you how to write lesson notes and plan teaching stages clearly. How to Teach English — Jeremy Harmer (2007). Chapter five explains how to keep records and write useful lesson summaries.

MINI STORY

My name is Sara and I am a student. Every day I have many lessons at school. My favorite subject is English. My teacher is very kind and she always explains new words clearly.

I like to write notes in my notebook during every lesson. When the teacher talks about an important topic, I write down the main points. I also make a list of new words and examples. After class, I review my notes to remember everything.

Today our teacher taught us how to write a short summary. She said we should include only the most important information. Writing good notes is very useful. It helps me understand the lesson better and do well on tests. I always keep my notebook clean and organized.

Reading Passage

Maria's Note-Taking Problem

Text type: Narrative
Maria is 15 years old. She is a student at Green Valley School. Every day she has six lessons. Maria always listens in class. But she has one big problem. She never writes notes about her lessons.

Last week, Maria had a test in science. She could not remember the lesson. She did not have any notes to read. Maria got a bad mark on her test. She felt very sad. Her teacher, Mr Brown, talked to her. He said notes

help you remember things.

Now Maria writes short notes after every lesson. She writes the date and the topic. She writes three or four important words. She also writes one or two questions. At home, Maria reads her notes. Now she remembers her lessons better. Her marks are getting better too.

Tom's Lesson Notes

Text type: Description
Tom has a blue notebook for his lesson notes. The notebook is small and easy to carry. Tom uses it every day at school. He keeps it in his school bag. The notebook has 100 pages. Tom writes on only one side of each page.

Tom's notes are very simple and clear. At the top of each page, he writes the date. Under the date, he writes the subject name. Then he writes the lesson topic in big letters. He uses a red pen for important words. He

draws small boxes around key ideas.

Tom also writes page numbers from his textbook in his notes. This helps him find information quickly. At the end of each note, Tom writes two questions. Later, he tries to answer these questions at home. Tom's notes help him study for tests.

Email From Miss Johnson

Text type: Notice

To: All Year 9 Students
From: Miss Johnson
Date: 15th March
Subject: Writing Notes in Class

Dear Students,

I want to help you with your lessons. Starting next week, we will practice writing short notes in class. This will help you remember important things. Please bring a notebook and two pens to every lesson.

At the end of each lesson, you will have five minutes. In this time, write short notes. Write the date and the topic. Write three important words from the lesson. Also write one question about the lesson.

Your notes are for you. They do not need to be long or perfect. Short notes are better than no notes. If you have questions, please ask me. Good notes will help you with homework and tests.

Best wishes, Miss Johnson Year 9 Class Teacher

contentRef.text:
How to Write Good Lesson Notes

Text type: Informational
Writing short notes after a lesson is easy. Good notes help you remember what you learned. Here are five simple steps to write good notes.

First, write the date at the top of the page. Then write the subject name and the lesson topic. Next, write down three to five important words from the lesson. Use your own words when possible. Do not copy

everything the teacher says. Also write one or two questions about the lesson.

Keep your notes short and simple. Use clear handwriting. You can use different colours for different parts. Draw small pictures if they help you remember. Read your notes again at home on the same day. This helps you remember the lesson better. If something is not clear, ask your teacher the next day. Good notes make studying easier.

contentRef.text:
Two Ways to Take Notes

Text type: Comparison
Lisa and Ahmed are both good students. But they take notes in different ways. Lisa writes long notes during the lesson. She writes everything the teacher says. She uses five or six pages for each lesson. Lisa's notes have many details. But sometimes she misses important points because she is writing all the time.

Ahmed writes short notes after the lesson. He listens carefully during class. He does not write much when the teacher is talking. After the lesson, Ahmed takes five minutes. He writes the date, the topic, and five key words. He also writes two questions. Ahmed's notes are only half a page long.

Both students do well in tests. But Ahmed finds it easier to study. His short notes are clear and quick to read. Lisa sometimes feels tired when she reads her long notes.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

I write short notes after every lesson. My notes have the date and the subject. I write the most important words from the lesson. Good notes help me remember what I learned. I keep my notes in a notebook or on my phone.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Do you write notes during your lessons? Why or why not?

Yes, I write notes during lessons. Notes help me remember important things. I can read them again before a test.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What information do you usually put in your lesson notes?

I write the date and the subject name. I also write new words and important ideas. Sometimes I draw small pictures too.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Where do you keep your lesson notes?

I keep my notes in a blue notebook. I have one notebook for each subject. Sometimes I take photos of my notes.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. When do you look at your notes again after class?

I read my notes at home in the evening. I also look at them before tests. This helps me study better.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What makes good lesson notes? Can you give an example?

Good notes are short and clear. For example, I write key words, not long sentences. I also use colours for important parts.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Past Simple

We use the past simple to write about things that happened in a lesson.

We add -ed to regular verbs.

Many verbs are irregular.

FORMS

FormExample
Regular verb: subject + verb + -edI learned new words yesterday.
Irregular verb: subject + past formWe wrote notes in class.
Negative: subject + did not + base verbShe did not understand the question.
Question: Did + subject + base verb?Did you finish the homework?
Common irregular verbsgo → went, make → made, have → had, see → saw

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ The teacher goed to the board.

✓ The teacher went to the board.

Go is irregular. The past form is went, not goed.

✗ I not finished my notes.

✓ I did not finish my notes.

Use did not (or didn't) before the base verb for negatives.

✗ We writed three sentences.

✓ We wrote three sentences.

Write is irregular. The past form is wrote, not writed.
