lessons.titleKm: Writing Short Notes About a Lesson — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)
lessons.titleEn: Writing Short Notes About a Lesson — Guided Writing Task 1 (40–60 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about what you learned in today's English lesson. Explain the main topic and one new thing you learned. (40–60 words)

  • Start with the date and lesson topic
  • Write what the teacher explained
  • Say one new word or idea you learned

Key structures: Past simple tense (learned, studied, talked about), We + verb (We learned, We studied)

Model
Monday, 15th January. Today we studied writing notes in English class. The teacher showed us how to write short sentences about lessons. We learned to write the date first, then the topic. I learned a new word: 'summarize'. It means to make something short. This will help me study better.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words of notes on today's English lesson: start with the date and topic, say what the teacher explained, and give one new word or idea you learned.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson, note, topic, explain, example, main point, summary, useful, remember, understand. Structures: Past simple (learned, studied, talked about); We + verb (We learned, We studied).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: The notes open with a date and a real lesson topic, say what the teacher explained, and name one specific new word or idea (for example 'summary' and what it means). Good: All three points are there, but one is thin, such as a topic named with no detail about what the teacher explained. Developing: Only one or two of the three points appear; the date is missing or the 'new word or idea' is just a general comment like 'I learned a lot'. Beginning: The text does not say what the lesson was about, or it is mostly the task instructions or unrelated sentences.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses past simple verbs such as studied, explained, learned and 'We + verb' naturally, plus at least three words like lesson, topic, note, explain, example. Good: Uses past simple and 'We + verb' at least twice and two or three week words, though one verb may be in present tense. Developing: Writes mostly in present tense ('We study notes today') and uses only one week word, usually 'lesson'. Beginning: No past simple verbs and no week words, or only phrases copied from the task.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Past forms are right, including common irregular ones (wrote, taught); only small slips like a missing -s or article. Good: Most past forms are right; a few errors such as 'We learn yesterday' or 'writed' do not stop understanding. Developing: Many verbs stay in the base form or are wrongly formed ('goed', 'writed'), so the reader must guess the time. Beginning: Nearly every sentence has a verb or word-order error and the meaning is unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Reads like real lesson notes: date and topic first, then the explanation, then the new word, in short complete sentences. Good: The order is mostly right, with one sentence that is run-on or missing a subject. Developing: Points are in a mixed order or written as loose fragments without full stops. Beginning: Disconnected words or phrases with no clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Date, topic, explanation and a specific new word are all present, in past tense, with few errors. | 75-89: All parts present and understandable; some past-tense slips or one thin part. | 60-74: Two of three parts clear; many verb errors but the lesson can be understood. | 40-59: Only partly answers the task; mostly present tense or very short. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (e.g. 'sumary', 'lesoon'); date written in a Khmer or short style (15/1); clear Khmer-influenced word order; missing articles (a/the); no capital letters on days or months.
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words: cap at 59 because the three points cannot all be covered.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real lesson topic is fine (not only English). The new item can be a word, a rule or a method. 'I learned' and 'we studied' are equally good. The model's 'summarize' is only one example. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted task instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 with a kind request to try again. Model answer copied word for word: 100 with a note to write own sentences next time. Notes about a lesson in present tense only: mark on content, and coach past simple.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the specific topic or new word the learner chose, quoting it. 2) Fix: Correct one past-tense error, e.g. 'We study about notes yesterday' -> 'We studied notes yesterday.' 3) Next step: Next time start with the date, then add one example sentence for your new word.

lessons.titleKm: Writing Short Notes About a Lesson — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Writing Short Notes About a Lesson — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write notes about a science or math lesson you had recently. Include the topic, what you did in class, and why it was important. (60–80 words)

  • Give the subject and topic clearly
  • Describe the activities you did
  • Explain why this lesson was useful or important

Key structures: First, then, finally (sequencing words), Because (to give reasons), Past simple for completed actions

Model
Science lesson - Plants and water. Date: 10th January. Today we learned about how plants drink water. First, the teacher showed us a video about plant roots. Then we did an experiment with flowers and colored water. We put white flowers in blue water and watched them change color. This was important because now I understand how water moves inside plants. Finally, we drew pictures of our experiment. I enjoyed this lesson because we could see everything clearly.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words of notes on a recent science or math lesson: give the subject and topic, describe what you did in order, and explain why the lesson was important.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: subject, topic, experiment, explain, example, important, useful, understand, information, review. Structures: First, then, finally; Because (reason); Past simple for finished actions.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names a science or math subject and a clear topic, describes two or three real class activities, and gives a reason why the lesson mattered (e.g. 'because now I understand fractions'). Good: Subject, activities and a reason are all there, but the activities are vague ('we did exercises') or the reason is very short. Developing: Gives the subject and one activity but no reason, or the lesson is not science or math. Beginning: No clear lesson is described; the text is general comments about studying.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses First / Then / Finally to order the activities, 'because' for the reason, and past simple throughout, with words like topic, experiment, important, understand. Good: Uses two sequencing words and 'because' at least once; vocabulary is correct but limited. Developing: Tries one sequencing word or 'because', but mostly joins ideas with 'and' or starts every sentence with 'We'. Beginning: No sequencing words, no reason, and no week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Past simple is mostly correct; 'because' is followed by a full clause ('because I understand...'); errors are small. Good: A few errors in past forms or 'because' sentences, but every sentence can be understood. Developing: Mixes present and past in the same paragraph, or writes 'because' alone as a sentence. Beginning: Errors in most sentences; the order of events cannot be followed.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Subject and topic as a heading, activities in time order, reason at the end, easy to scan. Good: Order is mostly clear; the heading or the reason is slightly out of place. Developing: Activities are not in order or run together without full stops. Beginning: Hard to tell what happened first or why.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear subject and topic, ordered activities with First/Then/Finally, and a real reason. | 75-89: All parts present; a few verb errors or a general reason. | 60-74: Subject and activities clear but reason or sequencing missing. | 40-59: Short or mostly present tense; parts missing. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling of science words (e.g. 'experement'); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; using 'Then' twice instead of 'Finally'; a simple topic like addition or the water cycle.
LENGTH: 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Under about 45 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any science or math topic works (plants, shapes, multiplication). Other sequencing words (next, after that) are fine. The reason may use 'because' or 'so'. It does not need an experiment like the model. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Instructions pasted or unrelated text: 0-20 with encouragement to retry. Model answer copied exactly: 100 with a note to use own lesson. A lesson in another subject (e.g. history): mark normally but note the task asked for science or math.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Name one activity or reason the learner described well. 2) Fix: Fix one past-tense or 'because' error, e.g. 'Because I understand now.' -> 'This was important because I understand fractions now.' 3) Next step: Next time use First, Then and Finally once each in your notes.

lessons.titleEn: Writing Short Notes About a Lesson — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write detailed notes to help you prepare for a test. Choose any lesson topic and explain the main points, give examples, and add your own study tips. (80–110 words)

  • Organize your notes with clear headings
  • Give specific examples for each main point
  • Add personal reminders or study tips at the end

Key structures: Bullet points or numbered lists in sentences, For example, such as (giving examples), Should/must (for study advice)

Model
History notes for test - Ancient Egypt. Date: 20th January. Topic: Daily life in ancient Egypt. Main points to remember: First, Egyptian people lived near the Nile River because they needed water for farming. Second, rich people and poor people had very different lives. For example, rich families had big houses and servants. Poor families worked on farms. Third, children went to school only if their family was rich. Most children helped their parents with work. The Egyptians used papyrus to write, not paper. Important dates: Ancient Egypt started around 3000 BC. Study tips: I should review my drawings of Egyptian houses. I must remember the three main points about daily life. I can make a timeline to help me remember the dates better.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words of test-preparation notes on any lesson topic: use a heading, list the main points with an example for each, and end with your own study tips.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: main point, topic, example, summary, review, remember, important, information, useful, list. Structures: For example / such as; Should / must for study advice; First, second, third (numbered points).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Has a heading with subject and topic, two or three main points each with a specific example, and at least one personal study tip. Good: Heading and main points are present and most have examples; the study tip is brief or generic. Developing: Lists points without examples, or gives examples without a clear topic; no study tip. Beginning: Does not read as test notes; no clear topic or points.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'For example' or 'such as' to give examples, 'should' or 'must' for the study tips, and numbering (First, Second) correctly, with words like main point and review. Good: Uses two of the three structures; the third is attempted or missing. Developing: Uses one structure, usually 'should', and little other week vocabulary. Beginning: None of the target structures; mostly very basic statements.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'Should/must' + base verb is correct ('I should review'), and facts are stated in clear simple sentences; only small slips. Good: Occasional errors such as 'I should to review' or 'she have'; meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in modal verbs and verb forms; some sentences need guessing. Beginning: Most sentences contain errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Heading first, numbered or clearly separated points, study tips last, so a student could revise from it. Good: Points are separated and mostly in a useful order; one part blends into the next. Developing: Points run together as one block, or tips appear before the content. Beginning: No visible structure.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Usable test notes: heading, 2-3 points with examples, and sensible study tips. | 75-89: Good notes with a few weak examples or small errors. | 60-74: Main points clear but examples or tips missing. | 40-59: Short list of facts; few target structures. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; bullet points or numbers instead of full sentences; facts that are slightly wrong (grade the English, not the history or science); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; short heading style like 'Math notes - fractions'.
LENGTH: 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subject is fine. Examples may be numbers, objects or events. Tips may use 'should', 'must' or 'can'. Numbered lists count as organisation. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 with encouragement. Model answer (Ancient Egypt) copied: 100 with a note to choose own topic. Notes with no study tips: mark normally but lower content.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear main point or good example from the learner's notes. 2) Fix: Correct one modal error, e.g. 'I must to remember' -> 'I must remember the three main points.' 3) Next step: Next time add one 'For example' sentence under each main point.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about how you take notes in your English lessons. Explain what you write and why it helps you. (40–60 words)

  • Say what you write first (date, topic, etc.)
  • Explain how you organize your notes
  • Tell why your notes help you learn
Model
I take notes in every English lesson. First, I write the date and the topic at the top of the page. I listen carefully and write down main ideas and examples. I use short sentences and bullet points. After class, I read my notes again. This helps me remember important things for tests. My notes are clear and useful.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a 40-60 word paragraph on how you take notes in English lessons: what you write first, how you organise it, and why it helps you learn.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: note, notebook, write, date, topic, main point, remember, review, useful, important. Structures: Present simple for habits (I write, I read); First / After class; This helps me + verb.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Says what the learner writes first (date, topic), how the notes are organised (short sentences, lists, headings), and a clear reason notes help (e.g. remember for tests).
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses present simple habit verbs correctly with First / After class and 'This helps me remember', plus words like notebook, topic, main point, review.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Habit sentences are correct in present simple, including 'it helps me' with -s; only small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: One paragraph with a clear order: what I write, how I organise, why it helps.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; 'I note' for 'I take notes'; missing articles; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; describing notes written in Khmer.
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-70. Under about 30 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Learners may describe colour pens, drawings, tables or Khmer notes. They may use 'because' instead of 'This helps me'. Past tense is not expected here. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Instructions pasted or unrelated text: 0-20 with encouragement. Model answer copied exactly: 100 with a note to describe own habits. Writing about teacher notes instead of own: mark on content.

Writing a Simple Reflection: What Went Well

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Reflective writing

Writing about what you did in your lesson. You say what was good and what you learned.

Example:Teachers write reflections after lessons to think about their teaching.
Connection:Teachers write reflections in teaching journals and teacher training courses.
  • 2. Positive teaching moments

Good things that happen in class. Students learn well or enjoy the lesson.

Example:The students understood the story and answered all my questions.
Connection:Teachers talk about positive moments in staff meetings and teaching reports.
  • 3. Past simple for reflection

We use past simple verbs to talk about finished lessons. We say what happened yesterday or last week.

Example:The lesson went well and the students learned new words.
Connection:Teachers use past simple in reflection journals and feedback forms.

Thinking about your own teaching to see what you do well. You find your strengths.

Example:I am good at explaining grammar and helping quiet students.
Connection:Student teachers do self-evaluation in teaching practice and portfolio writing.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
WWW
what went well
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I write WWW at the top of my reflection.
🔉 Spoken Example:
+
positive or plus
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I put a plus sign next to good things.
🔉 Spoken Example:
this went well or tick
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I put a tick next to things that succeeded.
🔉 Spoken Example:
:-)
happy or positive
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I draw a happy face when students enjoyed the lesson.
🔉 Spoken Example:
→
this led to or arrow
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
My clear instructions led to good student work.
🔉 Spoken Example:
e.g.
for example
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I helped students, for example I explained new words.
🔉 Spoken Example:
*
important or star
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I put a star next to my biggest achievement.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Mon 3rd Feb
Monday the third of February
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
I taught the lesson on Monday the third of February.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. reflection — Writing about what you did and how you feel about it.
  2. went well — Something was good or successful.
  3. proud — Feeling happy about something good you did.
  4. improve — To get better at something.
  5. achievement — Something good that you did successfully.
  6. experience — Something that happened to you that you learned from.
  7. skill — Something you can do well after practice.
  8. succeed — To do well and finish something successfully.
  9. lesson — A time when you learn something new.
  10. positive — Good, happy, or helpful.
  11. confident — Feeling sure you can do something well.
  12. helpful — Useful or giving help to someone.
  13. progress — Getting better at something over time.
  14. effort — Trying hard to do something.
  15. enjoyable — Fun and making you happy.
  16. complete — To finish doing something.
  17. task — A piece of work you need to do.
  18. goal — Something you want to do or achieve.
  19. strength — Something you are good at doing.
  20. perform — To do something or show your ability.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
You will learn twenty words about reflecting on teaching and success.
Reading
You will read teacher reflections and find positive adjectives and past verbs.
Listening
You will listen to teachers talking about what went well in lessons.
Speaking
You will tell a partner about one good thing from your lesson.
Grammar
You will practise past simple verbs that teachers use in reflections.
Writing
You will write a short reflection about what went well in your lesson.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary, past simple verbs and reflection writing; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Teachers who write reflections after every lesson improve their teaching skills three times faster than teachers who don't reflect!

REFERENCES

Learning Teaching — Jim Scrivener (2011). This book has simple examples of teacher reflections and reflection language. Reflective Practice in English Language Teaching — Thomas Farrell (2015). It shows how English teachers write about what went well in lessons.

▶ How to Write a Teaching Reflection — Teaching Tips ▶ Reflecting on Your Lesson — Cambridge English Teacher

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play the full vocabulary list with definitions and example sentences:

reflection noun

Phonetic: ri-FLEK-shun

Meaning: writing about what you did and how you feel about it

Khmer: ការឆ្លុះបញ្ចាំង

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I wrote a reflection about my school day.

proud adjective

Phonetic: went WEL PROWD

Meaning: something was good or successful feeling happy about something good you did

Khmer: មានមោទនភាព

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The test went well for me. I feel proud of my homework.

improve verb

Phonetic: im-PROOV

Meaning: to get better at something

Khmer: កែលម្អ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I want to improve my English.

achievement noun

Phonetic: uh-CHEEV-ment

Meaning: something good that you did successfully

Khmer: សមិទ្ធិផល

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Finishing the project was a big achievement.

experience noun

Phonetic: ik-SPEER-ee-ens

Meaning: something that happened to you that you learned from

Khmer: បទពិសោធន៍

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The trip was a good experience.

skill noun

Phonetic: SKIL

Meaning: something you can do well after practice

Khmer: ជំនាញ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Reading is an important skill.

succeed verb

Phonetic: suk-SEED

Meaning: to do well and finish something successfully

Khmer: ជោគជ័យ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I worked hard to succeed in class.

lesson noun

Phonetic: LES-un

Meaning: a time when you learn something new

Khmer: មេរៀន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Today's lesson was about writing.

positive adjective

Phonetic: POZ-i-tiv

Meaning: good, happy, or helpful

Khmer: វិជ្ជមាន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: She has a positive attitude about school.

confident adjective

Phonetic: KON-fi-dent

Meaning: feeling sure you can do something well

Khmer: មានទំនុកចិត្ត

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I feel confident about the exam.

helpful adjective

Phonetic: HELP-ful

Meaning: useful or giving help to someone

Khmer: ចេះជួយអ្នកដទៃ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The teacher was very helpful today.

progress noun

Phonetic: PROG-res

Meaning: getting better at something over time

Khmer: វឌ្ឍនភាព

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I made good progress in math.

effort noun

Phonetic: EF-urt

Meaning: trying hard to do something

Khmer: ការខិតខំប្រឹងប្រែង

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: She put a lot of effort into the project.

enjoyable adjective

Phonetic: en-JOY-uh-bul

Meaning: fun and making you happy

Khmer: គួរឱ្យរីករាយ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The activity was very enjoyable.

complete verb

Phonetic: kum-PLEET

Meaning: to finish doing something

Khmer: បញ្ចប់

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I will complete my homework tonight.

task noun

Phonetic: TASK

Meaning: a piece of work you need to do

Khmer: កិច្ចការ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The writing task was easy.

goal noun

Phonetic: GOHL

Meaning: something you want to do or achieve

Khmer: គោលដៅ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: My goal is to read more books.

strength noun

Phonetic: STRENGTH

Meaning: something you are good at doing

Khmer: ចំណុចខ្លាំង

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: Writing is my strength in English.

perform verb

Phonetic: per-FORM

Meaning: to do something or show your ability

Khmer: បង្ហាញសមត្ថភាព (ក្នុងការប្រឡង)

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: I performed well on the test.

MINI STORY

My First Reflection

Last week, I wrote my first reflection about my English lesson. The teacher asked us to write about what went well. I felt confident because I had a positive experience that day. I completed all my tasks on time. My goal was to improve my writing skill, and I think I succeeded.

I wrote about my achievement in class. I read a story and answered all the questions. The lesson was very enjoyable and helpful. I put a lot of effort into my work. I made good progress with my reading. My teacher said my strength is understanding new words.

Writing the reflection was an easy task. I felt proud of my work. I learned that thinking about what went well helps me feel more positive. Now I want to perform better in every lesson. I will continue to work hard and improve my English skills every day.

Reading Passage

Maria's Happy Notebook

Text type: Narrative
Maria is a student in Year 9. Every Friday, she writes about her week. She writes about the good things that happened. Last Friday, Maria wrote about her math test. She got a B grade. She was very happy. She also wrote about her art project. Her teacher said it was beautiful.

Maria keeps all her writing in a blue notebook. She reads her old notes sometimes. When she feels sad, she reads about good days. This makes her smile. Her mother likes this idea too.

Maria's friend Tom asked about the notebook. Maria showed him her writing. Now Tom writes about good things too. He has a red notebook. They talk about their weeks together. Writing helps them remember happy times. It makes them feel good about school.

contentRef.text:
A Special Book of Good Memories

Text type: Description
A reflection journal is a special book. Students write in it about their day or week. They write about things that went well. The journal has empty pages. Some journals have lines. Others have blank pages. Students can write or draw pictures.

In a reflection journal, you write about good moments. You can write about tests you passed. You can write about friends you helped. You can write about new things you learned. Some people write about sports or games. Others write about art or music.

The journal is private. You keep it in a safe place. You can read it anytime you want. Many students keep their journals for years. When they are older, they read them again. The journals help them remember good school days. They show how much they learned and grew.

Teacher's Message About Reflection Writing

Text type: Notice

To: All Year 8 Students
From: Ms. Johnson
Date: Monday, 15th January

Dear Students,

This week we start reflection writing. Every Wednesday, you will write about good things from your week. Write for 10 minutes in class. Think about what went well. Did you help someone? Did you learn something new? Did you finish your homework on time?

Bring a notebook on Wednesday. Any notebook is fine. You can use a new one or an old one. Write at least five sentences. Use simple words. Be honest about your feelings.

This writing is just for you. I will not read it. You do not get a grade for it. This is your special time to think. Reflection helps you see your progress. It helps you feel proud of yourself.

See you Wednesday!

Ms. Johnson

contentRef.text:
How to Write a Simple Reflection

Text type: Informational
Writing a reflection is easy. First, find a quiet place. Sit down with your notebook and pen. Think about your day or week. Remember the good moments.

Start with simple sentences. Write 'Today went well because...' or 'This week I was happy when...'. Then write what happened. Use easy words. Write about real things. Maybe you helped your friend with homework. Maybe you finished a difficult project. Maybe you played well in a game.

Next, write how you felt. Were you proud? Were you excited? Were you happy? Feelings are important in reflections. Write two or three sentences about your feelings.

Finally, read what you wrote. Does it make sense? That is all! Reflection writing is not difficult. You only need a few minutes. Do it every week. Soon you will have many happy memories in your notebook.

contentRef.text:
Two Students, Two Ways of Reflecting

Text type: Comparison
Jake and Lisa both write reflections. But they do it differently. Jake writes every evening before bed. He sits at his desk. He writes for five minutes. He writes about one good thing from his day. His reflections are short. He uses very simple words. Jake keeps his notebook next to his bed.

Lisa writes on Sunday afternoons. She sits in the garden. She thinks about the whole week. Then she writes for fifteen minutes. She writes about three or four good things. Her reflections are longer than Jake's. She sometimes draws small pictures too. Lisa keeps her notebook in her backpack.

Both ways are good. Jake remembers something every day. Lisa sees the big picture of her week. Jake's way is quick and easy. Lisa's way gives more detail. The important thing is this: they both write about good moments. They both feel happier when they reflect.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

A reflection is when you think about your work. We write about what went well in our lessons. I can write about the good things I did. My reflection helps me see my strong points. It is good to remember our happy learning moments.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What is one thing that went well in your English class this week?

I learned ten new words this week. I remembered all of them in the test. I felt very happy about that.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Can you tell me about a time when you did good work?

Yesterday I finished my homework early. My teacher said it was very good. I was really proud of myself.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Why is it important to write about what went well?

It makes me feel good about my work. I can see what I do well. It helps me try harder next time.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. What went well when you worked with other students?

My group worked well together on our project. We all helped each other. Everyone did their part of the work.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. How do you feel when you write about your good work?

I feel happy and confident when I write about it. It shows me I can do good things. I want to keep learning more.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Past Simple (Regular and Irregular Verbs)

We use the past simple to talk about finished actions in the past.

We add -ed to regular verbs.

Irregular verbs change in different ways.

FORMS

FormExample
Regular verbs: verb + -edI helped my friend yesterday.
Irregular verbs: special past formsWe made a poster last week.
Negative: did not + base verbShe did not forget the homework.
Question: Did + subject + base verb?Did you finish the project?
Time words: yesterday, last week, agoThey worked hard two days ago.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ I help my teacher yesterday.

✓ I helped my teacher yesterday.

Use past simple with 'yesterday', not present simple.

✗ She goed to school last Monday.

✓ She went to school last Monday.

'Go' is irregular — the past form is 'went', not 'goed'.

✗ We didn't finished the task.

✓ We didn't finish the task.

After 'did not', use the base verb without -ed.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write a short reflection about one thing that went well in your English class this week. Say what you did and why it was good. (40–60 words)

  • Say what lesson or activity you are writing about
  • Use past tense verbs like 'learned', 'worked', 'did'
  • Finish by saying how you felt about it

Key structures: Past simple tense (I learned, we worked), Because + reason

Model
This week in English class, I learned new words about animals. I worked with my partner and we made a poster. It was good because we used pictures and colours. I felt happy because I remembered all the words. The teacher liked our work too.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about one thing that went well in your English class this week: name the lesson or activity, say what you did and why it was good, and end with how you felt.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: went well, proud, improve, effort, enjoyable, confident, skill, positive. Structures: Past simple (I learned, we worked, I did); Because + reason; I felt + feeling word.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names one specific lesson or activity from this week, says what the learner did, explains why it went well, and ends with a feeling. Good: The activity, what was done and a feeling are clear, but the 'why it was good' is general ('it was good because it was fun'). Developing: Mentions an activity but gives no reason or no feeling; or lists several things without choosing one. Beginning: Does not describe something that went well in English class.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses past simple verbs (learned, worked, made), 'because' for the reason and a feeling word such as proud, happy or confident. Good: Uses past simple and either 'because' or a feeling word; one week word such as 'went well' or 'improve'. Developing: Uses past verbs in a few sentences but no reason with 'because'; vocabulary is basic. Beginning: No target structures; mostly present tense or copied wording.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Regular and irregular past forms (made, went, did) are correct; 'I felt happy because...' is correct; slips are small. Good: Some wrong past forms ('I learn', 'we maked') but the story is clear. Developing: Regular errors such as 'I help my friend yesterday' or 'I was happy because remembered'; meaning sometimes needs guessing. Beginning: Most sentences have errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Starts with the activity, then what was done, then why it was good, then the feeling, in complete sentences. Good: Mostly in order; one sentence is out of place. Developing: Ideas are mixed or very short with no linking. Beginning: Disconnected words.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: One clear success, with what, why and feeling, all in correct past tense. | 75-89: Clear reflection; small past-tense slips or a general reason. | 60-74: Understandable; reason or feeling missing. | 40-59: Very short or mostly present tense. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; simple feeling words like 'happy' instead of 'proud'; writing about a Khmer-class success told in English.
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any activity works: a game, a speaking task, a test, group work. 'It was good because' or 'I liked it because' are both fine. The model's poster is only one example. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 with encouragement. Model answer (animals poster) copied word for word: 100 with a note to write own experience. Writing about a failure instead: mark on English and gently redirect.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the specific activity or feeling the learner named. 2) Fix: Correct one past or 'because' error, e.g. 'I am happy because I remember the words' -> 'I felt happy because I remembered the words.' 3) Next step: Next time add one more sentence saying what you will do to improve.

lessons.titleKm: Writing a Simple Reflection: What Went Well — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Writing a Simple Reflection: What Went Well — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write a reflection about a group project that went well. Explain what your group did together and what you learned from working as a team. (60–80 words)

  • Say who was in your group and what the project was about
  • Describe what each person did to help the group
  • Explain what good things happened when you worked together

Key structures: We + past simple (we planned, we shared), Everyone / Some people + past simple, It was good because...

Model
Last month, my group made a presentation about healthy food. There were four students in my group. We planned the work together at the start. Maria found pictures of fruit and vegetables. Tom wrote about breakfast. I made the poster and Sara talked to the class. Everyone did their job well. It was good because we helped each other. We finished on time and the teacher gave us a good mark. I learned that teamwork is important.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words about a group project that went well: say who was in the group and what the project was, what each person did, and what good things happened because you worked together.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: group, project, teamwork, helpful, effort, complete, achievement, progress, proud. Structures: We + past simple (we planned, we shared); Everyone / Some people + past simple; It was good because....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives the group size or members and the project topic, says what at least two different people did, and explains one or two good results of teamwork. Good: Group, project and roles are given, but the good results are general ('it was nice'). Developing: Describes the project but not who did what, or does not say what was good about working together. Beginning: Does not describe a group project.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'We planned/shared...' and 'Everyone' or 'Some people' with past simple, plus 'It was good because...' and words like teamwork or helped each other. Good: Uses 'We + past simple' and one of the other two structures correctly. Developing: Mostly 'I' sentences; 'we' or 'everyone' appears once or not at all. Beginning: No target structures; present tense throughout.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Past forms for different people are correct (Maria found, Tom wrote, I made); 'everyone' takes a singular verb. Good: A few errors such as 'Everyone were' or 'We plan together'; meaning is clear. Developing: Past and present are mixed; roles are hard to follow. Beginning: Meaning is mostly unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Group and project first, then each person's job, then the results and what was learned. Good: Order is mostly clear; roles may be listed in one long sentence. Developing: Roles and results are mixed together. Beginning: Disconnected sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear project, several roles and real results in correct past tense. | 75-89: Clear; a few verb slips or general results. | 60-74: Project clear but roles or results thin. | 40-59: Short, mostly 'I' sentences. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling of names; spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'friends' for 'group members'; a very simple project such as cleaning the classroom.
LENGTH: 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Under about 45 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any group activity counts: a poster, a play, a garden, a teacher-training task. Roles can be given with names or 'one person'. 'Because' can come at the start or middle. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (healthy food presentation) copied exactly: 100 with a note to use own group. A solo project: mark on English but note the task asked about a group.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise how the learner described what one group member did. 2) Fix: Correct one verb, e.g. 'Everyone do their job' -> 'Everyone did their job well.' 3) Next step: Next time add one sentence saying what the group learned.

lessons.titleKm: Writing a Simple Reflection: What Went Well — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Writing a Simple Reflection: What Went Well — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write a longer reflection about a school day or week when many things went well. Describe different activities and explain why you feel positive about your learning. (80–110 words)

  • Write about two or three different things that went well
  • Give specific examples of what you did in each activity
  • Use positive feeling words and say what you will do next

Key structures: First / Then / Also (sequencing words), I felt... because..., Now I can... / Next time I will...

Model
Last week was very good at school. First, I did well in my Maths test. I studied hard and I answered eight questions correctly. I felt proud because Maths is difficult for me. Then, in Art class, I finished my painting of my family. The teacher said the colours were beautiful. Also, I helped a new student find the library. She was lost and I showed her the way. We are friends now. I felt happy because I was kind. This week taught me that hard work is important. It also showed me that helping others feels good. Now I can do better in tests. Next time I will help more new students too.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words about a school day or week when several things went well: describe two or three activities with examples, say how you felt and why, and say what you will do next.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: achievement, progress, proud, confident, effort, improve, positive, succeed, goal. Structures: First / Then / Also; I felt... because...; Now I can... / Next time I will....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes two or three different things that went well, each with a specific detail (a mark, a painting, a helpful act), shows feeling for each, and ends with a plan. Good: Two things are described with some detail; the feelings or the plan are brief. Developing: Only one thing is described properly, or the examples are very general ('I studied well'). Beginning: Does not describe things that went well at school.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses First / Then / Also to move between events, 'I felt ... because ...' with real reasons, and 'Now I can' or 'Next time I will' correctly. Good: Uses two of the three structures correctly; the third is missing or slightly wrong. Developing: Uses one sequencing word or 'felt', with basic vocabulary. Beginning: No target structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Past forms are correct and 'will' / 'can' plans use the base verb ('I will help'); errors are few. Good: Some slips ('I felt proud because I am study hard'), but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent tense mistakes, especially in 'because' clauses; some meaning lost. Beginning: Most sentences contain errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Each activity has its own short part in time order, and the plan comes last. Good: Order is mostly clear; one activity is mixed with another. Developing: Events and feelings are mixed with no clear order. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Several well-described successes with feelings, reasons and a next step. | 75-89: Clear reflection; small errors or a weak plan. | 60-74: Understandable; only one success well developed. | 40-59: Short and general. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'also' at the start or the end; simple feelings words instead of the model's; successes outside the classroom, e.g. helping a friend.
LENGTH: 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any school day or week works. 'Next' plans may use 'I want to' or 'I will'. Successes can be tests, art, sport or kindness. Order words such as 'After that' are fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (Maths test, painting, new student) copied: 100 with a note to use own week. A week with no good things: encourage and mark on language.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one specific success or good reason the learner gave. 2) Fix: Correct one error, e.g. 'I feel proud because I study hard' -> 'I felt proud because I studied hard.' 3) Next step: Next time end with 'Next time I will...' and one real plan.

questions.question: Q1. I ___ my homework on time last night.
questions.explanation: → 'Last night' shows the action is finished, so we need past simple.

questions.question: complete — finish
questions.explanation: → 'complete' and 'finish' both mean to bring to the end, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: lesson — mountain
questions.explanation: → 'lesson' and 'mountain' are about very different things, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: goal — window
questions.explanation: → 'goal' and 'window' have no link in meaning, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q5. We ___ a good plan for the presentation yesterday.
questions.explanation: → 'Yesterday' shows finished time, and the past of 'make' is the irregular form 'made'.

questions.question: Q25. The group ___ the classroom after the lesson yesterday.
questions.explanation: → 'Yesterday' shows the cleaning is finished, so we need past simple.

questions.question: Q1. I wrote a ___ about my school day.
questions.explanation: → A 'reflection' is writing about what you did and what you think.

questions.question: confident — nervous
questions.explanation: → 'confident' and 'nervous' have opposite meanings: confident is sure, nervous is worried, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: skill — banana
questions.explanation: → 'skill' and 'banana' do not connect in meaning or form, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q23. We ___ about the project for ten minutes yesterday.
questions.explanation: → 'Yesterday' signals the talking is finished, so past simple is correct.

questions.question: Q18. My ___ is to read more books.
questions.explanation: → A 'goal' is something you want to reach.

questions.question: succeed — win
questions.explanation: → 'succeed' and 'win' both mean to do well and reach a goal, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q22. I ___ a good score on my homework yesterday.
questions.explanation: → 'Yesterday' shows finished time, and 'get' is irregular with past form 'got'.

questions.question: Q16. I will ___ my homework tonight.
questions.explanation: → We 'complete' homework when we finish it.

questions.question: helpful — help
questions.explanation: → 'helpful' and 'help' share the root 'help', so they are a word family.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short reflection about something that went well for you at school recently. Say what happened and how you felt about it. (40–60 words)

  • Write about one good thing that happened at school
  • Say when it happened
  • Explain why it went well
  • Say how you felt about it
Model
Last week, I gave a presentation in English class. I talked about my favorite hobby. I practiced a lot at home. My teacher said my pronunciation was very good. My classmates asked interesting questions. I answered them all. I felt proud and confident. This presentation went much better than my last one. I learned that practice helps me improve.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a 40-60 word paragraph about one good thing that happened at school recently: when it happened, why it went well, and how you felt.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: went well, proud, confident, improve, practice, effort, achievement, enjoyable. Structures: Past simple with time words (last week, yesterday); It went well because...; I felt + feeling.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Tells one specific good event at school, says when it happened, explains what made it go well, and says how the learner felt.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses a past time phrase, past simple verbs, a reason with 'because' or 'so', and a feeling such as proud or confident.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Past forms are correct (gave, talked, practised, answered); only small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: One tidy paragraph: event, when, why it went well, feeling.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; simple reasons; events as small as answering a question.
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any school event works: a presentation, test, game, sports day. The model's presentation is only an example. 'Last week', 'yesterday' or a date are all fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Instructions pasted or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (English presentation) copied: 100 with a note to write own event. A non-school event: mark on language but note the task.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Educational Apps and Digital Tools

Apps are programs on phones or tablets that help teachers teach and students learn. They can show lessons, games, or activities on a screen.

Example:Open the app and click the icon to start your lesson.
Connection:Teachers use apps in the classroom to make lessons more interesting and fun.
  • 2. Operating Classroom Technology

To operate means to use or control a device or tool. Teachers need to know how to turn on, use, and explain technology to students.

Example:First, turn on the tablet, then click the app icon.
Connection:Teachers explain how to use tablets and apps during class time every day.
  • 3. Digital Instructions and User Guides

Instructions tell you what to do step by step. User guides are books or pages that explain how to use an app or device.

Example:Follow the instructions to download the app from the website.
Connection:You read instructions in textbooks, on screens, and in teacher handouts.

*[Embedded images on PDF page 878; see source PDF.]* When you are online, you can share files, messages, and work with other people. You need wifi or internet to connect.

Example:Connect to the wifi, then share your work with the class.
Connection:Students and teachers share homework and projects online every week.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
phone icon or mobile device
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Click the phone icon to open the app.
🔉 Spoken Example:
download arrow or download button
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Press the download arrow to get the file.
🔉 Spoken Example:
upload arrow or upload button
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Click the upload arrow to send your work.
🔉 Spoken Example:
search icon or magnifying glass
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Click the search icon to find information.
🔉 Spoken Example:
save icon or disk
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Press the save icon to keep your file.
🔉 Spoken Example:
delete icon or trash bin
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Click the delete icon to remove the file.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Wi-Fi symbol
wifi symbol or wireless internet icon
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Look for the wifi symbol to connect to the internet.
🔉 Spoken Example:
message icon or envelope
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Click the message icon to send words to your friend.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. tablet — A tablet is a small computer with a touch screen.
  2. app — An app is a program you use on a phone or tablet.
  3. screen — A screen is the flat part of a device that shows pictures.
  4. keyboard — A keyboard is the part with buttons you press to type.
  5. click — Click means to press a button on a mouse or screen.
  6. download — Download means to get a file from the internet.
  7. upload — Upload means to send a file to the internet.
  8. icon — An icon is a small picture on a screen you can click.
  9. password — A password is secret letters or numbers to enter a system.
  10. search — Search means to look for information on the internet.
  11. website — A website is a place on the internet with information.
  12. online — Online means connected to or using the internet.
  13. record — Record means to save sound or video on a device.
  14. save — Save means to keep a file on a computer.
  15. delete — Delete means to remove or take away a file.
  16. connect — Connect means to join two things together like internet.
  17. wifi — Wifi is wireless internet you can use on devices.
  18. message — A message is words you send to someone on a phone.
  19. share — Share means to let other people see or use something.
  20. charge — Charge means to put electricity into a device battery.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty technology words and their meanings for classroom apps and devices.
Reading
Read a simple user guide about an educational app and find the main steps.
Listening
Listen to a teacher explain how to use an app and identify the key features.
Speaking
Explain to a partner how to use a digital tool with clear instructions.
Grammar
Use imperative verbs to write and say commands for using technology in class.
Writing
Write step-by-step instructions for how to download and use an educational app.
Lesson Test
The test checks your technology vocabulary, listening, and instruction writing skills; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'app' is short for 'application' and was first used in 2008 when smartphones became popular around the world.

REFERENCES

Teaching English with Technology — Dudeney and Hockly (2007). This book explains basic technology words and how teachers use apps in class. English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). Unit 20 teaches simple technology words and expressions for everyday use.

▶ Basic Computer Skills: Getting Started with Technology — GCF Global ▶ English for Teachers: Using Apps in the Classroom — British Council LearnEnglish

Maria's First Video Lesson

Text type: Narrative
Maria is a teacher in a small town. Last month, she started using a tablet in her class. She was nervous at first. She did not know much about technology.

One day, Maria wanted to show a video about animals. She opened a video app on her tablet. The students watched lions and elephants on the big screen. They were very happy and excited. They asked many

questions about the animals.

Now Maria uses the tablet every week. She plays videos and shows pictures to her students. Sometimes the students use the tablet too. They play learning games and do quizzes. Maria is not nervous anymore. She thinks technology makes learning more fun. Her students love the new lessons.

How to Use a Quiz App

Text type: Informational
Quiz apps are popular tools for learning. They help students practice and remember information. Here is how to use a simple quiz app.

First, open the app on your phone or tablet. Choose your subject. You can pick English, math, science, or history. Then choose a topic. For example, in English you can choose 'verbs' or 'spelling'. Next, start the quiz. Read each question carefully. Click on the correct answer. The app will tell you if you are right or wrong.

After the quiz, you can see your score. The app shows which questions you answered correctly. You can try the quiz again to get a better score. Many apps also give you stars or points. Quiz apps make studying easy and fun!

Mr. Lee and Mrs. Brown are both English teachers. They teach in the same school. But they use different methods in their classrooms.

Mr. Lee loves technology. He uses a laptop and a projector every day. He shows videos and plays music in his lessons. His students use tablets to do exercises. They also use a chat app to ask questions. Mr. Lee thinks technology saves time and makes lessons interesting.

Grammar Practice

Imperative Form (Commands and Instructions)

We use the imperative to give instructions, commands, or tell someone what to do.

Start with the base verb (no subject).

Use 'Don't' + base verb for negative commands.

FORMS

FormExample
Affirmative: base verb + rest of sentenceOpen the app on your phone.
Negative: Don't + base verb + rest of sentenceDon't close the window yet.
Polite request: Please + base verbPlease turn on the computer.
Warning: Don't + base verb (stronger)Don't delete the file!
Multiple steps: verb, then verbClick here, then wait.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ You click on the link.

✓ Click on the link.

Don't use 'you' in imperative sentences — start with the verb.

✗ Not touch the screen now.

✓ Don't touch the screen now.

Use 'Don't' before the verb for negative commands, not 'Not'.

✗ Please you save your work.

✓ Please save your work.

Remove 'you' — even polite imperatives don't need a subject.

nodes.question: Q29. ___ the text size in the app settings if needed.

nodes.question: Q30. ___ use your phone for games during class time.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe one app you use for studying. Explain what it does and why you like it. (40–60 words)

  • Name the app in your first sentence
  • Say what you do with the app
  • Explain why it helps you

Key structures: I use... to + verb, It helps me + verb

Model
I use Duolingo to learn new English words every day. The app has games and short lessons. It helps me practice vocabulary and grammar. I like it because the lessons are fun and easy. I can study for ten minutes on the bus.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 40-60 words about one app you use for studying: name it in your first sentence, say what you do with it, and explain why it helps and why you like it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: app, download, tablet, screen, search, online, save, share, website. Structures: I use... to + verb; It helps me + verb; I like it because....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names a real app in the first sentence, says specifically what the learner does with it (for example learns words, watches videos, records a voice), and gives a clear reason for liking it. Good: Names the app and says what it does, but the reason is general ('it is good'). Developing: Names an app but does not say what the learner does with it, or does not explain why it helps. Beginning: Does not describe a study app.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'I use... to + verb' and 'It helps me + verb' correctly, with tech words such as app, download, online, screen, save. Good: Uses one of the two structures correctly and two tech words; the other is attempted. Developing: Writes 'I use the app' with no purpose verb, and few tech words. Beginning: No target structures and no tech vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: After 'to' and 'helps me' the base verb is correct ('to learn', 'helps me practise'); present simple is accurate. Good: Some slips such as 'I use it for learn' or 'it help me'; meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in verb patterns; reader sometimes guesses. Beginning: Most sentences contain errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: App first, then what it does, then why it helps, in short complete sentences. Good: Mostly ordered; one sentence is out of place. Developing: Ideas mixed or fragmentary. Beginning: Disconnected words.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Named app, clear use and reason, with both structures correct. | 75-89: Clear; small verb-pattern slips. | 60-74: Understandable; reason or use is general. | 40-59: Very short; structures missing. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling of app names; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; using 'phone' or 'YouTube' as the 'app'; 'for + verb-ing' instead of 'to + verb' when meaning is clear (coach gently).
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any study app or website works: Duolingo, Google Translate, YouTube, Khan Academy, a Khmer app. The model's Duolingo is only one example. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (Duolingo) copied: 100 with a note to use own app. If the learner uses no apps, accept an app they would like to use, written clearly.
NOTE: Week 23 grammar practice teaches imperatives (Click, Don't delete), but this task's key structures are 'I use... to + verb' and 'It helps me + verb'; the rubric follows the task text.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the app or the reason the learner gave. 2) Fix: Correct one pattern, e.g. 'I use it for learn words' -> 'I use it to learn words.' 3) Next step: Next time add one sentence about when you use the app.

lessons.titleKm: Using Simple Classroom Technology and Apps — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)
lessons.titleEn: Using Simple Classroom Technology and Apps — Guided Writing Task 2 (60–80 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about how your teacher uses technology in your classroom. Give two or three examples of what the teacher does. (60–80 words)

  • Start with a general sentence about technology in your class
  • Give specific examples of devices or apps
  • Say how this technology helps students learn

Key structures: My teacher uses... to + verb, We can also + verb, This helps us + verb

Model
My teacher uses technology in our English lessons every week. She uses a projector to show videos and pictures. We can see grammar examples on the big screen. Sometimes we use tablets to do vocabulary exercises together. My teacher also plays listening activities from a website. This helps us understand English better. The lessons are more interesting with this technology.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 60-80 words about how your teacher uses technology in class: start with a general sentence, give two or three examples of devices or apps, and say how they help students learn.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: projector, screen, tablet, website, online, record, share, connect, wifi, keyboard. Structures: My teacher uses... to + verb; We can also + verb; This helps us + verb.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Opens with a general sentence about technology in the class, gives two or three clear examples of what the teacher uses and does, and says how it helps learning. Good: General sentence and two examples are given, but how it helps students is short. Developing: Gives only one example, or lists devices without saying what the teacher does with them. Beginning: Does not describe the teacher's use of technology.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'My teacher uses... to + verb', 'We can also + verb' and 'This helps us + verb' correctly with device words (projector, tablet, speaker, website). Good: Uses two of the three structures correctly with some device words. Developing: Uses one structure; sentences are mostly 'The teacher has a...'. Beginning: No target structures; very few tech words.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Third person -s is correct ('She uses', 'it shows'); 'can' and 'helps us' take the right verb forms. Good: Some slips such as 'My teacher use' or 'we can to see'; meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in he/she verbs and modals; reader guesses. Beginning: Meaning unclear in most sentences.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: General sentence, examples one by one, closing benefit. Good: Mostly in order; examples run together. Developing: Examples and benefits mixed. Beginning: No clear order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: General opening, 2-3 clear examples, a benefit, correct structures. | 75-89: Clear; small third-person or modal errors. | 60-74: Understandable; one example or benefit thin. | 40-59: Short list of devices. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; 'smart board' for 'interactive whiteboard'; a teacher who uses only a phone or speaker.
LENGTH: 60-80 words; accept about 55-90. Under about 45 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real devices are fine: projector, TV, phone, speaker, laptop. If the school has little technology, writing about a teacher's phone or a speaker is acceptable. The model's English class is only an example. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (projector, tablets) copied: 100 with a note to describe own class. Writing about students' own devices instead of the teacher's: mark on language.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one clear example of what the teacher does. 2) Fix: Correct one error, e.g. 'My teacher use a projector show videos' -> 'My teacher uses a projector to show videos.' 3) Next step: Next time end with 'This helps us...' and name what we learn.

lessons.titleKm: Using Simple Classroom Technology and Apps — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)
lessons.titleEn: Using Simple Classroom Technology and Apps — Guided Writing Task 3 (80–110 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Imagine you are a teacher. Explain how you would use simple technology to teach a lesson about animals. Describe the tools and activities you would use. (80–110 words)

  • Say what technology you would use first
  • Describe two or three activities with this technology
  • Explain what students would learn

Key structures: I would use... to + verb, First/Then/Finally, Students could + verb

Model
I would use simple technology to teach a lesson about animals. First, I would show a short video about different animals on the projector. Students could see lions, elephants, and birds. Then, I would use a quiz app on tablets. Students would answer questions about animal names and where they live. They could work in small groups. Finally, I would ask students to take photos of animals with their phones. They could find pictures in books or outside. Students would show their photos to the class. This lesson would be fun and easy. Technology helps students remember new words about animals.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words as a teacher explaining how you would use simple technology to teach a lesson about animals: say what you would use first, describe two or three activities, and say what students would learn.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: projector, tablet, video, record, search, share, website, quiz, photo, screen. Structures: I would use... to + verb; First / Then / Finally; Students could + verb.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Says which technology comes first, describes two or three activities for an animal lesson (for example a video, a quiz, taking photos), and states what students would learn. Good: Describes two activities with the tools; what students learn is brief. Developing: Names tools only, with few activities, or the lesson is not about animals. Beginning: Does not describe a teaching plan.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I would use... to', 'Students could' and First / Then / Finally correctly, with tech words such as projector, record, search, share. Good: Uses two of the three structures correctly; the third is missing or slightly wrong. Developing: Uses 'I will' or present tense instead of 'would/could'; one sequencing word. Beginning: No target structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'Would' and 'could' are followed by the base verb ('students could see'); few errors. Good: Some slips such as 'I would to show' or 'students could saw'; meaning clear. Developing: Frequent errors in would/could and tense; plan is partly unclear. Beginning: Meaning unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps follow First, Then, Finally with the result at the end; easy to follow as a plan. Good: Mostly in order; one step unclear. Developing: Steps are mixed together without order words. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear 3-step animal lesson with correct would/could. | 75-89: Clear plan; small modal errors. | 60-74: Understandable; one step or the learning outcome missing. | 40-59: Short list of tools. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'I will' instead of 'I would' when meaning is clear (coach gently); ideas that are not realistic for a rural school; missing articles.
LENGTH: 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 60 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any simple technology works: phone camera, speaker, projector, tablet, offline videos. Activities may differ from the model. A different animal focus (farm, wild, pets) is fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (lions, elephants, birds) copied: 100 with a note to plan own lesson. If the learner describes a non-animal lesson, mark on language and note this.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one practical idea from the learner's plan. 2) Fix: Correct one error, e.g. 'Students could to see the video' -> 'Students could see the video.' 3) Next step: Next time end with one sentence about what students will learn.

questions.question: Q6. ___ share your password with other students.

questions.question: message — text

questions.question: Q26. ___ the brightness if you can't see the screen well.

questions.explanation: → 'online' and 'offline' have opposite meanings: online is connected to the internet, offline is not, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: Q4. Please ___ your name on the quiz app.
questions.explanation: → Polite imperatives use 'Please' + base verb, keeping the simple command form.

questions.question: Q3. The teacher points to the big ___.
questions.explanation: → The 'screen' is the part of a device where we see things.

questions.question: Q13. ___ your work in the cloud folder every day.
questions.explanation: → This is advice or an instruction repeated regularly, so imperative form is used.

questions.question: Q15. ___ to the teacher's screen on your tablet.
questions.explanation: → This is a classroom instruction, so we use the imperative base verb form.

questions.question: Q12. We take an ___ class every Monday morning.
questions.explanation: → 'Online' means on the internet.
