questions.explanation: → 'keyboard' and 'banana' have no link in meaning, so they are unrelated.

questions.explanation: → 'message' and 'text' both mean words sent to someone, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q16. Can you ___ your phone to the wifi?
questions.explanation: → We 'connect' a phone to wifi to use the internet.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about your favorite classroom technology or app. Explain what it is and why you like it. (40–60 words)

  • Say what technology or app you use.
  • Explain what you do with it.
  • Say why you like it.
Model
My favorite classroom technology is my tablet. I use it every day to read books and watch videos. I also do my homework on it and send it to my teacher online. I like my tablet because it is light and easy to carry. It helps me learn new things quickly. Learning with my tablet is fun and interesting.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a 40-60 word paragraph about your favourite classroom technology or app: say what it is, what you do with it, and why you like it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: tablet, app, screen, keyboard, online, download, save, share, connect. Structures: My favourite... is...; I use it to + verb; I like it because....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names one technology or app, describes specific things the learner does with it, and gives a clear personal reason for liking it.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'My favourite... is', 'I use it to + verb' and 'because' correctly, with words like screen, online, download.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Present simple and 'to + verb' are mostly correct; slips are small.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: One paragraph: what it is, what I do, why I like it.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; phone or TV as the favourite technology; British or American spelling.
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any device or app works. Past tense is not required. The model's tablet is only one example. The model answer is only a reference.

submodules.titleKm: Week 24: Chapter 4 Review: Reading and Writing for Teaching
submodules.titleEn: Week 24: Chapter 4 Review: Reading and Writing for Teaching

contentRef.text:
CHAPTER IV · WEEK 24

Chapter 4 Review: Reading and Writing for Teaching

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify key teaching strategies from spoken reviews of reading and writing instruction methods. L2 Understand
  • Apply educational terminology and simple past tense to describe completed teaching activities. L3 Apply
  • Discuss effective techniques for teaching reading and writing skills to different learner groups. L3 Apply
  • Evaluate sample lesson plans that focus on developing student reading and writing abilities. L3 Apply
  • Summarize main principles of teaching reading and writing in a structured paragraph format. L3 Apply
  • Collaborate with peers to reflect on personal growth in understanding literacy teaching approaches. L4 Analyze · HOTS

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

textbook noun

Phonetic: TEKST-book

Meaning: a book that students use to learn in school

Khmer: សៀវភៅសិក្សា

Example: I read my English textbook every day.

teacher noun

Phonetic: TEE-cher

Meaning: a person who helps students learn things

Khmer: គ្រូ

Example: My teacher explains the lesson very well.

lesson noun

Phonetic: LES-un

Meaning: a time when a teacher teaches something new

Khmer: មេរៀន

Example: We have an English lesson every Monday.

explain verb

Phonetic: eks-PLAYN

Meaning: to help someone understand something by telling them

Khmer: ពន្យល់

Example: The teacher will explain the new words.

practice verb

Phonetic: PRAK-tis

Meaning: to do something many times to get better

Khmer: ហ្វឹកហាត់

Example: I practice writing sentences at home.

homework noun

Phonetic: HOME-werk

Meaning: work that students do at home after school

Khmer: កិច្ចការផ្ទះ

Example: I finish my homework before dinner.

classroom noun

Phonetic: KLAS-room

Meaning: a room where students learn with a teacher

Khmer: ថ្នាក់រៀន

Example: Our classroom has twenty desks.

paragraph noun

Phonetic: PAR-a-graf

Meaning: a group of sentences about one main idea

Khmer: កថាខណ្ឌ

Example: Write a paragraph about your family.

notebook noun

Phonetic: NOTE-book

Meaning: a book with empty pages for writing notes

Khmer: សៀវភៅកត់ត្រា

Example: I write new words in my notebook.

grammar noun

Phonetic: GRAM-er

Meaning: the rules for using words in a language

Khmer: វេយ្យាករណ៍

Example: We study English grammar every week.

assignment noun

Phonetic: a-SYNE-ment

Meaning: a piece of work that a teacher gives

Khmer: កិច្ចការ

Example: The teacher gave us a writing assignment.

review verb

Phonetic: ri-VYOO

Meaning: to look at something again to remember it

Khmer: ពិនិត្យឡើងវិញ

Example: We review old lessons before the test.

mistake noun

Phonetic: mi-STAYK

Meaning: something wrong that you do or write

Khmer: កំហុស

Example: I found three mistakes in my writing.

correct verb

Phonetic: ko-REKT

Meaning: to fix something that is wrong

Khmer: កែតម្រូវ

Example: Please correct your spelling mistakes.

improve verb

Phonetic: im-PROOV

Meaning: to make something better than before

Khmer: កែលម្អ

Example: I want to improve my English writing.

instruction noun

Phonetic: in-STRUK-shun

Meaning: words that tell you how to do something

Khmer: សេចក្តីណែនាំ

Example: Read the instruction before you start writing.

summary noun

Phonetic: SUM-a-ree

Meaning: a short way to tell the main ideas

Khmer: សេចក្តីសង្ខេប

Example: Write a summary of the story.

question noun

Phonetic: KWES-chun

Meaning: something you ask when you want to know

Khmer: សំណួរ

Example: Students can ask questions in class.

answer verb

Phonetic: AN-ser

Meaning: to give information when someone asks you

Khmer: ឆ្លើយ

Example: Can you answer this question for me?

prepare verb

Phonetic: pri-PAIR

Meaning: to get ready for something before it

Khmer: រៀបចំ

Example: I prepare my lesson materials every

MINI STORY

My name is Dara. I am a teacher at a small school. Every morning I prepare my lessons carefully. I read my textbook and write notes in my notebook.

In the classroom, I explain new grammar rules to my students. They practice writing sentences and paragraphs. Sometimes students make mistakes, but that is okay. I correct their work and help them improve. The students do homework every night. They review their lessons before tests.

Today I gave my students a writing assignment. The instruction was simple: write a summary about your favorite teacher. One student asked a good question about spelling. I was happy to answer it. Teaching helps me learn too. I love my job very much.

nodes.text: GAP-FILL

nodes.question: Q1. I read my English ___ every day.
nodes.explanation: → A 'textbook' is a school book for a subject.

nodes.question: Q2. My ___ explains the lesson very well.
nodes.explanation: → A 'teacher' explains the lesson.

nodes.question: Q3. We have an English ___ every Monday.
nodes.explanation: → A 'lesson' is a class at a set time.

nodes.question: Q4. The teacher will ___ the new words.
nodes.explanation: → A teacher can 'explain' new words by saying what they mean.

nodes.question: Q5. I ___ writing sentences at home.
nodes.explanation: → We 'practice' writing by doing it often.

nodes.question: Q6. I finish my ___ before dinner.
nodes.explanation: → 'Homework' is work to do at home.

nodes.question: Q7. Our ___ has twenty desks.
nodes.explanation: → A 'classroom' is a room with desks.

nodes.question: Q8. Write a ___ about your family.
nodes.explanation: → A 'paragraph' is a group of sentences about one topic.

nodes.question: Q9. I write new words in my ___.
nodes.explanation: → We write new words in a 'notebook'.

nodes.question: Q10. We study English ___ every week.
nodes.explanation: → 'Grammar' is the rules of a language.

nodes.question: Q11. The teacher gave us a writing ___.
nodes.explanation: → An 'assignment' is a piece of work from the teacher.

nodes.question: Q12. We ___ old lessons before the test.

Reading Passage

Maria's First Lesson Plan

Text type: Narrative
Maria wanted to become a teacher. Last week, she wrote her first lesson plan. She sat at her desk with a notebook. She wrote down her ideas for teaching children.

First, Maria wrote the lesson topic at the top. Then she made a list of activities. She planned reading time, writing exercises, and games. She checked her plan three times. She wanted everything to be clear and simple.

The next day, Maria showed her plan to her teacher. Her teacher smiled and said it was very good. Maria felt happy and proud. She learned that good planning helps teachers do their job well. Now she writes a new plan every week.

A Teacher's Classroom Library

Text type: Description
Mr. Brown has a special corner in his classroom. It is a small reading area. There are two bookshelves with many books. The books have colorful covers. Some books are for reading. Other books are for writing practice.

The bottom shelf has picture books for young children. The top shelf has books with more words. There is also a small table. Students can sit and read there. Mr. Brown keeps pencils and paper on the table. Students can write about the books they read.

Every Monday, Mr. Brown adds new books to the shelves. He reads the titles to his students. The children get excited about new stories. This reading corner helps students love books. It makes reading and writing fun for everyone.

contentRef.text:
How to Make a Reading Activity

Text type: Informational
Teachers make reading activities for their students. This helps children practice reading. Here are some easy steps to make a good activity.

First, choose a short text. The text should be simple. It can be a story or some facts. Make sure your students can read most words. Then, think of some questions about the text. Write three to five questions. The questions should check understanding. Some questions can ask about details. Other questions can ask about the main idea.

Finally, prepare answer choices for each question. Give three or four possible answers. Make sure only one answer is correct. Test your activity first. Read it yourself. Check if the questions are clear. Now your reading activity is ready to use in class!

contentRef.text:
Two Ways to Teach Writing

Text type: Comparison
Teachers can teach writing in different ways. Two popular ways are free writing and guided writing. Both help students learn to write.

Free writing lets students choose their own topics. Students can write about anything they like. They write about their family, friends, or hobbies. This way is fun and creative. Students feel free. But sometimes students don't know what to write. They might make many mistakes.

Guided writing is different. The teacher gives students a topic. The teacher also gives helpful words and examples. Students follow steps to write. This way helps students learn structure. Students make fewer mistakes. But some students feel less creative. Good teachers use both ways. They know each way has good points.

Grammar Practice

Present Simple vs Present Continuous

We use present simple for habits and facts.

We use present continuous for things happening now or temporary situations.

Use -ing form for continuous.

FORMS

FormExample
Present simple: I / you / we / they + base verbI teach English every day.
Present simple: he / she / it + verb + s/esShe reads books to the class.
Present continuous: am / is / are + verb + -ingHe is writing a lesson plan now.
Present simple negative: do not / does not + base verbThey do not speak French in this class.
Present continuous negative: am not / is not / are not + verb + -ingI am not teaching today.
Present simple question: Do / Does + subject + base verb?Does she teach on Mondays?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ She teaching grammar now.

✓ She is teaching grammar now.

Present continuous needs am/is/are before the -ing verb.

✗ I am teach every morning.

✓ I teach every morning.

Use present simple, not continuous, for regular habits.

✗ He teach math on Fridays.

✓ He teaches math on Fridays.

Add -es for he/she/it in present simple.

Writing Good Lesson Plans (continuous) Teachers need to plan their lessons carefully. A lesson plan helps the teacher know what to do. It shows the aims of the lesson. It lists the activities students will do. Good lesson plans also include time for each activity.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about why lesson plans are useful for teachers. (40–60 words)

  • Say what a lesson plan is.
  • Explain why teachers use lesson plans.
  • Give one example of what is in a lesson plan.
Model
A lesson plan is a guide that teachers write before class. It helps teachers know what to teach and how to teach it. A lesson plan includes the lesson objective, activities for students, and time for each part. When teachers plan carefully, their lessons are clearer and students learn better. Lesson plans make teaching easier and more organized.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a 40-60 word paragraph on why lesson plans are useful for teachers: say what a lesson plan is, why teachers use one, and give one example of what is inside it.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson plan, lesson, teacher, explain, practice, activity, classroom, paragraph, textbook, homework. Structures: A lesson plan is...; Present simple for facts and habits (teachers write, it helps); It helps teachers + verb / ... because ....
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Defines a lesson plan in the learner's own words, gives at least one clear reason teachers use one (for example it shows what to teach and how), and names a specific item inside it (aim, activities, time for each part).
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'lesson plan', 'activities' or 'aim', and teacher/lesson words correctly, with 'A lesson plan is...' and present simple for facts.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Third person -s is correct ('a plan helps', 'it includes'), and present simple is used for general facts; errors are small.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: One short paragraph: definition first, then why, then an example, with a closing idea.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (e.g. 'lesson plane'); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; missing articles; using 'teach plan' for 'lesson plan' if meaning is clear; simple wording such as 'what to do in class'.
LENGTH: 40-60 words; accept about 35-65. Under about 30 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any correct contents of a lesson plan are fine: aim or objective, activities, materials, time, homework. Learners may mention reading and writing lessons. Reasons may be about preparation, time or student learning. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Instructions pasted or unrelated text: 0-20 with encouragement. Model answer copied exactly: 100 with a note to use own words. A paragraph about students' lesson notes instead: mark on language but note the topic.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Describing physical spaces in education

We talk about where things are in a classroom or learning space. We name the objects and say their positions.

Example:There is a whiteboard in the front of the classroom.
Connection:Teachers and students use this language when they give directions or describe their school rooms.
  • 2. Prepositions of place

These are small words that show where something is. They tell us the position of objects in a room.

Example:The clock is on the wall above the door.
Connection:You use prepositions when you write about classroom layouts in education studies assignments.
  • 3. Classroom environment features

These are the things that make a learning space useful and comfortable. They include furniture, equipment, and decoration.

Example:A spacious and bright classroom helps students learn better.
Connection:Education textbooks discuss how classroom features affect teaching and learning quality.
  • 4. Describing quantity and existence

We say what exists in a place using special grammar. We can talk about one thing or many things.

Example:There are thirty desks in the classroom and there is one teacher's desk.
Connection:You need this grammar when you write observation reports about schools or classrooms.

Vocabulary

  1. classroom — A room where students have lessons at school or university.
  2. whiteboard — A white board that teachers write on with special pens.
  3. desk — A table where students sit and do their work.
  4. chair — Furniture that you sit on with a back support.
  5. textbook — A book that students use to learn a subject.
  6. projector — A machine that shows pictures or videos on a wall.
  7. screen — A flat surface where you can watch pictures or films.
  8. poster — A large printed picture that you put on a wall.
  9. bookshelf — Furniture with shelves where you keep books.
  10. window — An opening in a wall with glass to let light in.
  11. clock — An object that shows what time it is.
  12. notice board — A board where you put important information and announcements.
  13. organized — Arranged in a tidy and planned way.
  14. bright — Having a lot of light or strong colors.
  15. spacious — Having a lot of space or room inside.
  16. in the front — At the forward part or beginning area of something.
  17. at the back — At the rear part or end area of something.
  18. on the wall — Attached to or hanging on the side of a room.
  19. arrange — To put things in a particular order or position.
  20. display — To show something so people can see it.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the names of classroom objects and the words that describe their positions.
Reading
Read a text that describes a classroom and find the furniture and equipment mentioned.
Listening
Listen to someone describe a classroom and identify where each object is located.
Speaking
Look at a classroom picture and say aloud where you can see different objects.
Grammar
Practice using there is and there are to say what exists in classrooms.
Writing
Write a paragraph describing the layout and arrangement of furniture in a classroom.
Lesson Test
The test checks if you can describe classroom pictures and use prepositions correctly; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'classroom' first appeared in English dictionaries in 1870, when schools began building separate rooms for each class instead of teaching everyone together in one large hall.

REFERENCES

English Vocabulary in Use Elementary — Cambridge University Press (2017). Unit 16 covers classroom language and prepositions of place with clear pictures. Oxford Picture Dictionary — Oxford University Press (2015). The classroom section shows labeled pictures of all the furniture and equipment words.

MINI STORY

My Classroom

I study in a bright and spacious classroom at the university. The classroom has large windows that let in lots of natural light. In the front, there is a big whiteboard where the teacher writes important information. Above it, a clock shows the time during our lessons. Next to the whiteboard, there is a screen and a projector for watching videos.

Each student has a comfortable desk and chair. We keep our textbooks on our desks during class. At the back of the room, there is a tall bookshelf full of interesting books. On the wall, you can see colorful posters about different subjects. There is also a notice board that displays important announcements and class schedules.

Our teacher likes to arrange the chairs in different ways. Sometimes we sit in a circle for group discussions. The classroom always looks very organized and clean. I really enjoy studying in this comfortable space every day.

Reading Passage

My First Day as a Teacher

Text type: Narrative
Maria walked into her new classroom on Monday morning. She felt nervous but excited. The room was empty and quiet. She looked around and saw twenty small desks in rows. There was a large whiteboard on the front wall. Next to it, there was a world map. On the teacher's desk, she found some colorful markers and a class list.

Maria took a photo of the classroom with her phone. She wanted to remember this special moment. In the picture, she could see the big windows on the left side. Sunlight came through and made the room bright and warm. There were some posters on the back wall about numbers and the alphabet. A bookshelf stood in the corner with many children's books.

Later, Maria showed the photo to her sister. She talked about where each student would sit. She explained that shy students could sit near her desk. Active children could sit near the windows. Maria felt ready now. She knew this classroom would become a special place. In a few hours, it would be full of young voices and energy. She smiled and put her bag down.

A Modern Language Classroom

Text type: Description
This classroom is in a language school in the city center. It is a bright and comfortable space for learning English. The room is not very big, but it has everything students need. There are twelve desks arranged in a U-shape. This helps students see each other when they talk. Each desk has a chair with a soft blue seat.

The front wall has a large interactive whiteboard. The teacher uses it to show videos and write new words. Above the board, there is a clock so everyone can see the time. On the right wall, there are three wide windows. Students can see the street and some trees outside. Between the windows, there are posters with common English phrases and grammar rules. The posters have bright colors that make the room more interesting.

At the back of the room, there is a small table with a computer and a printer. Next to it, there are two comfortable chairs where students can sit and read. There is also a bookshelf with dictionaries, grammar books, and some easy readers. The floor has a soft gray carpet. The walls are painted light yellow. This color makes the room feel warm and friendly.

Email About Classroom Photos

Text type: Notice

From: Principal Johnson
To: All Teachers
Subject: Classroom Photo Project
Date: September 15

Dear Teachers,

We are starting a new project this month. Please take a clear photo of your classroom. We will use these photos on our school website. Parents want to see where their children study every day. The photos will help them feel more connected to the school.

Please follow these simple steps. First, tidy your classroom before you take the photo. Put books on shelves and clean the whiteboard. Second, take the photo from the back of the room. This way, people can see the whole space. Make sure the photo shows the desks, the board, and any posters on the walls. Third, take the photo when students are not in the room. We want to show the classroom, not the students' faces.

After you take the photo, please write a short description. Explain what makes your classroom special. Talk about the learning areas, the displays, or the furniture arrangement. Your description should be about fifty words. Send both the photo and the description to me by September 30. If you have any questions, please visit my office. Thank you for helping with this project.

Best wishes, Mr. Johnson

How to Describe a Classroom Picture

Text type: Informational
When you talk about a picture of a classroom, follow a clear pattern. This will help other people understand what you see. Start with the general information. Say what kind of room it is and how big it looks. Mention if it seems modern or traditional. Then talk about the main features you can see.

Begin with the furniture and its arrangement. Describe how many desks and chairs there are. Explain where they are positioned in the room. Talk about the teacher's desk and its location. Next, describe the walls. Look at the front wall first. Mention the board and what type it is. Then describe the other walls. Talk about windows, doors, and any posters or displays. Use position words like 'on the left,' 'at the back,' or 'next to' to be clear.

Finally, mention smaller details that make the classroom special. These might include technology like computers or projectors. Look for bookshelves, plants, or student artwork. Comment on the colors of the walls and furniture. Talk about the lighting and whether the room looks bright or dark. End by saying what feeling or atmosphere the classroom has. Does it look busy, calm, creative, or organized? Good descriptions help listeners imagine they are standing in the room.

Two Different Classrooms

Text type: Comparison
Anna teaches English in a small village school. Her classroom is in an old building. The room has wooden floors and high ceilings. There are sixteen desks in rows facing a traditional blackboard. Anna uses chalk to write on the board. The windows are tall and thin. They let in natural light, but the room can be cold in

winter. There are no computers in the classroom. Anna has one bookshelf with some old textbooks and dictionaries. The walls are white and quite plain.

Tom teaches English in a city school. His classroom is in a new building. The room has carpet on the floor and modern lighting. There are twenty desks arranged in groups of four. This helps students work together easily. Tom has an interactive whiteboard connected to his laptop. He can show videos and play listening exercises. The windows are wide and have blinds for sunny days. There are three computers at the back for students to use. The walls are painted green and have many colorful posters and student projects.

Both teachers love their classrooms. Anna enjoys the quiet, peaceful feeling of her traditional room. Tom likes the technology and bright colors in his modern space. Different classrooms suit different teaching styles. The most important thing is helping students learn well.

posters about grammar and vocabulary. There are also photos of famous writers. Plants sit on the window
shelves. They make the room feel fresh. This classroom picture shows us what a modern learning
environment looks like. Every detail helps create a good place for studying.

Comparing Two Classrooms
B1 — Listen and Answer

I have two pictures of classrooms to compare today. The first picture shows a traditional classroom. It has
old wooden desks in straight rows. All the students face the front. There is a green chalkboard on the wall.
The teacher stands in front of it with chalk. The room looks quite dark because there are only two small
windows. The walls are plain white with no decorations. There is one bookshelf in the corner with a few old
books.


The second picture shows a modern classroom. It looks very different. The desks are new and light. They are
arranged in small groups of four. This helps students work together. There is a smart board instead of a
chalkboard. The room is very bright with big windows. Colourful posters cover the walls. They show maps,
famous people and useful phrases. There are computers on some desks. At the back, there is a comfortable
sofa for reading. Plants make the space feel alive. Both classrooms are for learning, but they create different
feelings. The modern one seems more active and friendly. The traditional one feels quiet and formal. Each
style has good points for different teaching methods.

B1 — Listen and Answer

Preparing a Classroom Display
B1 — Listen and Answer

Good morning class. I'm going to describe a picture I took yesterday. It shows our classroom before we
decorated it for the new term. In the picture, you can see empty walls and plain furniture. Now I want to
explain what we should add. First, we need to put up a large world map. It will go on the back wall above the
storage cupboards. This will help students learn about different countries and cultures during lessons.


Next, we should create a student work display board. I think the right wall is perfect for this. Students can
pin their best writing and artwork there. Everyone will feel proud to see their work. We also need a class
rules poster near the door. It will remind everyone about good behaviour. On the left wall, let's hang pictures
of famous educators and writers. They will inspire students to work hard. Finally, we should put a weekly
schedule on the wall beside the whiteboard. Students can check it every day to know what subjects they have.
We also need labels for the bookshelves. They will show where to find different types of books. With all these
additions, our classroom will become a warm and organized learning space.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

In this picture, I can see a bright classroom with rows of desks and chairs. There is a large whiteboard at the front where the teacher writes lessons for students. The walls have colourful posters that show maps, numbers, and the alphabet for learning. Several students are sitting at their desks and listening carefully to the teacher. The classroom looks clean and organised, which helps students focus on their work better.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What can you see in the classroom in this picture?

I can see many desks and chairs arranged in rows. There is a whiteboard at the front of the room. The walls have posters with educational information. Some students are sitting and working at their desks.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. How would you describe the atmosphere in this classroom?

The classroom looks calm and peaceful. The students seem focused on their work. The room is bright and well-organised. I think it is a good environment for learning and studying.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What teaching materials or equipment do you notice in the picture?

I can see a whiteboard and some markers for writing. There are educational posters on the walls. Each desk has books and notebooks on it. I also notice a teacher's desk at the front.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. How is this classroom similar to or different from your own classroom?

This classroom is quite similar to mine. We also have rows of desks and a whiteboard. However, my classroom has more technology like computers. The posters and layout look very familiar to me.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What do you think makes a good classroom environment for students?

A good classroom should be clean and well-lit. It needs comfortable furniture and useful teaching materials. The space should be quiet so students can concentrate. Having interesting posters and displays also helps students learn better.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

There is / There are

We use 'there is' with singular nouns and 'there are' with plural nouns to describe what exists in a place.

Use contractions 'there's' and 'there're' in spoken English, but 'there're' is rare.

FORMS

FormExample
There is + singular nounThere is a teacher in the classroom.
There are + plural nounThere are twenty desks in the room.
Negative: There isn't / There aren'tThere aren't any windows on this wall.
Question: Is there / Are there + noun?Is there a whiteboard in your classroom?
There is + uncountable nounThere is some chalk on the desk.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ There are a blackboard in the classroom.

✓ There is a blackboard in the classroom.

'A blackboard' is singular, so use 'there is'.

✗ There is three windows near the door.

✓ There are three windows near the door.

'Three windows' is plural, so use 'there are'.

✗ It is a map on the wall.

✓ There is a map on the wall.

Use 'there is/are' to say something exists in a place, not 'it is'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe what you can see in the classroom picture below. Write about the furniture, equipment, and layout. (100–140 words)

  • Start by describing the overall layout and size of the room
  • Mention specific furniture items like desks, chairs, and cupboards
  • Include any technology or teaching equipment you can see

Key structures: There is / There are, Prepositions of place (in front of, next to, on the wall)

Model
This classroom picture shows a simple and bright room. On the wall there is a big green chalkboard, and above it there is a round clock. Next to the chalkboard, there is a small bookshelf with many colourful books. A globe is on top of the bookshelf. On the left, there are wooden desks and chairs for the students. A brown backpack is on a chair, and a pencil case is on a desk. In front of the desks, there is the teacher's desk. There is a big window with wooden shutters, and a green plant is on the window sill. The door is on the right side of the room.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 100-140 words describing a classroom picture: begin with the overall layout and size, name the furniture, and mention any teaching equipment, saying where things are.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: classroom, desk, chair, chalkboard, clock, bookshelf, globe, window, plant, door. Structures: There is / There are; Prepositions of place (in front of, next to, on the wall); Adjectives for rooms (bright, organized, spacious).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Opens with the room's overall layout or size, names several pieces of furniture with numbers or positions, and includes at least one item of teaching equipment. Good: Layout, furniture and equipment are all mentioned, but one is only one short sentence or the description is general. Developing: Lists some furniture but gives no overall layout, or no equipment; very few details. Beginning: Does not describe a classroom or is mostly unrelated.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'There is' and 'There are' correctly many times, with at least three place phrases (in front of, next to, on the left wall, at the back), and room words such as desks, chalkboard, bookshelf, clocks. Good: Uses there is/are mostly correctly and two place phrases; several room words. Developing: Uses 'There is/are' once or twice or says 'It has'; place phrases are rare. Beginning: No there is/are and no place phrases.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Singular and plural agreement is correct ('there is a clock', 'there are twenty desks'); nouns have plural -s; errors are few. Good: Some slips like 'There are a board' or 'two window'; meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent there is/are and plural errors, or 'It is a map on the wall'; reader sometimes guesses. Beginning: Most sentences contain errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: A clear tour of the room (front, left, right, back) from the overview to the details, ending with a closing sentence about the room. Good: Mostly logical; one or two items jump around. Developing: Items listed in random order with no overall picture. Beginning: Separate words or phrases.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: A clear overview and detailed tour of the room with correct there is/are and place phrases. | 75-89: Clear description; small agreement slips. | 60-74: Understandable; limited place phrases or details. | 40-59: Short list of objects. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (e.g. 'whiteboad'); British or American spelling (colourful/colorful); 'blackboard' for 'chalkboard'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a rural or simple classroom with little equipment.
LENGTH: 100-140 words; accept about 85-150 because this is long for A2. Under about 65 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Learners may describe the course picture, a classroom they know, or a mix. Any layout is fine. A short list of objects is fine as long as there is/are is used. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20 with encouragement. Model answer copied word for word: 100 with a note to describe the learner's own picture or room.
NOTE: The task now shows a classroom picture: a green chalkboard with a clock above it, wooden student desks and chairs, the teacher's desk, a small bookshelf with a globe on top, a window with shutters and a plant, a backpack, a pencil case and a door. It has no whiteboard, projector, posters or computer, so do not expect them. Teaching equipment means the chalkboard, globe and books. Learners may also describe a classroom they know. The word range is long for A2, so be generous with length.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one clear detail, such as a well-placed object. 2) Fix: Correct one agreement error, e.g. 'There is twenty desks' -> 'There are twenty desks in four rows.' 3) Next step: Next time add one more place phrase, such as 'next to the door'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Explain how the classroom layout helps students learn effectively. Describe what makes it a good learning environment. (120–160 words)

  • Explain the connection between the classroom features and student learning
  • Discuss how the arrangement of furniture supports different teaching activities
  • Mention the importance of displays, lighting, and organization

Key structures: Because / so (showing cause and effect), This helps / allows students to

Model
The layout of this classroom helps students learn in several ways. The desks are close to the chalkboard, so students can see the lesson clearly. This helps everyone follow the teacher. The teacher's desk is at the front, so the teacher can see all the students and help them quickly. The big window brings in light and fresh air, so the room is bright and students can read easily. The clock on the wall helps the teacher and students to manage the time for each activity. The bookshelf allows students to take a book and read when they finish their work. The globe on the shelf helps students to learn about countries and the world. There is enough space between the desks, so the teacher can walk around. All these features work together to make a good place for learning.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 120-160 words explaining how the classroom layout helps students learn: link features to learning, show how the furniture supports different activities, and mention displays, lighting and organisation.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: layout, chalkboard, clock, bookshelf, globe, window, light, space, organized, bright. Structures: Because / so (cause and effect); This helps / allows students to + verb; There is / There are.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Connects at least three features (for example desks facing the board, clocks, light, space to walk) to specific ways students learn, and covers furniture, displays, lighting and organisation. Good: Links two or three features to learning; one of the required areas (e.g. lighting) is missing or only described. Developing: Describes features but rarely says how they help learning. Beginning: Does not explain how the classroom helps students learn.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'because', 'so' and 'This helps/allows students to' correctly several times, with room words such as arranged, display, bright, organized. Good: Uses 'because' or 'so' and 'This helps' at least twice, with some room words. Developing: Uses one reason word; most sentences are plain descriptions. Beginning: No cause-and-effect language.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: 'Helps students to see' and 'so students can' are mostly correct; there is/are agrees; slips are small. Good: Some errors such as 'it help students' or 'so students can to see'; meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in reason clauses; 'because' used as a full sentence. Beginning: Most sentences contain errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Each feature gets a sentence of cause and effect, grouped in a logical order, with a closing sentence. Good: Mostly logical; two features are mixed. Developing: Features and benefits are repeated or jumbled. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Several features clearly linked to learning with correct because/so/helps. | 75-89: Clear; small clause errors or one area missing. | 60-74: Understandable; mostly description. | 40-59: Short or no links to learning. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; simple reasons like 'students can see better'; missing articles; using 'good' repeatedly.
LENGTH: 120-160 words; accept about 100-170. Under about 80 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any logical benefit is fine (seeing the board, moving around, reading books, feeling comfortable). Learners may refer to a picture or a real classroom. 'This allows students to' and 'This helps students' are equal. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer copied word for word: 100 with a note to use own ideas. A plain description with no learning benefits: mark on content, coach 'because' and 'so'.
NOTE: The task now shows a classroom picture: a green chalkboard with a clock above it, wooden student desks and chairs, the teacher's desk, a small bookshelf with a globe on top, a window with shutters and a plant, a backpack, a pencil case and a door. It has no whiteboard, projector, posters or computer, so do not expect them. Teaching equipment means the chalkboard, globe and books. Learners may also describe a classroom they know. The word range is long for A2, so be generous with length.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one clear cause-and-effect sentence from the learner. 2) Fix: Correct one error, e.g. 'The desks are in rows because students can see' -> 'The desks are in rows so all students can see the board.' 3) Next step: Next time add a sentence about lighting or space.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Compare this classroom to one from your own school experience. Explain the similarities and differences you notice. (140–180 words)

  • Begin by briefly describing a classroom from your past
  • Point out what is similar between the two classrooms
  • Explain what is different and which features you prefer

Key structures: Comparative structures (more modern than, similar to, different from), However / On the other hand (showing contrast)

Model
This classroom is similar to the one in my primary school, but there are some differences. My old classroom was bigger and had about thirty wooden desks in four rows. Both classrooms have a green chalkboard, wooden desks and chairs, and a teacher's desk at the front, which are basic features in most schools. Both rooms also have a window, so there is natural light. However, the classroom in the picture has a bookshelf and a globe, but my old classroom had no books. It also has a clock and a plant, so it looks more welcoming. On the other hand, my old classroom had many more students, so it was noisy. Overall, I prefer the classroom in the picture because it is quiet and has books for reading. However, I have good memories of my old classroom because I made many friends there.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 140-180 words comparing the picture classroom with a classroom from your own school days: describe your old classroom, say what is similar and what is different, and say which features you prefer.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: classroom, desk, chalkboard, clock, bookshelf, globe, window, bright, bigger, smaller. Structures: Comparatives (more modern than, bigger than, similar to, different from); However / On the other hand; There was / There were for the old classroom.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes the learner's own past classroom, gives at least two similarities and two differences with specific features, and says which the learner prefers and why. Good: Gives similarities and differences, but only one of each is specific, or the preference is not explained. Developing: Describes only one classroom, or lists differences without similarities. Beginning: Does not compare two classrooms.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses comparatives (bigger than, more modern than), 'similar to / different from', and 'However' or 'On the other hand' correctly, plus there is/are and place phrases. Good: Uses comparatives and one contrast word correctly. Developing: Uses 'big' and 'small' without comparative forms, or only 'but'. Beginning: No comparison structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Comparative forms are correct (bigger than, more modern than), and the tenses for old and new rooms are consistent; slips are small. Good: Some errors like 'more big', 'bigger that' or tense slips; meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent comparative and tense errors; comparisons are hard to follow. Beginning: Meaning unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Old classroom, then similarities, then differences, then preference, using However/On the other hand to separate points. Good: Mostly in order; points are slightly mixed. Developing: Features of the two rooms are mixed without clear comparisons. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear comparison with similarities, differences, a preference, and correct comparatives. | 75-89: Clear; small comparative or tense slips. | 60-74: Understandable; unbalanced comparison. | 40-59: Mostly description of one room. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; a simple old classroom with few items; mixing past and present when clear; 'more big' if the comparison is understood (coach gently).
LENGTH: 140-180 words; accept about 115-190. Under about 90 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: The old classroom may be primary, secondary or college. The comparison may use 'but' as well as However. Preferences may go either way. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer copied word for word: 100 with a note to describe own school days. Description of two rooms with no comparison: mark on content.
NOTE: The task now shows a classroom picture: a green chalkboard with a clock above it, wooden student desks and chairs, the teacher's desk, a small bookshelf with a globe on top, a window with shutters and a plant, a backpack, a pencil case and a door. It has no whiteboard, projector, posters or computer, so do not expect them. Teaching equipment means the chalkboard, globe and books. Learners may also describe a classroom they know. The word range is long for A2, so be generous with length.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear similarity or difference the learner noticed. 2) Fix: Correct one comparative, e.g. 'My room was more small than this' -> 'My room was smaller than this one.' 3) Next step: Next time use On the other hand once to show a contrast.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Describe a classroom that you know well. Write about the furniture, equipment, and what makes it a good place to learn. Use clear details. (80–110 words)

  • Start by saying which classroom you are describing
  • Mention the furniture like desks, chairs, and shelves
  • Describe what equipment is in the room
  • Explain why it is a good learning environment
Model
I want to describe my English classroom at school. It is a medium-sized room on the first floor. There are twenty desks arranged in four rows with comfortable chairs. The walls are white and decorated with grammar posters. At the front, there is a smart board that the teacher uses for presentations. On the left side, there is a tall bookshelf full of dictionaries and novels. The room has large windows that let in lots of natural light. This makes the classroom feel bright and welcoming. There is also air conditioning to keep us cool. I think it is a good learning environment because everything is organized and we have all the equipment we need.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. School day narrative structure

A school day story has a clear order: beginning, middle, and end. You tell what happened first, next, and last.

Example:First, I arrived at campus at 8 a.m., then I attended my lecture, and finally I went home.
Connection:You use this structure when you write essays about your experiences or tell someone about your day.
  • 2. Time sequencing in education contexts

You show the order of events using time words like 'first', 'then', 'after that', and 'finally'. This helps listeners understand when things happened.

Example:After the break, we discussed the assignment and then the professor explained the deadline.
Connection:Teachers use sequencing words when they explain lesson steps or give instructions in class.
  • 3. Past tenses for completed and ongoing actions

Past simple describes finished actions in a story. Past continuous describes actions that were happening when something else occurred.

Example:I was preparing my notebook when the professor arrived and started the lecture.
Connection:You see both tenses in textbooks when they describe historical events or explain what people were doing.

Special words describe the people, places, and activities in education. These words help you talk about daily school life clearly.

Example:Students hand in their assignments before the deadline and participate in class discussions.
Connection:You meet these words in your schedule, on campus signs, and when professors give you instructions.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. arrive — To reach a place at the end of a journey.
  2. lecture — A long talk given to a group of students to teach them.
  3. assignment — A piece of work that a teacher gives students to do.
  4. cafeteria — A place in a school where students can buy and eat food.
  5. attend — To go to an event or be present at a place.
  6. break — A short period of time when you stop working to rest.
  7. classmate — A person who studies in the same class as you.
  8. discuss — To talk about something with other people.
  9. notebook — A book with empty pages for writing notes.
  10. prepare — To make something or yourself ready for something.
  11. professor — A teacher who works at a university or college.
  12. schedule — A plan that shows when things will happen.
  13. submit — To give something to someone in authority.
  14. participate — To take part in an activity with other people.
  15. review — To study or look at something again.
  16. textbook — A book that students use to study a subject.
  17. campus — The land and buildings of a university or college.
  18. deadline — The time by which something must be finished.
  19. exam — A formal test to show what you know.
  20. hand in — To give something to a teacher or person in charge.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words about school routines, places, and activities that you use every day.
Reading
Read a short story about a student's school day and find the order of events.
Listening
Listen to someone describe their school day and notice the time words and past tenses.
Speaking
Tell your own school day story aloud using past simple and sequencing words.
Grammar
Learn when to use past simple and past continuous in stories about your school experiences.
Writing
Write one paragraph describing the events of a typical school day in the correct order.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary, grammar, and ability to tell a school day story; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In English, the phrase 'school day' can mean one single day at school or the whole time you spend in education, so context helps you understand which meaning is correct.

REFERENCES

English Grammar in Use — Raymond Murphy (2019). Units 5 to 7 explain past simple and past continuous with clear examples for storytelling. Oxford Word Skills Basic — Oxford University Press (2015). The education section teaches useful words for talking about school routines and campus life.

▶ Past Simple vs Past Continuous — BBC Learning English ▶ Daily Routines and School Vocabulary — English with Lucy

Vocabulary

MINI STORY

Maria's School Day

Maria always arrives at campus early in the morning. She checks her schedule and prepares her notebook and textbook for the first lecture. Her professor talks about education and history. Maria and her classmate sit together and discuss the important points. They participate in the class activities and ask questions.

At noon, they have a break and go to the cafeteria for lunch. Maria reviews her notes while eating. In the afternoon, she attends another class. The professor gives them a new assignment. The deadline is Friday, so Maria must work quickly. She needs to hand in the work on time.

After classes finish, Maria goes to the library. She wants to prepare for the exam next week. She studies the textbook carefully and writes in her notebook. Before going home, she will submit her homework. Maria feels happy because she had a productive school day.

Maria's Busy Tuesday

Text type: Narrative
Maria woke up at seven o'clock on Tuesday morning. She felt tired because she stayed up late. She had homework to finish the night before. After a quick breakfast, she packed her bag and walked to school. The weather was cold and rainy.

Maria arrived at school at eight fifteen. Her first lesson was maths. The teacher gave the class a difficult test. Maria tried her best but some questions were really hard. After maths, she had English class. This was her favourite subject. The teacher told an interesting story about London. Maria listened carefully and took notes in her notebook.

At lunchtime, Maria sat with her friends in the cafeteria. They talked about their weekend plans. After lunch, Maria had science and history lessons. In science, they did an experiment with water. It was fun and exciting. The history lesson was about ancient Egypt. Maria found it interesting but felt sleepy. Finally, school finished at three thirty. Maria walked home slowly. She was happy the day was over. At home, she had dinner with her family and told them about her test.

A Typical Classroom at Green Valley School

Text type: Description
The classroom at Green Valley School is bright and welcoming. It has four large windows on one side. Natural light fills the room during the day. The walls are painted light blue. There are colourful posters about grammar and vocabulary everywhere. Students sit at wooden desks arranged in rows. Each desk has space for books and a pencil case.

At the front of the classroom, there is a big whiteboard. The teacher uses it to write important information during lessons. Next to the board, there is a small desk for the teacher. On the desk, you can see a laptop and some marking pens. Behind the teacher's desk, there are tall bookshelves. They are full of textbooks and story books. Students can borrow books when they want to read.

The classroom also has a notice board on the back wall. It displays student work and important dates. There is a clock above the door so everyone can see the time. In one corner, there is a small table with dictionaries. Students use them during English lessons. The floor is clean and made of grey tiles. Overall, the classroom is a comfortable place to learn. Students spend about six hours there every school day.

Messages About School Day Changes

From: Mr Thompson, Head Teacher
To: All Students and Parents
Date: Monday, 15th March
Subject: Important Changes This Week

Dear Students and Parents,

I am writing to tell you about some changes this week. On Wednesday, we will have a fire safety drill at ten o'clock. Please leave your classrooms quickly and quietly when you hear the alarm. Go to the playground and wait with your teacher. The drill will take about fifteen minutes. After that, return to your normal lessons.

On Thursday, the school cafeteria will be closed for cleaning. Please bring a packed lunch from home. You can eat in your classrooms or outside if the weather is nice. There will be no hot meals available that day. We are sorry for this inconvenience.

On Friday, we will have a special assembly in the main hall. A local author will visit our school. She will talk about writing stories and answer your questions. The assembly starts at two o'clock and finishes at three o'clock. All students must attend. It will be interesting and educational.

Please check the school website for more information. If you have questions, contact the school office. Thank you for your understanding and cooperation.

Best wishes, Mr Thompson

How to Tell a Good Story About Your School Day

Text type: Informational
Telling a story about your school day is a useful skill. It helps you practice speaking and writing in English. A good story has a clear beginning, middle and end. Start by thinking about the most interesting parts of your day. Did something funny or unusual happen? Did you learn something new?

When you begin your story, say what time you arrived at school. Mention the weather or how you felt. Then describe your first lessons. Use time words like 'first', 'then', 'after that' and 'finally'. These words help listeners follow your story easily. Talk about what happened during breaks or lunchtime. Include details about people you met or conversations you had. Don't forget to use past tense verbs because you are talking about things that already happened.

To make your story more interesting, add feelings and opinions. Say which lessons you enjoyed or found difficult. Explain why you felt happy, tired or excited. Use descriptive words like 'boring', 'fun', 'challenging' or 'easy'. At the end, summarise your day briefly. You could say something like 'It was a busy day' or 'I learned a lot today'. Remember to speak clearly and not too fast. Good storytelling takes practice, so keep trying!

Two Different School Days: Tom and Lisa

Text type: Comparison
Tom and Lisa are both students at the same school. However, their school days are quite different. Tom is in Year 10 and studies science subjects. Lisa is in Year 9 and prefers arts and languages. Their schedules and experiences show interesting differences.

Tom's school day starts at eight o'clock with chemistry. He likes doing experiments in the laboratory. His morning also includes physics and maths lessons. These subjects are challenging but Tom enjoys solving problems. At lunchtime, Tom usually eats quickly and then goes to the computer room. He works on a science project with his classmates. In the afternoon, Tom has English and history. These are his least favourite subjects. He finds them less interesting than science. Tom finishes school at four o'clock and goes to football practice.

Lisa's day is very different. She starts with art class at eight thirty. She loves painting and drawing. After art, Lisa has French and Spanish lessons. She is good at languages and wants to travel in the future. At lunch, Lisa sits with friends and talks for a long time. In the afternoon, she has music and drama. These creative subjects make her happy. Lisa finishes at three thirty. She sometimes stays late for drama club. Both Tom and Lisa enjoy school, but their interests and daily routines are completely different.

Grammar Practice

Past Simple vs Past Continuous

Use Past Simple for completed actions in a story.

Use Past Continuous for background actions that were happening when another action interrupted them.

Past Continuous shows what was in progress at a specific moment in the past.

FORMS

FormExample
Past Simple: subject + verb + -ed (or irregular)The teacher arrived at eight o'clock.
Past Continuous: subject + was/were + verb + -ingThe students were writing when the bell rang.
Interrupted action: Past Continuous + when + Past SimpleI was reading a book when the lesson started.
Two actions in progress: Past Continuous + while + Past ContinuousTom was doing homework while his sister was studying.
Negative Past Continuous: subject + wasn't/weren't + verb + -ingThey weren't listening during the class.
Question Past Continuous: Was/Were + subject + verb + - ing?Were you paying attention in the lesson?

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ I read a book when the teacher came in.

✓ I was reading a book when the teacher came in.

Use Past Continuous for the longer background action that was in progress.

✗ The students were arriving at 8:30 yesterday.

✓ The students arrived at 8:30 yesterday.

Use Past Simple for a completed action at a specific time, not Past Continuous.

✗ While I did my homework, my friend called me.

✓ While I was doing my homework, my friend called me.

Use Past Continuous after 'while' to show an action in progress when another happened.

nodes.text: EXERCISES

nodes.question: Q1. The students ___ quietly when the headteacher walked into the classroom.
nodes.explanation: → The students' work was in progress when the headteacher interrupted, so we need Past Continuous.

nodes.question: Q2. I ___ my PE kit at home, so I couldn't join the sports lesson.
nodes.explanation: → Leaving the PE kit was a completed action that caused a result, so Past Simple is correct.

nodes.question: Q3. While the teacher ___ the instructions, some students talked to each other.
nodes.explanation: → 'While' signals that the teacher's explanation was in progress when the students talked, so use Past Continuous.

nodes.question: Q4. The bell ___ at exactly nine o'clock and everyone went to class.
nodes.explanation: → The bell ringing at nine o'clock is a single completed event at a specific time, so Past Simple is needed.

nodes.question: Q5. While I ___ to school, I saw my best friend waiting at the bus stop.
nodes.explanation: → 'While' shows an action in progress when another thing happened, so we use past continuous.

nodes.question: Q6. Yesterday, the teacher ___ the homework answers on the board during the first lesson.
nodes.explanation: → 'Yesterday' and a finished lesson need past simple.

nodes.question: Q7. My classmates ___ for a test when the fire alarm suddenly went off.
nodes.explanation: → Revising was the ongoing background activity when the fire alarm interrupted, so Past Continuous is needed.

nodes.question: Q8. I ___ my hand to answer the question, but the teacher chose someone else.
nodes.explanation: → The sentence tells a finished past event, so we use past simple.

nodes.question: Q9. Yesterday at lunchtime, I ___ a sandwich and then I went to class.
nodes.explanation: → 'Then I went' shows a finished action in the past, so we use past simple.

nodes.question: Q10. The students ___ notes while the guest speaker talked about science careers.
nodes.explanation: → 'While' shows that taking notes was happening at the same time as the talk, so we use past continuous.

nodes.question: Q11. When the lesson ___, the teacher gave us homework for next week.
nodes.explanation: → The lesson ending is a single completed event that happened before the teacher gave homework, so Past Simple is needed.

nodes.question: Q12. I ___ with my partner on a project when our teacher asked us to change groups.
nodes.explanation: → Working with your partner was in progress when the teacher interrupted with a new instruction, so Past Continuous is correct.

nodes.question: Q13. Yesterday afternoon, our class ___ a video about climate change in geography.
nodes.explanation: → 'Yesterday afternoon' is finished time, so we use past simple.

nodes.question: Q14. The students ___ in the corridor when the deputy head told them to go inside.
nodes.explanation: → Standing was in progress when the deputy head spoke, so we use past continuous.

nodes.question: Q15. My friend ___ me a funny story during break time, and I laughed a lot.
nodes.explanation: → 'Laughed' shows the story is finished in the past, so we use past simple.

nodes.question: Q16. While I ___ for the bus after school, I remembered I left my bag in class.
nodes.explanation: → 'While' signals that waiting was in progress when you remembered about your bag, so Past Continuous is needed.

nodes.question: Q17. The science teacher ___ an interesting experiment at the front of the lab yesterday.
nodes.explanation: → 'Yesterday' shows a finished action in the past, so we use past simple.

nodes.question: Q18. When the history teacher ___ the door, everyone stopped talking immediately.
nodes.explanation: → Opening the door was a single quick action that caused everyone to stop talking, so Past Simple is needed.

nodes.question: Q19. My group ___ a poster about recycling when the art teacher praised our work.
nodes.explanation: → Making the poster was in progress when the teacher interrupted with praise, so Past Continuous is correct.

nodes.question: Q20. At break, I ___ to the library and borrowed a book for my English homework.
nodes.explanation: → Going to the library and borrowing a book are two completed actions in sequence, so Past Simple is needed.

nodes.question: Q21. The students ___ in the playground when it started to rain heavily.
nodes.explanation: → Playing was the ongoing activity when the rain started, so Past Continuous describes this background action.

nodes.question: Q22. I ___ my textbook in the morning and couldn't do the exercises in class.
nodes.explanation: → Forgetting the textbook was a completed action in the morning that caused a problem, so Past Simple is correct.

nodes.question: Q23. While the teacher ___ questions, I checked my answers in my notebook.
nodes.explanation: → 'While' shows that asking questions was in progress when you checked your answers, so Past Continuous is needed.

nodes.question: Q24. The head teacher ___ an important announcement in assembly this morning.
nodes.explanation: → Making the announcement was a completed action in assembly this morning, so Past Simple is correct.

nodes.question: Q25. When the maths lesson ___, I felt relieved because the test was difficult.
nodes.explanation: → The lesson finishing is a single completed event that made you feel relieved, so Past Simple is needed.

nodes.question: Q26. I ___ to my friend about weekend plans when the teacher called my name.
nodes.explanation: → Talking to your friend was in progress when the teacher interrupted by calling your name, so Past Continuous is correct.

nodes.question: Q27. Our English teacher ___ us a poem by Wordsworth in the last lesson.
nodes.explanation: → Reading the poem was a completed action in the last lesson, so Past Simple is needed.

nodes.question: Q28. While we ___ football after school, the coach gave us new training tips.
nodes.explanation: → 'While' signals that playing football was happening when the coach gave tips, so Past Continuous is needed.

nodes.question: Q29. The students ___ up quickly when the principal entered the room.
nodes.explanation: → Standing up was a quick completed action in response to the principal's arrival, so Past Simple is correct.

nodes.question: Q30. Yesterday at lunchtime, my classmate ___ his lunch money and I helped him.
nodes.explanation: → Losing the lunch money was a completed event that made you help him, so Past Simple is needed.
