lessons.titleKm: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Guided Writing Task 1 (100–140 words)
lessons.titleEn: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Guided Writing Task 1 (100–140 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write about your morning at school. Describe when you arrived and what you did before your first lesson. (100–140 words)

  • Start with the time you arrived at school
  • Describe where you went and who you met
  • End with your first lesson starting

Key structures: Past simple for completed actions, Time expressions (at, before, after), Sequencing words (first, then, after that)

Model
I arrived at school at quarter to nine yesterday morning. The weather was cold and rainy. First, I went to my locker and put away my coat and bag. Then I met my friends in the corridor. We talked about our homework for a few minutes. After that, I walked to my classroom on the second floor. Some students were already sitting at their desks. I sat down next to my friend Tom. We took out our books and notebooks. At nine o'clock, the teacher came in and our English lesson started. I felt ready to learn and work hard.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 100-140 words about your morning at school: start with the time you arrived, say where you went and who you met before your first lesson, and end with the first lesson starting.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: arrive, classmate, notebook, textbook, prepare, break, schedule, attend, discuss, review. Structures: Past simple for finished actions; Time expressions (at, before, after); Sequencing words (first, then, after that).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts with an arrival time, names where the learner went and who they met, describes at least two things done before class, and ends with the first lesson starting. Good: Arrival time, people and first lesson are covered, but events before class are only one or two short sentences. Developing: Says when the learner arrived but gives few events, or leaves out the first lesson. Beginning: Does not tell a morning at school.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses past simple, time phrases (at quarter to eight, before class, after that) and First / Then / After that correctly, with words like arrive, classmate, notebook. Good: Uses past simple and two sequencing or time words correctly; some week words. Developing: Uses one or two past verbs and mostly 'and'; time phrases are rare. Beginning: No sequencing or time words; mostly present tense.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Past forms are correct, including irregulars (went, met, sat, took); 'at' for clock times is right; slips are small. Good: Some slips such as 'I goed', 'I meet my friend' or 'in 7 o'clock'; story still clear. Developing: Many verbs stay in the present or are wrongly formed; the order of events is hard to follow. Beginning: Meaning unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Events follow the real order of the morning and are linked with sequencing words; the last sentence is the lesson starting. Good: Order is mostly clear; one event is out of place. Developing: Events listed with no linking words or in mixed order. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear morning story with time, people, ordered events and correct past tense. | 75-89: Clear; small tense slips. | 60-74: Understandable; few events or sequence words. | 40-59: Short; mostly present tense. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; time written as 7:30 or 'half past seven'; missing articles; a real but simple morning (walked to school, ate breakfast).
LENGTH: 100-140 words; accept about 85-150. Under about 65 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real or imagined school morning works, including as a teacher. Learners may include the journey. Present historic tense is not expected but accept if clear. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (quarter to nine, rain, locker) copied: 100 with a note to tell own morning. Writing about a typical morning in present tense: mark on content, coach past simple.
NOTE: Week 26 vocabulary includes university words (lecture, professor, campus) that do not fit this school-morning task; the rubric uses the school-appropriate words. The 100-140 word range is long for A2, so tolerance is generous.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear moment in the morning that the learner described. 2) Fix: Correct one past form, e.g. 'I goed to the classroom' -> 'I went to the classroom.' 3) Next step: Next time use After that once to link two events.

lessons.titleKm: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Guided Writing Task 2 (120–160 words)
lessons.titleEn: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Guided Writing Task 2 (120–160 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about an interesting lesson you had during the school day. Explain what you did and why it was interesting or enjoyable. (120–160 words)

  • Name the subject and describe the main activity
  • Explain what made the lesson interesting or fun
  • Include your feelings and reactions during the lesson

Key structures: Past simple and past continuous together, Because/so for reasons and results, Descriptive adjectives (interesting, exciting, difficult)

Model
My science lesson was really interesting yesterday afternoon. We were learning about plants and how they grow. The teacher showed us a video about different types of seeds. It was fascinating to watch. Then we did an experiment in small groups. We planted some seeds in small pots with soil. My group worked together very well. We had to measure the soil and add water carefully. I enjoyed working with my hands because it was more fun than just reading. The teacher explained everything clearly so we understood the process. At the end of the lesson, we labelled our pots with our names. Now we will watch our plants grow over the next few weeks. I felt excited about seeing the results of our experiment.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 120-160 words about an interesting lesson you had: name the subject and main activity, explain what made it interesting or fun, and include your feelings and reactions.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: lesson, discuss, participate, assignment, classmate, prepare, interesting, exciting, difficult, enjoyable. Structures: Past simple and past continuous together (We were learning when...); Because / so for reasons and results; Adjectives for feelings (interesting, exciting, difficult).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names the subject, describes the main activity step by step, gives at least one clear reason why it was interesting, and shares feelings during the lesson. Good: Subject, activity and a reason are clear, but feelings or the steps of the activity are brief. Developing: Names the lesson but gives little detail about the activity, or no reason. Beginning: Does not describe an interesting lesson.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses past simple for actions and past continuous for background ('We were learning about plants'), joined with when/while where natural, plus because/so and feeling adjectives. Good: Uses past simple well, tries past continuous at least once, and uses because/so and two adjectives. Developing: Uses only past simple (or present); reasons are limited to 'because it was fun'. Beginning: No target structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Was/were + -ing is formed correctly; past simple verbs are mostly right; slips are small. Good: Some errors such as 'We learning' or 'we was reading'; meaning clear. Developing: Frequent past-simple and continuous errors; reader guesses what happened. Beginning: Most sentences contain errors that block meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: The lesson is told in time order, with reasons placed close to the events and a feeling at the end. Good: Mostly in order; one reason is out of place. Developing: Events and reasons are mixed. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear story of the lesson with reasons, feelings, and past simple plus continuous. | 75-89: Clear; small tense slips. | 60-74: Understandable; thin detail or only past simple. | 40-59: Short; mostly present tense. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using only past simple if the story is clear (score vocabulary band lower, coach gently); simple adjectives like 'fun'; missing articles.
LENGTH: 120-160 words; accept about 100-170. Under about 75 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any subject works. Reasons can use because, so or 'that is why'. The model's science plant lesson is only an example. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer copied word for word: 100 with a note to describe own lesson. A story about a boring lesson is fine if reasons are given.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise one detail of the activity the learner described. 2) Fix: Correct one tense error, e.g. 'We learned about plants when the teacher showed a video' -> 'We were learning about plants when the teacher showed a video.' 3) Next step: Next time add one sentence about how you felt at the end.

lessons.titleKm: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Guided Writing Task 3 (140–180 words)
lessons.titleEn: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Guided Writing Task 3 (140–180 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about the end of your school day. Describe your last lesson, leaving school, and how you got home. (140–180 words)

  • Describe your final lesson and any homework you received
  • Explain how you left school and travelled home
  • Share your thoughts and feelings about the whole day

Key structures: Past simple for sequential events, When/while for connecting actions, Feelings vocabulary (tired, happy, relieved, satisfied)

Model
My last lesson on Tuesday was mathematics. We studied fractions and percentages for fifty minutes. The lesson was quite difficult but the teacher helped me understand the problems. She gave us some homework to finish for Thursday. I wrote down the page numbers in my notebook carefully. When the bell rang at half past three, everyone packed their bags quickly. I said goodbye to my friends at the school gate. Then I walked to the bus stop near the school. I waited for about ten minutes while I checked my phone. The number twelve bus arrived and I got on. The journey home took twenty minutes. I looked out of the window and thought about my day. I felt tired after all the lessons but I was also happy. I learned many new things and spent time with my friends. When I arrived home, my mother asked me about my day. I told her about the science experiment and she was very interested.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 140-180 words about the end of your school day: describe your last lesson and any homework, how you left school and travelled home, and your thoughts and feelings about the day.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: assignment, hand in, deadline, submit, prepare, review, arrive, classmate, tired, relieved. Structures: Past simple for sequential events; When / while to join actions; Feeling words (tired, happy, relieved, satisfied).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes the last lesson and homework, tells how the learner left school and travelled home with specific details (time, transport, people), and says how the learner felt about the day. Good: Covers lesson, journey and feelings, but one part is short or general. Developing: Covers only the lesson or only the journey, or gives no feelings. Beginning: Does not tell the end of a school day.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses past simple for the sequence, when/while to join two actions (for example 'When the bell rang, we packed our bags'), and two or more feeling words. Good: Uses past simple and when or while at least once, and one or two feeling words. Developing: Uses past simple for a few events, no when/while, and 'happy' or 'tired' only. Beginning: No target structures; present tense.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A1-A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Past forms are correct including irregulars (got, took, went, said, felt); when/while clauses are formed correctly. Good: Some slips such as 'I waited while I check my phone' or 'I take the bus'; story clear. Developing: Many wrong or present-tense verbs; the order of events is hard to follow. Beginning: Meaning unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: The story follows time from last lesson to home, with linking words and a closing feeling. Good: Order is mostly clear; one event is out of place. Developing: Events listed with no linking or in mixed order. Beginning: No visible order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Complete end-of-day story with lesson, homework, journey, feelings and correct past tense. | 75-89: Clear; small tense slips. | 60-74: Understandable; a part is thin. | 40-59: Short; mostly present tense. | 0-39: Off task, copied, or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; mentioning a moto, bicycle or walking instead of a bus; missing articles; very short feelings like 'I was tired'.
LENGTH: 140-180 words; accept about 115-190. Under about 90 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real or imagined day works, including a teacher's end of day. Transport can be any, including walking. 'When' and 'while' can be replaced by 'after' if the sequence is clear. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer (Tuesday mathematics, bus number twelve) copied: 100 with a note to tell own day. A present-tense description of a usual day: mark on content and coach past simple.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear detail about the journey or the homework. 2) Fix: Correct one error, e.g. 'When the bell ring, we pack our bags' -> 'When the bell rang, we packed our bags.' 3) Next step: Next time end with one sentence about how you felt and why.

lessons.titleEn: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day — Paragraph Writing (After the Test)

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about your typical school day. Describe what you do from morning until afternoon. Include what time you arrive, your lessons, and break time activities. (80–110 words)

  • Start with what time you wake up or arrive at school
  • Mention two or three lessons you have during the day
  • Describe what you do during break time or lunch
  • Use simple past or present tense consistently
Model
My school day starts at 8 o'clock every morning. I arrive at school and go to my locker. My first lesson is usually English or maths. I like English because we read interesting stories. At 11 o'clock, we have a short break. I go to the playground with my friends. We talk and play games together. After break, I have science and geography. At lunchtime, I eat in the canteen. I usually have a sandwich and some fruit. In the afternoon, I have two more lessons. My favourite is PE because I love playing sports. School finishes at 3 o'clock. I feel tired but happy at the end of the day.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write 80-110 words about your typical school day: say what time you wake up or arrive, name two or three lessons, and describe what you do at break or lunch, using one tense consistently.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: arrive, schedule, break, cafeteria, lesson, classmate, homework, exam, review, attend. Structures: Present simple for routines (I arrive, we have); Time expressions (at 8 o'clock, after break, in the afternoon); Consistent tense (all present or all past).
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Gives a start time, names two or three lessons, and describes break or lunch with specific details (who, where, what).
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses time phrases (at 8 o'clock, after break, in the afternoon), sequencing, and week words such as arrive, break, schedule, lesson, with the chosen tense.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: One tense is used throughout and is correct (I go, she teaches / I went, we ate); only small slips.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Day follows morning, break, lunch, afternoon, with linking words.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; times written 8:00 or 8 AM; school days with only two lessons; missing articles.
LENGTH: 80-110 words; accept about 70-120. Under about 55 words: cap at 59.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Present simple (typical day) or past simple (yesterday) are both fine if consistent. The learner may write as a student or a teacher. Lessons and foods can be anything real. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Model answer copied exactly: 100 with a note to describe own day. A weekend description: mark on language and note the task.

contentRef.text:
Video Evidence

This is your performance evidence for this lesson. Record a 3-minute video of yourself presenting this week's topic in English. Speak naturally — notes are fine, reading a script word-for-word is not.

Present in your own words: Telling a Simple Story About a School Day

CHECKLIST

  • ☐ Introduce the topic in one or two sentences

Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Activity Planning

Activity planning means writing down what children will do, what you need, and how to do it. A good plan helps teachers prepare and keeps children safe.

Example:Teachers should write a clear activity plan before they start working with young learners.
Connection:You read and write activity plans in teacher training courses, lesson preparation and classroom practice.
  • 2. Instructions and Steps

Instructions are the words that tell people how to do something in order. We use sequencing words like first, then, next and finally to make instructions clear.

Example:First, prepare the materials, then demonstrate the activity, and finally let children participate.
Connection:You use instructions when you explain activities in the classroom or write lesson plans for teachers.
  • 3. Safety and Supervision

Safety means protecting children from danger during activities. Teachers must supervise children to check they are safe and doing things correctly.

Example:Teachers must supervise young children carefully when they use scissors or other equipment.
Connection:You talk about safety in lesson plans, training sessions, parent meetings and classroom rules.
  • 4. Materials and Equipment

Materials are the things you need to do an activity, like paper, crayons or toys. Teachers should prepare all materials before the lesson starts.

Example:The teacher needs to check that all the materials are suitable for the children's age group.
Connection:You list materials in lesson plans and prepare them before teaching or training sessions.

Vocabulary

  1. activity — An activity is something that people do for fun or learning.
  2. plan — To plan means to think about and organize what you will do.
  3. instructions — Instructions are words that tell someone how to do something.
  4. materials — Materials are things you need to do an activity or make something.
  5. simple — Simple means easy to do or understand, not difficult.
  6. prepare — To prepare means to make something ready before you use it.
  7. demonstrate — To demonstrate means to show someone how to do something.
  8. age group — An age group is children or people of similar ages together.
  9. safety — Safety means being protected from danger or harm.
  10. supervise — To supervise means to watch people to make sure they are safe.
  11. goal — A goal is something you want children to learn or achieve.
  12. encourage — To encourage means to give someone support so they feel confident.
  13. equipment — Equipment means tools or things needed for a special purpose.
  14. participate — To participate means to join in and do an activity with others.
  15. steps — Steps are the different parts you do in order to complete something.
  16. arrange — To arrange means to put things in a good order or position.
  17. suitable — Suitable means right or appropriate for a particular person or situation.
  18. time limit — A time limit is the amount of time allowed to do something.
  19. enjoyable — Enjoyable means something that gives pleasure and makes you happy.
  20. check — To check means to look at something carefully to see if it is correct.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty key words about planning activities, materials, instructions and safety for children.
Reading
Read a simple activity plan and find the objectives, materials list and steps in order.
Listening
Listen to a teacher describing an activity and notice the modal verbs and sequencing words used.
Speaking
Explain a simple children's activity plan aloud using the vocabulary and grammar from this lesson.
Grammar
Study modal verbs like must, should and have to when writing rules and advice in activity plans.
Writing
Write your own short activity plan with an objective, materials list and clear numbered steps.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary, reading, grammar and writing about activity planning; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Teachers around the world use the same English words like objective, materials and steps when they share activity plans online. This means a teacher in Cambodia can easily read and use an activity plan written by a teacher in another country!

REFERENCES

Learning to Teach in the Primary School — Teresa Cremin and Joan Burnett (2018). This book shows clear examples of activity planning language that primary teachers use every day. Classroom Management Techniques — Jim Scrivener (2012). Read the chapters about instructions and demonstrations to see modal verbs used in real classroom contexts.

▶ How to Plan Activities for Young Learners — British Council TeachingEnglish ▶ Classroom Instructions and Demonstrations — Cambridge English Teacher

MINI STORY

Sarah is a new teacher and she needs to plan a simple activity for her class. Her goal is to teach children about shapes. She chooses an age group of four to five-year-olds. First, she must prepare all the materials she needs. She collects paper, crayons, and safety scissors.

Sarah writes clear instructions for the activity. She breaks it into easy steps so children can follow. She will demonstrate how to cut and paste shapes. The time limit is twenty minutes, which is suitable for young children. She must arrange the desks in groups before class starts. She also checks that all equipment is ready and safe.

During the activity, Sarah will supervise the children carefully. Safety is very important with scissors. She will encourage every child to participate and try their best. Sarah wants the lesson to be enjoyable for everyone. She knows that when children have fun, they learn better. This simple activity will help them understand shapes in an easy way.

Reading Passage

Sarah's First Story Time

Text type: Narrative
Sarah was nervous about her first day as a volunteer at the local library. She wanted to plan a simple story activity for young children. Sarah chose a book about animals because most children love animals. She practiced reading it at home three times. She also prepared some questions to ask the children after the story.

On Saturday morning, six children came to the library. Sarah sat on a small chair and showed them the book cover. The children looked excited. She read slowly and showed them all the pictures. When she finished, she asked the children about their favorite animals. Every child wanted to answer. One boy said he liked elephants. A girl talked about her pet cat at home.

After the activity, Sarah felt very happy. The children enjoyed the story and talked a lot. Sarah learned that simple activities work best with young children. She did not need expensive materials or difficult plans. Next week, she wants to do another story time. This time, she will add a simple drawing activity. The children can draw their favorite animal from the story.

A Perfect Activity Room

Text type: Description
The children's activity room at Greenhill Community Center is a bright and welcoming space. The room has large windows that let in natural light. There are colorful pictures on the walls. The pictures show children playing, learning, and having fun together. In the middle of the room, there is a soft blue carpet. Children sit on this carpet during activities.

The room has low shelves along one wall. These shelves hold simple materials for activities. There are colored papers, pencils, crayons, and safety scissors. There are also picture books and puzzles. Everything is at a height where children can reach it easily. A small white table stands in the corner. Teachers use this table to prepare activities before children arrive. Next to the table, there is a board. Teachers write the day's activity plan on this board.

The room can hold about fifteen children comfortably. It is not too big and not too small. The space feels safe and calm. Parents often say their children love coming to this room. The simple design helps children focus on activities. There are no loud colors or too many decorations. Everything in the room has a purpose and helps children learn through play.

contentRef.text:
Five Steps to Plan a Simple Activity

Text type: Informational
Planning a simple activity for children does not need to be difficult. You can follow five easy steps. These steps will help you create fun and safe activities. Children will enjoy learning and playing.

First, think about the children's age. Young children need shorter activities. They cannot focus for a long time. Children aged four or five need activities of about fifteen to twenty minutes. Older children can do activities for thirty minutes or more. Second, choose one clear goal. What do you want children to learn or do? Perhaps you want them to practice colors. Maybe you want them to work together as a team. Keep your goal simple and easy to understand.

Third, list the materials you need. Use things that are safe and easy to find. Paper, crayons, and glue work well for many activities. Fourth, write down the steps of your activity. Break the activity into small, clear actions. This helps you remember what to do. It also helps children follow along. Fifth, think about possible problems. What will you do if a child finishes early? What will you do if materials run out? Having backup plans helps activities go smoothly. When you follow these five steps, you can plan successful activities every time.

contentRef.text:
Two Ways to Plan: Maria and Tom

Text type: Comparison
Maria and Tom both work at a daycare center. They both plan activities for young children. However, they have different ways of planning. Maria likes to plan activities several days early. She writes everything down in a notebook. She draws pictures of the activity steps. She also prepares all her materials in advance. Maria puts everything in a box and labels it. When activity time comes, she feels calm and ready.

Tom has a different approach. He often plans activities the night before. Sometimes he plans on the same day. Tom keeps ideas in his head. He does not write detailed plans. He prefers to be flexible. If children seem tired, he changes the activity. If they are excited, he makes the activity longer. Tom finds materials quickly from the daycare cupboard. He believes that simple preparation works best. He says children are unpredictable, so detailed plans may not help.

Both ways can work well. Maria's method helps her feel organized and confident. She never forgets important materials. Her activities usually follow a clear structure. Tom's method gives him freedom to respond to children's moods. He can adapt quickly to unexpected situations. New teachers often feel more comfortable with Maria's planning style. Experienced teachers sometimes prefer Tom's flexible approach. The best method depends on your personality and experience.

contentRef.transcript:
Planning a Singing Game
B1 — Listen and Answer

Hello everyone. Today I want to talk about planning a simple singing game for young children. Singing
games are wonderful activities because children learn while having fun. They help children remember new
words and practice speaking together. First, choose a song that is short and easy. The song should have
simple words that children can repeat. Songs about animals, numbers, or body parts work very well. Make
sure the tune is easy to remember. You can use actions with the song, like clapping hands or jumping. This
makes the activity more interesting and helps children understand the words better.


Before you start, practice the song yourself several times. Sing it slowly at first so children can learn the
words. Then you can sing faster when they know it well. Plan to repeat the song three or four times in each
lesson. Children need repetition to learn new things. The whole activity should take about ten to fifteen
minutes. Remember to smile and use a happy voice. If you enjoy the activity, the children will enjoy it too.
Keep the group small, around eight to twelve children, so everyone can participate easily.

Organizing an Outdoor Game
B1 — Listen and Answer

Planning outdoor games for children requires careful thinking about safety and fun. Outdoor activities give
children fresh air and help them use their energy in a positive way. Today I'll explain how to plan a simple
running game for children aged four to seven years old. First, check the space where you'll play the game.
The area should be flat and have no dangerous objects like stones or broken glass. Make sure there's enough
space for all children to run safely without bumping into each other. A game called 'Traffic Lights' is perfect
for young children. It's easy to understand and very active.


Here's how the game works. You are the traffic light. When you say 'green light', children run forward. When
you say 'red light', they must stop immediately. You can add 'yellow light' which means walk slowly. Play the
game for about fifteen minutes because children get tired quickly. Before starting, explain the rules clearly
and show the children what to do. Always count the children before and after the activity. Stay where you can
see every child during the game. Remember to bring water for the children and plan a quiet activity
afterwards so they can rest and calm down.

contentRef.transcript:
Setting Up a Building Blocks Activity
B1 — Listen and Answer

Building with blocks is an excellent activity for young children's development. It helps children learn about
shapes, colors, and sizes while improving their hand control. Today I'll share how to organize a simple block-
building activity for children aged three to six years. First, prepare the materials you need. Collect enough
blocks so each child has at least ten to fifteen pieces. Use large, light blocks that are easy for small hands to
hold. Wooden blocks or soft plastic blocks both work well. Set up a clean space on the floor or on low tables
where children can build comfortably.


When you start the activity, sit with the children and show them what to do. Build a simple tower or a small
house as an example. Then let the children create their own designs. Some children will copy your example

and others will make something different. Both ways are fine. Walk around the group and talk to each child
about their building. Ask simple questions like 'What are you making?' or 'What color is this block?' This
helps children think and practice speaking. The activity should last about twenty to twenty-five minutes. At
the end, take photos of the children's work before you pack away the blocks. Children feel proud when you
show interest in their creations.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

When you plan an activity for children, you need to think about their age first. Simple activities like drawing or singing songs work well with young children.

You should prepare all the materials before the children arrive in the classroom. It is important to give clear instructions so the children understand what to do. Always have a backup plan if the activity finishes early or does not work.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What kind of simple activity would you choose for young children and why?

I would choose a colouring activity because it is easy and fun. Children can use crayons to colour pictures of animals or flowers. This activity helps them practice holding pencils and being creative. Most children enjoy art activities.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. How do you decide if an activity is suitable for a child's age?

I think about what the child can do at that age. Young children need simple tasks they can finish quickly. Older children can do more difficult activities that take longer. I also check if the activity is safe for them.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What materials do you need to prepare for a drawing activity?

For a drawing activity, I need paper and crayons or coloured pencils. I also prepare some example pictures to show the children. It is good to have extra paper in case someone makes a mistake. I put everything on the table before class starts.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Why is it important to give clear instructions to children?

Children need clear instructions because they might not understand complicated explanations. If the instructions are simple, they know exactly what to do. This helps them feel confident and enjoy the activity more. Clear instructions also save time in the classroom.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What would you do if children finish an activity too quickly?

I would have a backup activity ready, like a simple game or song. I could also ask them to help other children who need more time. Another idea is to let them add more details to their work. Planning extra activities is always helpful.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs for Obligation, Advice and Necessity

Modal verbs like must, should, can, need to and have to help us talk about rules, advice and what is necessary.

We use must for strong rules, should for advice, have to for external rules, and don't have to when something is not necessary.

FORMS

FormExample
must + base verb (strong obligation/rule)Children must wash their hands before eating.
should + base verb (advice/recommendation)You should bring extra paper for the activity.
have to / has to + base verb (external necessity)We have to finish by three o'clock.
don't have to / doesn't have to + base verb (not necessary)Children don't have to bring their own crayons.
can + base verb (permission/ability)The children can choose their favourite colour.
mustn't + base verb (prohibition)Children mustn't run in the classroom.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ Children must to sit down.

✓ Children must sit down.

Never use 'to' after modal verbs like must, should or can.

✗ You no must shout indoors.

✓ You mustn't shout indoors.

Use mustn't for prohibition, not 'no must' or 'must no'.

✗ We not have to buy new scissors.

✓ We don't have to buy new scissors.

Use don't/doesn't before 'have to' to make it negative.

nodes.question: Q1. The school has a safety rule, so all teachers ___ check the classroom before activities start.
nodes.explanation: → A safety rule from the school is a strong obligation, so we use must.

nodes.question: Q2. I think you ___ prepare extra craft materials because some children work very fast.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice from the speaker's experience, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q3. The activity is outdoors, so children ___ wear warm clothes today.
nodes.explanation: → Wearing warm clothes is good advice for outdoor activities, so we use should.

nodes.question: Q4. Children ___ use scissors without an adult watching them.
nodes.explanation: → This is a safety prohibition because scissors are dangerous, so mustn't is correct.

nodes.question: Q5. The library already has paper, so we ___ buy any for the drawing activity.
nodes.explanation: → Buying paper is not necessary because the library has it, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q6. The class finishes at two o'clock, so we ___ finish the game by then. There is no other time.
nodes.explanation: → There is no other choice, so we use 'have to'.

nodes.question: Q7. You ___ give children a choice of colours because it makes the activity more interesting.
nodes.explanation: → Giving choices is a good idea to improve the activity, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q8. Children ___ bring their own toys because we have games here.
nodes.explanation: → Bringing toys is not necessary because games are provided, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q9. The principal says every teacher ___ write a short activity plan before each class. It is a rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q10. It's a good idea to prepare more activities, so you ___ have a backup plan.
nodes.explanation: → Having a backup plan is good advice to prepare well, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q11. Children ___ touch the hot glue gun because it can burn them.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q12. The room is already clean, so we ___ tidy up before starting.
nodes.explanation: → Tidying is not necessary because the room is already clean, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q13. Fire regulations say we ___ keep all exits clear during activities.
nodes.explanation: → Fire regulations create a legal obligation, so must is correct.

nodes.question: Q14. You ___ test the activity yourself first because then you can see any problems.
nodes.explanation: → Testing first is helpful advice to find problems, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q15. The children are very young, so instructions ___ be very simple and clear.
nodes.explanation: → Young children need simple instructions, making this a strong necessity, so must is correct.

nodes.question: Q16. I recommend bringing extra pencils, so you ___ have enough for everyone.
nodes.explanation: → Bringing extra pencils is advice to be prepared, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q17. Children ___ leave the room during the activity without telling the teacher. It is a safety rule.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q18. Each child already has a chair, so you ___ bring more chairs.
nodes.explanation: → Bringing more chairs is not necessary because everyone has one, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q19. The school policy says teachers ___ arrive ten minutes before class starts.
nodes.explanation: → A school policy creates an obligation for teachers, so must is correct.

nodes.question: Q20. The weather looks bad, so we ___ move the activity indoors today. It is a good idea.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q21. Children ___ eat or drink near the computers because liquids damage them.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q22. We have plenty of time, so you ___ rush to finish the activity.
nodes.explanation: → It is not necessary, so we use 'don't have to'.

nodes.question: Q23. First aid training is required here, so every teacher ___ complete the course.
nodes.explanation: → A required training creates an obligation for all teachers, so must is correct.

nodes.question: Q24. It helps children focus, so you ___ give one instruction at a time.
nodes.explanation: → Giving one instruction at a time is helpful advice for teaching, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q25. Children ___ shout in the library because other people are reading there.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q26. The playground is dry today, so children ___ bring indoor shoes for playtime.
nodes.explanation: → Indoor shoes are not necessary because the playground is dry, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q27. The activity uses small parts, so parents ___ watch children under three years old. It is a safety rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q28. Children seem tired, so you ___ make the next activity shorter and calmer.
nodes.explanation: → Adjusting the activity for tired children is good advice, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q29. Children ___ run with scissors because they can fall and hurt themselves.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q30. There are spare crayons in the cupboard, so children ___ buy new ones.
nodes.explanation: → Buying crayons is not necessary because spare ones are available, so don't have to is correct.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe a simple drawing activity you could plan for children aged 5-7 years. Explain what the children will do and what materials they need. (100–140 words)

  • Name the activity clearly and state the age group
  • List the basic materials needed (paper, pencils, colours)
  • Describe the steps children will follow in simple order

Key structures: Future with 'will' (children will draw, will use), Sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally)

Model
I will plan a simple drawing activity for children aged 5 to 7 years old. The activity is called 'Draw Your Family'. The children will need white paper, pencils, and coloured crayons or markers. First, I will ask each child to think about their family members. Then, the children will draw pictures of their family on the paper. They can use pencils first and then add colours. After that, each child will write the names of their family members under the pictures. Finally, the children will show their drawings to the class. This activity helps children practice drawing and writing. It also helps them talk about people they love. The activity will take about 30 minutes to complete.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Describe a simple drawing activity for children aged 5-7: name it, state the age group, list the basic materials and give the steps in order.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: activity, plan, materials, instructions, prepare, steps, age group, suitable. Structures: Future with 'will' (children will draw, I will ask); Sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names the drawing activity, gives the 5-7 age group, lists materials such as paper, pencils and crayons, and describes several clear steps in a sensible order. Good: Names the activity and lists materials but the age group or the steps are thin (for example only two steps), though a reader could still run the activity. Developing: Mentions a drawing activity but leaves out the materials or the steps, or the steps are a jumble such as 'draw, paper, children happy'. Beginning: Does not describe a drawing activity for children, or writes one or two disconnected sentences.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'will' for the plan several times ('The children will draw...', 'I will ask...') and at least two sequencing words, with words like activity, materials, steps or prepare used correctly. Good: Uses 'will' and some sequencing words such as first and then, with only a few week words; one or two uses are slightly wrong. Developing: Writes mostly in present simple ('children draw') and uses first/then once or not at all; few week words appear. Beginning: No use of 'will' or sequencing words and almost none of the week's vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (25 points). Excellent: Most sentences are correct; only small slips such as a missing article ('draw picture') or 'children will drawing'. Good: Many correct sentences; errors with 'will + base verb', plural nouns or articles appear but meaning is always clear. Developing: Frequent errors such as 'children will draws', missing verbs or wrong word order make some sentences hard to follow. Beginning: Errors in almost every sentence, so the plan cannot be understood.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Reads like a short plan: activity and age first, then materials, then steps in order, with sequencing words linking the sentences. Good: Mostly in a sensible order; sequencing words are used but one step seems out of place or two ideas run together. Developing: Ideas are in a random order and the reader has to guess which step comes first. Beginning: No order; a list of unrelated words or sentences.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear activity plan with name, age, materials and ordered steps, using 'will' and sequencing words well. | 75-89: All main points present; a few grammar slips or one thin point. | 60-74: Plan is understandable but a point is missing or 'will' and sequencing are weak. | 40-59: Only part of the plan; many errors or very short. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (crayon/cryon, colour/color); a different drawing activity from the model's 'Draw Your Family'; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear (e.g. 'paper white'); missing 'the' before 'children'; using 'can' or 'need to' alongside 'will'.
LENGTH: 100-140 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 80 words: cap at 60. Over 160 words: do not penalise unless it becomes unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any simple activity for 5-7 year olds is fine (colouring, drawing a school, drawing animals), with any reasonable materials and any number of steps from three upwards. First-person 'I will ask' or third-person 'The teacher will ask' are both acceptable. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted task instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for the learner's own plan. Copying the model answer word-for-word: score 100 with a note to use their own sentences next time. Writing about a different topic: maximum 40.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the learner's own activity name, materials or a well-formed 'will' sentence they wrote. 2) Fix: Correct one common error, e.g. 'Children will drawing' becomes 'The children will draw a picture.' 3) Next step: Add one more step with 'after that' or 'finally' next time.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Explain how you will give instructions to children at the start of a simple game activity. Describe the steps you will follow to make sure everyone understands. (120–160 words)

  • Begin by getting the children's attention and stating the game name
  • Explain the rules using short, clear sentences and demonstrate actions
  • Check understanding by asking questions or doing a practice round

Key structures: Modal verbs (will, should, can, must), Imperatives for instructions (sit, listen, watch, try), Time markers (before we start, first, when)

Model
Before I start the game, I will ask all the children to sit in a circle and listen carefully. I will tell them the name of the game: 'Pass the Ball'. Then I will explain the rules in simple words. I will say, 'We will pass a soft ball around the circle. When the music plays, you pass the ball quickly. When the music stops, the person holding the ball must stand up and say their name.' After I explain, I will show the children what to do. I will pass the ball to one child and demonstrate. Then I will ask, 'Does everyone understand?' If some children look confused, I will explain again or do a practice round. This way, everyone knows what to do before we begin. Clear instructions help the game run smoothly and make it more fun for all the children.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Explain how you will give instructions at the start of a game: get attention and name the game, explain the rules in short sentences with a demonstration, and check understanding.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: instructions, demonstrate, game, rules, check, participate, encourage, simple. Structures: Modal verbs (will, should, can, must); Imperatives for instructions (sit, listen, watch, try); Time markers (before we start, first, when).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Covers all three points: gets the children's attention and says the game name, explains rules in short sentences with a demonstration, and checks understanding by a question or practice round. Good: Covers two points well; for example explains and demonstrates the rules but only briefly says how understanding is checked. Developing: Describes the game or the rules but does not say how the teacher gets attention or checks understanding. Beginning: Does not explain how instructions are given, or only names a game.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses imperatives in the teacher's spoken lines ('Sit down. Watch me.'), modals such as will/must/should, and time markers like 'before we start' or 'when the music stops'. Good: Uses will and at least one imperative or time marker correctly; modals like must or should are missing or used once. Developing: Uses only 'will' or only plain present tense; imperatives or time markers appear once with errors. Beginning: No modals, imperatives or time markers.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Teacher's spoken lines and explanations are mostly correct; slips are small, such as 'must to stand'. Good: Some errors with modal + base verb ('I will explains') or articles, but every sentence can be understood. Developing: Frequent errors mix up modals and verb forms, and some rules cannot be understood. Beginning: Nearly every sentence has an error and the explanation is unclear.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Steps follow the real order: attention, game name, rules, demonstration, question, with time markers linking them. Good: Order is mostly logical; one step, such as the check, is placed oddly. Developing: Steps are mixed up, so the reader cannot tell what happens before the game starts. Beginning: No clear order or sequence.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: All three stages of giving instructions explained clearly with imperatives, modals and time markers. | 75-89: Good explanation of the stages; some modal or verb-form slips. | 60-74: Rules explained but attention or checking understanding is missing or thin. | 40-59: Very short or unclear explanation with many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; a different game from 'Pass the Ball' (Simon Says, a counting game); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; omitting quotation marks around the teacher's words; using 'tell' or 'say' interchangeably.
LENGTH: 120-160 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 95 words: cap at 60. Over 185 words: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any simple game and any way of getting attention (clap, sit in a circle, count down). Checking understanding by a practice round, a question or asking a child to repeat the rule are all fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20 and ask for their own explanation. Model answer copied word-for-word: 100 with a note to use own sentences. Writing only about the game rules with no teaching steps: maximum 45.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a specific step the learner described or a good teacher line such as their own 'Listen and watch me'. 2) Fix: Fix one modal or verb-form error, e.g. 'I will explains the rules' becomes 'I will explain the rules.' 3) Next step: Next time add one sentence with 'before we start' to show what you do first.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write about why it is important to choose age-appropriate activities for children. Give reasons and include an example of what could go wrong with the wrong activity. (140–180 words)

  • State clearly that activities must match children's age and abilities
  • Give 2-3 reasons why this is important (safety, learning, confidence)
  • Include a specific example of a problem that can happen with wrong activities

Key structures: Conditionals (if...then, when...can), Because/so for giving reasons, Examples with 'for example, for instance'

Model
It is very important to choose age-appropriate activities for children. This means the activity should match what children at that age can do and understand. If an activity is too difficult, children will feel frustrated and lose confidence. They might give up quickly or feel bad about themselves. If an activity is too easy, children will feel bored and will not learn anything new. Age-appropriate activities help children feel successful and want to learn more. They also keep children safe because the tasks are suitable for their physical skills. For example, if you ask 4-year-old children to use sharp scissors or small beads, they could hurt themselves or swallow dangerous objects. Young children do not have good control of their hands yet. However, if you give them large crayons and thick paper, they can create art safely. When you plan activities, always think about the children's age first. This helps you choose the right materials and set tasks they can complete successfully.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Explain why activities must be age-appropriate, give two or three reasons (safety, learning, confidence) and one specific example of what can go wrong.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: suitable, age group, safety, supervise, equipment, goal, enjoyable, encourage. Structures: Conditionals (if...then, when...can); Because / so for giving reasons; Examples with 'for example' or 'for instance'.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: States that activities must match children's age and ability, gives two or three reasons (such as safety, learning, confidence), and includes a specific example of a problem with a wrong activity. Good: States the main idea and gives reasons, but the example is vague (for example 'children can be sad') or only one reason is developed. Developing: Says age-appropriate activities are good but gives one weak reason and no real example. Beginning: Does not explain why age matters, or writes about a different topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses if-sentences correctly ('If the game is too hard, children feel sad'), because/so to link reasons, and 'for example' to introduce the problem, with words like suitable, safety or age group. Good: Uses because or so and one if-sentence or 'for example' correctly; a second attempt has a small error. Developing: Gives reasons with simple 'and' sentences; because/if appear once, often with errors like 'because children is small'. Beginning: No conditionals, no reason words and no examples.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: If-sentences and reason sentences are mostly accurate; slips are small, such as 'if it too hard'. Good: Some errors in tense inside if-sentences ('if the game will be hard') or in 'children/child', but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in verb forms and sentence structure make several reasons hard to understand. Beginning: Most sentences are broken and the argument cannot be followed.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Opens with the main idea, then reasons in separate sentences, then the example, and closes with a short conclusion. Good: Main idea and reasons are clear but the example or conclusion is placed awkwardly. Developing: Reasons and example are mixed together without linking words. Beginning: No clear main idea or order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear opinion with 2-3 reasons and a specific example, using if/because/for example correctly. | 75-89: Good argument with a usable example; a few errors in if-sentences. | 60-74: Opinion and reasons present but example is vague or structures are weak. | 40-59: Very little reasoning; many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little to judge.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; a different example from the scissors and beads in the model (e.g. a running game for toddlers, a reading task for 5-year-olds); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'children' and 'kids' together; 'for example' without a following comma.
LENGTH: 140-180 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 110 words: cap at 60. Over 200 words: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sensible reasons (safety, confidence, boredom, learning) and any realistic example. The example may be about an activity that is too hard or too easy. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: score 0-20. Copying the model answer word-for-word: 100 with a note to use own sentences. A general essay on teaching that never mentions age: maximum 40.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the learner's best reason or their own example of a wrong activity. 2) Fix: Correct one conditional or reason sentence, e.g. 'If the activity is too difficult, the children feel sad' instead of 'If activity too difficult, children sad.' 3) Next step: Add a second 'for example' sentence with a different age group.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about how to plan a simple art activity for young children. Describe the materials you need, the steps to follow, and how to make it safe. (80–110 words)

  • Say what materials you need (paper, paints, brushes, etc.)
  • Explain the steps clearly and simply
  • Mention safety and how to protect clothes
Model
Planning a simple art activity for young children is easy. First, you need to get the materials ready. You need paper, paints, brushes, water cups, and old shirts. The old shirts protect the children's clothes from paint. Put everything on the tables before the children arrive. When they come in, show them how to use the brushes and paints. Tell them to dip the brush in paint and then paint on the paper. Walk around and help them if they need it. Make sure they wash the brushes in water when they change colors. After about 20 minutes, help them clean up. The activity should be fun and safe for everyone.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a short paragraph on planning a simple art activity: the materials needed, the steps, and how to keep it safe and protect clothes.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: materials, prepare, steps, safety, supervise, equipment, arrange, check. Structures: Sequencing words (first, then, after that); Imperatives for instructions (put, show, help).
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names the materials (paper, paints, brushes), gives clear steps for the activity, and says how to make it safe, including protecting clothes with shirts or aprons.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses first/then/after that and instruction verbs ('Put the paper on the table', 'Help the children') along with week words such as materials, prepare, safety.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Sentences are mostly accurate; small slips only, such as 'paints' for 'paint' or a missing 'the'.

DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips (paint/pant, brush/bruch); a different art activity such as clay or collage; Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; writing 'color' or 'colour'; a short paragraph near the lower word limit.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Teaching as a profession

Teaching is a job where you help students learn new things every day. Teachers need special training and skills to do this work well.

Example:Professional teachers must prepare lessons and support students to reach their goals.
Connection:You will read and hear this language in education textbooks, job interviews and teacher training courses.
  • 2. Teacher responsibilities

Teachers have many duties like planning lessons, grading work and giving feedback. They also motivate students and create a good learning environment.

Example:A teacher's responsibilities include preparing assignments and explaining new subjects clearly.
Connection:This language appears in job descriptions, teacher evaluations and professional development workshops.
  • 3. Qualities of effective teachers

Good teachers are patient, skilled and able to inspire their students. They interact well with students and encourage them to work hard.

Example:Effective teachers should be patient and must motivate students even when lessons are challenging.
Connection:You will use these words when writing about teaching methods or discussing classroom experiences with colleagues.
  • 4. Teaching contexts and cultures

Teachers work in different schools and countries with different rules and customs. Each classroom has its own challenges and rewards.

Example:Teachers can compare how they interact with students in different cultural contexts.
Connection:This language is useful for international teaching programmes, cultural exchange projects and education conferences.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. teacher — A person whose job is to help students learn in a school.
  2. classroom — A room in a school where students have their lessons.
  3. lesson — A period of time when a teacher teaches something to students.
  4. explain — To help someone understand something by describing it clearly.
  5. patient — Able to stay calm and not get angry when things are difficult.
  6. assignment — A piece of work that a teacher gives students to do.
  7. grade — To check student work and give it a mark or score.
  8. prepare — To make something ready before you use or do it.
  9. encourage — To give someone confidence and support to do something.
  10. subject — An area of knowledge that students study at school.
  11. challenging — Difficult in a way that tests your ability or skills.
  12. reward — Something good you get because you did something well.
  13. professional — Relating to a job that needs special training and skills.
  14. interact — To talk and work together with other people.
  15. motivate — To make someone want to do something or work hard.
  16. feedback — Comments about how well someone did something to help them improve.
  17. responsibility — A duty or job that you must do.
  18. skilled — Having the ability to do something very well.
  19. inspire — To make someone feel excited and want to do something.
  20. goal — Something you want to achieve in the future.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn twenty key words about teachers, classrooms and the work teachers do every day.
Reading
Read short texts about different teaching contexts and compare the challenges and rewards teachers describe.
Listening
Listen to teachers talking about their motivations and daily responsibilities in authentic interview recordings.
Speaking
Discuss your own reasons for choosing teaching and talk about teacher roles in different cultures.
Grammar
Study modal verbs like must, should and can to talk about teacher obligations and permissions.
Writing
Write a paragraph describing daily responsibilities and the qualities that make a teacher effective.
Lesson Test
Complete questions on vocabulary, grammar and the language of teaching to check your understanding, aiming for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

The word 'teacher' comes from an old English word meaning 'to show or point out.' Teachers around the world use hand gestures and body language to help students understand, even when they speak different languages!

REFERENCES

English for Academic Study: Vocabulary — Sheldon Smith (Garnet Education) (2017). This book helps you learn academic words about teaching and education in clear, simple English. Oxford Word Skills: Basic — Ruth Gairns and Stuart Redman (Oxford University Press) (2008). It teaches everyday vocabulary for work and professional contexts, including words teachers use.

▶ A Day in the Life of a Teacher — BBC Learning English ▶ Modal Verbs for Obligation and Advice — English with Lucy

Maria is a new teacher at a primary school. Every morning, she prepares her lessons carefully before going to the classroom. She teaches English, which is her favorite subject to teach.

Maria tries to be patient with all her students. She explains things clearly and gives helpful feedback on their assignments. When students do well, she encourages them to keep working hard. Maria's First Day as a Teacher

Text type: Narrative
Maria woke up early on Monday morning. She felt nervous and excited at the same time. Today was her first day as a primary school teacher. She put on her new blue dress and ate a quick breakfast. Then she drove to Greenfield Primary School.

When Maria walked into her classroom, twenty-five children were waiting for her. They looked at her with curious eyes. Maria smiled and introduced herself. She told the children about her hobbies and her dog. The children started to relax. They asked her many questions about her life. Maria felt happy because the children were friendly.

During the day, Maria taught English and Maths. She played games with the students and read them a story. By lunchtime, she felt less nervous. At the end of the day, a little girl gave her a drawing. The picture showed Maria standing in front of the class. Maria smiled and thanked her. That evening, Maria told her family about her wonderful first day. She knew she had chosen the right job. Being a teacher was hard work, but it made her feel proud and happy.

Inside Mr. Thompson's Classroom

Text type: Description
Mr. Thompson's classroom is on the second floor of the school building. It is a bright and colourful room with large windows. Sunshine comes through the windows every morning. The walls are covered with student artwork and posters about different countries. There is a big world map near the teacher's desk.

The classroom has six rows of desks. Each desk is for two students. The desks are made of light brown wood and they are always clean. At the front of the room, there is a large whiteboard. Mr. Thompson writes the daily schedule on it every morning. Next to the whiteboard, there is a bookshelf full of stories and textbooks. The books are organized by subject and level. Students can borrow them during reading time.

In the corner of the classroom, there is a comfortable reading area. It has soft cushions and a small carpet. Students like to sit there during break time. Mr. Thompson also has a special board where he puts gold stars.

Students get stars for good work and helpful behaviour. The classroom feels warm and welcoming. Students say they enjoy learning in this space because it feels safe and friendly.

Email from the Head Teacher

Text type: Notice

To: All Teachers
From: Head Teacher, Mrs. Johnson
Date: 15 September 2024
Subject: New Teacher Welcome Meeting

Dear Colleagues,

I am writing to invite you to our welcome meeting for new teachers. The meeting will take place next Wednesday at 4 PM in the staff room. We have five new teachers joining our school this year. They will teach different subjects including Science, Art, and Physical Education. This meeting is important because it helps new teachers feel comfortable in our school community.

During the meeting, I will explain our school rules and daily routines. We will also talk about lesson planning and classroom management. Each new teacher will receive a welcome pack with useful information and materials. The pack includes school maps, timetables, and contact details for all staff members.

After the meeting, we will have tea and cake together. This is a good time to meet the new teachers and chat in a relaxed way. Please try to attend if you can. Your support helps new teachers feel welcome and confident. If you cannot come, please send me an email before Tuesday.

I look forward to seeing you at the meeting.

Best wishes, Mrs. Johnson

What Makes a Good Teacher?

Text type: Informational

Good teachers have many important qualities. First, they need to be patient. Students learn at different speeds and they make mistakes. A patient teacher stays calm and helps students without getting angry. Second, good teachers know their subject well. They can explain difficult ideas in simple ways. They also answer student questions clearly and confidently.

Communication skills are very important for teachers. They need to speak clearly so everyone can understand. They also need to listen carefully to their students. Good teachers notice when students feel confused or worried. They create a friendly classroom where students feel safe to ask questions. Good teachers also communicate well with parents. They send regular updates about student progress and school activities.

Finally, good teachers are creative and enthusiastic. They make lessons interesting by using different activities and materials. They might use videos, games, or group projects. When teachers show enthusiasm for their subject, students become more interested too. Good teachers also continue learning throughout their careers. They attend training courses and read about new teaching methods. This helps them become better at their job every year. Teaching is a challenging job, but it is also very rewarding.

Two Different Teaching Styles

Text type: Comparison
Miss Roberts and Mr. Lee both teach at the same secondary school, but they have very different teaching styles. Miss Roberts teaches History and she prefers traditional methods. She usually stands at the front of the classroom and gives clear explanations. She writes important dates and facts on the board. Students take notes and then complete exercises from the textbook. Miss Roberts believes this method helps students remember information well. Her lessons are quiet and organized. Tests happen every month to check student progress.

Mr. Lee teaches Geography and he uses a more modern approach. He often arranges desks in groups so students can work together. He uses technology like videos and interactive maps. Students do projects and presentations instead of just textbook exercises. Mr. Lee thinks this method makes learning more interesting and helps students develop different skills. His classroom is usually noisier because students discuss ideas together. He checks progress through projects rather than regular tests.

Both teachers are popular with students for different reasons. Some students prefer Miss Roberts because they like clear structure and routine. Other students enjoy Mr. Lee's creative lessons and group activities. The school values both teaching styles. The head teacher says different methods work for different students and subjects. What matters most is that both teachers care about their students and help them learn successfully.

Good morning everyone. I'm Nimol and I teach at a secondary school in the city. I'd like to describe a typical

At midday, I have a lunch break for one hour. I usually eat in the school canteen with other teachers.
Sometimes we have meetings during lunch to discuss school events or student problems. In the afternoon, I
teach two more classes. After the last lesson at three thirty, I don't go home immediately. I stay at school to
prepare lessons for the next day or to mark homework. Sometimes students come to ask questions or get
extra help. I usually leave school around five o'clock. When I get home, I'm quite tired but happy. Teaching
keeps me very busy but I enjoy working with young people every day.
