Hi, I'm Rotha. I've been teaching for five years now and I want to share some thoughts about my job. Being a
teacher has many challenges. One big challenge is managing a classroom with many different students. Some
students learn quickly and some need more time and help. Some are quiet and shy, while others talk too
much. I have to find ways to help everyone learn well. Another challenge is the amount of work. I spend
many hours preparing lessons, checking homework, and writing reports. Sometimes I feel stressed and tired.


However, teaching also brings many rewards. The best reward is seeing students make progress and succeed.
Last year, one of my students couldn't read very well. I gave her extra support and practice every week. Now
she loves reading and borrows books from the library every week. That makes me feel proud and happy. I

also enjoy the relationships I build with my students. They trust me and share their ideas and feelings.
Teaching is definitely not an easy job but it's meaningful and important. When I help young people learn and
grow, I know I'm making a positive difference in their lives.

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Teachers help students learn new things every day in the classroom. Being a teacher means you need to be patient and kind with young people. Teachers plan lessons and check homework to make sure students understand everything. Many teachers say they love their job because they can make a difference.

Good teachers explain things clearly and answer questions when students need help.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. Why do you want to become a teacher?

I want to become a teacher because I enjoy working with young people. I like helping others learn new things and grow. I think teaching is a meaningful job where I can make a positive difference in students' lives.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What do you think is the most important quality for a teacher?

I believe patience is the most important quality for a teacher. Students learn at different speeds and sometimes need extra help. A patient teacher can explain things many times without getting frustrated. This helps students feel comfortable asking questions.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. What subjects would you like to teach and why?

I would like to teach English because I am good at languages. I enjoy reading books and writing stories. I think I could help students improve their communication skills. English is also useful for many different jobs in the future.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. What challenges do teachers face in their daily work?

Teachers often have to manage large classes with many different students. Some students need more attention than others, which can be difficult. Teachers also spend a lot of time preparing lessons and marking homework. Sometimes parents have high expectations too.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. How can teachers make their lessons more interesting for students?

Teachers can use games and group activities to make lessons fun. They can also use technology like videos and online tools. Real-life examples help students understand better. When lessons are interactive and practical, students stay more interested and learn more easily.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs of Obligation, Advice and Permission

Modal verbs like must, have to, should, can and may express obligation, advice or permission.

Must and have to show something is necessary.

Should gives advice.

Can and may show permission or possibility.

FORMS

FormExample
must + base verb (strong obligation)Teachers must arrive on time every day.
have to / has to + base verb (obligation)She has to plan lessons at home.
should + base verb (advice)You should ask questions in class meetings.
can + base verb (permission / ability)Students can leave after the bell rings.
may + base verb (permission / possibility)Teachers may use the staff room freely.
don't have to / doesn't have to + base verb (no obligation)We don't have to work on Saturdays.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ Teachers must to check homework every week.

✓ Teachers must check homework every week.

Must is followed directly by the base verb, never by 'to'.

✗ She musts prepare lessons carefully.

✓ She must prepare lessons carefully.

Must never adds -s, even with he/she/it subjects.

✗ Do I must attend the meeting?

✓ Must I attend the meeting? / Do I have to attend the meeting?

Must forms questions without 'do/does'; use 'have to' if you need 'do'.

nodes.text: EXERCISES

nodes.question: Q1. The headteacher says all staff ___ attend the training session next Monday. It is a rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q2. New teachers ___ ask experienced colleagues for help when they need it.
nodes.explanation: → Asking for help is good advice, not a rule, so should is the right choice.

nodes.question: Q3. Teachers ___ use their phones during lessons because it sets a bad example.
nodes.explanation: → Setting a bad example makes phone use prohibited, and mustn't expresses prohibition.

nodes.question: Q4. You ___ wear formal clothes every day; our school has a relaxed dress code.
nodes.explanation: → A relaxed dress code means formal clothes are not necessary, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q5. Students ___ enter the staff room without permission from a teacher.
nodes.explanation: → Needing permission shows that entry without it is not allowed, so can't expresses the prohibition.

nodes.question: Q6. Teachers ___ report any serious behaviour problems to the principal immediately. It is their duty.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q7. You ___ try different teaching methods to see what works best for your class.
nodes.explanation: → Trying different methods is helpful advice for improvement, so should is the right modal.

nodes.question: Q8. Teachers ___ keep student records confidential according to school policy. It is a rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q9. We have no choice: we ___ finish marking all the tests tonight because the deadline is tomorrow morning.
nodes.explanation: → There is no other choice, so we use 'have to'.

nodes.question: Q10. Teachers ___ leave the building during working hours without signing out first.
nodes.explanation: → The requirement to sign out shows that leaving without doing so is prohibited.

nodes.question: Q11. You ___ prepare every lesson in detail, but planning helps you feel more confident.
nodes.explanation: → The second part shows planning is helpful but not required, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q12. Student teachers ___ observe experienced teachers before they teach their own classes. This is good advice.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q13. All teachers ___ attend a first aid course because it is now a legal requirement.
nodes.explanation: → A legal requirement creates an absolute obligation, so must is the correct modal.

nodes.question: Q14. Teachers ___ give students homework every day; twice a week is usually enough.
nodes.explanation: → It is not necessary, so we use 'don't have to'.

nodes.question: Q15. You ___ arrive at school by 8:00 a.m. because classes start at 8:15. It is a rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q16. Teachers ___ use positive encouragement when students make mistakes in class.
nodes.explanation: → Positive encouragement is good teaching advice, not a rule, so should is the right choice.

nodes.question: Q17. We ___ speak loudly in the library because students are studying there.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q18. You ___ learn every student's name quickly; it helps build better relationships.
nodes.explanation: → Learning names helps relationships, which makes this good advice, so should is correct.

nodes.question: Q19. Teachers ___ work during school holidays unless they choose to prepare materials.
nodes.explanation: → The word 'unless' shows holiday work is not required, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q20. You ___ share your lesson plans with other teachers in your department. This is good advice, not a rule.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

nodes.question: Q21. All teachers ___ complete the online training module by Friday for safety certification.
nodes.explanation: → Certification requirements and a deadline create an obligation, so must is correct.

nodes.question: Q22. Teachers ___ give students the answers directly; they learn better by discovering themselves. This is advice, not a rule.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'shouldn't'.

nodes.question: Q23. You ___ check your email every hour, but read messages at least twice daily.
nodes.explanation: → It is not necessary, so we use 'don't have to'.

nodes.question: Q24. Teachers ___ maintain professional boundaries with students at all times. It is a strict rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q25. You ___ bring your own lunch or you can buy food in the cafeteria.
nodes.explanation: → The choice between bringing lunch and buying shows this is permission, so can is correct.

nodes.question: Q26. Teachers ___ use outdated textbooks when new materials are available online.
nodes.explanation: → New materials being available makes using old books poor practice, so shouldn't gives this advice.

nodes.question: Q27. All staff ___ wear identification badges inside the school building for security reasons. It is a rule.
nodes.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

nodes.question: Q28. You ___ attend every staff meeting, but it is helpful to join when you can.
nodes.explanation: → The second part shows attendance is helpful but not required, so don't have to is correct.

nodes.question: Q29. Teachers ___ ignore bullying behaviour; they need to report it immediately.
nodes.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'mustn't'.

nodes.question: Q30. You ___ use simple language when explaining new concepts to younger students. This is good teaching advice.
nodes.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Write a paragraph describing why you want to become a teacher. Explain your main reasons and motivation. (100–140 words)

  • Start by stating clearly that you want to be a teacher
  • Give two or three specific reasons for your choice
  • End with what you hope to achieve as a teacher

Key structures: I want to... because..., First / Second / Also

Model
I want to become a teacher because I love working with children. First, I enjoy explaining new ideas and helping students understand difficult topics. When a student finally understands something, it makes me very happy. Second, I believe education is very important for everyone. I want to give young people the best chance to succeed in life. Also, I like the idea of making a difference in my community. Teachers help shape the future by preparing the next generation. I hope to be a patient and kind teacher who inspires students to keep learning. Teaching is not just a job for me, it is my passion.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a paragraph saying clearly that you want to be a teacher, give two or three personal reasons, and end with what you hope to achieve.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: teacher, encourage, inspire, motivate, patient, subject, goal, responsibility. Structures: I want to ... because ...; First / Second / Also.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Opens by clearly saying 'I want to be a teacher', gives two or three personal reasons (for example loving children, helping students learn, serving the community), and ends with a hope or goal. Good: States the wish and gives two reasons, but the ending goal is missing or the reasons are very short. Developing: States the wish with one reason, or gives reasons that are copied general ideas with nothing personal. Beginning: Does not say why the writer wants to be a teacher, or is off-topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'I want to... because...' and First/Second/Also correctly, with words such as inspire, patient, motivate or goal. Good: Uses 'because' and at least two of First/Second/Also; a few week words are used correctly. Developing: Uses 'because' once, no ordering words, and only basic words like 'teach' and 'children'. Beginning: None of the structures and almost no week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Sentences are mostly accurate; only small slips such as 'I want be a teacher' or 'helps student'. Good: Some errors with 'want to + verb', third person -s or plurals, but the reasons are always clear. Developing: Frequent errors such as 'Because I like children' standing as a sentence alone, causing confusion. Beginning: Almost every sentence has an error that blocks meaning.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Clear shape: wish, reasons in order, hope for the future, joined by First/Second/Also. Good: Reasons are clear, but the opening or ending is weak. Developing: Reasons are mixed together, with no ordering words. Beginning: No order, just loose words.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear wish, 2-3 personal reasons and a closing goal, with 'want to... because' and ordering words well used. | 75-89: Wish and reasons clear; ending or accuracy slightly weak. | 60-74: Reasons present but short, or structures used only once. | 40-59: One reason only or many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different personal reasons from the model (family influence, love of learning); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'wish to' instead of 'want to'; writing about a future teacher role the writer already has.
LENGTH: 100-140 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 80 words: cap at 60. Over 160: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any sincere reasons; a teacher who already teaches can write why they chose to become one. 'First, Second, Also' may be replaced by 'Another reason is...'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model answer word-for-word: 100 with a note to use own reasons. Writing about another job: maximum 35.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a personal reason the learner gave in their own words. 2) Fix: Correct one error, e.g. 'I want to be a teacher because I love children' instead of 'I want be teacher because love children.' 3) Next step: Add one more reason beginning with 'Also'.

lessons.titleKm: Talking About Being a Teacher — Guided Writing Task 2 (120–160 words)
lessons.titleEn: Talking About Being a Teacher — Guided Writing Task 2 (120–160 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write a paragraph about the challenges teachers face in their daily work. Describe at least three different challenges and why they are difficult. (120–160 words)

  • Mention different types of challenges (classroom management, workload, student needs)
  • Explain why each challenge is difficult for teachers
  • Use linking words to connect your ideas smoothly

Key structures: One challenge is... Another challenge is..., This is difficult because...

Model
Teachers face many challenges in their daily work. One major challenge is managing classroom behaviour. When students talk too much or don't pay attention, it is hard to teach effectively. This is difficult because every class has different students with different personalities. Another challenge is the heavy workload. Teachers must plan lessons, mark homework, write reports, and attend meetings. They often work in the evenings and at weekends to finish everything. This leaves little time for their personal life. A third challenge is meeting the needs of all students. Some students learn quickly while others need extra help. Some have learning difficulties or personal problems at home. Teachers must try to support every student, but this is not always easy. Despite these challenges, many teachers find their work very rewarding.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Describe at least three challenges teachers face (such as classroom management, workload, student needs), explaining why each one is difficult and joining the ideas with linking words.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: challenging, assignment, grade, prepare, responsibility, patient, feedback, interact. Structures: One challenge is... Another challenge is...; This is difficult because....
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (40 points). Excellent: Describes three different challenges and gives a reason why each is hard (for example too many assignments to grade, noisy classes, students needing extra help). Good: Describes three challenges but explains the difficulty clearly for only one or two, or describes two challenges well. Developing: Names challenges as a list ('workload, behaviour, time') with little or no explanation. Beginning: Does not describe teacher challenges.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses 'One challenge is...', 'Another challenge is...' and 'This is difficult because...' correctly, with words like assignment, grade, prepare or challenging. Good: Uses two of the three frames; a few week words are used correctly. Developing: Uses 'challenge' once or twice but no 'because' sentences; basic words only. Beginning: No frames and almost no week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate sentences; small slips such as 'a lot of homeworks' or 'teacher have'. Good: Some errors with subject-verb agreement and uncountable nouns, but the explanations are clear. Developing: Frequent errors; some 'because' reasons cannot be understood. Beginning: Errors in nearly all sentences.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Each challenge has its own sentences with a reason, linked by Another/Also/However so the paragraph flows. Good: Challenges are separate but linking words are few or repeated. Developing: Challenges and reasons are mixed up in a long unclear block. Beginning: No linking or structure.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Three challenges each explained with a reason and smooth linking. | 75-89: Three challenges; one reason weaker; minor errors. | 60-74: Two challenges explained or reasons thin. | 40-59: Mostly a list with no reasons. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different challenges from the model (large classes, lack of materials, parent expectations); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'Next challenge is...' instead of 'Another challenge is...'; missing articles.
LENGTH: 120-160 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 95 words: cap at 60. Over 185: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic challenges for teachers in the learner's own school; local examples are welcome. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own examples. Writing only about why teaching is good (no challenges): maximum 35.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a challenge the learner described from their own school life. 2) Fix: Fix one sentence, e.g. 'This is difficult because teachers have many assignments to grade' instead of 'This difficult because many assignment grade.' 3) Next step: Add a linking word like 'Another challenge is' to introduce your third idea.

lessons.titleKm: Talking About Being a Teacher — Guided Writing Task 3 (140–180 words)
lessons.titleEn: Talking About Being a Teacher — Guided Writing Task 3 (140–180 words)

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Write a paragraph giving advice to someone who is thinking about becoming a teacher. Share three important things they should know or do. (140–180 words)

  • Start with an opening sentence about becoming a teacher
  • Give three clear pieces of advice with explanations
  • Finish with an encouraging final sentence

Key structures: You should... / It is important to..., First / Additionally / Finally

Model
If you are thinking about becoming a teacher, there are some important things you should know. First, you should spend time in real classrooms before you decide. Try to observe different teachers and see what their daily work is really like. This will help you understand if teaching is right for you. Additionally, you need to develop strong communication skills. Teachers must explain ideas clearly and listen carefully to their students. You should also learn to be patient because students make mistakes and need time to learn. Finally, it is important to be organized. Teachers handle many tasks at the same time, so good planning is essential. You will need to prepare lessons, manage paperwork, and remember important deadlines. Teaching can be stressful and tiring, but it is also incredibly rewarding. If you are passionate about helping others learn and grow, teaching could be a wonderful career for you.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Give advice to someone thinking about becoming a teacher: an opening sentence, three pieces of advice each with an explanation, and an encouraging final sentence.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: professional, skilled, patient, prepare, motivate, feedback, responsibility, inspire. Structures: You should... / It is important to...; First / Additionally / Finally.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts with an opening sentence about becoming a teacher, gives three clear pieces of advice each with a reason, and ends with an encouraging sentence. Good: Gives three pieces of advice but one has no explanation, or the opening or ending is missing. Developing: Gives one or two pieces of advice with little explanation. Beginning: Does not give advice, or writes about something else.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'You should...' and 'It is important to...' correctly several times, with First/Additionally/Finally and words such as patient, prepare or skilled. Good: Uses 'should' correctly and at least two ordering words; 'It is important to' is missing or has a small error. Developing: Uses 'should' once or with errors ('should to go') and no ordering words. Beginning: No advice structures and almost no week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Advice sentences are mostly accurate; small slips only, such as 'it is important be patient'. Good: Some errors with 'should + base verb' and 'important to + verb', but the advice is clear. Developing: Frequent errors in modals; some advice is hard to understand. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Opening, three pieces of advice in order with First/Additionally/Finally, then a warm closing sentence. Good: Advice is in order but the opening or closing is weak. Developing: Pieces of advice run together without order. Beginning: No structure.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Opening, three explained pieces of advice and encouraging close; should / it is important to well used. | 75-89: Three pieces of advice, mostly explained; small errors. | 60-74: Advice given but explanations or structures thin. | 40-59: One or two pieces of advice, many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different advice from the model (observe classes, learn the subject well, keep learning); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'must' instead of 'should'; addressing the reader as 'you' or 'a new teacher' consistently.
LENGTH: 140-180 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 110 words: cap at 60. Over 200: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any three sensible pieces of advice; 'Second' may replace 'Additionally'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to give own advice. Describing only why the writer likes teaching with no advice: maximum 40.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a piece of advice the learner explained well. 2) Fix: Correct one modal error, e.g. 'You should be patient with students' instead of 'You should to patient with student.' 3) Next step: Finish with one warm sentence like 'I believe you will be a great teacher.'

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph describing what you think makes a good teacher. Include at least three qualities and explain why they are important. (80–110 words)

  • Mention three qualities that good teachers have
  • Explain why each quality is important for teaching
  • Use clear examples to support your ideas
Model
I believe that good teachers need several important qualities. First, they must be patient because students learn at different speeds and some need more time. If teachers get angry or rush, students will feel stressed and learn less. Second, good teachers should be enthusiastic about their subject. When teachers show excitement, students become more interested and motivated to learn. Third, teachers need to be fair and treat all students equally. This creates a positive classroom where everyone feels respected. Finally, good teachers must be good communicators. They should explain things clearly and listen to student questions carefully. These qualities help teachers create a supportive learning environment where students can succeed.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a short paragraph naming at least three qualities of a good teacher, explaining why each is important and giving a clear example.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: patient, skilled, encourage, motivate, inspire, professional, explain, interact. Structures: A good teacher should / must be...; ...because...; First / Second / Third.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names three qualities (such as patient, fair, enthusiastic), explains why each matters for learning, and supports at least one with an example.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses quality words correctly (patient, skilled, inspire, motivate) with 'must/should be' and 'because'.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate; slips are small, e.g. 'teachers is patient'.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: One paragraph with qualities in separate sentences, linked by First/Second/Finally and a short closing sentence.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different qualities from the model (kind, creative, organised); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'a good teacher' vs 'good teachers' mixing; examples from the writer's own teachers.
LENGTH: 80-110 words, tolerance of about 8 words. Under 60 words: cap at 60. Over 130: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any three positive qualities; reasons can be personal or general. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own words. Writing about a bad teacher only: maximum 40.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Parent-teacher communication

Teachers and parents talk or write to each other about how a student is doing. They share information about schoolwork, behavior, and any problems.

Example:We need to communicate with parents when a student's behavior changes or their grades drop.
Connection:You use this English when you meet parents, write emails, or call them about their children.
  • 2. Professional tone in education

Using polite, clear, and respectful language when you talk to parents and colleagues. You stay calm and helpful, even when discussing problems.

Example:I appreciate your concern about the assignment, and I recommend we meet to discuss it.
Connection:You need this tone in parent meetings, emails to families, and conversations with other teachers.
  • 3. Describing student performance

Explaining how well a student is learning, behaving, and completing their work. You give examples and talk about what they can improve.

Example:Your son is making good progress in reading, but he needs to improve his writing skills.
Connection:You use this English in report cards, parent meetings, and feedback sessions at school.
  • 4. Making and responding to meeting requests

Asking someone to meet with you at a specific time, or answering when someone asks you. You check schedules and confirm the time and place.

Example:I am available on Tuesday at 3 p.m. if that time is convenient for you.
Connection:You see this in emails from parents, messages from colleagues, and school meeting invitations.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Vocabulary

  1. colleague — A person you work with in the same organization or school.
  2. progress — Improvement or development in learning or doing something.
  3. concern — A worry or problem that needs attention or discussion.
  4. discuss — To talk about something with another person and share ideas.
  5. meeting — A planned time when people come together to talk about something.
  6. attend — To go to or be present at an event or place.
  7. behavior — The way someone acts or conducts themselves with others.
  8. assignment — A task or piece of work given to students to do.
  9. schedule — A plan showing times when activities or events will happen.
  10. appreciate — To feel grateful or thankful for something someone does.
  11. feedback — Comments or advice about how well someone is doing something.
  12. support — To help or encourage someone to do something successfully.
  13. available — Free or ready to talk to someone or do something.
  14. permission — Official agreement allowing someone to do something or go somewhere.
  15. improve — To become better or make something better than before.
  16. issue — A problem or difficulty that needs to be solved.
  17. communicate — To share information or talk with someone clearly and effectively.
  18. responsible — Having the duty to take care of something or someone.
  19. recommend — To suggest that someone should do or try something.
  20. convenient — Suitable or easy for someone to use or do.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty words teachers use when talking about students, meetings, and communication with parents.
Reading
Read emails and messages from parents asking for meetings or sharing concerns about their children.
Listening
Listen to recordings of parent-teacher meetings and identify the main concerns and information shared.
Speaking
Practice having polite conversations about student progress and behavior with parents and colleagues.
Grammar
Study modal verbs like must, should, can, and may to give advice and talk about rules in school.
Writing
Write short professional emails to parents confirming meeting times and responding to their concerns.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary, grammar, and ability to communicate professionally; aim for 70 percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

In many countries, teachers say they are available for meetings during office hours or parent-teacher conferences. In Cambodia, parents often visit schools without appointments, so teachers use phrases like 'I appreciate you coming' to welcome unexpected visits politely.

REFERENCES

English for Academic Purposes: A Guide and Resource Book for Teachers — Ken Hyland (2006). This book helps you learn the polite, professional English used in education settings and meetings. Professional English in Use — Cambridge University Press (2007). It teaches the vocabulary and phrases for writing emails and speaking professionally at work.

▶ Parent-Teacher Conferences: Communication Tips — Edutopia ▶ Professional Email Writing — British Council LearnEnglish

MINI STORY

Sarah is a new teacher at Green Valley School. She needs to communicate with parents and colleagues every day. Yesterday, she had an important meeting with her colleague Tom to discuss their teaching schedule for next month.

After the meeting, Sarah met with Mrs. Chen, a parent. Mrs. Chen had a concern about her son's behavior in class. Sarah gave feedback about the boy's progress and said he is improving slowly. She recommended some extra practice at home. Mrs. Chen really appreciated Sarah's support and helpful advice.

Later, Sarah checked her schedule for next week. She needs to attend two parent meetings and finish grading student assignments. She also needs permission from the principal to change one class time. Sarah is always available to help students and parents. She knows that being responsible and giving regular feedback is very important. She feels convenient working with such supportive colleagues at her new school.

contentRef.text:
Reading Passage

Maria's First Parent Meeting

Text type: Narrative
Maria started her new job as a teacher last month. Yesterday, she had her first meeting with a parent. She felt nervous because she wanted to make a good impression.

The parent was Mrs. Johnson. She came to talk about her son, Tom. Maria smiled and offered her a chair. They sat down together in the classroom. Maria asked Mrs. Johnson how Tom was doing at home. Mrs. Johnson said Tom enjoyed school but sometimes forgot his homework. Maria listened carefully and took notes. She explained that Tom was a good student in class. He always helped other children and asked good questions. Maria suggested that Tom could use a homework diary. This would help him remember his tasks every day.

Mrs. Johnson thanked Maria for the helpful advice. She said she felt better after their talk. Maria felt relieved and happy. The conversation was easier than she expected. She learned that being friendly and listening well

are very important. Now Maria feels more confident about meeting other parents. She knows that simple, honest conversations help build trust. Good communication makes everyone feel comfortable and understood.

contentRef.text:
The School Staff Room

Text type: Description
The staff room is a special place in every school. It is where teachers meet and talk during their breaks. This room is usually quiet and comfortable. Teachers need this space to relax between lessons.

In most staff rooms, there are soft chairs and tables. There is often a coffee machine and a kettle for tea. Teachers sit together and share their experiences. They talk about their classes and students. Some teachers discuss lesson plans and new teaching ideas. Others share funny stories from their classrooms. The staff room helps teachers feel less stressed. When teachers talk to colleagues, they can get helpful advice. They can

ask questions about difficult situations. Experienced teachers often help new teachers solve problems. These informal conversations are very valuable. Teachers learn from each other every day.

The staff room is also a place for important meetings. Sometimes the head teacher makes announcements there. Teachers receive information about school events and changes. They can also check the noticeboard for messages. The staff room brings colleagues together as a team. It creates a friendly atmosphere in the school. Good relationships between teachers make the workplace more enjoyable and productive.

Message from the Principal

Text type: Notice

To: All Teaching Staff
From: Principal Sarah Chen
Date: 15th March 2024
Subject: Parent-Teacher Conference Day

Dear Colleagues,

Our next Parent-Teacher Conference Day will be on Friday, 22nd March. This is an important day for our school. We will meet parents between 9:00 AM and 4:00 PM. Each meeting will last fifteen minutes. Please check your schedule on the staff noticeboard. Your meeting times are listed there.

Please prepare for your meetings carefully. Bring your student records and grade books. Think about each student's progress and behavior. Parents want to know how their children are doing. They also want to hear about any problems or concerns. Remember to start each conversation with something positive. This helps parents feel comfortable. Then you can discuss any difficulties or areas for improvement.

If you need to speak to a parent for longer than fifteen minutes, please book another meeting. You can arrange this directly with the parent. Some parents cannot come on Friday. Please offer them an alternative time next week. Remember to be patient and friendly. Some parents feel nervous about these meetings. Your kind words and clear explanations will help them understand their child's situation better.

Thank you for your cooperation. If you have any questions, please come to my office.

Best regards, Sarah Chen

Tips for Good Professional Conversations

Text type: Informational
Good communication is essential in education. Teachers need strong conversation skills. These skills help them work well with parents and colleagues. Here are some practical tips for better professional conversations.

First, always listen carefully when someone speaks. Do not interrupt or finish their sentences. Show that you are listening by nodding and making eye contact. Ask questions to understand better. Use simple language and speak clearly. Avoid complicated words that might confuse people. When talking to parents, explain things in a friendly way. Remember that not all parents understand educational terms. Be patient and repeat information if necessary. Always stay calm, even in difficult situations. If someone is upset, listen to their concerns first. Then offer solutions or suggest ways to help.

Second, prepare before important conversations. Think about what you want to say. Write down key points if needed. This helps you stay organized and confident. Be honest but kind in your words. If there is a problem, explain it clearly. Also mention positive things to balance the conversation. End meetings with a clear plan. Make sure everyone understands the next steps. Thank people for their time and cooperation. Good conversations build strong relationships and create a positive working environment.

contentRef.text:
Two Different Communication Styles

Text type: Comparison
Mr. Brown and Ms. Lee are both experienced teachers. They work at the same school. However, they have very different communication styles with parents and colleagues.

Mr. Brown prefers formal conversations. When parents visit him, he sits behind his desk. He uses official language and speaks seriously. He focuses on facts and numbers. He shows parents test scores and written reports. Mr. Brown keeps meetings short and structured. He follows a clear plan for each conversation. Some parents appreciate his organized approach. They like receiving detailed information. However, other parents feel uncomfortable. They think Mr. Brown seems distant and unfriendly. His formal style can make people nervous.

Ms. Lee has a more relaxed communication style. She sits next to parents, not across from them. She smiles often and uses friendly language. She asks about the family and listens to parents' stories. Ms. Lee talks about students' feelings and interests, not just grades. She makes parents feel welcome and comfortable. Her meetings sometimes last longer because she enjoys chatting. Most parents prefer Ms. Lee's warm approach. They feel she truly cares about their children. However, some parents want faster meetings with clear information. Both styles can be effective, depending on the situation and the person.

contentRef.transcript:
Building Good Relationships with Colleagues
B1 — Listen and Answer

Good morning. I'm Lars and I work as a teacher trainer. Today I want to talk about working well with
colleagues. Good relationships at work make your job easier and more enjoyable. Here are some important
points to remember. First, be friendly and polite to everyone. Say hello in the morning and goodbye in the
evening. Smile and show interest in your colleagues. Ask them about their day or their weekend. Small
conversations help build strong friendships. Second, offer help when you can. If a colleague looks busy or

stressed, ask if they need support. Share your teaching materials and ideas. Working together makes
everyone's job easier.


Third, communicate clearly and regularly. If you have a problem, talk about it calmly and respectfully. Don't
wait until you feel angry or upset. Good communication prevents misunderstandings. Also, attend staff
meetings and social events when possible. This shows you are part of the team. Finally, respect differences.
Every teacher has their own teaching style and ideas. You don't have to agree with everyone, but you should
listen and be professional. Remember, when teachers work well together, students benefit the most. A
positive staff room creates a positive school environment for everyone.

contentRef.text:
Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Good communication with parents helps students do better at school. Teachers should listen carefully when parents share their concerns about their children. Working well with colleagues makes the school environment more positive for everyone. It is important to use polite and friendly language in all conversations. Regular meetings with parents and teachers help solve problems quickly and effectively.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. How do you usually start a conversation with a parent at school?

I usually greet the parent with a smile and introduce myself. Then I ask how they are doing today. I try to make them feel welcome and comfortable. This helps create a friendly atmosphere for our conversation.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. What topics do you think are important to discuss with colleagues?

I think we should discuss lesson plans and teaching methods. We can also talk about student progress and any problems. Sharing ideas with colleagues helps us improve our teaching. It is good to support each other at work.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. Why is it important to listen carefully during conversations with parents?

Parents know their children very well and have important information. When we listen carefully, we understand their concerns better. This helps us work together to support the student. Good listening builds trust between teachers and families.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. Can you describe a time when you had a difficult conversation at school?

Once I had to tell a parent their child was having problems in class. I felt nervous but stayed calm and polite. I explained the situation clearly and listened to their response. We worked together to find a solution that helped the student.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What advice would you give to someone having their first parent meeting?

I would say be friendly and professional at the same time. Prepare what you want to say before the meeting starts. Listen to the parent's questions and answer them honestly. Remember that you both want the best for the child.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Modal Verbs of Obligation, Advice and Permission

Modal verbs like must, should, can, and may express different meanings.

Must shows a strong obligation or rule.

Should gives advice or a recommendation.

Can and may show permission or ability.

FORMS

FormExample
must + base verbTeachers must attend the meeting on Friday.
should + base verbYou should talk to the parent about this problem.
can + base verbParents can visit the classroom after school.
may + base verbStudents may leave early if they feel sick.
don't have to / need not + base verbYou don't have to call every parent today.
must not + base verbWe must not share student information with others.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ You must to arrive on time.

✓ You must arrive on time.

Modal verbs are followed by the base verb without 'to'.

✗ She cans speak to the director now.

✓ She can speak to the director now.

Modal verbs do not add -s for he/she/it.

✗ I must not to forget the parent meeting.

✓ I must not forget the parent meeting.

Use the base verb after 'must not', without 'to'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe a situation when you need to talk to a parent about their child's progress. Explain what you would say and how you would make the conversation positive. (100–140 words)

  • Start by saying something good about the child before discussing any problems.
  • Use simple, clear language and avoid complicated educational terms.
  • End the conversation by suggesting ways to help the child improve together.

Key structures: Present simple for facts (e.g., 'Your child works hard'), Modal verbs for suggestions (e.g., 'We could try', 'You might want to'), Linking words: first, also, however

Model
When I talk to parents about their child's progress, I always start with something positive. First, I say what the child does well in class. For example, I might say 'Your son is very helpful to other students.' Then I explain any problems clearly. I use simple words so parents understand everything. I might say 'He sometimes finds reading difficult, but he is trying hard.' I always listen to what parents think and answer their questions. Finally, I suggest ways we can work together. I could say 'Maybe he can read for ten minutes at home each day.' This makes parents feel included and hopeful. Good conversations help children learn better at school.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Describe talking to a parent about a child's progress: start with something good, explain any problem in simple words, and suggest ways to help the child together.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: progress, concern, discuss, behavior, improve, support, feedback, recommend. Structures: Present simple for facts ('Your child works hard'); Modal verbs for suggestions ('We could try', 'You might want to'); Linking words: first, also, however.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Starts with praise for the child, states a problem in simple, kind words, and ends with a joint suggestion; includes example sentences the teacher would say. Good: Includes praise and a suggestion, but the problem is vague or there are no example sentences. Developing: Mentions only the problem or only the praise, with no suggestions for improving. Beginning: Does not describe a conversation with a parent about progress.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses present simple facts ('Your son reads well'), soft modals ('We could...', 'You might want to') and first/also/however, with words like progress, improve or support. Good: Uses present simple facts and one soft modal or linker correctly. Developing: Uses only simple 'is/has' statements; suggestions are commands such as 'You must do'. Beginning: No modals, no linkers, almost no week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Teacher's example sentences are mostly correct; slips are small, such as 'Your daughter work hard'. Good: Some third-person -s and modal errors ('We could to try') but all is clear. Developing: Frequent errors; some of the teacher's sentences would confuse a parent. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order is praise, problem, suggestion, with first/however used to link them and a positive close. Good: Mostly in order; 'however' or linkers are missing or repeated. Developing: Order is mixed, so the conversation sounds negative or confusing. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Positive, clear conversation with praise, problem and joint suggestion, with soft modals used correctly. | 75-89: All three stages present; some slips. | 60-74: Stages present but short, or suggestions are blunt. | 40-59: Only praise or only a problem; many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; a different child problem from reading difficulty (attendance, homework); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'can' instead of 'could'; no quotation marks around the teacher's words.
LENGTH: 100-140 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 80 words: cap at 60. Over 160: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any child, subject or problem; examples may be reported ('I tell the parent...') or direct speech. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own examples. Describing a conversation with a colleague instead: maximum 40.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise the kind opening or a good example sentence the learner wrote. 2) Fix: Correct one sentence, e.g. 'Your son works hard in class' instead of 'Your son work hard in class.' 3) Next step: Add one suggestion with 'We could...' for the parent and child.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Write about how you can build good relationships with your teaching colleagues. Give examples of useful conversations and why teamwork is important in education. (120–160 words)

  • Include specific examples of everyday conversations with colleagues, like sharing teaching ideas or asking for advice.
  • Explain how helping each other makes the workplace better for everyone.
  • Mention both formal meetings and informal friendly chats during breaks.

Key structures: Present simple for regular actions (e.g., 'We meet', 'I ask'), Conditional sentences (e.g., 'If we work together, we can...'), Time expressions: every day, sometimes, when, during

Model
Building good relationships with colleagues is very important in teaching. Every day, I try to have friendly conversations with other teachers. During break time, I ask them about their classes and share my own experiences. For example, I might say 'How did your science lesson go today?' or 'I have a problem with classroom management. Can you help me?' When we share ideas, everyone learns something new. Sometimes we meet after school to plan lessons together. If we work together, we can solve problems more easily. I also try to help new teachers when they feel worried. I listen to them and give them useful advice. Good teamwork makes our school a happier place. When colleagues support each other, teachers feel less stressed and students get better education. Simple conversations every day help us build strong professional friendships.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write about building good relationships with colleagues: give examples of everyday conversations (sharing ideas, asking advice, meetings and break-time chats) and explain why teamwork matters.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: colleague, discuss, meeting, support, schedule, available, communicate, appreciate. Structures: Present simple for regular actions ('We meet', 'I ask'); Conditional sentences ('If we work together, we can...'); Time expressions: every day, sometimes, when, during.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives specific examples of conversations (sharing ideas, asking advice), mentions both formal meetings and informal break-time chats, and explains how helping each other improves the workplace. Good: Gives some examples and a reason for teamwork, but formal or informal talk is missing. Developing: Says teamwork is good in general terms without examples of real conversations. Beginning: Does not discuss relationships with colleagues.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses present simple for habits, at least one correct 'If we..., we can...' sentence, and time words such as every day, sometimes, during break, with words like colleague or support. Good: Uses present simple habits and time expressions; the conditional is tried but has a small error. Developing: Uses simple present only; no conditional and few time expressions. Beginning: No target structures and little vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate; small slips such as 'we shares' or 'if we will work'. Good: Some errors in third-person -s and if-sentence tense, but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors; several sentences are difficult to follow. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Moves from daily chats to meetings to the reason teamwork matters, using time words as links. Good: Examples and reasons are present but the order is slightly loose. Developing: Ideas repeat or jump around without links. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Specific examples of formal and informal talk plus a clear reason for teamwork, with the conditional used correctly. | 75-89: Good examples; one area (formal/informal or reason) light; minor errors. | 60-74: Mainly general statements with few examples. | 40-59: Little content or many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different examples from the model (lesson planning together, lending materials); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; 'coworker' for 'colleague'; dialogue lines without quotation marks.
LENGTH: 120-160 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 95 words: cap at 60. Over 185: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic conversations in the learner's own school; 'When we..., we...' is acceptable in place of 'If'. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own examples. Writing about talking to parents only: maximum 40.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a real conversation example the learner gave. 2) Fix: Correct one if-sentence, e.g. 'If we work together, we can solve problems' instead of 'If we will work together, we can to solve problem.' 3) Next step: Add one example of a formal meeting with 'during' or 'when'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Imagine a parent is upset because their child is having problems at school. Describe how you would handle this difficult conversation and what language you would use to calm the situation. (140–180 words)

  • Show empathy by recognizing the parent's feelings first before explaining anything.
  • Stay calm and use polite, respectful language even if the parent is angry.
  • Focus on finding solutions together rather than blaming anyone for the problem.

Key structures: Phrases showing understanding (e.g., 'I understand that you feel...', 'I can see why you are worried'), Past simple to describe what happened, Future forms for solutions (e.g., 'We will', 'I'm going to')

Model
When a parent is upset, I know the conversation can be difficult. However, I always stay calm and polite. First, I listen carefully to everything the parent wants to say. I don't interrupt them or argue. I use phrases like 'I understand that you feel worried' or 'I can see why this is upsetting for you.' This shows that I care about their feelings. Then I explain what happened at school using simple, clear language. I might say 'Yesterday, your daughter had an argument with another student during lunch time.' I always focus on facts, not opinions. After that, I ask the parent for their ideas. I say 'What do you think we should do?' This makes them feel involved. Together, we make a plan to help the child. I might suggest 'We will check with her every day to see how she feels.' Before the parent leaves, I thank them for coming to talk to me. I say 'Please contact me anytime if you have more concerns.' Good communication helps solve problems and builds trust with families.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Describe how you would handle a conversation with an upset parent: show empathy first, stay calm and polite, explain what happened simply, and find solutions together.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: concern, issue, discuss, listen, support, communicate, responsible, improve. Structures: Understanding phrases ('I understand that you feel...', 'I can see why you are worried'); Past simple to say what happened; Future forms for solutions ('We will...', 'I'm going to...').
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Shows empathy first with phrases the teacher would say, stays polite, explains what happened using facts, and proposes solutions made together, without blaming anyone. Good: Shows empathy and a solution, but the explanation of what happened is thin or the calm, polite approach is not clear. Developing: Describes the problem or the parent's anger but offers few calming phrases or no solution. Beginning: Does not describe handling an upset parent.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses understanding phrases correctly, past simple to report events ('Your son had an argument'), and 'We will / I'm going to' for solutions. Good: Uses an understanding phrase and either past simple or a future form correctly. Developing: Uses only present tense; understanding phrases are missing or wrong. Beginning: No target structures.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate, including past forms; slips are small, such as 'He have' for 'He had'. Good: Some errors with past tense ('he fight') or 'going to', but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors; the parent's problem is hard to understand. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Order is listen, empathise, explain, plan together, thank, with linking words and a calm tone throughout. Good: Mostly in order; tone is polite but the sequence is a little jumbled. Developing: Steps are unclear or the tone becomes blaming. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Empathy first, polite tone, clear facts in past simple and shared solutions with 'will / going to'. | 75-89: All stages present; a few tense slips. | 60-74: Empathy or solutions thin, structures partly correct. | 40-59: Little of the conversation described; many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; a different problem from the argument at lunch time (a lost book, marks, bullying); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; irregular past forms with a small slip if the meaning is clear; no quotation marks.
LENGTH: 140-180 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 110 words: cap at 60. Over 200: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic school problem and any calm, polite solution; 'I will' and 'I'm going to' are both fine. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own words. A conversation where the teacher argues or blames the parent: maximum 50 with a gentle note.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a calming phrase the learner wrote in their own words. 2) Fix: Correct one tense, e.g. 'Yesterday your son had an argument' instead of 'Yesterday your son have argument.' 3) Next step: Add a sentence with 'We will...' to say what happens next.

questions.question: Q4. You ___ bring your own lunch to the staff meeting tomorrow if you want to.
questions.explanation: → The phrase 'if you want to' shows this is a choice or permission.

questions.question: Q5. We have a staff ___ every Monday morning at nine.
questions.explanation: → A 'meeting' is when people come to talk.

questions.question: Q2. You ___ speak to the child's mother before making any big decisions about his education. This is good advice, not a rule.
questions.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

questions.explanation: → We 'recommend' when we say that something is good to do.

questions.question: Q13. I am ___ after school if you want to talk.

questions.question: Q7. You ___ try to contact the father again tomorrow if the mother cannot come to school. It is a good idea, not a rule.
questions.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

questions.question: appreciate — criticize
questions.explanation: → 'appreciate' and 'criticize' have opposite meanings: appreciate is to say thanks, criticize is to find fault, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: Q8. Students ___ use their mobile phones during class time according to our school policy. It is a rule.
questions.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'must not'.

questions.question: schedule — butterfly
questions.explanation: → 'schedule' and 'butterfly' are about very different things, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: progress — progressive
questions.explanation: → 'progress' and 'progressive' share the root 'progress', so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q12. Teachers ___ share confidential student information with people outside the school. It is against the rules.
questions.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'must not'.

questions.question: Q9. We ___ arrange a meeting with both parents together if they prefer to come separately.
questions.explanation: → The parents' preference shows that a joint meeting is not necessary.

questions.question: Q21. Teachers ___ keep detailed records of every conversation with parents in case questions arise later. It is recommended, not required.
questions.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

questions.question: assignment — ocean
questions.explanation: → 'assignment' and 'ocean' are about very different things, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: improve — worsen
questions.explanation: → 'improve' and 'worsen' have opposite meanings: improve is to get better, worsen is to get worse, so they are antonyms.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about how to have a good conversation with a colleague at work. Explain what you should do and why it is important. (80–110 words)

  • Mention being polite and respectful
  • Talk about listening to your colleague's ideas
  • Explain why good communication helps at work
Model
Having a good conversation with a colleague is very important at work. First, you should always be polite and respectful. Listen carefully when your colleague speaks. Do not interrupt them. Ask questions if you do not understand something. Share your own ideas in a clear way. Good communication helps you work better together. It also makes the workplace more friendly. When colleagues talk well together, they can solve problems easily. This helps students learn better too. Remember that teamwork is very important in education. Always try to support your colleagues at work.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a short paragraph on how to have a good conversation with a colleague: be polite and respectful, listen to their ideas, and explain why good communication helps at work.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: colleague, communicate, discuss, support, appreciate, available, feedback, responsible. Structures: You should / Do not... (advice); Present simple for general truths; Linking words: first, also, because.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:

- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses advice forms ('You should listen', 'Do not interrupt') and words like colleague, communicate or support correctly, with because/also to link.

contentRef.text:
CHAPTER V · WEEK 30

Case Studies: Schools in Cambodia (Simple English)

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify key challenges facing Cambodian schools from a recorded interview with a teacher. L2 Understand
  • Use present simple and basic educational vocabulary to describe school facilities and conditions. L3 Apply
  • Compare educational resources between Cambodian schools and schools in your own country. L3 Apply
  • Summarise main problems and solutions presented in a case study about rural Cambodian education. L3 Apply
  • Write a short paragraph explaining one challenge that Cambodian students face at school. L3 Apply
  • Evaluate how different communities can support education in schools with limited resources. L4 Analyze · HOTS

questions.question: Q6. One ___ is the lack of books in schools.
questions.explanation: → A 'challenge' is a problem that is hard to solve.

questions.question: Q2. Over 200 students ___ this school since it started.
questions.explanation: → 'Since it started' shows a period from the past until now, so present perfect is needed.

questions.question: Q5. The head teacher ___ to improve attendance in 2021.
questions.explanation: → A specific year in the past takes past simple.

questions.question: literacy — literate
questions.explanation: → 'literacy' and 'literate' share the root 'liter-', about reading and writing, so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q14. The school canteen ___ free lunch to poor students since January.
questions.explanation: → 'Since January' shows a period from January until now, so present perfect is needed.

questions.question: Q22. Teachers ___ more training courses in the last two years.
questions.explanation: → 'In the last two years' is a period continuing to the present, requiring present perfect.

questions.question: remote — nearby
questions.explanation: → 'remote' and 'nearby' have opposite meanings: remote is far away, nearby is close, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: community — communal
questions.explanation: → 'community' and 'communal' share the root 'commun-', about a group of people, so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q1. ___ is very important for children in Cambodia.
questions.explanation: → 'Education' means learning at school.

questions.question: Q15. The ___ helps build new schools for children.
questions.explanation: → A 'community' is people living together in an area.

contentRef.text:
Lesson Overview

KEY CONCEPTS

  • 1. Educational challenges in developing countries

Problems that make it hard for children to go to school or learn well. These can include lack of buildings, teachers, or money.

Example:Many rural schools face challenges such as teacher shortages and limited classroom space.
Connection:You will read about these challenges in education textbooks and discuss them in teacher training courses.
  • 2. School facilities and resources

The buildings, equipment, and materials that schools need for teaching and learning. Examples are classrooms, books, desks, and computers.

Example:This primary school has good facilities, including a library and three new classrooms.
Connection:You describe school facilities when you write reports or talk about school conditions in meetings.
  • 3. Access to education

The opportunity for all children to attend school and receive teaching. Poor access means some children cannot go to school easily.

Example:Students in remote areas often have limited access to secondary education.
Connection:This phrase appears in education policy documents and when discussing equal opportunities in schools.
  • 4. Community support for schools

Help that local people give to schools, such as money, time, or materials. Communities can work together to improve education.

Example:The community donated books and helped build a new classroom for the primary school.
Connection:You will hear this when discussing school improvement projects and parent-teacher meetings.

Say It in English

Listen to the phrases and examples, then follow along in the table.

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play all phrases and example sentences:

Symbol or notation How to say it Example sentence
ages 6–12
ages six to twelve
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Primary school is for children ages six to twelve.
🔉 Spoken Example:
50% dropout rate
fifty percent dropout rate
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The school has a fifty percent dropout rate this year.
🔉 Spoken Example:
2:1 ratio
two to one ratio
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The textbook ratio is two to one, so students share books.
🔉 Spoken Example:
K–12
kindergarten to grade twelve
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The programme covers kindergarten to grade twelve education.
🔉 Spoken Example:
20 km away
twenty kilometres away
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
The nearest secondary school is twenty kilometres away.
🔉 Spoken Example:
3 out of 5 schools
three out of five schools
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Three out of five schools in the district need repairs.
🔉 Spoken Example:
2010–2015
from two thousand ten to two thousand fifteen
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
Enrolment increased from two thousand ten to two thousand fifteen.
🔉 Spoken Example:
Grade 1–6
grade one to six
🔊 Phrase Pronunciation:
This building has classrooms for grade one to six.
🔉 Spoken Example:

Vocabulary

  1. education — The process of teaching and learning in schools.
  2. rural — Relating to the countryside, not the city.
  3. primary school — A school for young children, usually ages six to twelve.
  4. facility — A building or equipment that provides a service.
  5. attend — To go to or be present at a place regularly.
  6. challenge — A difficult problem that needs to be solved.
  7. classroom — A room where students have lessons.
  8. improve — To make something better than before.
  9. district — An area or region within a country or province.
  10. resource — Something useful like money, materials, or equipment.
  11. enroll — To officially join or register at a school.
  12. dropout — A student who leaves school before finishing.
  13. funding — Money provided for a particular purpose.
  14. access — The ability or right to use or reach something.
  15. community — A group of people living in the same area.
  16. secondary — Relating to education after primary school.
  17. shortage — A situation when there is not enough of something.
  18. remote — Far away from cities or towns.
  19. literacy — The ability to read and write.
  20. donate — To give something to help others without payment.

How to Learn This Chapter

Vocabulary
Learn the twenty education words about schools, challenges, and community support.
Reading
Read a case study about rural Cambodian schools and find the main problems and solutions.
Listening
Listen to a teacher interview and identify the key challenges facing Cambodian schools.
Speaking
Compare educational resources between Cambodian schools and schools in your country.
Grammar
Study past simple and present perfect to describe school situations and changes over time.
Writing
Write a short paragraph explaining one challenge that Cambodian students face at school.
Lesson Test
The test checks your vocabulary, grammar, and understanding of school challenges; aim for seventy percent.

MOTIVATIONAL FACT

Cambodia has made great progress in education since 2000. Primary school enrolment has improved from sixty percent to nearly one hundred percent, showing that communities and government can work together successfully.

REFERENCES

Teaching English in Context: Cambodia — British Council (2018). This book explains education vocabulary with examples from real Cambodian schools. Education for All Global Monitoring Report — UNESCO (2015). It provides case studies and statistics about education challenges in developing countries.

▶ Education in Cambodia: Challenges and Solutions — UNICEF ▶ Teaching English for Education Studies — British Council LearnEnglish

Vocabulary

VOCABULARY

🎧 Listen & Practice: Play the full vocabulary list with definitions and example sentences:

Phonetic: ej-oo-KAY-shun

Meaning: the process of teaching and learning in schools

Khmer: ការអប់រំ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Phonetic: ROOR-ul

Meaning: relating to the countryside, not the city

Phonetic: fuh-SIL-i-tee

Meaning: a building or equipment that provides a service

Khmer: អគារ ឬបរិក្ខារបម្រើការសិក្សា

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The school has a new facility for science classes.

Phonetic: uh-TEND

Meaning: to go to or be present at a place regularly

Khmer: ចូលរៀន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: All students must attend school every day.

Phonetic: CHAL-enj

Meaning: a difficult problem that needs to be solved

Khmer: បញ្ហាប្រឈម

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: One challenge is the lack of books in schools.

classroom noun

Phonetic: KLAS-room

Meaning: a room where students have lessons

Khmer: ថ្នាក់រៀន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

improve verb

Phonetic: im-PROOV

Meaning: to make something better than before

Khmer: កែលម្អ

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Phonetic: DIS-trikt

Meaning: an area or region within a country or province

Khmer: ស្រុក

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: There are five schools in our district.

Phonetic: REE-sors

Meaning: something useful like money, materials, or equipment

Khmer: ធនធាន

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example
