Phonetic: en-ROHL

Meaning: to officially join or register at a school

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Phonetic: FUN-ding

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

access noun

Phonetic: AK-ses

Meaning: the ability or right to use or reach something

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: All children should have access to quality education.

community noun

Phonetic: kuh-MYOO-ni-tee

Meaning: a group of people living in the same area

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: The community helps build new schools for children.

Phonetic: SEK-un-der-ee

Meaning: relating to education after primary school

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: She finished secondary school and went to university.

shortage noun

Phonetic: SHOR-tij

Meaning: a situation when there is not enough of something

Khmer: កង្វះខាត

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

Example: There is a shortage of trained teachers in Cambodia.

remote adjective

Phonetic: ree-MOHT

Meaning: far away from cities or towns

Khmer: ដាច់ស្រយាល

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

🔊 Word🔉 Meaning🔉 Example

donate verb

Phonetic: DOH-nayt

Meaning: to give something to help others without payment

MINI STORY

Bopha lives in a rural district in Cambodia. She attends a small primary school in her community. Every morning, she walks two kilometers to reach her classroom. The school is in a remote area, far from the city.

Her school faces many challenges. There is a shortage of teachers and resources. The facility is old and needs repair. However, the local community works hard to improve the situation. Parents help enroll new students every year. International organizations donate books and provide funding for better education.

Bopha loves learning and wants to finish secondary school. She knows that literacy is important for her future. Some students become dropouts because they need to work, but Bopha dreams of going to university. Access to quality education gives her hope for a better life.

Sopheap's First Day as a Teacher

Text type: Narrative
Sopheap woke up early on Monday morning. She felt excited and nervous at the same time. Today was her first day as a teacher at a small school in Siem Reap. She put on her best dress and ate breakfast quickly. Then she rode her bicycle to the school. The road was dusty and bumpy. When she arrived, thirty children were waiting outside the classroom. They all smiled at her. Some children had no shoes. Others carried old books from their older brothers and sisters.

The classroom was small and hot. There were only two windows and no fan. Sopheap wrote her name on the old blackboard. The chalk was very short and difficult to hold. She asked the children to introduce themselves. Most children spoke quietly because they felt shy. One girl named Chenda said she wanted to be a doctor. A boy named Sovann said he liked reading books. Sopheap felt happy when she heard their dreams.

After the first lesson, Sopheap understood that teaching would be hard work. The school had very few books and pencils. Some children walked two hours to get to school. But all the children wanted to learn. Sopheap decided she would do her best to help them. She knew education could change their lives. That evening, she planned her lessons for the next day.

Inside a Village School in Kampong Cham

Text type: Description
The school in Kampong Cham province is located near rice fields. It is a simple building with four classrooms. The walls are painted light blue, but the paint is old and falling off in some places. The roof is made of metal sheets. During the rainy season, the rain makes a very loud noise on the roof. Sometimes teachers must stop talking because students cannot hear them.

Each classroom has about forty wooden desks. The desks are quite old and some have broken legs. Students usually share desks because there are not enough for everyone. At the front of each room, there is a blackboard and a teacher's desk. The blackboard is green but it looks almost white because teachers have used it for many years. There are no computers or projectors in the school. The school has a small library with about two hundred books. Many books are donations from organizations in other countries.

Outside the school, there is a large field where children play during break time. They play games like football and jump rope. There is a water pump where students wash their hands before lunch. The school has four toilets but they are very basic. Despite these simple conditions, the school is always clean. Teachers and students work together to keep it tidy. Everyone is proud of their school.

Letter from the Education Office

Text type: Notice

To: Mr. Veasna Kim, School Principal Rat Borey Primary School, Battambang Province
From: Provincial Education Office
Date: 15th March 2024
Subject: New Teaching Materials and Teacher Training

Dear Mr. Kim,

We are writing to inform you about two important programs for your school. First, your school will receive new teaching materials next month. These materials include textbooks for mathematics and science, pencils, notebooks, and posters for classrooms. A delivery truck will arrive on April 12th. Please make sure someone is available to receive the materials. You will need to sign a form to confirm delivery. After that, please send us photographs showing how you store the materials.

Second, we are organizing a training workshop for teachers. The workshop will take place on April 20th and 21st at Battambang Teacher Training Center. All teachers from your school are invited to attend. The training will focus on new teaching methods for reading and writing. Experienced trainers from Phnom Penh will lead the sessions. Teachers will learn how to make lessons more interesting for students. They will also receive certificates at the end.

Please confirm by March 25th how many teachers from your school will attend the workshop. We need this information to prepare enough training materials. If you have any questions, please contact our office. We look forward to working with your school to improve education quality.

Best regards, Mrs. Channary Sok Provincial Education Coordinator

Education Challenges in Rural Cambodia

Text type: Informational

Many schools in rural Cambodia face difficult challenges. One major problem is the lack of trained teachers. Some schools cannot find enough teachers, especially for subjects like English and science. This means students sometimes have only three or four lessons per day instead of six. Another challenge is that many teachers have not received proper training. They often use old teaching methods that do not help students learn effectively.

Poor infrastructure is another serious issue. Many school buildings are in bad condition. Some schools have no electricity, so students cannot study after dark. During the rainy season, dirt roads become muddy and dangerous. This makes it hard for students and teachers to reach school. Some children must walk several kilometers each day. When roads are very bad, attendance drops significantly. Schools also lack basic equipment like books, desks, and clean water. Some students must bring their own chairs from home.

Despite these problems, there is hope for improvement. International organizations are working with the Cambodian government to build new schools. They are also training more teachers and providing better materials. Community members are helping too. Parents sometimes volunteer to repair classrooms or paint walls. Students remain motivated because they understand that education offers opportunities. With continued support and investment, rural schools can provide better learning environments for all Cambodian children.

Two Different Schools: City vs. Village

Text type: Comparison
Phnom Penh International School is located in Cambodia's capital city. It has modern buildings with air conditioning in every classroom. The school has science laboratories, a computer room with fifty computers, and a large library. Students wear uniforms and arrive by car or school bus. Most classes have about twenty- five students. Teachers use projectors and interactive whiteboards. The school offers many subjects including music, art, and foreign languages. Students pay fees to attend this private school.

In contrast, Prey Veng Village School is in a rural area about one hundred kilometers from the city. The school has only three classrooms in a simple wooden building. There is no electricity or running water. Students sit on old benches and share textbooks. Most children walk to school, and some arrive late because they help their families with farming first. Classes are large, with up to fifty students in one room. Teachers write lessons on a blackboard with chalk. The school offers basic subjects like Khmer, mathematics, and social studies. Education is free but families still struggle to buy notebooks and pencils.

Both schools face challenges but they are very different. The city school needs to keep up with expensive technology. The village school needs basic resources like books and desks. However, students at both schools work hard and have big dreams for their futures.

Another challenge is teacher shortage. Rural schools need more qualified teachers. Young teachers often

Speaking Practice

READ ALOUD

🗣️ Listen and Repeat: Listen to the teacher's sentence stress, then read the sentences aloud:

Many schools in Cambodia face challenges like limited resources and large class sizes. Some rural schools do not have enough textbooks or chairs for every student. Teachers in Cambodia often work hard with very low salaries and few materials.

International organizations help build new classrooms and provide books to Cambodian schools. Despite difficulties, many Cambodian students are eager to learn and improve their lives.

QUESTIONS & MODEL ANSWERS

🎧 Listen to all questions and model answers:

Q1. What are some common problems that schools in Cambodia face today?

Schools in Cambodia often have large classes with too many students. They also lack enough books and teaching materials. Many rural schools don't have proper buildings or furniture. These problems make it difficult for students to learn well.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q2. Why do you think some children in rural Cambodia cannot attend school regularly?

Many families in rural areas are very poor and need children to work. Some villages are far from the nearest school, so travel is difficult. Parents sometimes cannot afford school supplies or uniforms. These reasons prevent children from attending classes every day.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q3. How do international organizations help improve education in Cambodia?

International groups build new school buildings and repair old ones. They provide textbooks, computers, and other learning materials to schools. Some organizations also train teachers to improve their teaching methods. This support helps create better learning environments for students.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q4. What challenges do teachers in Cambodian schools experience in their work?

Teachers often receive very low pay, which makes life hard for them. They have to teach large classes with limited materials and resources. Many teachers need extra training but cannot access professional development. Despite these challenges, they continue working to help their students.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Q5. What positive changes have you learned about in Cambodian education recently?

More children are now able to attend primary school than before. The government and charities have built many new classrooms in rural areas. Teacher training programs are helping improve the quality of education. These changes show that Cambodia's education system is slowly getting better.

▶ Listen: question and answer

Grammar Practice

Past Simple vs Present Perfect

Use past simple for finished actions at a specific time.

Use present perfect when the time is not stated or when past actions connect to now.

FORMS

FormExample
Past simple: subject + verb + -ed / irregular formThe school opened in 2015.
Present perfect: subject + have/has + past participleMany teachers have worked here for years.
Past simple question: Did + subject + base verb?Did the students pass their exams last year?
Present perfect question: Have/Has + subject + past participle?Has the government improved school buildings recently?
Past simple negative: subject + did not + base verbThey did not receive new books in 2020.
Present perfect negative: subject + have/has not + past participleThe village has not built a new classroom yet.

COMMON MISTAKES

✗ I have seen that school last week.

✓ I saw that school last week.

Use past simple with specific past time words like 'last week', 'yesterday', 'in 2020'.

✗ Many children learned English since 2018.

✓ Many children have learned English since 2018.

Use present perfect with 'since' or 'for' to show actions continuing from past to now.

✗ The school has opened in 2015.

✓ The school opened in 2015.

Use past simple when you say the exact year or date something happened.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 1 of 3

Describe the typical classroom environment in a rural Cambodian school. Write for education students who want to understand daily school conditions. (100–140 words)

  • Describe the physical classroom space and furniture
  • Mention the number of students and available resources
  • Explain what students and teachers use during lessons

Key structures: Present simple for facts (e.g., 'The classroom has...'), There is/are for describing what exists

Model
A typical rural school classroom in Cambodia is quite simple. The classroom usually has concrete walls and a tin roof. There are about forty to fifty students in one class. The students sit on wooden benches at old desks. Many classrooms do not have enough textbooks for every student. The teacher has one blackboard at the front of the room. Students share books with their classmates during lessons. The classroom often has no electricity or fans. Windows provide light and air during the day. Some schools have posters on the walls for learning. However, many rural classrooms need more supplies and better furniture. Teachers work hard with limited resources to help their students learn every day.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Describe a typical rural Cambodian classroom for education students: the space and furniture, number of students and resources, and what students and teachers use in lessons.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: classroom, rural, resource, shortage, primary school, access, community, improve. Structures: Present simple for facts ('The classroom has...'); There is / There are for describing what exists.
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Describes the room and furniture (walls, roof, benches, desks), says roughly how many students and what resources exist, and mentions what is used in lessons such as a blackboard or shared textbooks. Good: Describes the room and one other area, but either resources or the number of students is missing. Developing: Gives a few general statements like 'the classroom is small' without specific details of furniture or resources. Beginning: Does not describe a classroom, or describes a city school or a different topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses 'There is/are' and 'The classroom has' correctly several times, with words like rural, resources, shortage or primary school. Good: Uses 'There are' and present simple facts correctly; two or three week words appear. Developing: Uses 'There is/are' once or with errors ('There have many students'); few week words. Beginning: No target structures and almost no vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate; small slips such as 'There is forty students'. Good: Some errors in is/are agreement and plurals ('desk', 'benches'), but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors; several descriptions are unclear. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Moves logically from the building to students to resources, with a short closing sentence. Good: Facts are clear but not in a tidy order. Developing: Facts jump around with repeats. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear, factual picture of the classroom with furniture, numbers and resources, using there is/are accurately. | 75-89: Good description; one area light; small errors. | 60-74: General description with few details. | 40-59: Very few facts; many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different details from the model (no fans, mud floors, shared textbooks); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; approximate student numbers; writing about the learner's own school.
LENGTH: 100-140 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 80 words: cap at 60. Over 160: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic rural classroom details based on the learner's knowledge; statements may include some positives. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own details. Describing a non-school place: maximum 35.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a specific detail the learner added, such as furniture or class size. 2) Fix: Correct one sentence, e.g. 'There are forty students in the class' instead of 'There is forty student in class.' 3) Next step: Add one sentence about teaching materials with 'The teacher uses...'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 2 of 3

Explain the daily schedule and routine at a Cambodian primary school. Write for teacher trainees preparing to work in similar environments. (120–160 words)

  • Include specific times when school starts and finishes
  • Describe the different subjects taught during the day
  • Mention breaks and any special activities

Key structures: Time expressions (e.g., 'in the morning', 'at 7:30', 'after lunch'), Sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally)

Model
The school day at a Cambodian primary school starts early in the morning. Students arrive at school around 7:00 or 7:30 in the morning. First, all students gather for a morning assembly in the schoolyard. They sing the national anthem and listen to announcements. Then classes begin at 8:00. In the morning, teachers focus on important subjects like Khmer language and mathematics. Students have a short break at 10:00 for snacks and play. After the break, they study other subjects such as science or social studies. The morning session finishes at 11:30. Some schools have afternoon classes that start again at 2:00. These afternoon sessions include subjects like physical education and arts. The school day ends at 4:30 or 5:00. Students then go home to help their families or do homework.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Explain the daily schedule at a Cambodian primary school for teacher trainees: start and finish times, subjects taught, and breaks or special activities.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: primary school, attend, enroll, education, community, classroom, access, literacy. Structures: Time expressions ('in the morning', 'at 7:30', 'after lunch'); Sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally).
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Gives specific start and finish times, names several subjects in the day, and mentions breaks and a special activity such as morning assembly. Good: Gives times and subjects but breaks or special activities are missing. Developing: Mentions only that school starts and ends, or lists subjects with no times. Beginning: Does not describe a school day.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses exact times ('at 8:00') and phrases like 'in the morning' and 'after lunch' correctly, with first/then/after that/finally to order the day. Good: Uses several time expressions and some sequencing words, with a few small errors. Developing: Uses one or two time words; no ordering words. Beginning: No time expressions or sequencing.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate present simple; small slips such as 'school start' or 'on 7:00'. Good: Some errors with prepositions of time (in/at/on) and third-person -s, but the schedule is clear. Developing: Frequent errors; times and subjects are sometimes unclear. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Follows the day from arrival to home time in a clear time order. Good: Most of the day is in order; one part is out of place. Developing: Order is mixed, so the day is hard to follow. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear school day with times, subjects, breaks, accurate time words and good sequencing. | 75-89: Complete day; minor time-preposition slips. | 60-74: Times and subjects present; breaks or order weak. | 40-59: Little detail; many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different times from the model (a school with morning-only classes); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; using 'o'clock' or 24-hour style times; writing about the learner's own school.
LENGTH: 120-160 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 95 words: cap at 60. Over 185: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic timetable (one-shift or two-shift); subjects may differ. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own details. If the learner only writes the stray 'Discuss the main challenges...' prompt or answers it instead: maximum 40.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear time or subject the learner included. 2) Fix: Correct one time phrase, e.g. 'Classes begin at 8:00 in the morning' instead of 'Class begin on 8:00 morning.' 3) Next step: Add one sentence for the end of the day with 'finally'.

contentRef.text:
WRITING TASKS

Task 3 of 3

Describe the main problems in Cambodian schools and the solutions that are helping. Write for international education researchers studying developing countries. (140–180 words)

  • Identify two or three major problems clearly
  • Explain why these problems affect student learning
  • Describe solutions or programs that are helping

Key structures: Because/so for showing cause and effect, Present perfect for recent changes (e.g., 'Organizations have provided...')

Model
Cambodian schools face several important challenges that affect the quality of education. The first major problem is the lack of qualified teachers, especially in rural areas. Many teachers have not received proper training, so they struggle to use effective teaching methods. Another challenge is poverty in families. Many children must work to help their parents earn money. Because of this, students miss classes or drop out of school completely. Poor infrastructure is also a serious issue. Many school buildings are old and need repairs. Some schools do not have clean water or proper toilets. However, several solutions are being tried across the country. The government has started teacher training programs to improve teaching skills. International NGOs have provided new textbooks and learning materials to schools. Some organizations have built libraries and computer rooms in rural schools. Communities are also working together to keep children in school. They organize scholarship programs for poor families. These efforts are slowly making positive changes, but more support is still needed for Cambodian education.

aiGrading.instructions:
Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: For international education researchers, identify two or three major problems in Cambodian schools, explain how they affect learning, and describe the solutions or programmes that are helping.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: challenge, shortage, funding, dropout, resource, access, literacy, donate. Structures: Because / so for cause and effect; Present perfect for recent changes ('Organizations have provided...').
STEP 1: Check the off-task rule first. STEP 2: choose a level for each criterion (excellent=95%, good=80%, developing=60%, beginning=35% of that criterion's weight), add the four, and round to a whole number. If the total does not match the score bands, follow the bands.
CRITERIA:
- Task completion & content (35 points). Excellent: Names two or three clear problems (such as teacher shortage, poverty and dropout, poor buildings), explains how each affects learning, and describes solutions or programmes now helping. Good: Names two problems and some solutions, but the effect on learning is explained for only one. Developing: Lists problems with little explanation, or gives no solutions. Beginning: Does not discuss problems in schools, or is off-topic.
- Use of week's vocabulary & structures (30 points). Excellent: Uses because/so correctly for cause and effect and at least two present perfect sentences ('The government has built...'), with words like shortage, funding, dropout or resource. Good: Uses because/so and one correct present perfect; a few week words appear. Developing: Uses 'because' with errors; no present perfect; basic vocabulary. Beginning: No cause-effect or present perfect, almost no week vocabulary.
- Grammar & accuracy (at A2 level) (20 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate; present perfect has small slips such as 'has build' or 'have provide'. Good: Some errors with present perfect and plurals, but meaning is clear. Developing: Frequent errors; cause and effect sentences are unclear. Beginning: Almost every sentence is broken.
- Clarity & organisation (15 points). Excellent: Problems first, then effects, then solutions, written in a formal but simple tone for researchers. Good: Content is in order but linking words are few. Developing: Problems and solutions are mixed up. Beginning: No order.
SCORE BANDS: 90-100: Clear problems, effects on learning and solutions, with because/so and present perfect used accurately. | 75-89: All three parts present; small errors. | 60-74: Problems clear; effects or solutions thin. | 40-59: One part only; many errors. | 0-39: Off-task, copied or too little.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different problems from the model (distance to school, no toilets, language barriers); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; simple past instead of present perfect where meaning is the same; informal style if the ideas are clear.
LENGTH: 140-180 words, tolerance of about 10 words. Under 110 words: cap at 60. Over 200: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any realistic problems and programmes the learner knows; accept general statements about NGOs, government or communities. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own ideas. Because the task has no prompt, accept any writing that follows the three bullets; text on a different subject: maximum 35.
FEEDBACK (write in simple English, at most 3 short sentences, kind and specific): 1) Strength: Praise a clear problem or solution the learner named. 2) Fix: Correct one sentence, e.g. 'The government has started training programmes' instead of 'The government have start training programme.' 3) Next step: Add one 'because' sentence to explain how a problem affects students.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about how schools in Cambodia are improving. Describe the changes and who is helping. Use simple, clear sentences. (80–110 words)

  • Mention specific improvements like new buildings or teacher training
  • Say who is helping (government, NGOs, communities)
  • Explain how these changes help students learn better
Model
Schools in Cambodia are improving in many ways. The government is building new classrooms in rural areas. International NGOs provide money for books and computers. Teachers now attend training programs to learn better teaching methods. Many schools received donations of desks and textbooks. School lunch programs help hungry children concentrate better. Local communities help by painting classrooms and repairing buildings. Because of these changes, more students attend school regularly. Girls are staying in school longer than before. Student test scores are improving every year. Although challenges still exist, education in Cambodia is getting better.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a short paragraph on how schools in Cambodia are improving: name the changes, say who is helping (government, NGOs, communities), and explain how this helps students learn.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: improve, donate, funding, community, resource, access, education, attend. Structures: Present simple/continuous for current changes; Because / so for results.
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names specific improvements (new classrooms, teacher training, books), says who helps, and explains how these changes help students.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses improve, donate, funding or community correctly, with 'because' or 'so' to show results.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate; small slips only, such as 'NGO build' for 'NGOs build'.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: Changes first, then helpers, then results, in short clear sentences as the task asks.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different improvements from the model (school gardens, scholarships, water tanks); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; simple past or present perfect used for changes; 'NGOs' written in different forms.
LENGTH: 80-110 words, tolerance of about 8 words. Under 60 words: cap at 60. Over 130: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real or likely improvements; examples from the learner's own district are welcome. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to use own words. Writing only about problems: maximum 40.

CHAPTER V · WEEK 31

Final Assessment (Foundation Education English — A2 to B1)

Start by exploring the illustration, then move through this week's learning activities.

Lesson Learning Outcomes

  • Identify main ideas and supporting details in spoken educational contexts during assessment tasks. L2 Understand
  • Apply education-related vocabulary and present perfect tense accurately in assessment responses. L3 Apply
  • Demonstrate fluency discussing teaching methods and learning experiences in timed speaking tasks. L3 Apply
  • Analyse authentic educational texts to answer comprehension questions within time constraints. L3 Apply
  • Compose coherent paragraphs describing classroom practices using appropriate connectors and educational terminology. L3 Apply
  • Evaluate own language progress from A2 to B1 through reflective self-assessment. L4 Analyze · HOTS

Week 31 · Final Assessment

Lesson Test

VOCABULARYGRAMMARPISA READING

PISA READING

7 texts

Text 1continuous

My Journey Through Foundation English

When I started my Foundation English course last year, I felt nervous about learning a new language. My teacher explained that we would move from A2 level to B1 level slowly. She told us that practice and participation were very important for success.

During the course, we studied vocabulary, grammar and reading skills every week. We also wrote paragraphs and practiced speaking in small groups. The teacher gave us feedback on our work regularly. This helped us understand our mistakes and improve quickly.

Now I feel more confident using English in my education studies. I can read simple academic texts and write clear sentences. The final assessment will test everything we learned this year. I know I must revise all my notes and practice more before the exam. I believe that hard work will help me pass and continue my studies successfully.

contentRef.text:
WRITING — PARAGRAPH

Write a short paragraph about how you prepared for your final assessment. Describe what you studied and how you organized your time. (80–110 words)

  • Mention the different skills you revised (vocabulary, grammar, reading, writing)
  • Explain how you organized your study time
  • Describe one or two study methods you used
Model
I prepared carefully for my final assessment by revising all the important skills. First, I reviewed my vocabulary notebooks and practiced using new words in sentences. Then I completed grammar exercises to remember the rules we studied. I also read many short texts to improve my reading speed and understanding. Every day, I studied for two hours after class. I made a study plan and followed it strictly. I worked with a study partner twice a week, and we tested each other on grammar and vocabulary. Finally, I wrote practice paragraphs to improve my writing. This preparation helped me feel more confident about the exam.

How your paragraph is marked

Your paragraph is marked out of 100 points. Read the task carefully and use your own ideas.

CriterionPoints
Task completion and content
Answer the question and include the requested details.		35
Vocabulary and sentence structures
Use suitable vocabulary and sentence patterns from the lesson.		25
Grammar and accuracy
Use simple grammar and word order that make your meaning clear.		25
Clarity and organisation
Put your ideas in a clear, logical order.		15
Total100

Focus on answering the question clearly. Small spelling slips and understandable phrasing are treated fairly for your English level. Follow the word range in the task. Use your feedback to improve your next draft.

aiGrading.instructions:
MARKING RUBRIC (100 points): Task completion/content 35; vocabulary/structures 25; grammar/accuracy 25; clarity/organisation 15.
Give integer points per criterion: excellent 90-100%, good 75-89%, developing 50-74%, beginning 1-49%, no evidence 0% of its maximum. Judge against the topic expectations below at A1-A2 level; full marks are possible. Deduct each error once. Total MUST equal the four scores. Keep the length/off-task limits and copied-model policy below: apply caps by reducing task points first, then others as needed; keep breakdown equal to total, within each maximum. A copied-model award of 100 means full points in all four criteria.
FEEDBACK: 'Task: x/35; Vocabulary: x/25; Grammar: x/25; Organisation: x/15. Total: x/100.' Then up to 3 short, kind sentences: strength, corrected example, next step, based on the actual answer. Use simple English.

Learners are Cambodian primary-school teachers studying English at about A1-A2 level (A1 in early weeks). Grade the answer with this rubric and give feedback that helps them improve.
TASK: Write a short paragraph about how you prepared for the final assessment: which skills you revised (vocabulary, grammar, reading, writing), how you organised your study time, and one or two study methods.
TARGET LANGUAGE this week - vocabulary: revise, practice, vocabulary, grammar, reading, writing, feedback, confident, timetable. Structures: Past simple for what you did ('I studied', 'I made a plan'); Sequencing words (first, then, also, finally).
TOPIC-SPECIFIC EXPECTATIONS:
- Task completion and content (35 points). Excellent: Names at least two or three skills revised, says how study time was organised (for example two hours each evening or a weekly plan), and describes one or two methods such as a study partner or practice paragraphs.
- Vocabulary and sentence structures (25 points). Excellent: Uses past simple correctly for the preparation story, with first/then/finally, and words such as revise, practice, feedback or confident.
- Grammar and accuracy (25 points). Excellent: Mostly accurate, including past forms; slips are small, such as 'I readed'.
- Clarity and organisation (15 points). Excellent: One paragraph that goes from skills to time plan to methods, with linking words and a short ending about how the learner felt.
DO NOT PENALISE: spelling slips; different study methods from the model (flashcards, listening to audio, practice tests); Khmer-influenced word order that is still clear; an honest answer that the learner studied only a little; present perfect used instead of past simple.
LENGTH: 80-110 words, tolerance of about 8 words. Under 60 words: cap at 60. Over 130: no penalty unless unclear.
OTHER CORRECT ANSWERS: Any real study routine; the learner may mention work or family limits on time. The model answer is only a reference.
OFF-TASK: Pasted instructions or unrelated text: 0-20. Copied model: 100 with a note to describe their own preparation. Writing about a different exam or topic: maximum 40.

questions.question: Q12. My friend ___ art very much.
questions.explanation: → My friend is 'he' or 'she', so needs 'likes'.

questions.question: Q16. This class is very ___. I want to sleep.
questions.explanation: → 'Boring' means not interesting. We want to sleep in a boring class.

questions.question: Q5. Our class is in ___ 205 today.
questions.explanation: → 'Room' + number is the place where a class is held.

questions.question: Q16. All the children can ___ in the playground.
questions.explanation: → Children 'run' fast in the playground.

questions.question: Q23. We ___ cancel the staff meeting if fewer than five teachers can attend it. This is allowed, but not required.
questions.explanation: → The action is allowed, so we use 'can'.

questions.question: Q30. Yesterday at lunchtime, my classmate ___ his lunch money and I helped him.
questions.explanation: → Losing the lunch money was a completed event that made you help him, so Past Simple is needed.

questions.question: Q6. He ___ not like tests.
questions.explanation: → He needs does before not in present simple negative.

questions.question: Q8. Please ___ the sentence.
questions.explanation: → 'Read' the sentence means to look at it and say the words.

questions.question: Q18. Parents ___ wait in the reception area until a staff member comes to meet them. It is a security rule.
questions.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

questions.question: Q3. I ___ my pen, so I used a pencil.
questions.explanation: → The sentence explains a past situation and result, so we use past simple.

questions.question: fun — enjoyable
questions.explanation: → 'fun' and 'enjoyable' both mean giving pleasure, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q3. My ___ is very kind and helpful. She teaches us.
questions.explanation: → A 'teacher' teaches us, so she can be kind and helpful.

questions.question: Q11. You ___ prepare some questions before the parent meeting so the conversation goes well. This is a good idea, not a rule.
questions.explanation: → This is advice, not a rule, so we use 'should'.

questions.question: fun — enjoyable
questions.explanation: → 'fun' and 'enjoyable' both mean giving pleasure, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q5. Please ___ to me carefully.
questions.explanation: → This is a polite instruction using 'Please' with imperative form.

questions.question: Q17. Are ___ computers in the library?
questions.explanation: → We use 'are there' in questions about plural things.

questions.question: confident — nervous
questions.explanation: → 'confident' and 'nervous' have opposite meanings: confident is sure, nervous is worried, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: give — take
questions.explanation: → 'Give' and 'take' have opposite meanings, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: study — student
questions.explanation: → 'Student' comes from 'study', so they are in the same word family.

questions.question: brave — scared
questions.explanation: → 'brave' and 'scared' have opposite meanings: brave has no fear, scared has fear, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: freckles — bicycle
questions.explanation: → 'freckles' and 'bicycle' are about very different things, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q19. The teacher gives ___ on student work.
questions.explanation: → 'Feedback' tells students about their work.

questions.question: safety — danger
questions.explanation: → 'safety' and 'danger' have opposite meanings: safety means no harm, danger means possible harm, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: Q26. All visitors ___ wear an identification badge while they are inside the school building. It is a rule.
questions.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

questions.question: Q4. We ___ a big test today.
questions.explanation: → 'We' uses the base form 'have' when talking about having a test.

questions.question: Q29. My eight-year-old neighbour ___ cook simple meals like toast and eggs.
questions.explanation: → At age eight, the child has learned to cook simple things, so they have the ability.

questions.question: prepare — preparation
questions.explanation: → 'prepare' and 'preparation' share the root 'prepare', so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q16. Please ___ your answers with a partner.
questions.explanation: → We 'check' answers when we look at them to see if they are right.

questions.question: Q8. She writes new words in her ___.
questions.explanation: → A 'notebook' is where we write new words.

questions.question: Q5. He has ___ on his face.
questions.explanation: → 'Freckles' are small brown spots on the face.

questions.question: Q15. Your ___ is to write five sentences.
questions.explanation: → A 'task' is a job to do, like writing five sentences.

questions.question: ___ ten chairs in the room.
questions.explanation: → 'Ten chairs' is more than one, so we say 'There are'.

questions.question: study — learn
questions.explanation: → 'study' and 'learn' both mean to gain knowledge, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q25. The school ___ at half past three every day.
questions.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit. The school is one thing, so we add -es.

questions.question: Q18. Reading is your ___ in English class.
questions.explanation: → A 'strength' is something you do well.

questions.question: goal — aim
questions.explanation: → 'goal' and 'aim' both mean what you want to reach, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q11. We have a ___ at ten. We play and eat a snack.
questions.explanation: → A 'break' is a short rest when students play and eat a snack.

questions.question: test — flower
questions.explanation: → 'test' and 'flower' are about very different things, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: assignment — assign
questions.explanation: → 'assignment' and 'assign' share the root 'assign', so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q6. I have a new ___. I read it at home.
questions.explanation: → A 'book' is something we read at home.

questions.question: connect — connection
questions.explanation: → 'connect' and 'connection' share the root 'connect', so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q2. I always take ___ during class.
questions.explanation: → We take 'notes' when we write short points to remember. The plural is used here.

questions.question: Q2. Many ___ schools in Cambodia need more teachers.
questions.explanation: → 'Rural' means in the countryside.

questions.question: Q24. Parents ___ collect their children late without calling the school to explain the delay. It is a school rule.
questions.explanation: → The action is not allowed, so we use 'must not'.

questions.question: instructions — butterfly
questions.explanation: → 'instructions' and 'butterfly' do not connect in meaning or form, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: ___ not any erasers here.
questions.explanation: → 'Erasers' is plural, so after 'not any' we say 'There are'.

questions.question: task — job
questions.explanation: → 'task' and 'job' both mean a piece of work to do, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q18. We ___ try to arrive five minutes early. It is good to be ready.
questions.explanation: → Being ready is a benefit, so arriving early is good advice.

questions.question: Q9. ___ the door when you leave.
questions.explanation: → This instruction tells someone what to do at a certain time.

questions.question: effort — window
questions.explanation: → 'effort' and 'window' do not connect in meaning or form, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q1. I ___ homework every day.
questions.explanation: → We say 'do homework' with I, you, we, they.

questions.question: instruction — instruct
questions.explanation: → 'instruction' and 'instruct' share the root 'instruct', so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q12. ___ the video and answer the questions.
questions.explanation: → This gives students two instructions for the lesson activity.

questions.question: question — inquiry
questions.explanation: → 'Question' and 'inquiry' mean almost the same, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: write — writer
questions.explanation: → 'Writer' comes from 'write', so they are in the same word family.

questions.question: Q12. My sister ___ to music after class every day.
questions.explanation: → 'Every day' shows a habit, so we use present simple. 'Sister' is one person, so add -s.

questions.question: Q5. He ___ practise reading every day to improve his English.
questions.explanation: → Daily practice is necessary for improvement, so 'needs to' is correct.

questions.question: suitable — inappropriate
questions.explanation: → 'suitable' and 'inappropriate' have opposite meanings: suitable is right for a purpose, inappropriate is not, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: test — quiz
questions.explanation: → 'Test' and 'quiz' mean almost the same, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: disturb — bother
questions.explanation: → 'disturb' and 'bother' both mean to trouble someone, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q14. Work in a ___ of four people.
questions.explanation: → A 'group' is a few people working together.

questions.question: Q26. We ___ in class now.
questions.explanation: → We use 'are' with 'we' to say where we are.

questions.question: homework — shoe
questions.explanation: → 'homework' and 'shoe' belong to different ideas, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: early — late
questions.explanation: → 'Early' and 'late' have opposite meanings, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: Q27. You ___ bring your own materials to the workshop, but the school will provide everything needed.
questions.explanation: → Because the school provides materials, bringing your own is not necessary.

questions.question: Q28. While we ___ football after school, the coach gave us new training tips.
questions.explanation: → 'While' signals that playing football was happening when the coach gave tips, so Past Continuous is needed.

questions.question: Q14. Sports day is always ___ June every year.
questions.explanation: → We use 'in' with months.

questions.question: succeed — win
questions.explanation: → 'succeed' and 'win' both mean to do well and reach a goal, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q3. Reading is an important ___ for children.
questions.explanation: → A 'skill' is something you can do well, like reading.

questions.question: hard — simple
questions.explanation: → 'hard' and 'simple' have opposite meanings: hard is difficult, simple is easy, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: door — banana
questions.explanation: → A 'door' and a 'banana' have no connection, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: big — small
questions.explanation: → 'big' and 'small' have opposite meanings: big is large, small is little, so they are antonyms.

questions.question: question — flower
questions.explanation: → A 'question' is something you ask and a 'flower' is a plant, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: bright — light
questions.explanation: → 'bright' and 'light' both mean full of light, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q18. ___ villages often have small schools.
questions.explanation: → 'Remote' means far away from towns.

questions.question: Q24. The teachers ___ a meeting today.
questions.explanation: → Teachers is 'they', so use 'have'.

questions.question: concern — worry
questions.explanation: → 'concern' and 'worry' both mean a feeling of being troubled, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q15. ___ he like sports?
questions.explanation: → He needs 'Does' in questions.

questions.question: Q18. My little sister is still ___ now.
questions.explanation: → 'Short' means not tall. A little sister is still small.

questions.question: Q1. I read my English ___ every day.
questions.explanation: → A 'textbook' is a school book for a subject.

questions.question: arrive — reach
questions.explanation: → 'arrive' and 'reach' both mean to get to a place, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: Q8. I write notes in my ___.
questions.explanation: → We write notes in a 'notebook'.

questions.question: attend — attendance
questions.explanation: → 'attend' and 'attendance' share the root 'attend', so they are a word family.

questions.question: ___ twenty desks in the big classroom.
questions.explanation: → 'Twenty desks' is more than one, so we say 'There are'.

questions.question: Q7. ___ in pairs for this activity.
questions.explanation: → The teacher is instructing students to work together in pairs.

questions.question: Q8. The government wants to ___ schools in Cambodia.
questions.explanation: → We 'improve' schools when we make them better.

questions.question: Q8. Teachers ___ students to ask questions.
questions.explanation: → 'Encourage' means to give someone courage to try.

questions.question: Q2. She ___ her homework after school.
questions.explanation: → She needs a verb with -s or -es.

questions.question: Q23. The boy ___ his pencil every day.
questions.explanation: → Boy is one person, so add -s to the verb.

questions.question: whiteboard — banana
questions.explanation: → 'whiteboard' and 'banana' have no link in meaning, so they are unrelated.

questions.question: Q25. We ___ forget to sign out when we leave early. It is important.
questions.explanation: → Something important that we must not forget is a prohibition on forgetting.

questions.question: encourage — support
questions.explanation: → 'encourage' and 'support' both mean to help someone to do well, so they are synonyms.

questions.question: explain — explanation
questions.explanation: → 'explain' and 'explanation' share the root 'explain', so they are a word family.

questions.question: Q6. Local families ___ money for the library recently.
questions.explanation: → 'Recently' signals a time close to now without a specific date, so present perfect is used.

questions.question: Q28. We ___ close the windows before we leave. The teacher gave a rule, so we have no choice.
questions.explanation: → 'It is a rule' means there is no choice, so we use 'must'.

questions.question: motivate — motivation
questions.explanation: → 'motivate' and 'motivation' share the root 'motivate', so they are a word family.

questions.question: teacher — teach
questions.explanation: → 'Teacher' comes from 'teach', so they are in the same word family.

questions.question: Q19. ___ forget to do your homework for tomorrow.
questions.explanation: → This is a negative instruction reminding students about homework.

questions.question: Q27. ___ a calendar on the wall showing the school year.
questions.explanation: → A calendar is singular, so 'there is' is the correct choice.

questions.question: Q30. She ___ the classroom rules very well yesterday.
questions.explanation: → 'Yesterday' shows past time, and 'understand' is irregular with past 'understood'.
